DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN 
BY THE MINISTRY 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC

OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 After considering the elaborate mandate of the Department, the number of schemes 
and funds allocated to it does not seem commensurate with each other.   The Committee is 
therefore of the view that the department should devise more schemes and programmes 
aimed at improving the Human Resource potential and productivity of the government and 
project their funds requirements to the MoF accordingly. (2.10)  
Action Taken  
2.1 The Department has undertaken several initiatives / programmes such as revamping 
of publi c Grievance system, setting up call center on public grievances, internal process 
reviews to increase efficiency in decision making in the government, reducing pendency in 
govt offices, regular swachhata campaign to build a healthy and clean work environme nt etc. 
These are new activities   aimed at improving the Human Resource potential and productivity 
of the government. The scheme for Administrative Reforms has accordingly been revised 
with enhanced outlay. However, M/ Finance has approved the scheme with  a total outlay of 
Rs 125 crore only for the time being. Therefore, depending upon the pace of implementation 
and requirements additional financial need may be projected to Ministry of Finance.  
Further observation 
2.2 The Committee appreciates the efforts  of Department to come up with new 
initiatives aiming to improve the Human Resources potential and productivity of the 
Government. 
 

 
 
 
 17 
CPGRAMS Reforms 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.3 The Committee also takes note of the fact that a very large number of the pub lic 
grievances are limited to some specific aspects of certain organizations/ Departments. The 
Committee desires that all those areas where a large number of grievances are received, 
should be examined and in those common areas of grievances, after analyzi ng the root cause, 
systemic changes wherever necessary should be brought without any delay which in turn will 
reduce the volume of grievances to a large extent. (3.8) 
Action Taken 
2.4 DARPG has set up data Strategy Unit (DSU) to develop in -house capacity to analyze 
grievances for root cause and suggest areas that requires systemic improvement through 
evidence based approach.   
Further observation 
2.5 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. The Committee further 
recommends the Department to apprise  the Committee about the suggestions made by 
DSU for systemic improvement of any Organization or Department. 
E-Office-Mission Mode Project 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.6 The Committee observes that e -Office is one of the key e -Governance reforms 
brought by  the Department in the recent past. It has helped not only in making the 
government's work faster and more efficient, but has also made a marked difference in the 
decision making process. It has proven its worth during the recent lockdowns due to COVID 
pandemic in the work-from-home scenario. (3.16) 
 2.7 The Committee is therefore of the view that the e -office should be implemented in 
all Central Government Ministries / Departments / organizations on priority basis. Proper 
training on e -Office should be imp arted to the officials. Every effort must be made to 
encourage officials to carry out their office work through e -office only. Further, at an 
appropriate time, it should be made binding for all Government Departments/organizations, 
in a phased manner, to carry out all their official work through e-office only. (3.17) 

 
 
 
 18 
2.8 The Department, along with NIC/MeitY should also keep on improving the e -office 
software based on the inputs received from all stakeholders, on a continuous basis. The e -
office should also be made compatible with all widely used browsers. As e -office has the 
potential for making lot of savings for the government in terms of office space, stationery 
etc., the Committee therefore, recommends the DARPG to approach the MoF, with proper 
justifications, and seek funds to implement the e -office project on a faster pace in all 
Ministries. (3.18) 
  
 Action Taken 
2.9 e-Office has been implemented in all 77 Ministries / Departments along with their 
Attached / Subordinate/ Autonomous organisations. Training is imparted by National 
Informatics Centre (NIC) to the officers on various features of e office and their usages. As 
on date 180 organisations, 14 Apex Bodies and 56 PSUs are working on eOffice.  
 2.10 e-Office has kept on improving    based on the input and suggestion of users.   The 
latest version of e office 7.0 much advanced software with browser neutral 
capability.  However, due to continuous upgrades/patches released by browsers; the operating 
environment is extremely dynamic and continuous efforts are made to make the eOffice 
Product work on all the browsers.  
2.11 Currently NIC follows a subscription -based model for fina ncial sustainability of e 
office.  The respective Ministries have to meet the subscription from their budget.  
Further observation 
2.12 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in 
implementation of e -office. However, the Committee recom mends the Department to 
find the feasibility of making e -office binding for all Government 
Departments/Organizations in a phased manner. 
Administrative Reforms 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.13 The Committee observes that apathy of civil servants in implementation of 
Government schemes/programmes is one of the major impediments in the implementation of 
government schemes and delivery of services and therefore, recommends DARPG to make

3.0 Department is able to spend only 61.7% of the budgetary allocation made under RE

restricted to 33% ceiling and in last month (March) expenditure has to be restricted to 15%  of 
ceiling.  Thus, the performance of the Department in terms of utilization of funds needs 
considerable improvement. A Focused planning and close monitoring of utilization of funds 
is required on the part of the Department.   As restrictions imposed due t o COVID on 
expenditure are waning, the Department should have met the quarterly expenditure targets set 
by the MoF without fail.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should 
identify the bottlenecks responsible  for not being able to mai ntain the pace of utilization 
required as per the instructions of the MoF and take remedial measures to improve its 
performance in utilization of funds in future. (2.5)

financial year 2021 -2022. The major activities of Department    are    usually taking place in 
the last quarter   towards Prime Minister‟s award for Excellence in Civil Services, National e 
governance conference and e-gov awards etc. Therefore, higher expenditure takes place in the 
last quarter of the financial year.  However, efforts have been made to improve expenditure in 
sync with quarterly expenditure target set by MoF. The activities have been outlined with 
clear milestones and expenditure a re reviewed regularly in Senior Officers Meeting. As a 
result   this financial year about 20% of BE has already been incurred as on 22 June 2022.

Time Bound Delivery of Services 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.6 The Committee recommends the government to bring a scheme for a time -bound 
delivery of goods and services for citizens. Initially the scheme may be started by including a 
few basic services only, which may later be expanded to include other services also. The 
Scheme should include appropriate measures for reward and punishment of government 
functionaries so that it remains effective. (3.12) 
 Action Taken 
3.7 The Government has so far adopted promotional approach to   strengthen   servic e 
delivery architecture in the country. More and more services are delivered online.  Services 
like pension, banking etc have reached door step delivery mode.  National e Service Delivery 
(NESDA) frame work has been introduced to assess the efficacy of var ious e service delivery 
platforms.  Under the scheme Prime Minister‟s Awards for excellence in Public 
Administration a separate category of award for Improving Service Delivery and Redressal of 
Public Grievances was introduced. The proposed grievance redre ssal Index would also rank 
the performance of Ministries on the basis of citizen satisfaction and other parameters of 
service delivery and grievance redressal.    
3.8 The DARPG has published the Good Governance Index 2019 & 2021 as an 
incentivise action taken towards effective service delivery. All the above measures effectively 
cover the recommendation of this committee towards time bound delivery of Goods and 
Services. However, scope of these schemes could be further reviewed to reflect the 
recommendations of the Committee.

NESDA, 2021 has very limited scope as it covers only 13 Central Ministry Departments 
and 15 Departments of States and UTs. Moreover, the Co mmittee is of the view that in 
addition to awards and rankings, accountability of concerned officers dealing with the 
services should also be laid down to ensure delivery of services to common citizens in 
time-bound manner.

DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE 
Pensioners’ Portal 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.13 The Committee observes that as per last five years data provided by the Department 
on satisfaction ratings, about 40% of complainants have rated their grievance redressal as 
poor. Such ratings reflect poorly on the overall grievance handling by different organ izations. 
Further, about twelve Ministries/Departments in the year 2021 and twenty two 
Ministries/Departments in the year 2020 have failed to resolve more than 30% of pensioners' 
grievances pertaining to them within the stipulated time. This shows apathy o f those 
organizations towards handling of pensioners' grievances and the Committee feels dismayed 
over indifference shown by government officials to the grievances of their retired colleagues.  
(3.40) 
3.14 The Committee accordingly recommends the DPPW to de velop a 
mechanism/guidelines/policy to ensure accountability of the government officials dealing 
with the pensioners' grievances and suggest action against the erring officials. The appellate 
authority should be empowered to award monetary penalties and sa nction disciplinary action 
against those officials who are habitually responsible for delayed action or summary disposal 
of grievances without any qualitative action. (3.41) 
Action Taken 
3.15 DoPPW has issued advisory to all Ministries/Departments vide OM dated 04.04.2022 
(copy enclosed). 
Further observation 
3.16 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. The Committee recommends 
the Department that particular Ministries/Departments which are failing to resolve 
more than 30% of pensioners grievances s hould be issued separate advisory to furnish 
reasons for not resolving a high percentage of grievances within the stipulated time.

R E P O R T 
  
 This Action Taken Report of the Department-related Parliamenta ry Standing 
Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice deal s with the action taken by 
the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on th e 
recommendations/observations made by the Committee in its One Hundred twelfth Report on 
the Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Ministry, which was pre sented to the Rajya Sabha 
and laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha on the 24th March, 2022. 
2. The Committee had made as many as 37 recommendations/observa tions in its One 
Hundred twelfth Report. Replies of the Ministry of Personnel, P ublic Grievances and 
Pensions thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under th ree chapters on the basis of 
satisfaction of the Committee. Out of 37 recommendations where final replies have been 
received as many as 26 (70 percent approximately) of total reco mmendations are satisfactory. 
These replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations (09) which have been accepted by  t h e  
Ministry, i.e. in respect of paras 2.16, 4.4, 4.13, 5.5, 5.6, 5 .12, 5.18, 5.22 
and 6.32 of the Report. The Committee is pleased to note that t he Ministry 
has accepted those recommendations. 
Chapter – II:   Recommendations/observations (17) which the Committee does n ot desire 
to pursue in view of the replies given by the Ministry, i.e. in  r e s p e c t  o f  
paras 2.13, 2.38, 2.42, 3.6, 3.22, 3.25, 3.26, 3.30, 3.31, 4.16 , 4.20, 4.29, 
5.17, 6.14, 6.22, 6.26 and 6.30 of the Report. The Committee is  satisfied 
with the explanations advanced by the Ministry and does not wis h to 
pursue those as of now.  
Chapter – III:  Recommendations/observations (11) in respect of which Committ ee has 
not accepted the replies of the Ministry, i.e. with regard to paras 3.13, 3.17, 
3.21, 4.7, 4.10, 4.25, 5.11, 6.8, 6.9, 6.10 and 6.21 of the Rep ort. The 
Committee does not accept the reasons given for not accepting i ts 
recommendations of the Committee and reiterates the same. 
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish poi nted and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendation s/Observations made by the 
Committee in this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have b een discussed in the respective  Chapters in the 
succeeding pages.

Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee believes that opt imal utilization of funds is  as important as allocation

2.26 Since the Ministry of Personnel Public Gr ievances and Pensions is the nodal agency 
for policy matters relating to personnel management  as per the Allocation of Business Rules, 
the Committee desires the Ministry to enlighten it whether the term ‘Central Government’ or 
‘Union Government’ was used at the time of framing of the Constitution.                          3.26              
Action Taken  
2.27 The matter was referred to Legis lative Department, Ministry of Law and 
Department of Legal Affairs with the following observations:  
i) Interpretation of the Constitution or genesis of the terms m entioned in the 
Constitution does not come under the Business allocated to DoPT  a s  p e r  
Allocation of Business Rules, 1961; 
ii)  Recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the three organs of 
the Union (Executive, Legislatur e and Judiciary) are governed b y separate set 
of Rules framed under separate Articles viz. Article 309, Artic le 98 and Article 
146 respectively of the Constitu tion. The persons serving the t hree organs are, 
accordingly, governed by the Rules framed under the separate provisions of the 
Constitution and their service conditions are also not uniform. Combining them 
together will have wider implications which may go beyond the s cope of 
Business allocated to Department of Personnel and Training; 
22

iii)  All the service rules e.g. CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964; CCS  (CCA) Rules, 
1965; CCS(TS) Rules, 1965, CCS(L TC) Rules, 1988, CCS (Leave) Ru les, 
1972, Fundamental Rules, CCS(RP) Rules, 2016, TA Rules, etc. ha ve used the 
term ‘Central Government’. Rule 2 of the CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1 964 states 
that  “ The Government ” means the Central Government; and “ Government 
servant” means any person appointed by Go vernment to any civil service  o r  
post in connection with the affairs of the Union and includes a  civilian in a 
Defence Service; 
iv) The use of this term “Centra l Government” for the Governmen t of India is 
ubiquitous and is used in the common parlance to mean employees  serving the 
Union as per Part XIV of the Constitution. 
2.28 DoLA then informed that the  term ‘Centre’ or ‘Central Gove rnment’ is 
nowhere used in the Constitution. The makers of the Constitutio n specifically 
discarded it and instead used th e word ‘Union’. The members of the Constituent 
Assembly were very cautious of not using the word ‘Centre’ or ‘ Central Government’ 
in the Constitution as they intended to keep away the tendency of centralising of 
powers in one unit. The ‘Union Government’ or the ‘Government o f  I n d i a ’  h a s  a  
unifying effect as the message sought to be given is that the government is of all.  
 2.29 In this regard it is significant to mention though, the t erm 'Central Government' 
was not used at the time of framing of Constitution, in The Con stitution (Seventy-
third) Amendment Act, 1992 done in 2012, the terminology ‘Centr al Government’ 
was used. DoLA has also observed that the Union Legislature and  State Legislature 
identify their boundaries and are circumspect to not cross thei r boundaries when it 
comes to the subject matter on which laws are made.  
2.30  Taking corollary from the above observation of DOLA, it i s again emphasized 
that any initiative for regulating the service conditions of the Legislature and the 
Judiciary by the Executive would be tantamount to encroaching upon the powers 
vested in them. Moreover, it would also demolish the spirit of the Constitution.  
2.31 In view of the foregoing, DoPT submits that changing the n omenclature from   
‘Central Government’ to ‘Union Government’ categorically does n ot come under the 
purview of DoPT as per the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961.

2.32 It is again emphasized that Recruitment and conditions of service of persons 
serving the three organs of the Union (the Executive, the Legis lature and the 
Judiciary) are governed by separate set of Rules framed under s eparate Articles viz. 
Article 309, Article 98 and Arti cle 146 respectively of the Con stitution. The persons 
serving the three organs are, ac cordingly, governed by the Rule s framed under the 
separate provisions of the Const itution and their service condi tions are also not 
uniform. As such, combining them together will have wider impli cations which is 
beyond the scope of Business a llocated to Department of Personn el and Training. In 
view of the above, it is requested that DRPSC may kindly drop t he above 
recommendations.

compared to pendency of 401 cases at the end of previous F.Y. 2020-21.  
3.21 Further, the Commission issued 535 advice letters during F .Y. 2021-22, which is the 
highest number of advice letters issued in the last 15 financia l years and 24% increase over 
the 433 advice letters issued in previous F.Y. 2020-21, despite  two waves of Covid-19 
37

pandemic during the F.Y. 2021-22. UPSC has made efforts at seve ral fronts and has taken 
multiple remedial measures like engaging experienced and retire d officers as consultants and 
also motivating existing officers to dispose of higher number of cases.  
Further observation 
3.22 The Committee appreciates the Department for striving hard  to bring down the 
pendency of disciplinary cases. T he Committee recommends the De partment to take 
measures to reduce the pendency further.   
Recommendation/Observation 
3.23 The Committee notes that Union Cabinet had given its approval to set up a National 
Recruitment Agency as far back as in 2020. The Committee also notes that NRA has utilized 
₹58.32 crore in 2021-22 and an outlay of ₹ 396 crore has been earmarked in BE 2022-23. 
However, NRA has not seen the light of the day yet. The Committee would like to be informed 
as to why NRA has not been operationalized yet. The Committee recommends DoPT to 
apprise the Committee by when NRA will become fully functional.                                     4.25 
Action Taken 
3.24 National Recruitment Agency  (NRA) has been made functional from LIC’s Jeevan 
Bharati Building at New Delhi. However, in order to conduct Com mon Eligibility Test

normalization, etc. for which an Expert Advisory Committee (EAC ) has been set up. The 
EAC will give recommendation and guidance on assessment, beside s technologies to be 
adopted for conducting the tests. Further, in order to build a digital platform for NRA, the

examination.  
3.25 There are 33 posts in NRA headquarters at New Delhi. Besid es Chairman and 
Secretary-cum-CoE, there are 31 posts at NRA HQ. 24 posts for R egional Offices have been 
created, which will be filled up on deputation basis. NRA is in  the process of filling up of

completed shortly. In view of the above, it is anticipated that  in next eight (8) to ten (10) 
months, NRA will be made functional.  
Further observation 
3.26 The Committee is unhappy to note that Common Eligibility T est has not been 
conducted yet. The Committee reco mmends National Recruitment Ag ency to 
operationalize it as soon as possible.

resource deficit. The Committee has been appris ed that the shortage of faculty has arisen,

The Committee reiterates that ISTM needs to reduce its dependence on deputed officials. It

digital library, training modules accessible to general public.                                            5.11

being monitored at higher level in the Department.

INTEGRITY, VIGILANCE, TRANSPARENCY AND SERVICE MATTERS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.34 On the question of pendency, CBI in its written reply submitted that a total of 1025 
cases are pending investigation with it and out of them 66 cases are pending for more than 5 
years as on 31 st January, 2022. The Committee feels that  this pendency can be effectively 
reduced if the manpower requirements are ta ken care of.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Government to undertake Cadre restructuring of CBI at the earliest. The 
Committee also recommends that CBI should make efforts to reduce its dependence on 
deputation and strive to recruit permanent staff atleast upto the rank of Deputy 
Superintendent of Police. The Committee is of the view that delayed justice is no justice at all 
and cases cannot linger on without a definite closure for decades. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that CBI may prepare a roadmap for disposal of cases pending with them and 
inform the Committee accordingly.                                                                                         6.8

(iii) As regards the roadmap for disposal of cases pending with CBI, it is to be intimated that 
the following steps have been taken to improve quality of inves tigation, conviction 
percentage and disposal of cases from trial :- 
Steps taken to improve the quality of investigation - 
3.36 A good investigation is sine qua non for better prosecutio n in a court of law. For 
improving the quality of investigation, the following steps have been taken by CBI:- 
a. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Crime Manual have b een upgraded and 
updated, keeping in view the ch anging necessities, technologica l advancement, 
changing legal requirement and direction of the Courts. 
b. CBI has introduced a system of using ICTs for processing and  monitoring files 
electronically through Core Application Software (CAS), to ensu re that prompt and 
quality investigation is carried  out and suggestions / instruct ions by the senior 
formations are dissipated well in time to the Investigating Officers for compliance. 
c. For better coordination and enhancing the quality of investi gation, the practice of 
synergetic working of Executive Officers in tandem with law off icers has been 
introduced. 
d. Investigation reports are prepared in a detailed proforma, h ighlighting the relevant 
material collected and the admissibility of evidence thereof. 
e. The explanation of the accused during investigation is taken  and evidence collected 
to verify and rebut the defence of the accused. 
f. Scrutiny of investigation report is carried out by Law Offic er as well as senior 
formations to assess the quality of evidence for launching prosecution. 
g. While conducting investigation and submitting the final repo rt, a detailed Calendar 
of evidence is prepared, highlighting both oral and documentary evidence in detail. 
h. For building up of domain expertise of CBI officers, regular  training is being 
imparted to them at CBI Academy, Ghaziabad. During the year 202 1, 32 specialised 
training courses have been organized for 434 Investigating Offi cers of CBI for 
improving their skill and knowledge of investigation. 
i. Executive and Legal officers have been given access to the l atest legal data through 
Manu Patra, an online data base for legal research, so that the y may keep themselves 
41

abreast of the latest case laws and rulings passed by the Hon’b le Supreme Court and 
High Courts. 
j. An MoU has been signed by CBI with National Forensic Science  University 
(NFSU) Gandhinagar (Gujarat) to promote collaboration and facil itate advancement 
of knowledge on the basis of reciprocity and frequent interacti on. NFSU will assist in 
the training and capacity building of officers of CBI and suppo rt in strengthening its 
forensic capabilities. 
Steps taken to improve the conviction percentage and disposal of cases from trial – 
3.37 The following steps have been taken by CBI for improving t he conviction percentage 
and better disposal of cases from trial:- 
a. Committee with the Director of Prosecution (DOP) as member a nd involvement of 
other senior law officers has been constituted at Zonal level f or suggesting steps and 
preparing strategy for addressing and speeding up the trial of cases pending for over 
20 years. 
b. In other cases pending trial for less than 20 years, efforts  like pruning of witnesses, 
ensuring the appearance of witnesses in Courts of law and their  timely examination 
etc. are being made for expeditious disposal of cases from trial. 
c. Appropriate steps are being taken for vacating stay in cases , as per the parameters 
laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the matter of Asian R esurfacing of Road 
Agency Pvt. Ltd. and Anr. Vs. Central Bureau of Investigation. 
d. The training programmes for law officers of CBI are being co nducted in 
coordination with the Law Universities for the enhancement of their capability. 
e. The concept of peer group learning is being promoted. 
f .  P r o s e c u t o r s  a n d  L a w  O f f i c e r s  o f  C B I  a r e  b e i n g  n o m i n a t e d  t o  attend the various 
training courses/ workshops conducted by the CBI Academy, Ghaziabad. 
g. Training has been organized on legal nuances of Forensic Inv estigation and 
Admissibility of Electronic Evidence and Meta Analysis in cases  under Investigation. 
Training was imparted by Law Faculty of Rashtriya Raksha Univer sity, Lavad 
(Gujarat) at CBI Academy and it was attended by 44 Law Officers  and Prosecutors of 
CBI. 
h. Monthly workshop of Director of Prosecution with the Law Off icers of CBI has 
been conducted, both physically as well as on virtual platform. 
i. Training need analysis for all the Law officers of CBI is be ing done to identify the 
areas for upgrading their knowledge and skills. 
j. A proposal is under process for organizing training programm es for prosecutors and 
Law Officers to be conducted by a reputed law institution

3.49 The Committee is concerned to note that 09 states have wit hdrawn their general

Recommendation/Observation 
3.50 The Committee notes that as many as 72 vigilance cases, including those involving 
serious allegations are pending sanction for prosecution beyond the stipulated time limit of 
three months. The Committee is strongly concerned to note that not granting sanction for 
prosecution within the stipulated time limit has become a routine affair. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends the Government to amend the relevant provisions and empower CVC 
to take necessary action in such cases where the competent authority fails to grant sanction 
for prosecution within stipulated time limit without valid reasons.                                      6.21 
 
Action Taken  
3.51 In this connection it is stated that the Prevention of Cor ruption Act, 1988 has already 
been amended vide the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 dated 26.07.2018. 
3.52 The matter of time limit for sanction for prosecution was considered in detail at the 
time of amendment of the PC Act. Various decisions of Hon’ble S upreme Court of India 
regarding sanction for prosecution within three months were con sidered. The Select 
Committee of the Parliament also exhaustively considered the am endment, undertaking a 
pan-India consultative exercise with a spectrum of stakeholders . On the basis of all these 
deliberations the relevant provision of Section 19 has been ame nded vide the aforesaid 
amendment of 2018. 
45

3.53 The statutory provision now provides that the appropriate Government or authority 
shall, after the the receipt of the proposal requiring sanction  for prosecution of a public 
servant under the sub-section, endeavour to convey the decision  on such proposal within a 
period of three months from the date of its receipt. Further, i t has also been provided that in 
case where, for the purpose of grant of sanction for prosecutio n, legal consultation is 
required, such period may, for th e reasons to be recorded in wr iting, be extended by a further 
period of one month. 
3.54 Thus, it may be seen that the aspect highlighted by the Ho n’ble Committee relates to 
implementation of statutory provisions of Section 19 of Prevent ion of Corruption Act, 1988, 
as referred to above. Adherence to the timeline by virtue of the amendment to the Act already 
has a force of law. 
Further observation 
3.55 The Committee notes that, as per the provisions of Prevent ion of Corruption Act, 
sanction for prosecution should be granted by the competent aut hority within a period 
of three months, which may be extended by a further period of o ne month. The 
Committee would like to know whether the Act or the Rules framed thereunder provide 
for any remedy in the event of sanction for prosecution not bei ng granted within the 
stipulated period.

     R E P O R T  
 This Action Taken Report of the  Committee deals with the actio n taken 
by the Department of Justice (Ministry of Law & Justice) on the  
recommendations / observations of the Department-related Parlia mentary 
Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Jus tice in its 
One Hundred Sixteenth (116 th) Report on Demands for Grants (2022-23) 
pertaining to the Department of Justice (Ministry of Law & Just ice), which was 
presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of the Lok S abha on the 24th 
March, 2022.  
2. The Committee had made 19 r ecommendations/observations in it s 116th 
Report. Replies of the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized 
under three chapters on the basis of satisfaction of the Committee. These replies 
have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations ( 3) which have been accepted 
by the Department, i.e. in respect of paras 3.17, 3.32 and 3.40 of 
the Report. The Committee is pleased to note that the 
Department has accepted those recommendations. 
Chapter – II:  Recommendations/observations ( 5) which the Committee does 
not desire to pursue in view of  the replies given by the 
Department, i.e. in respect of paras 2.6, 2.7, 2.15, 2.20 and 3 .15 
of the Report. The Committee is satisfied with the explanations  
advanced by the Department and does not wish to pursue those 
as of now.  
Chapter – III:  Recommendations/observations (9) in respect of which 
Committee has not accepted the replies of the Department, i.e. 
with regard to paras 2.12, 2.18, 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.23, 3.24, 3. 33 
and 3.34 of the Report. The Committee does not accept the 
reasons given by the Department and reiterates the same. 
Chapter - IV: Recommendations/observations ( 2) in respect of which final 
replies of the Department have not been received, i.e. in respe ct 
of paras 2.23 and 3.2 of the Report, the Committee has not 
received replies.  
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish poi nted and 
detailed Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further 
Recommendations/Observations made by the Committee in this report. 

9 
 
4. The details of the ATR have b een discussed in the respective  Chapters in 
the succeeding pages. For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report 
(i.e. of 116 th Report) have been mentioned at the end of each 
recommendation/observation.

10 
 
CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee appreciates the concept of DISHA scheme that endeavors to address 
the legal needs of the people and to empower them with knowledg e of their rights, 
entitlements and different redress al mechanism. However, the co mmittee observes that, on 
the face of it, many components of  the DISHA scheme appears to be the same as that of 
NALSA. The Committee accordingly, recommends that all programme s under the scheme 
before being implemented be thoroughly analysed to ensure optim al utilization and non-
duplication of resources. (3.17) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 Article 39 A under the Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP) Part IV of the 
Indian Constitution obligates the State to provide equal opport unities for securing justice and 
free legal aid either though legislation or scheme or any other  way. In securing this equal 
opportunity to justice wherein no citizen is neither denied nor  deprived to access justice due 
to economic or any other disability, Government of India introd uced a scheme titled 
“Designing Innovative Solutions for Holistic Access to Justice (DISHA)” in 2021. 
 
1.2 In addition, the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 mandate s Department of Justice 
(DoJ) to carry out functions under “Legal Aid to Poor and Acces s to Justice”.  In taking this 
forward DoJ has been implementing various programmes on access to justice since 2009 in a 
phased manner, in collaboration with United Nations Development  Programme (UNDP). 
During these phases the programme focused on improving institut ional capacities of key 
justice service providers enabling them to effectively serve th e poor and disadvantaged 
particularly women, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to ad dress the barriers they face 
in social, economic and political domains. On the other hand, i t focused on directly 
empowering the poor and the disadvantaged men and women to seek  and demand justice 
services. To have a more meaningful and holistic impact, DoJ pa rtnered with national, state 
and local justice institutions including the judiciary, legal services authorities (at the state and 
district level) developing legal and representational capacities of the CSOs and their networks 
working at the local level to improve access to justice for vulnerable groups. Major focus was 
on developing an affordable and replicable model of legal aid a nd empowerment that could 
be scaled up using government resources. 
 
1.3 Based on the success and learning of the DoJ – UNDP A2J pro ject, DoJ initiated 
implementation of A2J project in Jammu & Kashmir and the North Eastern States 
(hereinafter NEJK) in 2012. Aiming to address legal needs of th e marginalized and support 
justice delivery and legal service institutions, DoJ successful ly implemented 38 projects 

11 
 
through innovative models and practices including partnership w ith State Legal Service 
Authorities, State Institute of Rural Developments, Government Departments, CSOs, 
Academic Institutions etc. This a pproach has enabled DoJ in nar rowing down the gap 
between formal and traditional justice delivery system. 
 
1.4 Subsequently in 2017, DoJ launched three key legal aid and empowerment 
programmes under Access to Justice which included Tele Law (mai nstreaming legal aid at 
grassroots through technology); Nyaya Bandhu (promoting Pro bon o legal services) and 
Nyaya Mitra (facilitating reduction of pendency of 10+ year old cases). 
 
1.5 All these programmes made a gradual headway in achieving th e intended results. 
Subsequently, an evaluation study was conducted in 2020 through  National Council of 
Applied Economic Research (NCAER) that recommended for scaling up these programmes 
at an all India level. This resulted in formulation of a compre hensive, holistic, integrated and 
systemic solution on access to justice scheme titled “Designing  Innovative Solutions for 
Holistic Access to Justice in India” (DISHA). The recitals of the Scheme aims to supplements 
and complements the mandate given under the Constitutional prov isions, but also abides by 
the statutory requirement of Legal Services Authority Act, 1987  giving impetus to the 
implementation of SDG-16 in order to ensure Access to Justice f or All in the country. DoJ is 
implementing DISHA with a total outlay of Rs.250 crore for a pe riod of 2021-2026. The 
approach of DISHA includes: - 
 
i. Strengthening of Pre-litigation advice and consultation at the grassroots–  
 
 This approach is being implemented through leveraging indigeno us technological 
tools and platforms that have presence in the village or at gra m panchayat level. 
This approach is being carried forward through DoJ’s programme called Tele-Law: 
Reaching the Unreached, where in people are empowered to seek p re –litigation 
and advice and consultation through Panel Lawyers via tele/vide o conferencing 
facilities available at the Common Service Centres situated in the villages or 
through Mobile App. NALSA has presence only till the Taluk level.  
 
ii. Pan India Dispensation framework for Pro Bono Delivery of Legal Services-  
 
 This approach is being executed through Nyaya Bandhu (Pro Bono ) Legal 
Services Programme where in DoJ has four pronged strategies for  unlocking the 
Pro bono potential in the country. This includes creating a dat abase of probono 
lawyers, facilitating direct connect between the beneficiary an d Pro Bono Lawyer 
though mobile / web based application and following up through an online 
monitoring mechanism; embedding culture of pro bono in Law Scho ols through 
Pro Bono Club Scheme and engaging with CSOs and Law firms inclu ding 
NALSA to build a consensus for a comprehensive policy on Pro Bo no in the 
country.  
 
iii. Address pendency of 15 yearlong pending cases at the District Courts- 
 

12 
 
 To address pendency, DoJ started the Nyaya Mitra programme whe re in retired 
judge or a senior advocate has to be engaged in consultation wi th the Registrar 
General (RG) to assist in identifying gaps and effective ways t o dispose of long 
pending cases. The District courts with highest and lowest pend ency have been 
identified through the NJDG portal. Offer letter to 20 Nyaya Mi tra in 20 Districts 
in 9 States have been issued for who will work for a period of two years. There is 
no similar programme in NALSA.  
 
iv. Pan India Legal Literacy and Legal Awareness Programme-  
 
 DoJ has developed a working paper wherein five pronged strateg y is being 
promoted to build a pan India legal literacy and legal awarenes s programmes 
which includes- integration of legal literacy in and building c apacities of the 
frontline functionaries, across various ministries and departme nts, developing e-
legal literacy library, identifying indicators to assess and me asure the impact of 
legal literacy and awareness programme on the masses. 
 
v. Use of Definite Information, Education and Communication and In formation 
Communication and Technology (ICT) tools to embed the desired s ocial and 
behaviour changes to increase legal empowerment.  
 
1.6 In view of the above, it is submitted that the DISHA Scheme  is a Central Sector 
Scheme that is propounded to meet the needs, changes and concer ns of the present times and 
has been formalized to supplement and complement the delivery o f legal services in the 
country. DoJ concurrently assess the need and feasibility of th e approaches/ programmes 
before intervention and ensures optimum utilization and non-dup lication of resources. 
Embedding within each project is mandatory monitoring and evalu ation mechanism for any 
mid-course correction thereby to curate more new models/approac hes for scale up and 
replication by Legal Service Institutions or other bodies worki ng to strengthen the legal aid 
system in the country.  
 
Further Observation 
 
1.7 The Committee takes note of the reply. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.8 The Committee appreciates the efforts of NALSA, especially during the last few 
years, for doing exceedingly well in providing Legal Services a nd spreading legal awareness 
about their entitlements to the poor and vulnerable sections of  the country. NALSA had 
declared 2021 as the year of Lok Adalats and in which a record number of cases were 
disposed off. It had also launched a 44 days campaign on 2 nd October, 2021 to enhance their 
outreach of legal services to all 6.7 Lakh villages and 4100 pl us municipal town across the 
country. The NALSA also launched a mobile app and a web portal for giving an online push 
to the legal services they are offering to the people. The Comm ittee lauds such efforts of the 
NALSA and hopes that such efforts would continue in future with even more vigour. (3.32) 

13 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.9 The Department of Justice conveys gratitude expressed by NA LSA for appreciation in 
its endeavor in providing legal services, spreading legal aware ness in particular and also 
virtual propagation (online push) through NALSA Mobile App & We b Portal. NALSA has 
assured that it would continue to make efforts with more vigour  and will try to excel in the 
field. 
 
Further Observation 
 
1.10 Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.11 The National Judicial Academy, Bhopal has the advantage of  having a quality faculty, 
infrastructure and location.  However, the Committee feels that  the institution has remained 
underutilized and there is a tremendous scope for        enhanc ing its mandate and to make it 
an institution of eminence.  Accordingly, the Committee recomme nds the Academy to 
prepare a road map for enhancing the scope of its mandate and t o seek higher allocation 
accordingly. (3.40) 
Action Taken 
 
1.12 The Academy has been established and designed to cater to the enhancement of 
judicial skills to achieve excellence amongst High Court Judges and Judicial Officers through 
the country.  This module is successfully continuing since the inauguration of the Academy 
in 2002 and its activities have also expanded thereafter as ove r and above, Judges from 
foreign nations are regularly trained in special programmes tha t are conducted on weekdays 
so as not to disturb the weekend programmes for domestic Judges .NJA is conducting training 
programmes of Judicial Officers from Bangladesh, Maldives, Nepa l ,  S r i  L a n k a ,  M y a n m a r ,  
etc. 
 
1.13 The Academy was compelled during the pandemic to switch ov er to online mode, but 
despite the odds, the sessions of the various programmes were s cheduled and executed 
successfully with substantial participation of Judges and Judicial Officers. 
 
1.14 Apart from regular programmes that are conducted on Saturd ays and Sundays, since 
Judges and Judicial Officers are c onveniently available at week ends only, the Academy also 
runs parallel programmes at times simultaneously to accommodate  the topics as decided by 
the National Judicial Academic Council. 
 
1.15 Some special programmes are designed for officials and per sonnel involved in the 
adjudicatory process in the administration like for Income-Tax Commissioners and other 
Senior Officials, Public Prosecutors, Senior Officials of the C ustoms & Excise Department, 
Legal Services Authorities, Central Administrative Tribunal Off icials, etc.  This is ever 
increasing as for e.g. in the current year, the Academy is about to host a 4-day programme for 

14 
 
Senior Officials of the Governor’s Secretariat to acquaint them  about the constitutional and 
other statutory duties of a Governor under the Constitution. 
 
1.16 Consequently, with the given infrastructure and available resources, the Academy 
continues in its endeavour to enhance the skills of Judges, Judicial Officers and other officials 
to the best of its capacity with a vision to encompass all stak eholders connected with judicial 
governance. 
 
1.17 The Academy additionally has been able to conduct programm es for its participants in 
collaboration with foreign instit utions like the Federal Judici al Centre-Washington, CEELI-
Prague, SIFoCC-UK, Singapore Inte rnational Arbitration Centre, etc. ensuring the 
availability of a substantial number of renowned personalities of international fame enriching 
the quality of discourses at the Academy. 
 
1.18 For further supplementing the activities of the Academy, t he same would be discussed 
at the NJAC meeting to visualize more benefits for the audience  and participants at the 
Academy. 
 
Further Observation 
 
1.19 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
--- 
 
 
  

15 
 
CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN 
BY THE MINISTRY 
OVER ALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 The Committee observes that the Department has been able to  spend only about 55% 
of the overall funds earmarked for RE 2021-22 and about 45% of the funds are still left with 
to be spent in the remaining two months of the financial year. In this connection it may be 
stated that as per the instructions issued by the MoF, expendit ure in the last quarter has to be 
restricted to 33% ceiling and last month (March) expenditure to  15% ceiling. Thus 
performance of the Department in terms of utilization of funds leaves much to be desired. A 
focused planning and close monitoring of utilization of funds i s required on the part of the 
Department. As restrictions imposed on expenditure due to COVID  a r e  w a n i n g ,  t h e  
Department should meet the quarterly expenditure targets set by the MoF. (2.6) 
 
2.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department sh ould identify the 
bottlenecks responsible for not being able to maintain the pace  of utilization required as per 
the instructions of the MoF and take remedial measures to impro ve its performance in 
utilization of funds in future.  (2.7) 
 
Action Taken  
2.2 In the financial year 2021-22, against allocation of Rs.770 .44 crore for the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) on development of judicial infrastructur e in district and 
subordinate courts, the expenditure was Rs. 684.14 crore (89%),  involving a saving of 
Rs.86.30 crore or 11% of allocated amount. The reasons for low expenditure are as under: 
 
(i)         The COVID 19 pandemic affected the construction activities adversely. 
 
(ii)        Introduction of revised Public Financial Management  System (PFMS) procedure for 
release of funds to the CSS in terms of Ministry of Finance’s o rders dated 23.03.2021 
which entails wide range of activities on the part of the State s/UTs  to migrate to the 
new system which includes changes in interface, modification in  s o f t w a r e  
applications, pilot testing, opening of separate budget heads/l ines for routing the 
Central and State share of funds for which a separate dedicated  account is required. In 
this dedicated account the unspent balance available with the S tate (both Central and 
State share) along with interest thereon is required to be depo sited, after withdrawing 
it from different accounts where this fund was lying. This requires involvement of line 
Department of the State, their Finance Department, the High Cou rts, Legislatures and 
banking institutions in the States. All the States have not bee n able to make the 
necessary changes as mandated by the new PFMS system.   

16 
 
(iii)      Further, as per the n ew guidelines, the release can be made to a State, only if funds 
upto 75% of the last release made earlier have been utilized by  the State. On account 
of COVID pandemic, the construction activities were also advers ely affected, as a 
r e s u l t  o f  w h i c h  s o m e  s t a t e s  a r e  n o t  a b l e  t o  g i v e  t h e  U t i l i z a t i on Certificate for the 
releases made earlier.   
 
2.3 Thus on account of unspent balance and non-transition to th e revised PFMS procedure, 
the release of funds was at a slower pace. However, through tra inings on PFMS and regular 
review meetings through video conferencing the States/UTs are b eing sensitized, so that all 
the States comply with PFMS procedures and funds can get releas ed and utilized timely in 
the current financial year 2022-23.  
 
Further observation

3.22 With respect to best practices followed by other countries ,  i t  h a s  b e e n  f o u n d  t h a t

the delivery of judgment within 6 weeks of trial through the ab olition of pleadings,

3.23 However, this department has recommended a disposal plan f o r  t h e  F T S C s  t o  b e  
followed. Each FTSC is expected to dispose of, 41-42 cases in e ach quarter and at least 165 
cases in a year in order to remove the pendency. As on 31.03.20 22, 722 FTSCs including 406 
e-POCSO have been made functional in 28 States/UTs which have d isposed of more than 
87,100 cases since their inception. 
 
 

27 
 
Further Observation 
 
3.24 The Committee takes note of the reply. There is a need to revamp the FTSCs in 
accordance with the recommendations of the 'Third Part Party Ev aluation' referred 
above and the disposal plan for the FTSCs suggested by the Depa rtment. These reforms 
should be implemented and monitored on continuous basis in orde r to make these 
Courts truly 'fast track'.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.25 NALSA has recently completed 25 years of its establishment , accordingly, it is also 
the right time to ponder over reforms which are required in NAL SA and legal aid movement 
in India. Majority of Indians are eligible to receive legal aid , but the number of people 
actually receiving legal aid is a miniscule percentage of those  entitled. In the previous 
chapter, the Committee has already recommended a significant in crease in NALSA's budget 
and expects NALSA to make best use of it in performing its assigned mandate. (3.33) 
Action Taken 
 
3.26 It has been informed by NALSA that although majority of In dians are eligible to 
receive legal aid, only minuscule percentage of those entitled are actually availing the 
services provided by Legal Services Authorities, since a large number of categories are 
eligible even without application of means test. 
 
3.27 It has been further informed by NALSA that the National Me et of SLSAs is proposed 
to be organized shortly, wherein Hon’ble  Executive Chairperson s  o f  S t a t e  L e g a l  S e r v i c e s  
Authorities and Ld. Member Secretaries of State Legal Services Authorities will also 
participate with Central Authority i.e. NALSA, and will discuss  the issues pertaining to court 
based legal services i.e. Strengthening Front Offices as One St op Centre , Free Legal Aid, 
Advice, Counselling, Legal Aid Defence Counsel System, Legal As sistance at Pre-Arrest, 
Arrest and Remand Stages, Legal Aid To Prisoners, Pro Bono Lega l Services etc. will be 
deliberated and the strategy and methodology will be prepared. 
 
3.28 Strengthening Legal Services Institutions at grassroot lev el always remains the 
priority area and NALSA is focusing on several measures includi ng but not limited to 
following:  
 
1. People Centric Approach
: Work on “Beneficiary (Litigant) First Approach”, which 
w i l l  p l a c e  t h e  l i t i g a n t  a t  t h e  c e n t r e  o f  l e g a l  s e r v i c e  p r o v i s i on. NALSA will ensure 
increased monitoring and evaluation of legal services, in order  t o  e n s u r e  t h a t  m o r e  
effective and competent services are provided to meet the expec tations of legal aid 
beneficiary. 
 
2. One Nation-One DLSA : NALSA has already issued Regulations and SOPs for Pan 
India uniformity but still it is felt that more clearer and ela borative business rules are 
required for grassroot level district authority thus Uniform ru le of business in all 
District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) is need of the hour  a n d  N A L S A  i s  

28 
 
working over the same. Improvised processes to be incorporated to increase the 
outreach and legal literacy initiatives, for increasing vibrancy for legal services. 
 
3. Use of Digital Platform : Use of AI and digital platform from top to bottom for 
deliverable services as well as for monitoring quality of servi ce will be put in place 
during current year. An ODR platform for Pre-Institution Mediat ion (PIM) in 
commercial matters and also for all other Mediations in court a nnexed ADR/ 
Mediation centres of Legal services institutions will be launch ed soon, which will be 
first Online dispute resolution (ODR) platform in Government se ctor. We have 
already facilitated online filing of application for commercial  mediation through 
NALSA mobile App and portal in 10 languages. NALSA is already i n deliberations 
with NIC for a robust monitoring platform for accountability and efficiency.  
 
 In the period of turbulence caused by the COVID pandemic, Lega l Services 
Authorities appropriately responded by creatively adapting to t he new normal and 
successfully moved the conventional Lok Adalat to the virtual p latform enabling 
doorstep delivery of justice to common man. 
 
4. Incremental Expansion of Legal Aid Defence Counsel System:
 After successfully 
running the pilot project of Legal Aid Defence Counsel System (LADCS) at 13 places 
in 13 States, the Committee, constituted by the Central Authority has recommended to 
adopt full time lawyers engagement system for providing qualita tive and competent 
legal services to poor, marginalised and needy after comparing with counsel 
assignment system (Panel Lawyers scheme) at DLSA level. This sy stem is in line 
with Public defender system and will be fully operationalized i n  c u r r e n t  y e a r  i n  
following manner: 
 
i. 250 places (HQ- as per selection & availability of space) lates t by 15
th 
August 2022, 
ii. 250 more places (HQ) latest by 9th November 2022, 
iii. Remaining 200 District/ Judicial HQs by 26th January 2023. 
 
 At Outline or Taluka or sub-divisional places, which are not s eat of Principal District 
& Session Judge, existing Panel Lawyer (Counsel assignment) sys tem will continue 
with modified scheme.  
 
5. NALSA’s Early Access to Justice & Effective Legal Aid for inmat es:
 Effective 
implementation of NALSA's Early Access to Justice at Pre-Arrest , Arrest and 
Remand stage across the country. Further NALSA will conduct reg ular campaigns on 
mission mode basis for timely release of jail inmates. NALSA wi ll conduct regular 
campaigns on mission mode basis for timely release of jail inma tes. Increased focus 
on provision of legal services within the Juvenile Justice Mechanism. 
 
6. Integrity Code for Panel Lawyers:  As far as harassment of beneficiaries and demand 
of fee by panel lawyers is concerned, NALSA is already consider ing issuance of 
integrity code for legal aid lawyers. Even in upcoming SOPs pro visions for timely 

29 
 
interaction and filing timeline is also proposed. This Integrit y code for panel lawyers, 
in legal aid matters, will ensure adherence with professional standards and ethics. 
 
7. More vibrancy in Lok Adalat:  NALSA is committed to deliver prompt and 
inexpensive justice to the citizens and it has decided to lay m ore emphasis on 
contribution of National Lok Adal at in effectively reducing the  number of pending 
cases through Alternative Dispute Mechanisms. Lok Adalats are one of the most 
effective and successful Alternative Disputes Resolution mechan ism. The Lok Adalat 
has jurisdiction to take up any civil matters and all criminal compoundable matters 
which is either pending before any court or which has yet not b een brought to the 
court. In the year 2021, a total number of 1.27 crore cases hav e been settled in 4 
National Lok Adalat and out of which 55 Lakhs cases were alread y pending before 
the Courts of the country. It is proposed to further strengthen the Lok Adalats. 
 
3.29 However, there are certain challenges for NALSA, in streng thening the Legal 
Services Institutions at grassroots level and some of them are: -   
 
1. Strengthening of Legal Services Institutions at Grassroot level :
 There are 673 Legal 
Services Institutions at the District level. Section 9 (3) of t h e  L e g a l  S e r v i c e s  
Authorities Act, 1987 provides that the State Authority, in con sultation with the 
Chairman of the District Authority, appoint a person belonging to the State Judicial 
Service not lower in the rank than that of a subordinate Judge or Civil Judge as 
Secretary of the District Authority. Section 9 (5) of the Legal  Services Authorities 
Act, 1987 provides that the District Authority may appoint such  number of officers 
and other employees as may be prescribed by the State Governmen t in consultation 
with the Chief Justice of High Court for the efficient discharge of its functions. 
 
 Section 9 (7) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 prov ides that the 
administrative expenses of every District Authority, including the salaries, allowances 
and pensions payable to the Secretary, officers and other emplo yees of the District 
Authority shall be defrayed out of the Consolidated Fund of the  State. Out of 673 
District Legal Services Authorities, in 102 DLSAs, part time Se cretaries have been 
posted/appointed. The posts of the Secretary in all the DLSAs n eed to be created by 
the State Government and full time Secretaries have to be appoi nted in the remaining 
DLSAs. More over fix tenure is required for the Secretary, DLSAs.  
 
2. Inadequate support for State and District Legal Services Author ities by the State/UTs 
Governments: There is lack of staff and infrastructure in the State Legal Services 
Authorities and District Legal Services Authorities. Therefore,  to discharge the 
functions of the SLSAs and DLSAs, sufficient human resources ar e required to be 
deputed in the Legal Services Institutions. It is the statutory  duty of the State and UT 
Governments to create the necessary posts for the SLSA and DLSA s and to provide 
funds for administrative expenses  of the Legal Services Institu tions in the State for 
creation of proper infrastructure. It is submitted that barring  few States, most of the 
States/UTs are not supporting State/Legal Services Authorities with proper structural 
organisation framework. 

30 
 
 
3. Inadequate funds for victim compensation and non-adoption of NA LSA VCS for 
women survivors :      U n d e r  s e c t i o n  357-A of Cr PC, the operation of the Victim 
Compensation scheme is with the Legal Services Authorities and states have framed 
their schemes in pursuant to the provision. In case of Nipun Sa xena vs UOI, on the 
directions of Hon’ble Supreme Court, NALSA has prepared a victi m compensation 
scheme in 2018 for women survivors which is available on NALSA’ s website 
(enclosed for ready reference). This scheme is applicable to th e POCSO victims as 
well because there is no separate scheme for POCSO victims. There are two issues:- 
 
a. Adequate fund is not provided for victim compensation, so large  number of 
victims are not paid. 
b. A good number of states have not adopted NALSA Model Scheme, so  the victims 
are not getting adequate compensation. 
Further Observation 
3.30 The Central and State Governments are duty bound constitut ionally, legally and 
morally to ensure "access to justice for all". However, the ser iousness and attention 
from the various stakeholders of the legal aid movement is rath er missing. None other 
than the CJI has opined that the legal aid services are neglect ed in our country. So it is 
high time to pay adequate attention and seriousness to the lega l aid movement in India 
it deserves. State/UT Governments are equal partners in extending the legal aid services 
t o  t h e  e l i g i b l e  p o p u l a t i o n .  A s  i n f o r m e d  b y  N A L S A  t h e  i n f r a s t r u cture and manpower 
requirements at the grassroots levels are awfully inadequate. T hus the DoJ and NALSA 
are expected to have an effective consultation with the SLSAs a nd State/UT 
Governments and to impress upon them to provide all necessary i nfrastructure and 
manpower in order to provide a decent quality of legal aid to the people at grassroots.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.31 The Committee observes that the majority of the funds for NALSA are utilized for 
administrative services, rather than providing legal aid. Also,  p a n e l  l a w y e r s  a r e  n o t  b e i n g  
adequately compensated and their remuneration has remained stag nant for long. This affects 
the quality of legal aid service provided to the clients. This also often leads to lawyers found 
harassing beneficiaries or demanding ‘fees’ from them. The Comm ittee accordingly, 
recommends NALSA to compensate lawyers adequately, so that they  are able to sustain 
themselves and remain motivated in their job. On other hand, a robust system of monitoring 
the efficacy and accountability of legal aid services provided to the beneficiaries should also 
be put in place by NALSA. (3.34)  
Action Taken 
 
3.32 It is submitted that after observation of the Hon’ble Comm ittee regarding utilization 
of majority of funds for administrative services, a set of guid elines for spending funds have 
been issued by NALSA after obtaining with the approval of Hon’b le Executive Chairman, 
NALSA. 
 

31 
 
3.33 Regarding remuneration and adequate compensation to Panel Lawyers, it is submitted 
that after the resolution in Chief Justices and Chief Ministers  Conference – 2016, the 
State/UTs have taken note of the same and most of the States ar e paying as per 
recommendations of NALSA. In the year 2019, monthly remuneratio n (Retainer fee) of 
retainer lawyers have been increased across the country. Further, this issue will be taken up in 
the National Meet proposed to be organized shortly. 
 
Further Observation 
 
3.34 It is an undeniable fact tha t a majority of the people who are entitled to free legal 
aid see it as an option only when they cannot afford a private lawyer. The reason behind 
this is the lack of trust on the Legal Aid Counsels (LACs). The  q u a l i t y  o f  l e g a l  
representation and lack of commitment of the LACs towards the b eneficiary's case is a 
matter of concern. Quite often the LACs are meagerly paid and they are engaged on ad-
hoc basis. Thus there is a dire need to provide adequate remune ration to them and to 
revise it on regular basis. Further, appointing them on full ti me basis will certainly 
going to improve the level of commitment amongst the LACs.

POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.2 The Committee notes that even after 12 years of its separat ion from the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and becoming an independent Department, the Depart ment of Justice is still 
dependent on the MHA for all its man power requirements. The va cancies in the Department 
are particularly staggering at the middle and operating level o f SO, ASO (50% vacancy), 
UDC (100% vacancy), PA (100% vacancy) and Steno (100% vacancy).   It is surprising that 
the DoPT is posting officers of the rank of US and above direct ly to the Department, but 
other officials are posted by the MHA. There is hardly any just ification for this type of 
cumbersome arrangement being followed in the case of the Depart ment of Justice, where it is 
being given a step-motherly treatment in this matter. The Depar tment of Justice has been 
mandated with a significant role in appointment of judges, acce ss to justice and justice 
delivery. Accordingly, it should be provided with sufficient re sources and manpower to fulfil 
its mandate. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Depa rtment of Justice should be 
given full autonomy in case of personnel management and all cad re controlling authorities, 
including DoPT, should post all encadred posts directly to the Department of Justice. The 
Department of Justice is directed to bring this recommendation o f  t h e  C o m m i t t e e  t o  t h e  
notice of DoPT and MHA. (3.2)

Recommendation/Observation

st Report on Demands for Grants (2020-21) had made observations w ith 
regard to drafting errors and ambiguity in law/statutes and des ired for pre-legislative 
consultation and periodic review of legislations.  The Committe e is of the view that 
legislation enacted are not able to keep pace with changing soc io-economic developments 
leading to excessive litigations, financial loss to exchequer, disconnect with social milieu and 
so forth. (Para 3.15) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.15, it is to mention that:  
i. The process of legislation involves the study of social and financial costs, benefits and 
the key challenges that required to be settled before undertaki ng the legislations. The 
administrative Ministry/Department also identifies the problems  in the policy that 
needs to be addressed, the options it has considered and the re asons thereof in 
bringing forward a legislation.  
ii. Further, the Chapter 9 of the Manual of Parliamentary Procedure  in the Government 
of India (relating to legislation) provides that the concerned Ministry/Department has 
to formulate the legislative proposals in consultation with the  interested persons and 
authorities concerned, including holding discussions on the nec essity for the proposed 
legislation and on all matters of substance to be embodied therein. 
iii. Moreover, as per the Government of India (Allocation of Busines s) Rules, 1961, 
different subject matter or policies are allocated to different Ministries/Departments of 
the Government of India. Accordingly, the Ministries/Department s concerned with 
the subject matter initiates pre-legislative Consultations, hol ds deliberations with the 
public and all stakeholders and on that basis, finalise its leg islative policy and 
subsequently conduct the impact assessment after the legislations is enacted.  
iv. It is further pertinent to mention here that the Legislative De partment prepares draft 
laws in consultation with the administrative Ministry concerned  in accordance with 
the procedure laid down in the Manual of Parliamentary Procedur es, ordinarily within 
thirty days from the date of receipt of the proposal and after clearance from the 
Department of Legal Affairs. The refore, the Legislative Departm ent is merely a 
service provider Department catering its drafting services to t he 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India.  
 
Further Observation 
1.2 The Committee notes the Reply of the Department.

                                  CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE 
GOVERNMENT             
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 The Committee desires that a general consensus is required on the issue of Legislative 
Impact Assessment (LIA), and accordingly of the considered view that there has to be a nodal 
Ministry/Department for dealing with the issues related to LIA,  and believes that the 
Legislative Department, due to its expertise in legislative/cab inet note drafting is the most 
suitable Department under the Government of India for the purpo se. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Department to prepare a white paper  on the Legislative Impact 
Assessment in the country by taking learning experiences of oth er developed countries. (Para 
3.16) 
Action Taken 
2.1 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.16, it is to mention that:  
i. The Legislative Impact Assessment or Analysis is a transparent and informed process 
with the participation and involvement of all stakeholders so that the preparedness and 
availability of requisite administrative, financial and infrast ructural support for 
successful implementation of intended legislation is known befo re hand and the 
desired object can be achieved. 
ii. The Legislative Impact Assessment is wide enough to encompass w ithin its scope 
Judicial Impact Assessment, Social Impact Assessment, Financial Impact Assessment, 
Environment Impact Assessment, Employment Impact Assessment, etc.  
 Judicial Impact Assessment  helps in preserving Courts ability to keep pace 
with growing workload, ensures, adequate funding of Courts and improves 
administration of justice. 
 Social Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the socio-economic impact of 
legislation on people, particularly those from the economically  weaker section 
and marginalized section of society. 
 Financial Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the economic costs of 
proposed legislation.  
 Environment Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the beneficial and 
adverse impact of new legislation on environment, optimization of natural 
resources, reducing or mitigating potential negative impacts an d achieving 
9

sustainable development.  
 Employment Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating employment creation 
through proposed legislation. 
iii. A law is reviewed by the concerned Ministry/Department for exam ining its 
effectiveness and setting right m ischief, if any, created by su ch law on the basis of 
feedback, if any, received from the stakeholders and the other concerned persons, the 
data, if any, collected in this behalf, the comments/suggestion s, if any, received from 
the public, etc. Thereafter, the concerned Ministry/Department takes up necessary 
l e g i s l a t i v e  a c t i o n  e i t h e r  f o r  a m e n d m e n t  o r  r e p e a l  o f  t h e  l a w .  Post-enactment 
legislative impact assessment is also done by the Law Commissio n of India or such 
other body or commission set up specifically for such purpose, which is normally 
limited to the specific terms of reference. 
iv. Under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1 961, each 
Ministry/Department has been allocated subject matters on which  t h a t  
Ministry/Department initiates, possess and implements legislati ve proposals and also 
studies social, economic, environmental and judicial impact of such  legislative 
proposals. 
v. In view of the above, pre-legislative consultations, legislative impact assessment /post 
legislation consultation are within the domain of the concerned  Ministry/Department. 
Hence, the pre and post Legislative Impact Assessment should be  done by the 
concerned Ministry/Department which piloted the legislation. Th erefore, the subject 
matter relating to legislative impact assessment does not come under the purview of 
the allocation of work to Legislative-I Section of this Department. 
vi. However, the Committee is of view that there has to be a nodal Ministry/Department 
for dealing with the issue related to Legislative Impact Assess ment and believes that 
the Legislative Department possess the expertise in legislative /cabinet note drafting 
and therefore, Legislative Department is considered as most sui table Department for 
the purpose. In this regards, it is to state that as explained above the legislative impact 
assessment /post legislation consultation is a wide concept and  involves intricacies, 
specialized knowledge, expertise, manpower, research work and i nfrastructure and as 
the Legislative Department does not intervene in the policy mat ter of the legislation 
rather only provides its drafting services to the Ministries/De partments. In view of the 
a b o v e ,  L e g i s l a t i v e  D e p a r t m e n t  i s  e x a m i n i n g  v a r i o u s  a s p e c t s  r e l ating to the 
recommendation made by the Department related Parliamentary Sta nding Committee, 
and the manner of its implementation and suitable decision take n by the competent 
authority will be communicated in due course of time. 
 
Further Observation
