smaller states like Manipur, Tripura etc. where the bench strength is small, high 
levels of vacancies leads divisional benches not being constituted for want of judges 
and if  there is some retirement or elevation or transfers the working of such High 
Courts are brought to a standstill. In the High Court of Tripura, where the Committee 
visited in the month of January, 2023, out of the sanctioned strength of 5, only 2 
Judges wer e in -position, including the acting Chief Justice, making it difficult for 
them to constitute a divisional bench. Thus, the peculiarities  of the smaller High 
Courts should be kept in mind while making appointment.      (Para 1.53)

Further observation of the Committee 
3.9 The Committee notes that the  situation of the smaller High Courts  like 
Manipur, Tripura etc,  is very different from the rest of the High Courts of the 
Country.  In these High Courts, where the bench strength is very small, 
transfers and retirements lead to acute shortage of judges and hence the entire 
judicial mechanism and justice administration  comes to a standstill. This leads 
to piling up of pending cases in the se Courts for unknown duration of time and 
litigants of these small states waiting for justice are left totally helpless in such a 
scenario. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department may impress 
upon the Chief Justice  of the concerned High Court/  who oversee the se Courts 
to initiate the process of appointment of judges  six months prior to  occurrence 
of vacancies, so that the Government is able to make the appointments  on time 
and the courts can run smoothly.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS 
ON EMPANELMENT OF ADVOCATES FOR UNION OF INDIA 
 
Q.1 What is ‘Panel Counsel’ for Union of India? 
Department of Legal Affairs has been mandated with conduct of litigations on behalf of 
Union of India before various courts / tribunals in India . For this purpose, Department of 
Legal Affairs empanels Advocates for various courts / tribunals in the country generally 
for a period of three years or until further orders, whichever is earlier. There are several 
categories (court -wise) in which this De partment empanels Advocates and such 
empanelled Advocates are collectively called as „Panel Counsel‟ for Union of India.  
However, „Panel Counsel‟ is not a civil post and as such they are not regular Government 
Servant.  
 
Q.2 Documentation/details required in the application for empanelment as a Panel 
Counsel for Union of India? 
 (a)   Name of court / tribunal seeking empanelment for. 
(b) Desired category of Panel Counsel available in that court /  
tribunal.  
(c) Certification on part of willing Advocate that he/she will be bound by all the 
terms & conditions (including fee) applicable to desired category of „Panel 
Counsel‟ in the desired court/tribunal. 
(d) A detailed and duly signed Bio -data may be enclosed with application 
incorporating the necessary details lik e name, postal address, contact numbers, 
email, legal qualifications, full enrollment number with the Bar Council 
concerned.

Q.4 What emoluments are paid to ‘Panel Counsel’? 
 
As „Panel Counsel‟ for Union of India are not Government Servant, they are not paid 
salaries and allowances. They are paid professional fee on case to case basis in lieu of 
their services as per the fee schedule applicable to their panel category. However,  there 
are a few categories of „Panel Counsel‟ which are paid retainership fee on monthly basis 
throughout their term in the entitled category. The fee schedule in this regard is as per 
this Department‟s OM No. 26(1)/2014-Judl. dated 01.10.2015 to be read with other OMs 
containing detailed terms & conditions applicable to „Panel Counsel‟. 
 

 
15 
 
 
Q.5 What is procedure for allotment of cases to ‘Panel Counsel’? 
  
Except in the Supreme Court of India, in all other courts / tribunals, allotment of cases to 
Panel Counsel is made by the Litigation In -charge of court concerned. The Litigation In -
charges have  been decided by the Department of Legal Affairs in OM No. J -
12017/1/2019-Judicial dated 21.10.2019. While in Supreme Court, Ld. Attorney General 
for India selects cases for his own  appearance while other cases are marked by the Ld. 
Solicitor General of India to Additional Solicitors General of India and Panel Counsel 
vide OM No. J-12017/1/2022-Judicial dated 13.09.2022.  
 
Q.6 Is there any sanctioned strength of Panel Counsel (Court-wise)? 
As stated earlier „Panel Counsel‟ for Union of India is not a civil post hence, the concept 
of sanctioned strength is not applicable in case of „Panel Counsel‟. Advocates a re 
empanelled for a particular court / tribunal by Department of Legal Affairs in numbers as 
required from time to time.   
 
Q.7 Are the Panel Counsel for Union of India allowed for private practice? 
Panel Counsel for Union of India may continue their private practice but with restriction 
to the extent that they cannot appear / advise in matters against Union of India in any 
manner vide Department of Legal Affairs OM No. J -16/11/2017-Judicial dated 
08.02.2018.

12 posts of Judicial Members and 09 posts of Accountant Members in the Income Tax Appellate 
Tribunal. The Department of Legal Affairs, in the month of September, 2022, has issued fresh 
vacancy circular to fill up the 18 posts of Judicial Members and 22 posts of Accountant Members 
in the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The process of selection of candidates for Members 
(Judicial /Accountant) has made substantial progress and t he interaction process with applicants 
has been concluded and the Search-cum-Selection Committee (SCSC) under the Chairpersonship 
of a sitting Judge of the Hon'ble Supreme Court has submitted a list of recommended candidates 
for the consideration of the Government and further appropriate action.  
 
1.20 Also the 'Vivad Se Vishwas Scheme' is doing well to reduce the number of pending cases 
in ITAT. The Central Government's efforts to fill up the existing vacancy in ITAT during the 
current year, will further facilitate in reducing the pending cases of ITAT in the next few years.  
 
INDIA INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION CENTRE (IIAC) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.21 With the operationalization of the IIAC the Committee expects the Centre to strive and 
achieve the vision with which it has been created i.e. to strengthen an independent & 
autonomous arbitration regime; to compete with other reputed international arbitration centres; to 
arbitrate on big ticket infrastructure projects disputes involving Central or State Governments, 
PSUs a parties or PPP projects; and to aid in effort in making India a hub of international 
commercial arbitration. In this endeavour, the Comm ittee expects the Government and 
Department of Legal Affairs, in particular, to whole heartedly support the Centre. (3.35) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.22 The Centre aims to implement advanced technology in order to offer a completely digital, 
paperless experience for all stakeholders. From registering arbitrators to managing the entire 
arbitration process, everything is proposed to be done digitally, making  the process more 
transparent, efficient and accessible globally. Necessary steps are being taken for development of 
the process/web and software application by the Centre.   
  
1.23 Further, considering requirements of an Arbitration Centre of international standards, the 
Centre is being considered to be re -designed/revamped and requisite action in this regard has 
also been initiated. 
  
1.24 The Centre has signed a MoU with IIM Rohtak to undertake collaborative activities to 
develop awareness and promotion campaigns that will align the goal of creating awareness in the 
field of arbitration and making India an international hub for arbitration. 
  

 
18 
1.25 The IIAC has finalized and notified various regulations for making it operational and 
fully funct ional. The Department is in the process of writing to all the Government 
Ministries/Departments and CPSEs that IIAC may be earmarked as the designated arbitral 
institution to facilitate resolution of the disputes pertaining to them with private parties etc ., 
wherever the option of Arbitration is to be taken recourse to. 
  
1.26 The Department of Legal Affairs is committed towards providing all requisite support to 
the Centre, in order to enable it to achieve its objectives.

CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY 
THE DEPARTMENT 
STAFF STRENGTH IN THE DEPARTMENT 
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
2.0 The Department of Legal Affairs has been functioning with about 50% of the sanctioned 
strength for quite a long time, across its grades. The Department has admitted that the shortage of 
manpower for such long duration is affecting their smooth functioning. The Committee has been 
for long; in almost every DFG reports, is recommending the Dep artment to take remedial actions 
to get rid of this perennial shortage of manpower in the Department. (3.10) 
2.1 The ILS, which is the mainstay of the Department and whose cadre control rests with the 
Department itself, has a vacancy of above 50%. The Depa rtment has further informed that they 
have initiated reforming the RRs of the cadre and vacancies will be filled thereafter. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to complete the revision of the RRs, at the 
earliest and start filling up of th e vacant position in a dedicated manner. Further, the RRs should 
be revised in such a way so as to avoid possibility of future litigations, as litigations have been 
one of the reasons for vacancies remaining unfilled. The eligibility conditions and career 
prospects in the ILS should be framed in such a manner, that it attracts the best and the brightest 
candidates from the market. (3.11) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.2 Indian Legal Service (ILS) is an organized Group -A Service, which is governed by the 
Indian Legal Serv ice Rules, 1957. A cadre review of this service is under process, which is the 
first cadre review since this service came into being in 1957. 
 
2.3        In its various meetings, the Cadre Review Committee (CRC) of the Department of 
Personnel & Training di scussed proposals of Department of Legal Affairs, which include 
improving flexibility in allocation of Indian Legal Service (ILS) officers to various Ministries 
and Departments, issue related to provision of reserves in the ILS cadre, merger of the cadre o f 
ILS to facilitate requirement based horizontal mobility and career progression, creation of posts 
above the SAG level, change in existing sanctioned strength (cadre wise) of ILS cadre as well as 
change in method of recruitment in ILS cadre. This cadre re view will help in mitigating potential 
legal disputes in the service as well as enhancing the overall efficiency and fairness of the 
recruitment process of ILS cadre. 
 
2.4.         These recommendations of CRC is under consideration of the Government and is 
expected to be finalized shortly. 
 

 
20 
CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE 
DEPARTMENT AND REITERATES ITS RECOMMENDATIONS 
Overall Assessment of the Demands for Grants 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 From the submission of the Institute and analysis of the functioning of the ILI over the 
years, the Committee is constrained to observe that a premier institution founded for promoting 
and conducting legal research is becomin g insignificant day-by-day due to lack of funding from 
the Government. Faculty positions are remaining vacant, basic renovation and upkeep of the 
institution are held up due to lack of funds. Only a skeletal faculty/staff are maintained with the 
limited grants provided by the Government. As we don't have many institutions in the country 
for legal research and thus, the Government should maintain this institution and not let it die a 
slow death. The Committee wants to see the Institute to become a centre of excellence in the 
field of legal research, for which it requires the support of the Government. However, the 
Committee feels that if the Government is not in a position to maintain this institute, it is better 
to hand it over to some other institutions like Supreme Court of India or BCI etc., like they did in 
case of Institute of Constitutional & Parliamentary Studies (ICPS) which was handed over to the 
Lok Sabha Secretariat. (2.15) 
Action Taken  
3.1 The Department of Legal Affairs provides recurring Grants -in-Aid to the Indian Law 
Institute (ILI) for salary and general purposes. The Department also provides Grants -in-Aid to 
ILI for special purpose, whenever it was required. The Department released Rs. 6.50 crore to ILI 
as special Grants-in-Aid for payment of property tax in the Financial Year 2021 -22 and Rs.1.00 
crore to ILI as additional Grants -in-Aid for payment of arrears of salary to employees of ILI on 
implementation of the recommendations of the 7 th CPC in the Financial Year 2018 -19. The 
Department has also increased the Grants -in-Aid „salary‟ of ILI by Rs.3.00 crore i.e. Rs.3.00 
crore in BE -2022-23 to Rs.6.00 crore in RE -2022-23. The Department of Legal Affairs has 
provided financial supports as well as administrative support to ILI, whenever they required.  
3.2 ILI has also shared their views on merger of ILI with either the Supreme Court of India 
or the Bar Council of India and stated that the ILI has been functioning effectively under the 
aegis of the Ministry of Law and Justice. ILI has also, therefore, opined that looking to the 
distinct and unique nature and work scope of the Indian Law Institute, it is not viable to merge it 
with either the Supreme Court of India or the Bar Council of India. 
3.3Therefore, it would be appropriate if the ILI continues to maintain its independent existence 
with the financial support of the Department and functions under the aegis of the Ministry of 
Law and Justice. The Department has from time to time accepted mo st of the requests of ILI for 
financial and administrative support.  

 
21 
Further Observation  
3.4 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. Indian Law Institute (ILI) was 
founded in 1956 primarily with the objective of promoting and conducting legal 
research. The Committee observes that either the fund or Grants -in-Aid provided by the 
Department is not sufficient to cater to its basic needs like proper infrastructure, filling up 
of faculty positions and other Academic and Non-Academic activities. The Committee notes 
that even after 60 years of its establishment a premier institute like ILI is struggling to 
cater to meet its essential requirements. The Committee wishes to see ILI as a centre of 
excellence in the field of legal research and therefore strongly recommends the Department 
to increase its allocation. 
VACANCIES OF NOTARIES 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.5 On observing the State/UT-wise sanctioned posts of Notaries it can be observed that their 
distribution is quite uneven. For instance for a much bigger state like Uttar Pradesh the 
sanctioned posts for public notaries is 2650 only, whereas for Gujarat, whic h is a comparatively 
much smaller state in terms of population the strength of notaries is 8000. It is also not known 
what criteria are being used to sanction a particular number of notaries in a State. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends the Government to use a fair yardstick and take into account the 
factors like population, litigations etc. while sanctioning the posts of Public Notaries in a 
particular State. (3.19) 
Action Taken 
 
3.6 It is submitted that the number of vacancies for Central Government Notaries in the State 
of Uttar Pradesh was inadvertently mentioned as 2650 and the correct figure is 5150, which was 
increased vide Notification G.S.R. 746(E) dated 18th October, 2021. Further, the vacancies in 
the state are increased in accordance with the number of applications received for appointment of 
Notaries for the particular state.  
 
Further observation  
 
3.7 The Committee is of the view that increasing the vacancies in accordance with the 
number of applications received is not a good criterion to decide vacancies for appointment 
of notaries. The Committee desires that the sanctioned strength of notaries in a particular 
state should be determined only on the basis of its population, number of litigation, 
economic and commercial activit ies in that state, etc., and it should  also be reviewed 
regularly.  
 
 
 
 

 
22 
VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.8 The Panel Counsels are engaged all over the Country by the Central Government to 
conduct litigations before the High Courts/Tribunals and other courts. They bear the major 
burden of litigations against the Central Government. From the submissions made by t he 
Department, it is observed that the fees paid to these counsels are very meagre, which is much 
below the market rates. The last revision of their fees was done about 7 years back. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends the Department to revise the fees p aid to the panel lawyers suitably, 
considering the current market rates, so that they remain interested and committed in their jobs. 
It will also help in attracting competent lawyers for being empanelled as a panel lawyer for the 
Central Government. (3.23)  
Action Taken 
3.9 Presently there are more than 6000 panel counsels before various Courts across the 
country. The present fee structure to these panel counsel was finalised in year 2015, vide OM 
No. 26(1)/2014/Judl.dated 01.10.2015, which still seems to b e sufficient. As such increase in fee 
structure at this stage does not seem to be required. 
Further observation 
3.10 The Committee  notes the reply. T he fee structure for notaries was  finalised way 
back in the year 2015 and the same fee structure is continuing till date . The Committee 
therefore recommends the Department to revise the fees taking into account the inflation 
rate over the past 8 years.

ment/ECI, hence this huge reduction. The Committee is therefore of the view that while ma k-
ing projections to the Ministr y of Finance in future, the Department should ensure that its 
projections are rational and appropriate to meet its requirements. (Para 2.22) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 Legislative Department is concerned with the Elections related expenditure including 
cases of settlement of Election Accounts of all States/UTs of India, which contains following 
steps: 
• For the purpose, Governments of States/UTs concerned, forward the valid Audit Ce r-
tificates obtained from the Accountant General (AG) offices concerned of the Stat e Govern-
ment, to Legislative Department, conveying the election expenditure incurred by that 
State/UT in a particular financial year, under the Major Head 2015- Elections.  
• Subsequently, all the records/ Audit Certificates are thoroughly scrutinized in t he De-
partment and the dues of Government of India‟ share for that particular financial year is se t-
tled and conveyed to the Government of State/UT concerned, along with the Election Co m-
mission of India. 
• Based on the settlement of dues of Government of Ind ia‟ share for a financial year in 
respect of States/UTs from where Audit Certificates have been received, projections of total 
dues is made at in R.E stage to Ministry of Finance (MOF).  
• After receipt of the amount in R.E. stage, the same is distributed among the State/UT 
concerned. 
1.2 On the basis of above procedure, in the year 2022 -23, Election accounts of 11 States 
(viz. Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Mah a-
rashtra, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tamil Nadu and West Be ngal) have been settled till 27.02.2022 
on the basis of Audit Certificates received from their respective AG Offices. Accordingly, a 
demand of Rs.3166.08 Crore was made in the second and final batch supplementary from 
Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, an amount of Rs.3166.08 crore has been received for 
Major Head-2015 (Elections) in the Second and Final Batch Supplementary.  Thereafter, 
the amount of Rs. 3166.08 crore has been released to the aforesaid 11 State Governments.

2.1 As regards the Committee‟s observation, Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP) has stated 
that it is a wing of Legislative Department, dedicated for promotion and propagation of Hindi 
in the legal field under the mandate of Constitution of India (Article 351), recommendations 
of Parliamentary Committee on Official Language and Orders of Hon‟ble President of India. 
In the year 1958, the Committee of Parliament on Official Languages recommended that ar-
rangements be made to bring out authorised Hindi version of all reportable judgements of the 
Supreme Court of India and various High Courts for the purpose of promotion and propaga-
tion of Hindi in the legal field and this work should be entrusted to a Central Office under the 
supervision of Law Ministry. Thereafter, on the recommendations of the Hindi Advisory 
Committee, a “Journal Wing” was set up in the Legislative Department in the year 1968 with 
the object of promoting Hindi in the legal field which was later on known as “VIDHI SA-
HITYA PRAKASHAN”. Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan has published Hindi text of about fifty 
thousand judgements passed by Hon‟ble Supreme Court, various High Courts and Privy 
Council. Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan has also published high standard 38 Law Text Books in 
Hindi on various legal topics. These books are under the copyright of Government of India.

(b) Awarding various prizes for the best publication of Hindi Text Books on various subjects 
in the field of law; 
(c) Sale of Hindi Law Journals and Hindi Text Books on various legal subjects, Central Acts 
in diglot edition, Constitution of India, Election Manual and Legal Glossary etc.;  and 
(d) Holding conferences, seminars, workshops and book exhibitions in different parts of the 
country for propagation and popularisation of Hindi in the legal field;

Kashmiri, Maithili, Nepali, Odia, Santhali and Sindhi to the Central Institute of Indian La n-
guages (CIIL established under the Ministry of Education, Government of India). 

pg. 20 
 
Further Observation 
3.15 The Committee acknowledges  and appreciates the fact that the Constitution of 
India has been updated in four more languages vis -à-vis Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi 
and Tamil by  the Department this year. However, the committee reiterates its reco m-
mendations made in its previous Reports  viz. 96th, 101st, 114th and 130th Report to bring 
out publication of the Constitution of India in all the Schedule d languages of the Consti-
tution as soon as possible. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.16 The Committee also observes that there are no officer for Kannada, Urdu, Dogri, G u-
jarati, Manipuri, Konkani, Assamese, Sindhi, Nepali, Sanskrit, Odia, Bodo, Santhali, Maithili 
and Kashmiri. The Committee also takes note of the proposal initiated to re -structure the ex-
isting cadre st ructure The Committee also observes that the department has not been able to 
fill these vacancies for some time now despite repeated recommendations of the Committee 
in its 101st, 107th and 114th report. (Para 2.35) 
3.17 The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the work related to translation and u p-
dation of the Constitution of India in all the Scheduled languages of the Constitution be e x-
pedited. In the mean-time, where the department has not been able to find suitable candidates 
for the regional language posts, people from those languages can be employed on contractual 
basis so that work related to translation of Constitution may be initiated. The vacancies can 
also be filled by floating a employment advertisement on its India Code Information Sy stem 
(ICIS) portal. The Committee also recommends the department to apprise the Committee of a 
status note on proposal for filling these regional language posts on real time basis and also 
inform about the bottlenecks faced by it. (Para 2.36) 
Action Taken 
 
3.18 As regards the Committee‟s observation in Para 2.35 and 2.36, Official Language 
Wing (OLW) (Admn.) has submitted that the presently 21 posts of Regional Languages o f-
ficers are lying vacant which are to be filled from various languages i.e. Kannada, U rdu, Do-
gri, Gujarati, Manipuri, Konkani, Assamese, Sindhi, Nepali, Sanskrit, Odia, Bodo, Santhali, 
Maithili and Kashmiri. A proposal for re -structuring of Group „A‟ posts of Regional La n-
guages has also been initiated and under consideration. After amendmen t of recruitment rules 
and re-structuring the cadre of Group „A‟ posts of Regional Languages, all the posts of R e-
gional Languages officers will be filled up expeditiously. As suggested by the Committee, 
this Wing also initiate the proposal for engaging sui table candidate on contract basis after en-
hancing the budget in sub -head „Professional Services‟. It is further submitted that after the 
proposal for revising existing cadre structure receives the approval of the competent author i-
ty, it is hoped that all o ut efforts shall be made to fill up all the posts in the Regional La n-
guages officers‟ cadre. It is pertinent to mention here that a proposal to assign the translation 

pg. 21 
 
work to the Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysore is also under consideration in the 
Department formalities.  . 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.19 The Committee observes that the filling of vacant post s in various languages is 
pending for approval of competent authority to revise the existing cadre structure  for 
quite some time . The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts may be taken to 
get the approval of competent authority at the earliest so that the vacant posts can be 
filled without any further delay. The Committee notes that the proposal to assign the 
translation work to the Central Institute of Indian Language, Mysore, is under consi d-
eration, which is a welcome step. The Committee desires that the above proposal may be 
finalised as soon as possible so that work related to translation of constitution in other 
languages may be initiated at the earliest.. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.20 The India Code Information System is a very noble initiative developed by the D e-
partment. However, the Committee found various loopholes in the functioning of the We b-
site. The Committe e found only some important acts which were translated in regional la n-
guages like Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, 
Tamil, Telugu and Urdu there. The Committee wishes to point out that there was no transl a-
tion of any act in Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Nepali, Sanskrit, Sa n-
thali and Sindhi. The Committee also found mention of Hindi version of the Acts upto the 
year 2020 only which should have been done till 2022. The Committee understands that th e 
process of the development of such a noble initiative is still at a nascent stage. The Commi t-
tee therefore recommends that ICIS platform be updated regularly with the help of Artificial 
Intelligence tools so that it becomes a one stop destination for all  the legal data related qu e-
ries for the people from all the regions of the country. (Para 2.42) 
Action Taken 
 
3.21 As regards the Committee‟s observation, India Code Updation Unit of Legislative 
Department (LD) has stated that the recommendation is not directly concerned with them. 
They uploads and updates the enforced Acts in English version only while the subordinate 
legislations are being uploaded and updated by the concerned Ministries/ Departments on the 
India Code website. The Acts in Hindi and reg ional languages are uploaded on the websites 
of the Legislative Department and India Code by the Official Languages Wing of the D e-
partment. 
 
3.22 Further, regarding the Committee‟s observation, Regional Language Unit (RLU) of 
Official Language Wing (OLW) o f Legislative Department has submitted that there is no 
translation of Central Acts have been started in Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, 
Manipuri, Nepali, Sanskrit, Santhali and Sindhi languages as there is no officer app ointed for 
the above languages. 

pg. 22 
 
 
Further recommendation/observation 
3.23 The Committee notes that uploading of Hindi version of the Acts on the websites of 
the legislative Department is not updated and therefore, recommends that the Official Lan-
guage Wing of the Department should expedite the uploading of the Hindi version of Acts on 
the website upto the year 2022. 
3.24 The Committee also recommends that appointment of officers for languages me n-
tioned in above para i.e., Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Nepali, San-
skrit, Santhali and Sindhi languages  should be expedited so that translation of Acts in these 
languages may also be done. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.25 The Committee also observes allocations have been increased under Revenue heads - 
Salary and Voters‟ Awareness, which the Committee believes are important components of 
electoral processes. Voter's Awareness is an important programme for the betterment of the 
democracy. The Commi ttee hopes that the Commission will be able to fully uti lize the i n-
creased allocation under the head Voters' Awareness for the financial year 2023 -24. (Para 
3.11) 
Action Taken 
 
3.26 Vacancies  arising  in  the  grade  of  ASO,  JSA, Stenographer  C&D  &  MTS  for 
direct recruitment are reported to the Staff Selection Commission  (SSC)  every  year. Vacan-
cies in these posts are mostly due to delay in sele ction of candidates by the SSC. Some posts  
of SSA  are lying vacant due to delay in conducting the UD grade departmental exam by SSC 
since 2016 . Further, th e vacant posts in the Commission are being filled by deputation whe-
rever the RRs provide for the same. 
 
3.27 It is also informed that the Commission has already reported its  DR  vacancies  for

CHAPTER–I
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS
FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the coordinating agency of
the Central Government in personnel related matters especially in respect of the issues concerning
recruitment, training, career development, staff welfare as well as post-retirement dispensation. The
Ministry is also concerned with promotion of responsive, people-oriented, modern administration.
The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely:—
(i) The Department of Personnel and Training;
(ii) The Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare; and
(iii) The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
1.1 The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister assisted by a Minister of
State. All the three Departments of the Ministry function under the charge of Secretary who is
presently assisted by four Additional Secretaries, three Joint Secretaries and other supporting
officers and staff. The Ministry is divided into seven Divisions, each of which is headed by an
officer of the level of Joint Secretary or above. The Divisions are:
(i) Establishment Officer;
(ii) Services and Vigilance;
(iii) Establishment;
(iv) Administrative Tribunal and Administration;
(v) Training;
(vi) Pension and Central Services; and
(vii) Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
1.2 The Ministry has under its administrative control four attached offices, namely:
(i) Staff Selection Commission (SSC);
(ii) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM);
(iii) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie; and
(iv) Central Bureau of Investigation.
1.3 The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are:
(i) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), a constitutional body;
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), a statutory body;
(iii) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), a statutory quasi-judicial body; and
(iv) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB), a body set up by a resolution of the
Central Government.

set up for the welfare of Government employees and their families. These societies are:—

(iii) Kendriya Bhandar; and
(iv) Civil Services Officers Institute.

1.16 The Union Public Service Commission is a Constitutional body, created under Article 315
of the Constitution. The Commission’s charter of duties is given in Articles 320 and 321 of the
Constitution. In brief, it is the duty of the Commission to conduct examinations for appointment
to services of the Union and to advise Government on all matters relating to framing of recruitment
rules, method of recruitment and the principles to be followed in making promotions and transfers
from one service to another. The Commission is also required to be consulted in respect of
disciplinary matters affecting a civil servant including appeals and memoranda filed by individual
Government servants.
1.17 Article 322 of the Constitution envisages, inter-alia, that the expenses of the UPSC
including salaries, allowances and pensions payable to members and staff of the Commission shall
be ‘charged’ on the Consolidated Fund of India.

CHAPTER–II
MAJOR INITIATIVES AND SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
Right to Information Act, 2005
2.0 The Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions while making
presentation on the Demand for Grants (2006-07) of the Ministry, deposed before the Committee
that according to their latest reports, 20 State Governments had already implemented the Right to
Information Act.
2.1 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry (2005-06), seven workshops were conducted at
the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management on Right to Information Act for Public
Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers nominated from various Ministries/
Departments to the Government of India.
2.2 The Committee appreciates the setting up of the Central Information Commission.
The Committee also appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry in this regard. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure that all Ministries/Departments/
Organisations do implement the provisions of the Right to Information Act, 2005 in its true
letter and spirit. The Committee also recommends that a mechanism should be put in place
to monitor and evaluate its status of implementation. Right to Information Act is a
milestone in the efforts made to promote transparency and accountability in the working of
public authorities. Therefore, the Ministries should persuade/motivate all the Ministries/
Departments/Organisations to implement pr ovisions of the Act. At the same time, the
Government should also ensure that the provisions of the Act are not misused, failing which
the very purpose of the Act will be defeated.
Training Policy and Programmes
3.0 In the era of globalisation, with the advent of latest information technology methods,
enriching of human resources has become an imperative need. Training and capacity building have
emerged as an important prerequisite for an efficient administration.
3.1 On the Cadre Training Plan, the Annual Report of the Ministry states that a Committee
of Senior Officers was set up in February, 2001 to devise a Comprehensive Training Plan for
CSS Officers and that its Report was submitted in February, 2005 making far reaching
recommendations.
3.2 The Ministry, in its reply on the issue, inter alia, stated that the recommendations were
examined in details by the Department and were accepted by the Government with certain
modifications. It was also stated that the Training Division of the Department and the ISTM had
been directed to provide necessary training to the officers at various levels in the CSS and that
the training programmes are likely to start in the current financial year.
3.3 The Committee is pleased to note that some initiatives have been taken in the
direction of implementation of its recommendations. The Committee recommends that the
training programmes should be started without further delay. The Committee hopes that its
recommendations would be implemented and pursued in order to ensure career growth and
development of CSS officers.
8

9
3.4 The Secretary apprised the Committee about the training programmes as follows:
“...we have taken a decision to start high quality programmes in India itself and the first
such programme was started in IIT, Bangalore....Then Sir, capacity building, especially in
the matters of Right to Information, is an important component of our programme. We have
an UNDP funded project.....for capacity building, including training modules and training of
trainers of national, State and district level...”
3.5 The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry in this regard and
recommends that the Ministry should pursue the initiatives in right earnest so that the
desired objectives are achieved.
Welfare of pensioners
4.0 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry (2005-06), the Ministry/Departments are having
a variety of mechanisms for redressal of pensioners’ grievances, which are not uniform and
compatible with each other. The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ welfare has, accordingly,
taken up a proposal for putting in place a “Pensioners Portal” which would adopt a uniform system
by harnessing IT resources.
4.1 The Committee is pleased to note that a good proposal has been initiated for the
guidance and welfare of the pensioners. The Committee recommends that the Ministry
should ensure that the proposal is implemented in a meaningful, effective and responsive
manner.
Information and Facilitation Counters
5.0 It has been stated in the Annual Report of the Ministry that computerised Information and
Facilitation Counters (IFCs) have been set up to provide information and assistance to the public
regarding the programmes and procedures of the concerned organisations as well as
acknowledgment and status report of the individual applications and grievances. Evaluation studies
of these IFCs are undertaken at random basis for suggesting further improvement in their
functioning.
5.1 The Secretary, Ministry of Personnel deposed before the Committee as follows:
“...Information for citizens is an important aspect of democratic functioning of the
Government and, Sir, in order to achieve this, we have been instrumental in getting
Information and Facilitation Counters set up in different Central Government Ministries and
Departments. And, so far, till the end of last year, 106 such facilitation counters were set
up in various Ministries in the Government of India...’’
5.2 The Committee appreciates this initiative of the Ministry and is of the opinion that
the suggestions made after completing the evaluation studies of these Information and
Facilitation Counters should be implemented in totality and should not remain confined to
paper alone.
Civil Services Reforms
6.0 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry, the UPSC on the 19th July, 2000 had constituted
the Yoginder Kumar Alagh Committee to review the existing scheme of the Civil Services
Examination. The said Committee has since submitted its report and its recommendations are under
Government’s examination.

10
6.1 The reply of the Ministry regarding the action taken so far on implementation of the
recommendations of the Alagh Committee is as follows:—
“(i) The salient points/recommendations of the Committee inter alia pertain to the eligibility
parameters of candidates appearing for Civil Services, schemes of Preliminary and
Main Examinations, Personality Test, allocation of Services and post-induction issues
of training and management of services.
(ii) The Government has set up an Administrative Reforms Commission to prepare a
detailed blue print for revamping the public administration System. The Commission,
while finalizing its recommendations, shall take into account the recommendations
made in the past by various Committees including the Alagh Committee.”
6.2 The Committee takes a serious note that the reply is not in consonance with the
Committee’s observation as contained in its 5th Report (page No. 43, para 3.41) that the
appointment of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission should not come in the way
of implementation of the recommendations made by various Committees in the past. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier considered view that the recommendations of
the Alagh Committee should be examined and implemented expeditiously; otherwise it will
be a callous wastage of public money, time and energy of the Committee which had worked,
hard to make recommendations as per its mandate.
Citizen’s Charter
7.0 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry, the Citizen’s Charter initiative was started by
Government of India in the year 1996-97. In the Chief Ministers’ conference held in May 1997,
it was decided that Central Government and State Governments would formulate Citizen’s Charters
starting with those organisations which have a large public interface.
7.1 As on 30th November 2005, 30 Ministries/Departments have brought out 111 Citizen’s
Charters and 24 State Governments/UT Administrations have brought out 656 Citizen’s Charters.
7.2 The Ministry has furnished the following reply regarding the present status of its
implementation:—
“(i) The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, being the nodal
Department for the Citizen’s Charter initiative is constantly pursuing with Central
Government Ministries/Departments/Organizations and State Government/UT
Administrations regarding formulation and implementation of the Citizen’s Charters. The
Central Government Ministries/Departments and State Governments/UT Administrations
are regularly impressed upon to formulate Citizen’s Charters in case of Departments/
Organizations where no Citizen’s Charter has been formulated so far. A Core Group
under the Chairmanship of the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions with the Secretary, Department of Consumer Affairs; the Principal Information
Officer and the Director General of National Informatics Centre (NIC) as Members and
the Additional Secretary, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances
(DARPG) as Member-Secretary is functioning in the Government of India to examine
and review the Citizen’s Charters of Central Government Ministries/Departments/
Organizations. Till date, 111 Charters of Central Government Ministries/Departments/
Organisations have been formulated and reviewed. Similarly 656 Charters of State
Governments/Union Territory Administrations have been formulated.
(ii) The Department shall continue its efforts in persuading/motivating Central Government
Ministries/Departments and State Governments/UT Administration in this direction.”

11
7.3 While deposing before the Committee, the Secretary stated as follows:
‘‘...One of the major initiatives, which have been taken by the Ministry, is to finalise the
Citizen’s Charter initiative. And this will result in ‘charter mark’ to be given to various
Ministries. They would agree to certain standards of delivery of services to the citizens, and
after this has been vetted and agreed to, we shall be awarding the ‘charter mark’ to them.
We are almost in the final stages. Towards the end of the last month, we had discussions
with various NGOs and Civil Society representatives on  this. Now, we are finalizing the
various components of  the ‘charter mark’. Once it is finalized, the process of awarding the
‘charter mark’ to various agencies and departments and offices of the Government of India
will be beginning...”
7.4 The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry to implement the
Citizen’s Charters. However, the Committee is of the considered view that all Ministries/
Departments/Organisations should be impressed upon to expedite formulation of their
Citizen’s Charters. The Ministry should continue to persuade/motivate the defaulters in this
regard. The Ministry should accelerate the process of finalizing the various components of
the Charter Mark.
7.5 The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has acted upon the
recommendations as contained in its 5th Report that publicity should be given to Citizen’s
Charter via. electronic media also. The Committee is of the opinion that this would create
better awareness among the general public.
7.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure that the feedback on
the implementation of the Charters is furnished by the respective Ministries/Departments/
Organisations. The implementation of Citizen’s Charter must also be reviewed in a
systematic manner and necessary steps should be taken to rectify the drawbacks, if any.
7.7 The Committee also observes that a proposal has been mooted for  institution of  an award
titled ‘Prime Minister’s Award for Excellence in Public Administration’ in recognition of meritorious
service and outstanding contributions made by the civil servants.
7.8 The Committee expects that such initiatives would serve as incentives to civil servants
in the pursuit of excellence in developing and maintaining high quality public services.
Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism
8.0 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry, detailed policy guidelines have been formulated
by the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances for redressal of grievances by
the Ministries and Departments of Government of India and while selecting grievances/complaints
for monitoring, the Department keeps in view the gravity and nature of the grievances as well as
the frequency of similar grievances arising in any particular field of work of the Government
Departments.
8.1 The Ministry has stated that a mechanism of ‘Fast Track’ is also in place. Complaints of
a serious nature as forwarded by the Prime Minister’s Office, Member of Parliament/Member of
Legislative Assembly, references and complaints received by Ministry of State (Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions) and Secretary (Personnel) and about 30% of the serious complaints
received in the Department are put on Fast Track. The cases are pursued intensively with regular
interventions at the highest level for speedy redressal.
8.2 The uniform software called Public Grievances Redress and Monitoring System (PGRAMS)
developed by the National Informatics Centre has been installed in a number of Ministries/
Departments/Organisations.

12
8.3 In response to a query regarding the PGRAMS, the Ministry has given the following
reply:
“(i) The Department is endeavouring to further improve the system and a Centralized Web
enabled PGRAMS module has been developed and is being installed to facilitate the
Public Grievances Officers of various Ministries/Departments/Organisations to log in
and view the grievances forwarded by Department of Administrative Reforms and
Public Grievances to the concerned Ministries for expeditious redressal.
(ii) Reports are generated periodically from the System to indicate the grievance prone
areas of different Ministries and Departments of Government of India.
(iii) An annual advertisement is issued in all national dailies and other newspapers
covering the entire country for wide publicity of the name and address of the public
grievance redress officers of different Ministries and Departments of Government of
India.”
8.4 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensure to install PGRAMS
software in all Ministries/Departments/Organisations so that the grievances of the public
are redressed quickly and efficiently and public grievance redress officers should be
appointed and notified in all the Departments and Ministries. The Committee further
desires that the Ministry should ensure that follow-up action is taken by the officers
promptly and effectively.
8.5 In response to a written query, the Committee has been informed that a Standing Committee
of Secretaries for Grievances Redress headed by the Cabinet Secretary was constituted in 1998 to
consider proposals for systemic reforms and grievances redressal in respect of Central Government
with public interface. The Committee, which has been meeting at regular intervals to conduct the
reviews, has so far reviewed 30 and re-reviewed 12 Ministries/Departments of Government of
India.
8.6 The Committee notes that only Report from the Ministry of External Affairs
(Passport Division), which was re-reviewed on July 1, 2005 by the Standing Committee of
Secretaries for Grievances Redress, has been received so far. The Committee recommends
that the review of the Public Grievances Redress Mechanism in the remaining Ministries/
Departments should be completed expeditiously and that Ministry should ensure that the
other Ministries/Departments submit their compliance reports well in time.
8.7 As per the reply of the Ministry, the Department of Administrative Reforms and
Public Grievances has been taking up studies to examine the Public Grievances Redress Mechanism
in the States/Union Territories and that the study in the State of Uttar Pradesh was completed
in 2005.
8.8 The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that it should ensure that
the recommendations made by the Department, after such studies, are duly implemented so
that its endeavour would become fruitful. The Committee recommends that such studies
should be carried out in the other States also. The Committee is of the opinion that the
Ministry should evolve a mechanism so that the public is kept informed about such studies
and findings thereof by way of publication in the Gazette of India or laying the same in the
form of a statement in both the Houses of Parliament periodically.
8.9 The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the local languages should
be used extensively to disseminate information regarding Public Grievances Redressal
Mechanism amongst the public in line with the various recommendations of the Commission
on Linguistic Minorities of Government of India.

Good Governance
9.0 According to the Annual Report of the Ministry, a day-long Conference of Chief Secretaries
was held on 2.11.2004 under the Chairmanship of Cabinet Secretary focusing on good governance,
administrative reforms and related issues and the Government had agreed to have a Model Code
of Governance which would enshrine the fundamental principles and would look at governance
from the point of view of the citizens and outline the framework for good governance, based on
identifiable benchmarks for comparison and evaluation, which can be a model for States to follow.
Accordingly, a Model Code of Governance, which is in the form of a road-map for the
administration was finalized and sent to all Chief Secretaries of States/UTs on 14.4.2005. The main
components of the Model Code covers action points under the heads (i) Improving Service
Delivery, (ii) Development of Programmes for Weaker Sections and Backward Areas,
(iii) Technology and System Improvement, (iv) Financial Management and Budget Sanctity,
(v) Accountability and Transparency, (vi) Public Service Morale and Anti-Corruption Measures and
(vii) Incentivising Reforms.
9.1 The Secretary, while deposing before the Committee, stated as follows:
“....We took two more initiatives to further the cause of good governance. With this aim
in view, a meeting of the Chief Secretaries was held in November 2004, where it was
decided that a model code of governance would be drawn up. And, the model code of
governance, which is in the form of roadmap for the administration, has been finalized and
sent to various Chief Secretaries...”
9.2 In its reply furnished to the Committee, the Ministry has stated as follows:
“(i) While forwarding the Model Code of Governance to the States/UTs, it was mentioned
that a number of its recommendations might have already been implemented in some
form or the other by the State Governments. It was further mentioned that the Model
Code had attempted to systematize all those in the form of a road-map for the
administration and could be a guide as well as a reference point. It was expected that
the Code could lead to the evolution of a common approach to governance issues all
over the country.
(ii) Government of Andhra Pradesh acknowledged the above position and stated that it
would take specific action in certain areas mentioned in the Model Code. Government
of Nagaland has constituted a Committee to chalk out a plan of action on good
governance. Governance is a detailed and comprehensive action plan and would lead
to the evolution of a common approach to governance issues all over the country.
Other States have also responded positively confirming their agreement with the basic
ideas in the model code. Implementation of the code will be an ongoing process in
which the Government, citizens and other stakeholders have all to participate.”
9.3 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should prevail upon all the State
Governments/Union Territory Administrations to chalk out a plan of action on good
governance and implement the same at the earliest.

10.1 In its reply furnished to the Committee, the Ministry has stated as follows:

10.2 The Committee is happy to note that the Second Administrative Reforms

10.3 The Members of the Committee expressed doubts regarding the setting apart of Rs. 2

10.4 In the reply furnished by the Ministry, it is stated as follows:
“The proposed allocation of Rs.2 crores towards foreign visits by the Commission to study

Backlog of vacancies
14.0 The Committee takes serious view of the backlog of vacancies in the various
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government. The Committee is of the opinion that
this would adversely affect the efficiency of the Government.
14.1 The Committee, therefore, recommends that in this era of globalisation, modern
management methods should be adopted. The Ministry should issue guidelines to the
various Ministries/ Departments so that the vacancies are anticipated at least one year in
advance and steps are taken to recruit new personnel to fill up the vacancies expeditiously,

vacancies in various Departments as on June, 2006.
United Nation’s Convention Against Corruption
15.0 The Secretary apprised the Committee as follows:
“...An important Convention, which we have signed recently, in December, 2005, in order
to fight the menace of corruption, is the United Nation’s Convention Against Corruption.
The Government of India became a signatory to this Convention on 9th December, 2005.
This Convention covers the basic formulation and implementation of effective anti-
corruption policies, practices and constitution of, within the national Governance, preventive
anti-corruption bodies, public access to information about various activities of the
Government and instituting a regulatory and supervisory regime for financial institutions in
order to tackle money laundering and other financial malpractices. So, we signed the
Convention on 9th December, 2005. As a result, we have to make various changes in our
own infrastructure relating to fighting corruption and make certain changes in our own
domestic rules and laws. We have written to the various Ministries of the Government of

recommends that the provisions of the Convention should be implemented whole heartedly
in a time bound manner.
Reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes
16.0 Clause (4) of Article 16 of the Constitution of India enables the State to make provisions

17
for reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the
opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State. Clause (4A) of
the same Article enables the State to provide reservation for the members of the Scheduled Castes
and Scheduled Tribes in the matter of promotion. Article 335 declares that the claims of the
members of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes shall be taken into consideration,
consistent with the maintenance of efficiency of administration in the making of appointments to
services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State. Proviso to the said
Article empowers the State to make any provision in favour of the members of the Scheduled
Castes and Scheduled Tribes for relaxation in qualifying marks in any examination or lowering the
Standard of evaluation, for reservation in matters of promotion to any class or classes of services
or posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State.
16.1 As per the Annual Report of the Ministry, armed with powers given by these provisions of
the Constitution, the Government has issued various instructions providing for reservation in
services for the members of the Scheduled Castes (SCs), the Scheduled Tribes (STs) and the Other
Backward Classes (OBCs).
16.2 The Secretary deposed before the Committee on this issue as follows:
“...Then, Sir, you had mentioned about the Scheduled Tribes and the Scheduled Castes and
Other Backward Classes reservation. You may be aware that there is already a Bill in
Parliament. The Parliamentary Committee attached to our Ministry had made detailed
comments on this Bill. In the light of that, the Government of India had decided to
Constitute a Group of Ministers, and the matter is now before the Group of Ministers. Sir,
we are also enquiring about the steps taken by the Government of India and the various
Ministries to fill up the backlog vacancies. We have had a very detailed exercise on this.
In fact, our Minister of State has taken personal initiative in the matter. He has had a series
of meetings with various Ministries — first, to identify the detailed number of vacancies
which are the backlog vacancies; then, to take concerted steps to fill up those backlog
vacancies. I can’t say that the target that we have put up that all the vacancies would be
filled up within the given timeframe. But there has been significant improvement in this
regard. Over 50 per cent of the backlog vacancies have been filled up. The drive was
extended up to March, 2006. So, we are trying to find out the latest position. Almost on
a weekly basis, we are monitoring the situation. We are trying to overcome the problem that
might be there in filling up the backlog vacancies...”
16.3 The Committee is of the opinion that since this is a Constitutional obligation, the
Ministry should adopt concerted efforts to fulfill the same. The Committee feels that there
is already a system in the Ministry by which the SCs, STs and OBCs vacancies should be
anticipated well in advance and recruitment process has to begin in advance, so that all the
vacancies are filled up as soon as they arise. The Committee recommends that the backlog
of vacancies should be cleared without any further delay through special recruitment
drives and other means. The Committee also desires to be apprised of the latest position
regarding existing vacancies in the SC, ST and OBC categories in various Departments as
on June, 2006.
