CHAPTER–III
RECRUITMENT AGENCIES
17.0 The Union Public Service Commission and the Staff Selection Commission are the two
designated recruitment agencies of the Central Government. The UPSC makes recruitment for
Group A services/posts and Group ‘B’ gazetted posts in Ministries/Departments etc. SSC makes
recruitment for non-gazetted posts in Ministries/Departments and their attached and subordinate
offices, carrying the pay scale of Rs. 6500-10,500 and non-technical Group ‘C’ posts. While the
UPSC is a Constitutional body set up under Article 315 of the Constitution, the SSC has been set
up by a Resolution of the Government and has the status of an attached office of the Department
of Personnel and Training.
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
18.0 The UPSC comprises of a Chairman and ten Members. The functions of the Commission
are as specified in Article 320 of the Constitution. The functions of the Commission prescribed in
Article 320 of the Constitution, inter alia , are:
(a) Recruitment for all civil services and civil posts by
(i) written examination with or without a viva voce examination or interview to
supplement them;
(ii) interview;
(iii) promotion.
(b) Advising Government on disciplinary matters relating to Government servants holding
civil posts.
So far as the working of the Commission is concerned, Article 323 of the Constitution
provides for submission of Annual Report on the working of the Commission and its laying before
the Parliament.
18.1 The Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, while considering the
Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and the UPSC
for the year 2006-07 requested the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions to ask the representatives of UPSC and concerned Officer of the Ministry not below the
rank of Joint Secretary to appear before the Committee to express their views on the Demands for
Grants of UPSC which was under consideration with the Committee. In a letter to the Rajya Sabha
Secretariat, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions conveyed the views of the
UPSC as follows:
“The undersigned is directed to refer to Rajya Sabha Secretariat Letters No. RS.3/1/2006-
P&L dated 21.3.2006 and 3.4.2006 and to say that while the Director (CBI) and Secretary
(SSC) will be making the presentation as scheduled, the UPSC has intimated vide their letter
No. 31.3.2005-A/cs-III dated 23rd March, 2006 that as per Article-322 and Article 113 of
the Constitution of India, expenses of Public Service Commission shall be charged on the
Consolidated Fund of India. The functions of the Commission are different from those of
other Ministry or Department. UPSC has a Constitutional Status as per Articles 315-323 of
18

19
the Constitution. All major decisions in the Commission are taken by the full Commission.
In the past the questions received from Standing Committees have been replied to after due
consideration of the Commission. Secretary, UPSC or any other functionary cannot take a
decision or reply to queries of Parliamentary Committee without approval and without
deliberation of the Commission. Any query by the Parliamentary Committee may be
forwarded to the Commission so that the Commission may deliberate and an appropriate
reply may be furnished.’’
18.2 As per Rule 84 of the Rules Of Procedure and Conduct Of Business In Rajya Sabha, a
Select Committee shall have power to require the attendance of persons or the production of papers
or records if such a course is considered necessary for the discharge of its duties and that if any
question arises whether the evidence of a person or the production of a document is relevant for
the purposes of the Committee, the question shall be referred to the Chairman whose decision shall
be final. As such, a Committee can take evidence of the experts, public bodies, associations,
individuals or interested parties. Rule 270 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in
Rajya Sabha states as follows:
Each of the Standing Committees shall have the following functions, namely:—
(a) to consider the Demands for Grants of the related Ministries/Departments and report
thereon. The report shall not suggest anything of the nature of cut motions;
(b) to examine Bills, pertaining to the related Ministries/Departments, referred to the
Committee by the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, and report thereon;
(c) to consider the annual reports of the Ministries/Departments and report thereon; and
(d) to consider national basic long term policy documents presented to the Houses, if
referred to the Committee by the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, and
report thereon:
Provided that the Standing Committees shall not consider matters of day-to-day
administration of the related Ministries/Departments.
18.3 There is no doubt about the Constitutional status of the UPSC. Under Article 323 of the
Constitution, the UPSC presents its Annual Reports to the President as to the work done by the
Commission, who in turn causes a copy thereof to be laid before each House of the Parliament.
Such reports are also debated in the Parliament from time to time. On the 22nd of December, 1954
the Rajya Sabha discussed the Annual Reports of the UPSC for the years 1951-52 and 1952-53.
18.4 Again on the 16th March, 1956 the House discussed the Annual Reports of the UPSC for
the years 1953-54 and 1954-55. The then Deputy Chairman had ruled that the discussions on the
motion would be restricted to criticism of the Government for any acts or omissions in the
exercise of their functions under the Constitution in relation to the UPSC and all criticisms of the
actions of the Commission or of its members will have to be avoided.
18.5 It is pertinent to note that the Committee on Subordinate Legislation of the Rajya Sabha had
examined the Union Public Service Commission (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958.
The Estimates Committee of the Lok Sabha examined the working of the UPSC in 1967-68. In the
introduction chapter of the 47th Report of that Committee on the subject, as well as in the Minutes
of its meetings held on 24th and 25th October, 1967, it has been stated that the Committee had
taken oral evidence of the then Chairman as well as the Secretary, UPSC.
18.6 Further, the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, while
drafting its 20th Report on the Working of the UPSC, heard the representatives of the UPSC on
the subject, in its sitting held on the 11th February, 1994. In its sitting held on the 26th May, 1994,

20
the Committee further discussed the subject and sought clarifications from the representatives of
the UPSC. Further the Committee, in its sitting held on 19th July, 1994 sought, clarifications from
the representatives of the UPSC. The Committee on Home Affairs in its 20th Report had inter alia
observed that “the UPSC has been impressing upon the Government to treat the Commission as
a Ministry for financial purposes and to delegate the financial powers accordingly. In other words,
it favours the financial autonomy as enjoyed by other Constitutional bodies, namely, the Election
Commission and the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India...The Committee has also been
informed by UPSC that in this regard UPSC is treated as an Attached/Subordinate Office of the
Department of Personnel and Training in the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
resulting in a situation when the UPSC is sometimes constrained to take decisions which are not
compatible with its Constitutional position.”
18.7 The Committee on Home Affairs had, therefore, made the following recommendation: “The
Committee finds no reason whatsoever for discrimination of the UPSC with other Constitutional
bodies, namely the Election Commission and the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India in
financial matters and feels that in this respect UPSC should enjoy the same status as other
Constitutional bodies.”
18.8 Regarding monitoring agency for UPSC, the Committee on Home Affairs had observed as
under: “A suggestion was mooted that there should be an independent body to critically examine,
scrutinize, monitor and supervise the functioning of the UPSC and to deal with all complaints and
representations against it as the present arrangement authorizing the UPSC to examine its own
failures may lead to inefficiency and miscarriage of Justice. The Committee having considered all
aspects of the suggestions found it to be impracticable. The UPSC is a Constitutional body and
in the scheme of the Constitution relating to UPSC there is no provision for an independent body
to examine and monitor its functioning. However, under Article 323, the Commission is required
to present annually to the President a Report as to the ‘Work done by it and the President causes
a copy of the Report to be laid before each House of Parliament, thus providing ample scope for
thorough discussion of the Commission’s functioning by Parliament. The Parliament through the
discussion can also make suitable observations.”
18.9 Taking into account the facts mentioned in the preceding paragraphs, the Committee
notes that by granting Constitutional status to certain bodies/organisations, the Constitution
of India has not deprived the Parliamentary body of examining/scrutinizing its working/
functioning within the permissible “limits particularly when such examination is in the
larger interest of that Constitutional body. The Committee desires to convey its view that
it regards and sanctifies the status of UPSC as a Constitutional body, but at the same time
it can hardly satisfy itself with this contention as is being interpreted in their own manner.
18.10 The Committee notes that the refusal of UPSC for sending representative of its Secretariat
to appear before the Committee amounts to shirking of its accountability to public through
Parliament. Both the Houses of Parliament are represented in the Committee which is known as a
mini Parliament. Had they attended the meeting of the Committee, they would have been able to
narrate/justify the Demands for Grants and activities described in the Annual Report submitted to
the Parliament for discussion.
18.11 The Committee is not at all convinced with the contention of the UPSC Secretariat
regarding its accountability to the Parliament. The Committee urges that the Annual
Reports of the UPSC are placed before both the Houses of Parliament for discussions and
takes cognizance of the fact that the Minister as an executive head of Government, on
behalf of the UPSC, answers the Questions in both the Houses. In view of the foregoing,
the Committee is of the view that as per the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business
in the Rajya Sabha, the Committee is well within its powers and jurisdiction to examine the

21
Budget of the Commission. Moreover, the representatives of the UPSC Secretariat could
have made a presentation in respect of its Demand for Grants and respond to the queries
if any, of the Committee in respect of the activities as mentioned in their Annual Report.
The Committee is, therefore, unable to examine the Demands for Grants of UPSC due to
the wilful avoidance of the Secretariat of UPSC, which avoidance ipso facto is against public
probity and contravenes Constitutional norms.
18.12 This Committee finally observes that the Demands for Grants of a particular financial
year of a Constitutional body can be examined in a better and effective manner if
representatives of the Secretariat of that Body depose before the Committee to throw light
on the areas/operations which may need more finances. Ultimately, scrutiny of Demands for
Grants in the presence of the representatives of UPSC Secretariat would help it in the long
run to make an assessment and evaluation of its fund starved plans/polices/programmes.
18.13 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should deliberate on the
issue with all sincerity at an appropriate level and take corrective measures to restore its
accountability towards people through Parliament.
STAFF SELECTION COMMISSION
19.0 As per Article 320 of the Constitution, the examinations for recruitment to all the posts and
services of the Union Government are to be conducted by the UPSC. As per recommendations of
the Estimates Committee (1967-68) of the Lok Sabha regarding setting up a separate Service
Selection Commission for taking over from UPSC, examination for recruitment to lower category
of posts, the Government made an interim measure by creating an examination wing under ISTM.
Finally on 26th September, 1977 a separate Commission SSC came into being. Later on, pursuant
to the recommendation of Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs
(20th Report) wherein the Government was requested to identify more areas where consultation
with UPSC could be dispensed with so as to decrease the work load of UPSC, certain
modifications were made in the UPSC (Exemptions from Consultation) Regulations, 1958 so as to
transfer some more areas from UPSC to SSC.
19.1 The S taff Selection Commission has been entrusted with the duty to make recruitment to
Group ‘C’ (non-technical) and Group ‘B’ (non-gazetted-both technical and non-technical) posts in
various Ministries/Departments of Government of India, its attached and subordinate offices except
those for which recruitment is made by the Railway Recruitment Boards and Industrial
Establishments.
19.2 The Staff Selection Commission has nine Regional/Sub-Regional Offices in different parts
of the country. These Regional/Sub-Regional Offices are responsible for smooth and peaceful
conduct of the examinations. They provide administrative support to the Headquarters for
performing various activities involved in the smooth conduct of examinations, like receipt of
applications from the candidates, processing of these applications, data entry into computer and
then issue of Admit Cards (ACs) to the candidates for the examination, booking of venues at the
various centres in consultation with the District Authorities, sending of examination material (other
than centrally dispatched Test Papers) to the Centre Supervisors, appointment of invigilators and
Inspecting Officers at various examination centres. Further, Regional Offices are also responsible
for holding the interviews/Physical Endurance Test (PETs), wherever required, either at the
Regional Headquarters or at other major cities within the respective regions.
19.3 The Regional Offices are also responsible to contact the various Government of India
offices located in the States of their jurisdiction and collect the vacancies from these departments.
These vacancies are collected and intimated by the Regional Offices to the SSC Hqrs.

22
19.4 After declaration of the result by the SSC Hqrs., the Regional Offices are required to
allocate the candidates to the user departments as per their requirement intimated to the Regional
Offices earlier. The policy decisions taken by the SSC Hqrs, which govern the recruitment/selection
are implemented by the Regional Offices in totality.
19.5 During the meeting of the Committee, the Members observed as follows:
“...the entire functioning of your organisation should be decentralized and given to
respective heads of department. Whether evaluation of your organisation has been done in
respect of its utility, its functionality and also whether it continues as it is. These are three
or four aspects in which comprehensive report has to be made about its existence and
continuance.......by decentralisation some purpose could be served...”
19.6 When asked about the number of persons recruited last year by SSC, the Secretary of the
Commission replied that they had recruited 3869 persons as on 31st March, 2005 through open
examination and 104 persons after selection. When enquired about the time taken to recruit
persons, the Secretary replied that it is done within one year.
19.7 The Committee feels that as far as reservation for SCs, STs and OBCs candidates
are concerned, the organisation has not met the required standards.
19.8 The Committee, notes that the BE for the year 2006-07 is Rs.6.91 crore under the
head salaries and that for professional services is Rs.15 crore. The Secretary had deposed
before the Committee that they had recruited about 4000 candidates in the last year. The
Committee feels that the allotment of such huge resources is not commensurate with the
recruitment of such less number of candidates.
19.9 The Committee is of the opinion that the long process of recruitment process leads
to a backlog of vacancies. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the recruitment
process in respect of lower posts should be delegated to the respective Departments wherein
vacancies arise. This may be viewed in the backdrop of SSC outsourcing major portion of
its recruitment process. The Committee feels that outsourcing can be done by the respective
Departments rather than incurring huge expenditure by SSC for recruitment of such less
number of candidates. The Committee is of the view that the respective Departments can
call for data from the employment exchanges from all regions throughout India, when
vacancies arise. This will ensure that the rural population derives maximum benefit out of
the recruitment process. So far as the recruitment for posts of superior grades being
handled by SSC is concerned, UPSC has sufficient infrastructure and expertise therefor.
19.10 Now since no yearly examinations to various grades are being held by SSC as were
being held in the past and very lesser number of recruitments are being recommended by
SSC, the Committee feels that it is high time for the Ministry to consider the winding up
of SSC in the public interest, efficiency and economy.
19.11 The Committee is also seized of the fact that out of the total 507 staff in SSC, 280
are ministerial staff and 4 are from the Department of Official Language. Only 223 staff
are from SSC cadre.
19.12 The Committee is of the opinion that if it is decided to wind up the SSC, the
ministerial staff can be repatriated to their respective Departments and out of the staff of
SSC cadre, those who are well conversant with the conduct of examinations may be
absorbed in UPSC and the rest of the staff may be absorbed in other Departments of the
Government of India.

23
CHAPTER–IV
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
20.0 The CBI came into existence in the year 1941 with a rather limited role and responsibility
to investigate offences of bribery and corruption connected with transactions relating to War and
Supply Department, Government of India. Over the last 64 years, the organisation has evolved
from an anti-corruption agency to a multi-faceted, multi-disciplinary Central police-law enforcement
agency with capability, credibility and legal mandate to investigate and prosecute offences anywhere
in India. At present, CBI has the following Divisions:
(1) Anti Corruption Division;
(2) Economic Offences Division;
(3) Special Crimes Division;
(4) Directorate of Prosecution;
(5) Administration Division;
(6) Policy and Coordination Division; and
(7) Central Forensic Science Laboratory.
20.1 The CBI derives the power to investigate from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act,
1946 (DSPE). As per section 2 of the Act, DSPE has jurisdiction to investigate offences in the
Union Territories only. However, the jurisdiction can be extended by the Central Government to
other areas including Railway areas and States under section 5(1) of the Act, provided the State
Governments have accorded consent under section 6 of the Act.
20.2 During the discussion on Demands for Grants (2006-07) of the Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions; the Director, CBI made a brief presentation before the Committee.
He narrated the mission and functions of CBI and the problems existing in the organisation.
20.3 In the reply furnished by the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, it has
been stated that a consolidated Plan Document for modernization of CBI is awaited from the CBI.
Their proposal is likely to include:
(i) Purchase of latest gadgetry like laptops, cellular phones, digital video cameras.
(ii) Purchase of vehicles.
(iii) Construction of 2nd phase of CBI Academy.
(iv) Replacement of existing distributed database architecture with central database.
20.4 The Committee is pleased to note that the recommendation as contained in its 5th
Report regarding the modernization of CBI has been seriously considered. The Committee
hopes that the consolidated plan document for modernization of CBI, which is awaited,
would be prepared and implemented at the earliest. The Committee commended the working
of CBI but were also of the opinion that much more needs to be done regarding
modernization in terms of investigation, interrogation and training.
23

24
20.5 The Committee notes that though funds to the tune of Rs.1.25 crores was allocated
for modernization of Training Centre in the RE 2005-06, an expenditure of Rs.8,87,000 only
has been incurred so far. The Committee feels that there has been under utilization of
funds and recommends that in future the funds should be utilised optimally.
20.6 As per the reply furnished by the Ministry, the total sanctioned strength of CBI as on
31.12.2005 was 5891. However, the actual manpower available was 4711 and as many as 1180
posts were lying vacant at the end of the year. These vacancies were mainly in the ranks of
Sr. Supdt. Of Police-8, Supdt. of Police-17, Addl. Supdt. of Police-13, Dy. Supdt. of Police-95,
Inspectors-174, Sub. Inspectors-130+ 14, Asstt. Sub Inspector-23, Head Constables-42,
Constables-134+95. Besides there were vacancies of 81 Law Officers at various levels. 95
Technical posts were also lying vacant.
20.7. The Committee takes the prevailing vacancies in the CBI as a disturbing
phenomenon and feels that if this trend continues, there could be serious repercussions in
the functioning of the CBI. The Committee notes with grave concern the factors responsible
for decline in quality and pace of investigation such as shortage of investigating officers and
27 to 40% of vacancies in the prosecuting staff. The Committee feels that the existence of
vacancies especially in the deputationist cadre, affects the effective functioning of the
premier investigating agency. The Committee also notes that on one hand, while the
deputation vacancies in CBI are allowed to remain unfilled for quite a long time, on the
other hand, the cadre officers of CBI, who  are quite eligible from the professional point of
view, but ineligible on the basis of service conditions, are not given the opportunity for
promotion. The Committee is afraid that this trend may result in frustration and hatred
among cadre officials against the deputationists and thus affect the over-all performance of
the investigating agency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in the event of
vacancies not being filled in the deputationist cadre, steps should be taken to fill up those
vacancies by seeking recruitment from the permanent cadre of CBI. The Committee
strongly recommends that in any case, the vacancies in CBI should be filled up at the
earliest, but in any case not later than 31st December, 2006.
20.8 The Committee had, in its 5th Report, recommended that a separate Act has to be
promulgated for CBI in tune with the requirements of the time to ensure credibility and impartiality.
20.9 The Committee regrets to note that no proactive steps have been taken in this
regard. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry should
consider bringing forward a separate enactment for CBI rather than deriving powers from
the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946 for its smooth functioning.
20.10 The Committee had also recommended in its previous Report that CBI should be
empowered by a suitable legislation to investigate all the offences under the Central laws like
Prevention of Corruption Act, the Income Tax Act, the Central Customs and Excise Act etc. in any
part of the country after obtaining the concurrence of the Central Government; but things have not
moved in this direction.
20.11 The Committee, therefore once again reiterates its earlier recommendation that CBI
should be empowered by a suitable legislation to investigate all the offences under the
Central laws in any part of the country after obtaining concurrence of the Central
Government.
20.12 The Committee, in its 5th Report, had recommended enhancement of financial powers of
CBI. It had also suggested that an Internal Financial Advisor may be appointed to render advice
on financial matters in CBI since similar system is already functioning in Central Police
Organisations.

25
20.13 In the reply of the Ministry, it is stated that the proposal to enhance the delegation of
powers of Director, CBI and to appoint an Internal Financial Advisor was being examined.
20.14 The Committee is pleased to note that its recommendation that the financial powers
of Director should be enhanced and an Internal Financial Advisor (IFA) be appointed is
being considered. However, the Committee notes that the proposal must be implemented
without further delay, since it is imperative to ensure the functional independence of CBI.
20.15 The Director, CBI deposed before the Committee that the decline in conviction rates of CBI
is due to many factors such as investigating faults, witnesses turning hostile and prolonged trial.
He also deposed that the statistical data in reference of CBI are the best anywhere in the world
except Japan.
20.16 The Committee recommends that steps should be taken to arrest the decline in
conviction rate. The Committee is of the opinion that better training and orientation
imparted to the officers and staff would improve the functioning of CBI and result in higher
rate of conviction.
20.17 The Committee notes that the satisfaction level in respect of housing all over the CBI is
26.92% only. As per the reply furnished by the Ministry, CBI Head Office has asked various
branches to submit proposals for purchase of ready built flats to meet the requirement of residential
accommodation and to raise the minimum satisfaction level upto 60%.
20.18 The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the minimum satisfaction
level of housing should be 60%. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should
augment its efforts to improve the accommodation facilities extended to CBI personnel.
20.19 The Committee, in its 5th Report, had recommended that the Ministry should ensure that
the construction of CBI Head Quarters Building takes place within the stipulated period.
20.20 The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation that the Ministry
should ensure that construction of CBI Head Quarters Building takes place within the
stipulated period of three years.

26
CHAPTER–V
CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION AND KENDRIYA BHANDAR
KENDRIYA BHANDAR
21.0 The Central Government Employees Consumer Cooperative Society Ltd. operating in the
name of KENDRIYA BHANDAR, is a welfare project of Government of India, under the Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. It was set up in 1963 as a welfare project of the
Government for the benefit of Central Government employees, their families and other customers.
Its objectives are as follows:—
(a) Providing essential commodities of daily needs to the customers at reasonable prices,
representing assured standards of quality and value for money.
(b) To play an effective role in the public distribution system and to become a pace setter
in retail market.
(c) To assist the Government in holding the price line and ensure distribution of scarce
commodities at controlled prices.
(d) To create an attractive and congenial shopping environment for customers.
21.1 The Report of the Kendriya Bhandar for the year 2004-05 states that the new Multi State
Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 has come into force w.e.f. 19.08.2002 and accordingly new Bye-
laws of the Society have been framed in consonance with the provisions of Multi State Cooperative
Societies Act, 2002 and the rules made thereunder are in operation.
21.2 In 2003, the Kendriya Bhandar registered en-block amendments to its bye-laws under
Section 11  of the Multi State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002. As a result there were many
changes in the administrative structure of the Kendriya Bhandar. The recruitment rules for
appointment of Managing Director was revised to such extent that there was no need to appoint
a Joint Secretary of the Government of India to that post which existed till its registration under
the above mentioned Act.
21.3 In the reply furnished by the Ministry, it is stated that there are only three Government
nominees in the Board of Directors, out of a total strength of 13 and that the Government
therefore, does not have effective control on the day to day functioning of Kendriya Bhandar. It
is also stated that the Government holds 81.43% of the shares of Kendriya Bhandar.
21.4 It is understood that in December 2005, the Board of Directors of Kendriya Bhandar passed
the following resolution which is already pending with the Government for consideration:—
“(a)...the Government may be requested to amend the Multi State Co-operative Societies
Act, 2002 for incorporating a provision that Chairman, Board of Directors, Kendriya
Bhandar shall be nominated by the Central Government as in the past.
(b)...the Government may nominate a nominee of the level of Additional/Joint Secretary on
the Board of Kendriya Bhandar who will be unanimously elected as Chairman, Kendriya
Bhandar...”
26

27
21.5 The Committee fails to understand why the Ministry’s control in the Governing Body
of Kendriya Bhandar is negligible when it holds 81.43% of shares. Also, it is not clear
whether the Ministry’s nominees in the Board of Directors hold vital posts or whether they
do not play an active role. The Committee has no objection to the functional autonomy
granted to Kendriya Bhandar; but is of the opinion that there should be strict and efficient
monitoring by the Ministry on the financial activities of Kendriya Bhandar. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should look into the functioning of Kendriya
Bhandar so that it may not go the ‘Super Bazar’ way. The Committee also desires to take
up this issue separately after the receipt of action taken reply from the Government in the
matter.
21.6 The Ministry, in a written reply stated that with the withdrawal of special dispensation of
Kendriya Bhandar from the procedure of inviting tenders/quotations by the Ministry of Finance,
Kendriya Bhandar may become prone to machinations and that there would be uncertainity about
Kendriya Bhandar being able to obtain the supply orders.
21.7 The Committee is of the considered view that Kendriya Bhandar should upgrade
itself to compete with other players in tenders/quotations, rather than being apprehensive
of competition.
CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
22.0 The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was established in 1964, as an apex body for
exercising general superintendence and control over vigilance administration, through the
Government of India Resolution of 11.2.1964. The main mandate of the Commission was based
on the report of the Committee on Prevention of Corruption, popularly known as the Santhanam
Committee. The establishment of the Commission was considered essential for evolving and
applying common standards in deciding cases involving lack of probity and integrity in
administration.
22.1 The Resolution empowered the CVC to undertake inquiry into any transaction in which a
public servant is suspected or alleged to have acted for an improper purpose or in a corrupt
manner irrespective of his or her status. Through subsequent ordinances and legislations, the
Government has added to the functions and powers of the Commission. Subsequent to the
directions of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the judgement in the Writ Petition filed in public interest,
by Shri Vineet Narain and others in Jain Hawala Case, the Government promulgated an Ordinance
in 1998. The Ordinance of 1998 conferred statutory status to the CVC and the powers to exercise
superintendence over functioning of the Delhi Special Police Establishment, and also to review the
progress of the investigations perta ining to alleged offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act,
1988 conducted by them.
22.2 In 1998, the Government introduced the CVC Bill in the Lok Sabha in order to replace the
Ordinance, though it was not successful. The Bill was re-introduced in 1999 and remained with
the Parliament till September, 2003, when it became an Act after being duly passed in both the
Houses of Parliament and with the President’s assent. The provisions of the Act include inquiries
into offences alleged to have been committed by certain categories of public servants of the Central
Government; corporations established by or under any central Act; Government companies;
societies; and local authorities owned or controlled by the Central Government; and for matters
connected therewith or incidental thereto. To give effect to the provisions of the Act of 2003, the
Commission exercises all powers and functions entrusted to it under the Government of India
Resolution No.24/7/64-A VD dated 11.2.1964, which are not inconsistent with this Act.
22.3 Three years have passed since the enactment of CVC Act of 2003, and prevention of
corruption continues to be the prime concern of the country. Recently, in response to a Public

28
Interest Litigation which was filed in the Supreme Court on account of the murder of Satyendra
Dubey, the Supreme Court directed the Government to designate a suitable machinery to act on
complaints from “whistle blowers” till such time as a suitable legislation was enacted to that effect.
The Central Government while implementing the directive of the Supreme Court, has reposed its
faith on the CVC. Through a Resolution dated 21st April, 2004 the Government has designated the
Central Vigilance Commission as the agency to act on complaints from “whistle blowers” till such
time as the Parliament passes a law on the subject. According to the Government Resolution on
“Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informer”, 2004 the Commission has been entrusted
with the additional responsibility of keeping the identity of the complainant secret and the power
to take action against complainants making motivated or vexatious complaints. There is no
restriction on jurisdiction of the Commission in the said Resolution.
22.4 As per the reply of the Ministry, the recommendations of the CVC to make the vigilance
set up more effective in the Central PSUs and Government Departments by appointment of full time
CVOs in Departments/Ministries is under consideration of this Department. Views/comments of
various Ministries/Departments have since been obtained and the implications are being examined.
22.5 The Committee recommends that the recommendations of the CVC regarding better
vigilance mechanism should be implemented without further delay.
22.6 The Committee has taken a serious view that no reply has been furnished by the
Ministry on its query on the status of implementation of the suggestions of CVC regarding
unauthorised constructions in Delhi. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
suggestions should be examined and the outcome thereof be informed to the Committee,
along with the action Government proposes to take in the matter.

R E P O R T 
I. NOTARIES - AN OVERVIEW 
 
Historical Background 
 
1.0 1Notary, also called  a notary public, is a public official whose chief 
function in common-law countries is to authenticate contracts, deeds, and other 
documents by an appropriate certificate with a notarial  seal. In ancient times, 
notaries recorded matters of judicial importance and important private 
transactions or events where an official authenticated record was necessary or 
advisable.  
 
1.1 The profession of notaries in India is presen tly regulated by the Notaries 
Act, 1952, and the Notaries Rules, 1956. Before India's independence, the 
Master of Faculties in England appointed notaries in India to perform all 
recognized notarial functions. After India attained independence, it became 
necessary to empower the Central and State Governments to appoint notaries. 
Therefore, a bill on the subject was introduced in the Parliament on 19 th April 
1951, passed by both Houses of Parliament, and received the assent of the 
President. It came on the St atue Book as the Notaries Act, 1952 (53 of 1952) 
and came into force on 14.02.1956. Subsequently, in exercise of the powers 
conferred by section 15 of the Notaries Act, 1952, the Central Government 
made the Notaries Rules, 1956, to carry out the purpose of  the Notaries Act, 
1952. 
 
1.2 The Notaries Act is a Central Act but the subject "Legal Profession" falls 
in the Concurrent List of the Constitution. Hence, the Central and State 
Governments are administratively competent to appoint notaries.  
 
Relevance of Notaries under various other Legislation 
 
1.3 Besides the Notaries Act, 1952 role of notaries has been prescribed under 
some other legislation also. A list of such legislations is as under:

Key provisions of the Notaries Act, 1952 and the Notaries Rules, 1956 
 
Powers to appoint notaries 
 
1.4 Section 3 of the Notaries Act, 1952, vests in the Central Government the 
power to appoint any legal practitioners or persons who possess the prescribed 
qualifications as notaries for the whole or any part of India. Similarly, the said 
section also empowers the State Government to appoint notaries for the whole 
or any part of the State. The maximum number of notaries to be appointed by 
the Central and State Governments is specified in the Schedule of the Notaries 
Rules, 1956.  
 
Eligibility for appointment as a Notary 
 
1.5 Rule 3 of the Notaries Rules, 1956 prescribes eligibility criteria for 
appointment as a Notary. As per the said rule, the qualifications are as follows: 
 
(i) At least ten years of practice as an Advocate; or, 
(ii) At least seven years of practice as an Advocate for a person 
belonging to SC/ST and OBC, or, 
(iii) At least seven years of practice as an Advocate for a woman or, 

10 
 
(iv) A person who had been a member of the Indian Legal Service 
under the Central Government or, 
(v) A person who had been at least for ten year s - (i) a member of 
Judicial Service; or (ii) held an office under the Central 
Government or a State Government requiring special knowledge of 
law after enrolment as an advocate; or (iii) held an office in the 
department of Judge Advocate General (JAG) or the legal 
department of the armed forces. 
 
Duties performed by Notaries 
 
1.6 The functions of notaries are provided under section 8 of the Notaries 
Act, 1952, which are as follows: 
 
(i) verify, authenticate, certify, or attest the execution of any 
instrument; 
(ii) present any promissory note, hundi, or bill of exchange for 
acceptance or payment or demand better security; 
(iii) note or protest the dishonor by non -acceptance or non -payment of 
any promissory note, hundi, or bill of exchange or protest for better 
security or prepare acts of honor under the Negotiable Instruments 
Act, 1881 (XXVI of 1881), or serve notice of such note or protest; 
(iv) note and draw up ship's protest, boat's protest, or protest relating to 
demurrage and other commercial matters; 
(v) administer the oath to, or take affidavit from, any person; 
(vi) prepare bottomry and respondentia bonds, charter parties, and other 
mercantile documents; 
(vii) prepare, attest, or authenticate any instrument intended to take 
effect in any country or place outside India in such form and  
language as may conform to the law of the place where such deed 
is entitled to operate; 
(viii) translate, and verify the translation of any document from one 
language into another; 
(ix) act as a Commissioner to record evidence in any civil or criminal 
trial if so directed by any court or authority; 
(x) act as an arbitrator, mediator, or conciliator, if so required. 
 

11 
 
1.7 The Government has informed that as per annual returns received – 
notaries perform almost all the above functions, albeit in varying degrees. 
However, a s ignificant volume of their work is related to verifying or 
authenticating the execution of an instrument and administering oaths or taking 
affidavits from any person. 
 
Powers of the Central Government to make rules 
 
1.8 Section 15 of the Notaries Act vests in the Central Government's power 
to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act. In exercising this power, the 
Central Government has made the Notaries Rules, 1956. The said Rules provide 
for, among other things, q ualifications for appointment as a notary; form and 
manner of submission of application for appointment as a notary; process to be 
followed for appointment of a notary; extension of area of practice; fees to be 
paid for issue and renewal of certificate of practice and extension of area; fees 
payable to a notary for doing any notarial act; transaction of business by a 
notary; action on allegations of professional or other misconduct of a notary; 
etc. 
 
Procedure followed for appointment of central notaries 
 
1.9 The Government, in their submission before the Committee, has informed 
that presently, the following procedure is being followed for the appointment of 
central public notaries:  
 
(i) Receipt of online applications:  Online applications are invited from 
the candidates eligible for appointment as notaries on the Notary 
Online Application Portal (NOAP) at 
https://notary.legalaffairs.gov.in. 
 
(ii) Interview of the candidates:   The Interview Boards, constituted for 
the purpose under Rule 7A of the Notaries Rules, 1956, assess the 
suitability or otherwise of the candidates through interviews in terms 
of their personality, basic legal knowledge, awareness of the roles and 
functions expected of them as notaries.  
 

12 
 
(iii) Verification of documents:  To ascertain whether the candidate 
fulfills the eligibility criteria, the following documents of the 
applicants are verified – (i) High School/Class X Certificate; LLB 
Degree Certificate; Enrolment Certificate issued by the Bar C ouncil; 
Caste/Disability Certificate (wherever applicable); and Aadhar Card. 
 
(iv) Final selection :  Based on the Interview Boards' recommendation, 
candidates are selected for appointment as notaries. After completing 
all formalities, certificates of practice a re issued to the successful 
candidates. 
  
Period of validity of the Certificate of Practice 
 
1.10 Section 5 of the Notaries Act provides for issuing or renewing the 
certificate of practice to the notaries. Notaries may be entitled to practice for 
five years, which may be renewed for five years. There is no restriction on the 
number of times a notary can renew their certificate of practice.

II. VIEWS OF THE STAKEHOLDERS 
 
2.0 During the deliberations of the Committee, the Committee interacted with 
various stakeholders related to this subject, viz., the Department of Legal 
Affairs (Ministry of Law & Justice, Govt. of India)  on 05.04.2023 and 
23.08.2023, Bar Council of India (BCI)  on 27.07.2023 , and Notaries 
Associations on 15.09.2023 . The Committee a lso invited suggestions, in 
writing, from all the High Court Bar Associations. The gist of the views 
expressed by these stakeholders is as follows: 
 
Bar Council of India (BCI) 
 
▪ Lack of Transparency in Appointments: The appointment process should 
be made tr ansparent and accessible to all aspirants and applicants. This 
can be achieved by the prominent publication of the proposal recruiting 
notaries online and offline mode. There are complaints of nepotism and 
favouritism in the appointment process that should  be addressed 
appropriately. 
▪ Qualification Criteria and the Role of the Bar Council of India: The 
appointment criteria for notaries are reasonable, but involving the Bar 
Council of India is essential. The BCI regulates the legal profession, 
maintains ethical standards, and ensures the competence of advocates. By 
involving the BCI in the appointment process, the credibility and 
reliability of notaries can be strengthened, as it verifies candidates are 
duly enrolled advocates with good standing. 
▪ Inclusivity and Diversity: The Act should provide for inclusivity and 
diversity to enrich the notarial system and address the diverse legal needs. 
▪ Adherence to Section 85 of the Indian Evidence Act: BCI proposed a 
regulatory system for notaries that oversees and s creens their conduct as 
Notary in conformity with the provisions of the Notaries Act and rules 
and provisions contained in section 85 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 
and other provisions of law. 
▪ Technology Integration: Technological advancements in the le gal sector 
require notaries to handle electronic transactions, digital documents, and 
online notarization with proper training. 
 

14 
 
▪ Renewal Process and Periodic Review of Notaries: The Act should 
provide for notary license renewal after five years of performa nce 
evaluation to ensure that notaries maintain the required standards 
throughout their tenure. 
▪ Coordination with Bar Councils and Specialization: The BCI can foster 
coordination between Bar Councils and Notary authorities to ensure 
notaries possess adequate legal knowledge and stay up -to-date with legal 
developments. 
▪ Ethical Guidelines and Accountability: The Notaries Act should establish 
a comprehensive ethics code for notaries, with the BCI ensuring 
implementation and promoting accountability through regular publication 
and transparency. 
▪ Designated Areas Needed: There must be designated areas for the seats of 
Notaries in every Court Complex and other tribunals and Quasi -Judicial 
Forums. 
▪ Need for Regulatory Mechanism: A strict regulatory mechanism 
regarding the performance and activities of Notaries must be 
implemented to weed out malpractices, undesirable people, and 
objectionable activities happening in notary-related functions. 
 
Notaries Associations  
 
▪ The present system of appointment of notaries is 'ad  hoc', and it needs to 
be reformed. 
▪ Many notaries who are given the certificate of practice have experience 
as an advocate on paper only. Thus, the eligibility criteria should include 
having experience of 100 cases practiced in the court. 
▪ Appointment of notaries should be based on a written examination 
followed by an interview. There is a general perception that one can 
become a notary if they have some sort of influence. This image needs to 
be corrected. 
▪ Another significant issue is the in ordinate delay in renewing the 
certificate of practice. As notaries cannot practice without a certificate of 
practice, inordinate delay in renewal leads to loss of practice, income, and 
reputation. Thus, in case of delay in renewal of the certificate of pr actice 
beyond a specific time limit, they may be allowed to carry out their 
practice. 

15 
 
▪ The fees for notarial acts have not been revised for the past nine years. 
The present fees are not in tandem with the current rate of inflation. 
Accordingly, the fee should be revised regularly, and it should be in sync 
with the level of inflation. 
▪ Presently, the number of notaries sanctioned for different states is very 
low. It should be in accordance with the population/litigations in that 
area. 
▪ In appointment of Notarie s, all sections of society, including women and 
differently-abled people, should be given due representation in appointing 
notaries. 
▪ Every notarized document must bear the certificate number and 
corresponding entry in the ledger/register maintained by the public 
Notary. Also, records maintained by the notaries should be digitalized to 
avoid fraud, deceit, and tempering of records. 
▪ Those notaries who are not submitting the periodic report with the 
registrar should be suspended from practicing till submission of the report 
with acceptable reasons for delay. 
 
High Court Bar Association 
 
▪ The cap on the maximum number of notaries in the State should be 
reviewed/revisited in view of the burgeoning population and exponential 
growth of commercial activities in the S tate, creating a need for notarial 
services and the appointment of more notaries. 
▪ The existing fees/rates be reviewed/revised and enhanced in tune with the 
high cost of living and all-round escalation of prices. 
▪ Penal provisions in the rules should be made  to rein in those notaries 
charging excessive fees. 
▪ Renewal of the certificate of practice of notaries should be made 
automatic subject to being fit to perform duties entrusted by removing the 
discretionary powers given to the government. 
 
Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law & Justice, Govt. of India 
 
2.1 In their presentation before the Committee, the Department informed that 
the Notary Online Portal has been entirely revamped. Entire functions like 
appointment, renewal, extension/change of area, annual returns, etc., are being

brought on one portal to ensure efficient management of the entire gamut of 
functions related to Notaries. 
In the future, the Department contemplates the following steps for making the 
entire process of appointment of notari es and related matters more robust and 
fast: 
▪ to make the whole process faceless, i.e., without any human intervention 
▪ make the entire process easy and user-friendly 
▪ Issuing of certificates in electronic form

III. DELIBERATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE 
COMMITTEE  
 
3.0 The Committee, during the course of deliberations on this subject, 
interacted with many stakeholders. In such deliberations, many issues and 
concerns arose before the Committee. Accordingly, those is sues and the 
recommendations of the Committee have been dealt with in the succeeding 
paras.  
Raising the stature of Notaries in India 
3.1 It is an undeniable fact that Notary Public is an essential office in our 
judicial system. The functions of notaries p rescribed under Section 8 of the 
Notaries Act, 1952 are very elaborate and important. The documents 
authenticated by the Notary have prima facie validity and are presumed genuine 
everywhere. However, it is also a sad truth that over the years, the notaries ' 
profession in India has degraded substantially. There have been instances where 
notaries have been operating from cars and taxis and have been criticized for 
lowering the dignity of the legal profession. Notaries have been known to issue 
false certificates, which can lead to fraud and other legal issues. Even though 
fees have been prescribed in the Rules, notaries charge exorbitant fees. Further, 
the notary profession in India is largely unregulated, which leads to 
malpractices and unethical behaviour. 
3.2 To overcome this challenge, first, there is a dire need to make the 
notaries' profession more attractive so that competent lawyers are attracted to 
this field. Presently, lawyers having a good practice  do not prefer to be a notary 
public.   
3.3 Notaries do not receive any remuneration or pay from the 
government. The only source of their income is the fees they charge from 
their client. The fees to be payable to a notary for doing any notarial act 
are prescribed under Rule 10 of the Notaries Rules , 1956. The prescribed 
fee is meagre, and it was last updated in the year 2014. Thus, there is a 
need to appropriately raise the fees commensurate with inflation so that the 
notaries can have a decent standard of living. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that the government  to increase the fee payable to notaries 
and make it inflation -linked. It should be revised at regular intervals, 
preferably every five year.  

18 
 
Appointment of Notaries 
3.4 The present interview-based appointment system for notaries nee ds more 
transparency and objectivity. There is no objective criterion for holding 
interviews for the selection of notaries. Given the number of applications, 
hardly 2 -4 minutes are given to each candidate, and about 200 applicants are 
interviewed daily. Th e entire process of conducting Interview looks ritualistic. 
Thus, the entire process of appointment of notaries requires a relook. 
3.5 The government of India has already dispensed interviews for Group B 
and C to stamp out corruption in appointment and to make the selection process 
objective and fair.  
3.6 The Committee accordingly recommends doing away with interview -
based appointment of notaries. Instead, the selection should be based on an 
objective type written examination along the lines of the All India Bar 
Examination (AIBE) conducted by the Bar Counc il of India (BCI). In fact, 
the Central Government may consider using the same examination i.e. 
AIBE, which is conducted twice a year by the BCI, for getting the panel of 
central notaries.  
Sanctioned Strength of Notaries 
3.7 The maximum number of notaries  to be appointed by the Central 
Government and the State/UT government is prescribed in the schedule to the 
Notaries Rules, 1956. Further, rule 8(4A) of these rules provides for the 
enhancement of the quota of notaries in the states/UTs inter alia consider ing 
their population. However, in their replies to the Committee’s questionnaire, the 
Department of Legal Affairs informed that the sanctioned strength of notaries 
for states/UTs is determined based on the number of applications received for 
appointment as a notary.  
3.8 It is observed that the number of notaries is limited and unevenly 
distributed across the country, leading to difficulties in accessing notarial 
services, especially in rural and remote areas. 
3.9 Accordingly, it is the considered view of the Committee that the 
criteria for deciding the sanctioned strength of notaries in a state is very 
vague and lacks objectivity at all. The sanctioned strength of notaries in a 
particular state should be determined on the basis of its population, volume 

19 
 
of litigation, economic and commercial activities in that state, etc., and it 
should be reviewed regularly.  
Qualification for Appointment of Notaries 
3.10 Rule 3 of the Notaries Rules, 1956, inter alia, stipulates 10 years of 
practice as a qualification (7 years for women, SCs, STs, OBCs, etc.). However, 
the stakeholders have informed the Committee that there are many instances 
where applicants having no exp erience of practicing in courts are appointed as 
notaries based on their years of enrolment as advocates.  
3.11 On this, the Committee opines that the 10 years of practice as 
eligibility for the appointment is on the higher side, and it should be 
reduced to 5 years to attract young aspirant lawyers to this profession. At 
the same time, it should also be made mandatory for the applicant to have 
appeared in at least 100 cases.  
Renewal of certificate of practice 
3.12 As per Section 5 of the Notaries Act, 1952 , every public notary has to 
apply for renewal of his/her certificate of practice before the expiry of the 
previous term. The renewal is done for a period of 5 years. For renewal of the 
certificate of practice, the notaries have to apply to the Department of Legal 
Affairs along with the prescribed fees. On approval of the Competent Authority, 
the renewal certificate is issued. 
3.13 Various stakeholders, in their deposition before the Committee, have 
informed that even after timely submission of the renewal application, there are 
huge delays in the disposal of their application. Because of this, many notaries 
find themselves without a certificate of practice, and legally, they can’t carry 
out their work. Accordingly, they lose their practice, income, and reputation.  
3.14 Almost all the stakeholders flagged the  issue of delay in the renewal 
of certificate of practice. They all brought to the notice of the Committee 
that there are allegations of corruption and misuse of discretion in the 
renewal process. On the  renewal process, the Committee think that it is 
being done only  to know about the antecedents of the applicant and to 
ensure that the applicant is alive and nobody else is practicing in their 
place.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that renewal of certificate 
of practice every five years should be done away with. After their 

20 
 
appointment, notaries may be allowed to practice till a particular age 
prescribed by the government. As the government has the power to 
suspend or remove notaries on a complaint received against them, this will 
empower the government to tame the erring/defaulting notaries. In order 
to access the antecedent of the notaries and confirm they are alive, the 
Committee desires that a system like online self -certification or otherwise  
may be suitably devised by the government. 
Use of technology in appointment and notarial work 
3.15 Presently, the Notary Portal of the Department of Legal Affairs 
(https://notary.legalaffairs.gov.in/) is used for submitting applications and 
declaring results only. With the advancement of technology, the 
Department needs to harness its full potential for making significant 
improvements in the appointment process. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the g overnment make this portal a one -stop place for 
advertising vacancies of notaries, making applications, submitting fees, 
publishing results, and downloading e -certificates of practice. The entire 
process of renewal of the certificate of practice should be made through 
this portal only. Further, the annual returns under rule 14 of the Notaries 
Rules, 1956, should also be filled online through this portal. 
3.16 Additionally, the general public should be provided with a state -wise 
list of public notaries, updated on a real -time basis, for verifying the 
credentials of notaries.  The public may also be allowed to raise 
grievances/complaints against notaries through this portal. In the long run, 
the services of this portal may be extended to the States and UTs so that the 
common public can access central and state notaries in one place.  
3.17 Notaries should be equipped to handle electronic transactions, digital 
documents, and online notarization. For this training of notaries should be 
made.  
Diversity in notaries' profession 
3.18 Currently, there is no provision for reservation in the appointment of 
notaries, though such categories (SC, ST, OBC, Women, Physically 
Challenged) are given 3 years of relaxation in qualification. The Department, in 
their submission before the Committee, has informed that they do not maintain 
category-wise data of notaries as the same is not required under the rules. 

21 
 
3.19 On this issue, the Committee feels that notaries' profession should 
reflect the diversity of the State in which they are appointed. This will 
further enrich the notarial profession and the legal system. Accordingly, it 
is recommended that the government should appropriately give 
representation to SCs, STs, OBCs, Women, Physically Challenged, 
Minorities, etc., in the appointment of notaries. Further, at the application 
stage, the candidate should be asked to furnish their category so that the 
Department maintains category -wise data. Accordingly, the rules may be 
amended to that extent.  
Designated areas for sitting of notaries 
3.20 The Bombay High Court, in Writ Petition No. 4947 of 2021, has 
observed that notaries have been found notarising documents from public 
vehicles and t axis, raising concerns about the legal profession’s dignity. On 
visiting court premises in different parts of the country, it can be seen that 
notaries roam all around the premises and even notarize documents from their 
vehicles parked outside the court.  
3.21 Accordingly, the Committee recommends the government  to ensure 
designated areas for the sitting of notaries in every Court complex from 
where they can do their notarial work in a dignified manner.  
Change of Notarial Year for furnishing the annual return 
3.22 Public notaries have to send their annual returns in the month of January 
each year. In the return, they are required to furnish details of notarial work 
done during the preceding year and the amount of fees received. Some notary 
associations have  demanded that the Notarial year (January to December) be 
changed to (April to March) coinciding with the financial year, to save them 
from the hardship they face in calculating and submitting their returns. 
3.23 The demand for changing the Notarial  Year from calendar year to 
financial year seems logical, and this will help the notaries to synchronize 
their returns with that of Income Tax returns. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends changing the Notarial Year from Calendar to Financial Year.   
Notarizing of documents  

22 
 
3.24 The notarial work is largely paper-based and manual, which increases the 
risk of fraud, forgery, and tampering of documents. There is a lack of 
digitisation, standardisation, and verification of notarial records and certificates. 
3.25 Further, t here are complaints that the  Public Notaries notarize the 
document without even taking a cursory look at it, sometimes the documents are 
antedated, and some notaries  are alleged to have attested blank pages. To 
overcome this, there is a need  to reform and strengthen the Notary Public 
activity in India to prevent the fabrication of false documents affecting the 
credibility and legality of business transactions. The falsification of documents 
is today’s foremost problem in scores of legal dispu tes, whether civil or 
criminal. 
3.26 The notarial work should be modernised and digitised, and the use of 
electronic signatures, stamps, and seals should be encouraged. The notarial 
records and certificates should be stored and maintained in a centralised 
online database, which can be accessed and verified by the concerned 
authorities and parties. The notaries should also adopt uniform formats 
and standards for their documents and certificates. 
3.27 The Committee accordingly, recommends the government to en sure 
that all public notaries maintain a digital register to keep records of 
documents notarised by them. Digitalizing records  will help avoid fraud, 
deceit, and tampering of records. The concept of digital signature should be 
introduced so that records are not antedated and to identify such notaries 
who indulge in fabrication or falsification of documents. 
Training of Notaries 
3.28 The notaries in India are not adeq uately trained and supervised, and there 
is no mechanism for ensuring their accountability and quality of service. There 
is also a lack of awareness and clarity among the public about the role and 
functions of notaries. 
3.29 Thus the Committee is of the vi ew that the notaries should be 
provided with regular training and guidance, and their performance and 
conduct should be monitored and evaluated by an appropriate 
government/authority. Also, some ethical and professional standards 
should be laid out by such government/authority to which notaries should 

23 
 
adhere to. Further,  any complaints or grievances against the  Notaries 
should be promptly addressed and resolved. 
*** 
  

24 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS - AT A GLANCE 
 
DELIBERATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE 
COMMITTEE 
Raising the stature of Notaries in India 
1. Notaries do not receive any remuneration or pay from the 
government. The only source of their income is the fees they charge from 
their client. The fees to be payable to a notary for doing any notarial act 
are prescribed under Rule 10 of the Notaries Rules , 1956. The prescribed 
fee is meagre, and it was last updated in the year 2014. Thus, there is a 
need to appropriately raise the fees commensurate with inflation so that 
the notaries can have a decent standard of living. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends that the government to increase the fee payable 
to notaries and make it inflation -linked. It should be revised at regular 
intervals, preferably every five year. (Para 3.3) 
Appointment of Notaries 
2. The Committee accordingly recommends doing away with 
interview-based appointment of notaries. Instead, the selection should be 
based on an objective type written examination along the lines of the All 
India Bar Examination (AIBE) conducted by the Bar Council of India 
(BCI). In fact, the Central Government may  consider using the same 
examination i.e. AIBE, which is conducted twice a year by the BCI, for 
getting the panel of central notaries. (Para3.6) 
Sanctioned Strength of Notaries 
3. It is the considered view of the Committee that the criteria for 
deciding the sanctioned strength of notaries in a state is very vague and 
lacks objectivity at all. The sanctioned strength of notaries in a particular 
state should be determined on the basis of its population, volume of 
litigation, economic and commercial activities  in that state, etc., and it 
should be reviewed regularly.(Para 3.9) 
 
 

25 
 
Qualification for Appointment of Notaries 
4. On this, the Committee opines that the 10 years of practice as 
eligibility for the appointment is on the higher side, and it should be 
reduced to 5 years to attract young aspirant lawyers to this profession. At 
the same time, it should also be made mandatory for the applicant to have 
appeared in at least 100 cases. (Para 3.11) 
Renewal of certificate of practice 
5. Almost all the stakeholders flagged the issue of delay in the renewal 
of certificate of practice. They all brought to the notice of the Committee 
that there are allegations of corruption and misuse of discretion in the 
renewal process. On the renewal process, the Committee think that  it is 
being done only to know about the antecedents of the applicant and to 
ensure that the applicant is alive and nobody else is practicing in their 
place.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that renewal of certificate 
of practice every five years  should be done away with. After their 
appointment, notaries may be allowed to practice till a particular age 
prescribed by the government. As the government has the power to 
suspend or remove notaries on a complaint received against them, this will 
empower the government to tame the erring/defaulting notaries. In order 
to access the antecedent of the notaries and confirm they are alive, the 
Committee desires that a system like online self -certification or otherwise 
may be suitably devised by the government. (Para 3.14) 
Use of technology in appointment and notarial work 
6. Presently, the Notary Portal of the Department of Legal Affairs 
(https://notary.legalaffairs.gov.in/) is used for submitting applications and 
declaring results only. With the advancement of technology, the 
Department needs to harness its full potential for making significant 
improvements in the appointment process. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the government make this po rtal a one -stop place for 
advertising vacancies of notaries, making applications, submitting fees, 
publishing results, and downloading e -certificates of practice. The entire 
process of renewal of the certificate of practice should be made through 
this portal only. Further, the annual returns under rule 14 of the Notaries 
Rules, 1956, should also be filled online through this portal. (Para 3.15) 

26 
 
7. Additionally, the general public should be provided with a state -wise 
list of public notaries, updated on a rea l-time basis, for verifying the 
credentials of notaries.  The public may also be allowed to raise 
grievances/complaints against notaries through this portal. In the long run, 
the services of this portal may be extended to the States and UTs so that the 
common public can access central and state notaries in one place. (Para 
3.16) 
8. Notaries should be equipped to handle electronic transactions, digital 
documents, and online notarization. For this training of notaries should be 
made. (Para 3.17) 
Diversity in notaries' profession 
9. On this issue, the Committee feels that notaries' profession should 
reflect the diversity of the State in which they are appointed. This will 
further enrich the notarial profession and the legal system. Accordingly, it 
is recommende d that the government should appropriately give 
representation to SCs, STs, OBCs, Women, Physically Challenged, 
Minorities, etc., in the appointment of notaries. Further, at the application 
stage, the candidate should be asked to furnish their category so that the 
Department maintains category -wise data. Accordingly, the rules may be 
amended to that extent. (Para 3.19) 
Designated areas for sitting of notaries 
10. The Committee recommends the government to ensure designated 
areas for the sitting of notaries in every Court complex from where they 
can do their notarial work in a dignified manner. (Para 3.21) 
Change of Notarial Year for furnishing the annual return 
11. The demand for changing the Notarial Year from calendar year to 
financial year seems logical, and this will help the notaries to synchronize 
their returns with that of Income Tax returns. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends changing the Notarial Year fro m Calendar to Financial Year.   
(Para 3.23) 
 
 

27 
 
Notarizing of documents  
12. The notarial work should be modernised and digitised, and the use of 
electronic signatures, stamps, and seals should be encouraged. The notarial 
records and certificates should be s tored and maintained in a centralised 
online database, which can be accessed and verified by the concerned 
authorities and parties. The notaries should also adopt uniform formats 
and standards for their documents and certificates. (Para 3.26) 
13. The Committee accordingly, recommends the government to ensure 
that all public notaries maintain a digital register to keep records of 
documents notarised by them. Digitalizing records  will help avoid fraud, 
deceit, and tampering of records. The concept of digital signature should be 
introduced so that records are not antedated and to identify such notaries 
who indulge in fabrication or falsification of documents. (Para3.27) 
Training of Notaries 
14. Thus the Committee is of the view that the notaries should be  
provided with regular training and guidance, and their performance and 
conduct should be monitored and evaluated by an appropriate 
government/authority. Also, some ethical and professional standards 
should be laid out by such government/authority to which  notaries should 
adhere to. Further, any complaints or grievances against the Notaries 
should be promptly addressed and resolved. (Para 3.29)

R E P O R T 
JUDICIAL INFRASTRUCTURE IN THE NORTH-EASTERN STATES OF INDIA 
1. Justice is an essential precondition for harmonious functioning of any 
society. It refers to the establishment or determination of rights according to the 
rules of law or equity. It is the enforcement of what is just i.e. equitable, fair and 
reasonable, by unbiased assessment of  conflicting claims . One of the most 
important functions of  a State is to ensure justice to its  citizens. Every state must 
always possess the capability to administer justice according to its legal system. In 
fact, in a parliamentary democracy, how justice is ad ministered in the society is a 
fairly accurate measure to assess its success. 
2. Constitution of India under Articles 14 to 18, guarantees equality of all 
citizens, in various spheres of life.  Access to justice to all citizens is inherent in 
these rights. Access to justice is the foundation of a fair and equitable society 
ensuring that all individuals have the right to seek legal remedies. It ensures 
equality of all citizens regardless of their background or socio -economic status. It 
is essential for social  cohesion and social harmony. It ensures peaceful and 
progressive development. 
3. Existence of adequate judicial infrastructure capable of delivering efficient, 
economic and timely delivery of justice is pivotal to ensuring access to justice to 

8 
 
the citizens. However, in a geographically large and culturally diverse country like 
India, achieving this goal is an en ormous challenge . The challenge get s further 
aggravated in remote and inaccessible regions of the Country like the N orth-
Eastern states. Keeping th is unique situation in mind , the Committee decided to 
review the status of Judicial infrastructure in the North-eastern states.  
4. To get first hand information , the Committee visite d Imphal, G auhati and 
Agartala from 19th to 23rd January, 2023 and to kohima, Shillong and Itanagar from 
9th to 13th May, 2023. The Committee interacted with the Chief Justices and other 
Judges of these High Courts  and district courts , Members of the Bar, officials of 
the Ministry of Law & Justice, Government of India , offic ials of State 
Governments and other stakeholders to understand the challenges being faced in 
augmentation of judicial infrastructure in the North-Eastern states. The main issues 
that emerged from these interactions include the following:- 
(i)  Severe space crunch is being faced in majority of court rooms . There 
is shortage of judges chambers, lack of sufficient parking space and lack of 
adequate number of toilets. It was emphasized that space is required to 
accommodate new departments, Record Roo ms, Secretariats and Offices 
such as Juvenile Justice Secretariat, Chief J ustices ' Conference Hall, 
Mediation Centers, Judges Libraries and Libraries for advocates.  

9 
 
(ii) Lack of robust digital infrastructure and poor network connectivity in 
remote areas is a major impediment in carrying out court proceedings 
through virtual mode.  The IT hardware and software need to be upgraded 
from time to time. 
(iii) The issue of adequate security of the court premises as well as that of 
the judicial Officers and lawyer s need to be addressed . In some cases there 
isn't separate compound, with boundary walls and gates , to secure the court 
complex which causes security issues for the judges, prosecutors, bar 
members, vulnerable witnesses etc. 
(iv) Steps need to be taken to ensure adequate water supply, fire safety 
measures, provisions for lifts and ramps, separate toilets for men/women. 
5. The Committee was apprised that the primary responsibility of c reation of 
judicial infrastructure at district and subordinate  level primarily lies with the State 
Government. However, the Department of Justice , Government of India  has been 
implementing the Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) for development of 
infrastructure facilities for the subordinate judiciary in the country since 1993-94.  
6. A brief description of the scheme is as under:- 
 
 

10 
 
Objective of the Scheme 
 
7. The objective of the scheme is to improve the physical infrastructure of the 
subordinate courts including court buildings and the housing needs for judicial 
officers of district and subordinate courts in the country with a view to facilitate 
better justice  delivery. The scheme does not cover construction of High Court 
buildings.  
Funding Pattern 
8. Presently, the fund sharing pattern of the Scheme is 90:10 (centre: state) for 
the 8 North -Eastern and 2 Himalayan states (Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh) 
and 60:40 for remaining States. There is 100% assistance for Union Territories.  
Components 
9. The scheme used to cover construction of court buildings and residential 
quarters for Judges/Judicial Officers of District and Subordinate Courts. The 
scheme now als o covers the construction of toilets, digital computer rooms and 
lawyers’ hall in the district and subordinate courts. The Scheme has been extended 
for a further period of five years from 01.04.2021 to 31.03.2026.  
Allocation of funds 
10. A sum of Rs. 9866.59 crores have been allocated to State Governments / 
Union Territories. Out of this, an amount of Rs. 6422.28 crores has bee n provided 

11 
 
since 2014-15 till 31st March 2023 (65.09%), which includes Rs. 684.14 crore in 
2021-22 and Rs. 857.20 crore released during 2022-23. 
 
    
 Modalities for Release of Fund under the scheme 
11. To ensure that proper utilization of funds takes place, and funds earmarked 
for a scheme are exclusively utilized for that particular scheme , the Government 
has introduced a new procedure for release of  funds through Public Financial 
Management System ( PFMS) for all CSS .  The revised PFMS  procedure includes 
designation of a Single Nodal Agency (SNA) for each CSS; registration of SNA in 
PFMS and opening of bank acc ount of each SNA and its mapping on PFMS and 
other p rocedures laid down by the Ministry of Finance .   Scheme wise single 
account are to be opened at the State level, wherein the central share (within 20 
days of receipt of central share) and  the state share (within 40 days of receipt of 
central share) is to be deposited  by the state in   stipulated time. Thus all release s 
under a particular scheme is to  be routed through PFMS in dedicated accounts

12. As per the new PFMS guidelines, further instalment of funds to the
