increasing during the past few years.  BE for the financial year 2025-26 of DARPG is 
Rs. 174.37 crores, which is an increase of Rs. 42.412 Crores (32.14% approximately) 
over RE 2024-25.  The Committee notes that except for the year 2022-23, where the 
Department was able to spend almost the entire budget allocation, in subsequent years, 
the Department has not been able to fully utilise the allocation, while the allocations 
kept on increasing.  The Committee hopes the Department would be able to spend the 
allocation as it has already done in 2022-23.  
(Para 2.2) 
 
2. The Committee observes that the Department should ensure timely 
implementation and efficient utilization allocated funds of Rs. 97.00 crore by 
establishing well-defined performance indicators. The enhancement of CPGRAMS 
through AI-driven analytics and regional language support is imperative to improve the 
accessibility and inclusivity. The Committee hopes that the proposed Data Strategy Unit 
will leverage advanced technologies to enhance governance efficiency.  Strengthening 
collaborations with premier institutions like IIT Kanpur will further drive innovation 
and technological advancements, in upgrading CPGRAMS.   
(Para 2.5) 
 
3. The Committee notes that there is an increase of 81.91% in Non-Scheme 
allocation.  The Committee desires that the key areas driving the rise may be identified 
to ensure that administrative and operational expenses remain constant and do not lead 
to excessive overheads.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to 
utilize the funds more uniformly throughout the year. 
(Para 2.7) 
 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR GOOD GOVERNANCE (NCGG) 
 
4. The Committee notes that there is a significant variation of 52.81% between BE 
2024-25 and BE 2025-26.  The Committee feels that improved forecasting and budget 
management processes may be used to reduce the variation.  Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that regular monitoring of expenditures by the Department should be 
done to optimize fund utilization. 
(Para 2.9)

Public Grievances

grievance redressal.

initiatives for Grievance Officers (GROs) by strengthening partnerships with ISTM,

INTRODUCTION 
 
  I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee to 
submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred Forty Seventh                 
Report on Demands for Grants 2025-26 pertaining to the Department of Justice (Ministry of 
Law and Justice). 
 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of Ministries/Departments of Government of India projected under various 
Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year need to be voted by the Parliament. 
Subsequently, the Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand referred 
to the concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close 
scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States. While making scrutiny of Demands for Grants, the Committee has made 
an appraisal of performance, programmes, schemes and policies of the Department Justice 
vis-à-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of India. 
 
3. In the Report, scrutiny of Demand No. 65 pertaining to the Department of Justice; and 
Demand No. 67 pertaining to the Supreme Court of India for the Financial Year 2025-26 has 
been made by the Committee. 
 
4. During the course of examination of the above Demands, the Committee heard the 
views of the Secretary, Justice; Member Secretary, National Legal Services Authority 
(NALSA); Director, National Judicial Academy; and Registrar, Supreme Court of India in its 
sittings held on the 19th February, 2025.  
 
5. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied 
upon the following:-  
(i) Detailed explanatory note on DFG 2025-26 submitted by the Department of 
Justice and Supreme Court of India; 
(ii) Replies of Department of Justice on Questionnaire (General Issues); 
(iii) Replies of Department of Justice and Supreme Court of India on Questionnaire 
(Budget Specific); 
(iv) Presentations made by the Secretary, Justice; Member Secretary, National Legal 
Services Authority (NALSA); Director, National Judicial Academy; and 
Registrar, Supreme Court of India in meeting of the Committee held on 
19.02.2025; 
(v) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Law and Justice.  
 
6. The Report is based on facts, figures and submissions (both oral and written) tendered 
by the Department/Institutions/Organizations to the Committee.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
 
Functions of the Department 
 
1.4 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, functions of the 
department are as under: 
 
i. Appointment, resignation and removal of the Chief Justice of India and Judges 
of the Supreme Court of India; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of 
absence (including leave allowance), pensions and travelling allowances; 
ii. Appointment, resignation and removal etc. of Chief Justice and Judges of 
High Courts in States; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of absence 
(including leave allowances), pensions and travelling allowances; 
iii. Appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial Officers in Union 
Territories; 
iv. Constitution and organization (excluding jurisdiction and powers) of the 
Supreme Court (but including contempt of such Court) and the fees taken 
therein; 
v. Constitution and organization of the High Courts and the Courts of Judicial 
Commissioners except provisions as to officers and servants of these courts; 
vi. Administration of justice and constitution and organization of courts in the 
Union Territories and fees taken in such courts; 
vii. Courts fees and Stamp duties in the Union Territories; 
viii. Creation of All India Judicial Service; 
ix. Conditions of service of District Judges and other Members of Higher Judicial 
Service of Union Territories; 
x. Extension of the Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory or exclusion 
of a Union Territory from the Jurisdiction of a High Court; 
xi. Legal Aid to the poor; 
xii. Administration of Justice; and 
xiii. Access to Justice, Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms. 
 
1.5 The Department of Justice is the administrative Department for the following 
institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives: 
a) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA):- The National Legal Services 
Authority has been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. The 
Chief Justice of India (CJI) is the patron-in-chief and the second senior-most judge of 
the Supreme Court is the Executive Chairman of the Authority. NALSA monitors and 
evaluates implementation of legal aid programmes, and lays down policies, principles, 
guidelines and frames effective and economical schemes for the State Legal Services 
Authorities (SLSA) to implement the legal services programmes throughout the 
country. The State Legal Services Authorities, District Legal Services Authorities 
(DLSA), Taluk Legal Services Committees (TLSC), etc. provide free legal services to 
underprivileged litigants and organize Lok Adalats for speedy resolution of disputes. 

 11 
The prime objective of NALSA is speedy disposal of cases and reducing the burden 
of the judiciary. 
b) Family Courts:- The Family Courts Act, 1984 was enacted with a view to providing 
for establishment of Family Courts by the State Governments in consultation with the 
High Courts to promote conciliation and secure speedy settlement of disputes relating 
to marriage, family affairs and related matters. In accordance with the provisions of 
Section 3 of the Act, the State Government has to mandatorily establish Family Court 
for every area in the State comprising a city or a town population of which exceeds 
ten lakh. In other areas of the States, the Family Courts may be set up if the State 
Governments deem it necessary. 
c) Special Courts for trial of criminal cases involving elected MPs/MLAs:- In 
compliance to Hon’ble Supreme Court Judgment in Ashwini Kumar Vs UoI (WP (C) 
699 of 2016)10 Special courts (02 Special Courts in Delhi, and 01 each in the State of 
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, 
Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal) are functional for expeditious trial and disposal of 
criminal cases involving elected MPs/MLAs. 
d) Fast Track Special Courts:- In pursuance of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 
2018, and direction of Hon’ble Supreme Court in Suo Motu Writ (Criminal) No. 1/2019 
dated 25th July, 2019, Union of India started a Centrally Sponsored Scheme in October 
2019 for setting up of 1023 Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs) including 389 
exclusive POCSO (e-POCSO) courts across the country for expeditious trial and disposal 
of pending c ases related to rape and Protection of Children from Sexual Offences 
(POCSO) Act, 2012.  
e) National Judicial Academy (NJA):- The National Judicial Academy (NJA), Bhopal 
is an autonomous body established in 1993 under the Societies Registration Act, 
1860. This independent body functions with its office at the Supreme Court of India 
and its campus at Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. This is an Apex body which imparts 
judicial training to Judges/Judicial Officers of the country and provides facilities for 
training of ministerial officers working in the Supreme Court, study of court 
management and administration of justice in the State/Union Territories, organizing 
conferences, seminars, lectures and research in matters relating to court management 
and administration. The core objectives of the said Academy have been to foster 
development of national judiciary in the country and strengthen administration of 
justice, judicial education, research and policy formulation. 
f) National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms: The Mission was set up 
with twin objectives of increasing judicial access by reducing delays and arrears in the 
system and enhancing accountability at all levels through structural changes and 
setting performance standards and facilitating enhancement of capacities for 
achieving such performance standards. The schemes/initiatives under the Mission are 
Action Research and Studies on Judicial Reforms, Access to Justice for all, E-Courts 
Mission mode, Infrastructure development of Subordinate Judiciary, judicial 
performance evaluation, etc. 
 

 12 
g) Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities 
for the Judiciary: The government has been implementing a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary since 1993-94. 
The scheme covers construction of court buildings and residential accommodations 
for Judicial Officers/Judges of District and Subordinate Courts. The fund sharing 
pattern of the Scheme has been revised to 60:40 (Centre: State) and 90:10 (Centre: 
State) for the North-Eastern and two Himalayan States, and 100% for Union 
Territories. The Union Cabinet, in its meeting on 14th July 2021, approved the 
continuation of the scheme from 2021-22 to 2025-26, with a financial outlay of Rs. 
9,000 Crore, including a central share of Rs. 5,357 Crore. In the current financial year 
(2024-25), Rs. 909.29 crore has been released to the States, bringing the total funds 
disbursed under the scheme to Rs. 11,838.30 crore. 
h) Computerization of District and Subordinate Courts: E-Courts Mission Mode 
Project (MMP) Phases – I, II & III: - This Project is being implemented by the 
Department under the guidance of e-Committee, Supreme Court of India primarily for 
universal computerization of all District and Subordinate Court complexes. Initiated 
in 2010, the Phase-I of the Project concluded at a total cost of Rs 639.14 crore. The 
Phase II of the Project with an outlay of Rs 1670 crore, of which Rs. 1,668.43 Crore 
has been utilized.  Phase III of the e-Courts Project, with a total financial outlay of Rs. 
7,210 Crore spread over four years, was approved by the Cabined on 13.09.2023. The 
Project aims to enhance the use of technology in the judiciary to improve efficiency, 
transparency and accessibility of justice. Building upon the success of Phase II (2015-
23), which focused on the ICT enablement of district and subordinate courts, Phase III 
is designed to strengthen digital case management, enhance virtual court 
functionalities and promote AI-driven legal research tools. Under Phase II, 3452 court 
complexes and 18,735 courtrooms were computerized, WAN connectivity was 
established across courts and digital case management tools such as the National 
Judicial Data Grid (NJDG) were implemented. Under the eCourts Project Phase-III, 
Rs. 1200 crore has been allocated under RE 2024-25 and the actual expenditure is 
mere Rs. 317.43 Crore as on date. A sum of Rs. 2151.57 crore is projected for BE 
2025-26, as per the requirement submitted by eCommittee, Supreme Court of India. 
i) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 :- The 
Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for the 
establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of 
providing speedy and inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps. 
The Central funding for Gram Nyayalayas includes one-time (non-recurring) 
assistance of Rs. 18 lakh per Gram Nyayalaya. Additionally Government meets fifty 
percent of the recurring assistance incurred in the first three years, subject to a ceiling 
of Rs. 3.20 lakh per Gram Nyayalaya per annum. 
j) Designing Innovative Solutions for Holistic Access to Justice In India (DISHA):- 
Department of Justice has created a new scheme Designing Innovative Solutions and 
Holistic Access to Justice - DISHA for a period of five year 2021 -2026 .To prioritize 
citizen-centric justice delivery system by integrating access to justice with 
technology, DISHA has the objective - : 

 13 
 To strengthen pre -litigation mechanism through Tele -Law; 
 To develop an effective dispensation of pro bono legal services through 
Nyaya Bandhu programme; and 
 To empower citizens through pan India Legal Literacy and Legal Awareness 
programme . 
SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
1.6 The Supreme Court of India is at the apex of a pyramidal, unified and integrated 
judicial system. Though the political system of the country is federal in nature, the judicial 
system is unitary. The Supreme Court came into existence on 28th January, 1950 and it 
comprises the Chief Justice of India and 33 Judges. The strength of the apex court was 
enhanced over the years from 8 in 1950 to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1977, 26 in 1986, 31 
in 2009 and 34 in 2019, with the increase of case load on it. The Constitution of India 
provides for the Supreme Court to be a court of record, guardian of liberties & rights and also 
as the final arbiter in most disputes. It is an appellate court, can review its own judgement and 
in its advisory capacity may answer references by the President on any question of law of 
public importance. The Supreme Court is designated as the custodian of fundamental rights 
and the 'rule of law'. It has power of judicial review and the law declared by the Supreme 
Court is binding on all courts. 
1.7 The administrative wing of the Supreme Court is called 'Registry'. The Registry is 
divided into two wings - (i) Administrative Wing; and (ii) Judicial Wing. These wings are 
further divided into various Divisions, Branches, Sections and Cells. The Chief Justice of 
India is the Administrative head of the Supreme Court. The highest Administrative Officer of 
the Supreme Court is the Secretary General, the post manned by a judicial officer of the rank 
of a District & Sessions Judge and is of the rank of Secretary to the Government of India. The 
Secretary General is assisted by Registrars, Officers on Special Duty, Additional Registrars, 
Deputy Registrars, officers of other lower ranks and subordinate staff. 
1.8 The Department of Justice is the nodal Department for the Supreme Court of India. 
There is a separate demand, Demand No. 67 pertaining to the Supreme Court of India, which 
is entirely charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India and cannot be submitted to the vote 
of Parliament. However, Article 113 of the Constitution provides for those estimates to be 
discussed in either House of Parliament.

CHAPTER - III 
POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
Vacancies in the Department of Justice 
 
3.0 The Department of Justice was separated from the Ministry of Home Affairs and set 
up as an independent Department under the Ministry of Law and Justice and was made 
operational w.e.f. 01.01.2010.  In the beginning it was decided that the manpower to be 
provided to the Department of Justice will be held on the common cadre with the Ministry of 
Home Affairs. In this joint cadre, all posts are first allotted to Home Affairs and thereafter as 
per the assessment of need of the Department of Justice they allot the staff.  Under this 
arrangement, in the Department of Justice as against the sanctioned strength of 102, only 60 
officials are working resulting in vacancies to the tune of 41%.   
 
3.1 The Department of Justice has apprised this Committee that at different times, the 
matter of posting sufficient strength of officials in the Department of Justice has been taken 
up with the Ministry of Home Affairs and other cadre controlling departments like DoPT.  
However, there continues to be an acute shortage of manpower in the Department. After 
becoming an independent Department, the matter of sanctioning additional posts was taken 
up with the Ministry of Finance and additional posts have also been sanctioned by the said 
Ministry. However, these posts continued to remain vacant as adequate staff has not been 
posted by the Ministry of Home Affairs. This manpower shortage is having an impact on 
functioning of the Department, which is inter alia performing important functions like justice 
delivery and access to justice.  The Department of Justice  has also informed the Committee 
that to cope up with the extreme shortage of staff, besides requesting MHA and DoPT to fill 
the vacancies, this Department has engaged retired Government servants as Consultants and 
also hired outsourced staff i.e. DEOs/MTSs.  
 
3.2 The Committee notes that even after 15 years of its separation from the Ministry 
of Home Affairs and becoming an independent Department, the Department of Justice 
is still dependent on the MHA for all its man power requirements. The vacancies in the 
Department are particularly staggering at the middle and operating level of SO(32% 
Vacancy), ASO (50% vacancy), UDC (100% vacancy), PA (100% vacancy). The 
Committee feels that Department of Justice (DoJ) should implement the 
recommendation made in this regard by this Commitee in its 113th Report on 
establishing a separate cadre unit. This should be done in collaboration with the DoPT 
and MHA, with a clear-cut timeline.   Also, the Committee desires that DoJ may submit 
a detailed proposal for the creation of a separate cadre to DoPT and MHA for approval, 
without any further delay.

3.8 The Committee observes that the process of judicial appointment and pendency  
of cases are critical issues that require urgent attention. There must be synergy between 
the Judiciary and the Government to ensure timely processing of recommendations and 
appointments. The Committee feels that a coordination mechanism should be developed

between the Judiciary and the Ministry of Law and Justice to track the status of 
appointments delays.  
3.9 The Committee feels that an institutional mechanism may be developed wherein 
the process of the retirement of a judge and the appointment of his/her successor is 
aligned which would  ensure that the vacancy is filled immediately after the retirement.. 
The High Courts with the most significant backlog (Allahabad, Bombay, and 
Rajasthan) should be prioritized for judicial appointments.  The Committee feels that 
judicial workforce may be augmented by hiring more administrative staff, junior 
judicial officers, and court assistants to ensure smooth and efficient operations.  
3.10 During its recent study visit to the Kerala High Court, the Committee observed 
the successful deployment of Mobile Legal Aid Units (Mobile E-sewa Kendras) which 
get stationed periodically in the districts in remote areas. These units have been actively 
providing legal services to people in far-flung locations, particularly in large tribal 
population, where they have played a crucial role in delivering justice. Based on this 
effective model, the Committee recommends the expansion of this services to other 
remote areas to conduct awareness sessions and assist people in accessing legal services, 
in the Country.

3.13 The Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for the development of judicial infrastructure 
has been in place since 1993-94 and was revised in 2011. Under this scheme, the Central 
Government supplements the resources of State Governments by providing financial 
assistance based on a prescribed fund-sharing pattern: 60:40 (Centre: State), 90:10 for the 
North-Eastern and two Himalayan States, and 100% for Union Territories. However, central 
funding is subject to budgetary allocations. In the current financial year (2024-25), Rs. 
909.29 crore has been released to the States, bringing the total funds disbursed under the 
scheme to Rs. 11,837.30 crore. 
3.14 As of 31.12.2024, there are 21,974 court halls/rooms available in District and 
Subordinate Courts, with 3,166 under construction. Additionally, 19,682 residential units 
have been completed, while 2,638 are under construction. The Union Cabinet, in its meeting 
on 14th July 2021, approved the continuation of the scheme from 2021-22 to 2025-26, with a 
financial outlay of Rs. 9,000 Crore, including a central share of Rs. 5,357 Crore, of which Rs. 
50 crore is earmarked for Gram Nyayalayas. Beyond the construction of court halls and 
residential units for judges and judicial officers, the scheme now also covers the construction 
of Lawyers' Halls, Toilet Complexes, and Digital Computer Rooms in Subordinate Courts. 
3.15 Further, the central funding for Gram Nyayalayas includes one-time (non-recurring) 
assistance of Rs. 18 lakh per Gram Nyayalaya. Additionally, recurring assistance covers 50% 
of the expenditure, subject to a ceiling of Rs. 3.20 lakh per annum per Gram Nyayalaya for 
the first three years. The Government has extended the Gram Nyayalaya scheme from 2021-
22 to 2025-26 with a financial outlay of Rs. 50 Crore for operationalizing Gram Nyayalayas. 
The functioning of Gram Nyayalayas in 15 States/UTs is being monitored through an online 
portal. However, the release of funds is subject to the following conditions: 
 Gram Nyayalayas must be notified and operational. 
 Nyayadhikaris (judicial officers) must be appointed. 
 Details must be updated on the Gram Nyayalayas Portal of the Department of Justice.

their respective High Courts, may establish one or more Gram Nyayalayas for each 
Panchayat at the intermediate level. However, the establishment of these courts is not 
mandatory for States. The functioning of Gram Nyayalayas in 15 States/UTs is being 
monitored through an online portal. The Status of Gram Nyayalayas Notified and

3.19 The Department in their written submission has informed that  as per data available, 
total number of 4,21,081 cases (Criminal and Civil) were registered on Gram Nyayalays, out 
of which 2,98,122 cases have been disposed oﬀ during the period December, 2020 to 
October, 2024. The Department further in their written submission also informed that they 
have found out following challenges in operationalization and implementing of Gram 
Nyayalayas in implementing States: 
 It is not mandatory on the part of State Governments to set up Gram Nyayalayas. 
 The Gram Nyayalayas in most of the States do only 2 days sitting (Example MP 
and Kerala) in a week, which need to be done on regular basis on every working 
day. 
 There is a need to provide basic infrastructure, ICT facilities and CIS system for 
efficient conduct of Mobile Courts for the Gram Nyayalayas. 
 The creation of Nyayadhikari post and filling up of vacancies of independent 
Nyayadhikari is the key to success of the Gram Nyayalayas. 
 Mobile courts are not functional in all the States where Gram Nyayalayas are 
functioning. 
 Non-availability of public prosecutors, notaries and other facilities and lack of 
interest shown by advocates for working in the Gram Nyayalayas is another 
challenge. 
 Training of the Gram Nyayadhikari is needed to make him aware of legal 
procedural requirements. 
 There is need to give wide publicity about the date and place of holding of mobile 
courts and adequate security for Mobile Courts is also needed. 
 Overlapping jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas with regular courts.  
 Shortage of First Class Judicial Magistrates to man the Gram Nyayalayas;  
 Reluctance of police and other state functionaries to appear before them.   
 
3.20 The Committee notes that out of 488 entities notified across various states, only 
319 are functional. It is observed that states like Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and UTs 
like Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh have notified entities but none are functional. The 
Committee feels that these states/UTs should prioritize operationalization of the notified 
entities through development of their infrastructural facilities and deployment of 

 32 
required workforce. The Committee also opines that that states with partially functional 
entities (e.g., Odisha, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Punjab, Haryana) should address their 
challenges such as funding allocation, administrative bottlenecks, and workforce 
shortages.   
3.21 The Committee feels that Gram Nyayalayas should operate every working day so 
that the backlog of cases can be handled more effectively instead of just two days a 
week. The current limited sitting schedule  of just two days a week significantly reduces 
the capacity of these courts to deal with the volume of cases. The Committee opines that 
prioritizing the recruitment of Nyayadhikaris (Judicial Officers) and ensuring the 
timely filling of vacancies may help in providing uninterrupted functioning of Gram 
Nyayalayas. 
3.22 The Committee suggests that an extensive public awareness campaign may be 
launched about Gram Nyayalayas which will  include information on the schedule of 
mobile courts, the process for filing cases, and the availability of legal support. The 
Committee further recommends the jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas may be clearly 
defined to avoid overlap with regular courts.

3.34 Article 39A of the Indian Constitution provides free legal aid to ensure that 
opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other 
disabilities.  Articles 14 and 22 (1) mandate the state to ensure equality before law.  The 
Parliament enacted the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 on 9th November 1995 to 
establish a nationwide uniform network for providing free and competent legal services to the 
weaker sections of society based on equal opportunity. The principal objective of NALSA is 
to provide free and competent legal services to the weaker sections of society to ensure that 
opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other 
disabilities, and to organize Lok Adalats for amicable settlement of disputes.

cases which are at the pre-litigation stage. Another objective was to implement a cost 
effective and time saving mechanism of dispute resolution for the effected parties. E- Lok 
Adalat has been conceptualized in a way that it facilitates party interaction and the 
exchange of information, allowing an opportunity to effectively solve a dispute. Pre-Lok 
Adalat sessions are held to identify cases fit for settlement and to facilitate settlement 
between the parties.

MANPOWER REQUIREMENT AT NALSA 
3.51   National Legal Services Authority was established in the year 1995 to facilitate Access 
to Justice to the poor and marginalized sections of the country with the sanctioned staff 
strength of 27 posts. Since its establishment, in about 30 years, only 6 additional posts have 
been created. However, the functions, activities and even the mandate of NALSA has 
increased manifold during the period leaving a huge gap between the required and sanctioned 
staff strength which ultimately impacts NALSA’S working.   
3.52 In their written submission to the Committee NALSA  has informed that they are 
facing difficulties in executing and monitoring its schemes and programs due to shortage of 
staff, especially at the lower levels. This staffing shortage has also affected their ability to 
maintain accurate data, proper accounts, and other essential records. To address these 
challenges, NALSA initially submitted a proposal to the Department in February 2022 for 
creation of 40 additional posts. Following the advice of the Department, NALSA revised the 
proposal and in April 2024, submitted an updated request for creation of 46 posts. In January 
2025, NALSA sent a proposal for revival of 12 posts, which were abolished earlier. 
 3.53 The Committee recommends that the Department should prioritize the approval 
of NALSA's proposals for creation of 46 additional posts and revival of 12 posts. The 
Committee feels that this will help bridge the significant gap between the current and 
required staff strength, enabling NALSA to efficiently execute and monitor its 
programs and schemes. 
National Judicial Academy, Bhopal 
3.54 The National Judicial Academy (NJA) is entrusted with the judicial education and 
capacity building of Judicial Officers across the country and Hon’ble Judges of the High 
Courts. In line with the Resolution adopted during the Chief Justices' Conference, 2016 
(Agenda Item No. 9), the National Judicial Academic Council (NJAC) was established under 
the aegis of the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India (CJI). The NJAC comprises: 
 Two Senior Puisne Judges of the Supreme Court of India 
 Chairpersons of State Judicial Academies 
 Judges-in-Charge (Judicial Education) of High Courts 
 Secretary, Department of Justice 
 Director, National Judicial Academy 
 
The NJAC is chaired by the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India and is responsible for: 
 Advancing the cause of judicial education  
 Formulating the academic calendar of NJA 
 Approving and prescribing academic calendars for State Judicial Academies(SJAs) 
 Enhancing resources for judicial training and education 
 Coordinating and monitoring NJA & SJA activities 
 Suggesting improvements in judicial education and fostering cooperation among NJA 
and SJAs 
Both NJA and SJAs are required to submit their annual academic calendars to the NJAC 
for finalization and approval.

reduction in allocation may impact key training and capacity-building programs 
undertaken by the NJA. Additionally, the variation of ₹1.66 crore between BE 2024-25 
and BE 2025-26, and ₹0.88 crore between BE 2024-25 and RE 2025-26, suggests a 
pattern of conservative budgeting, potentially limiting the Academy’s ability to expand 
its initiatives. To ensure smooth functioning of  NJA, it is recommended that the budget 
allocation aligns more closely with actual requirements. The shortfall of ₹4.34 crore 
between projections and allocation for 2025-26 should be reviewed, and funds may be 
provided as and when required. 
(Para 2.12) 
Assessment of Budget allocated to the Supreme Court of India (Demand No.  67) 
5. The Committee further notes that for 2024-25, the BE was ₹525.49 crore but was 
revised upward to ₹588.55 crore, indicating a higher requirement than initially 
projected. However, the BE for 2025-26 has been set at ₹547.15 crore, which is lower 
than the RE of the previous year, raising concerns about whether this allocation would 
be sufficient to meet actual financial needs. This pattern suggests that initial budget 
estimates may not be accurately reflecting the financial demands, leading to significant 
revisions and adjustments. To ensure better financial planning and resource utilization, 
it is essential that budget projections align more closely with actual requirements to 
avoid underfunding or over-allocation. The underutilization in 2022-23 points to the 
need for improved expenditure planning and timely fund disbursement.  
(Para 2.15) 
--- 
CHAPTER - III - POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
 
POLICIES, PROGRAMMES AND SCHEMES 
Vacancies in the Department of Justice 
 
6. The Committee notes that even after 15 years of its separation from the Ministry 
of Home Affairs and becoming an independent Department, the Department of Justice 
is still dependent on the MHA for all its man power requirements. The vacancies in the 
Department are particularly staggering at the middle and operating level of SO(32% 
Vacancy), ASO (50% vacancy), UDC (100% vacancy), PA (100% vacancy). The 
Committee feels that Department of Justice (DoJ) should implement the 
recommendation made in this regard by this Commitee in its 113th Report on 
establishing a separate cadre unit. This should be done in collaboration with the DoPT 
and MHA, with a clear-cut timeline.   Also, the Committee desires that DoJ may submit 
a detailed proposal for the creation of a separate cadre to DoPT and MHA for approval, 
without any further delay. 
                                                                                                                       (Para 3.2) 

 49 
Vacancy of Judges and Pendency of Cases in Higher Judiciary 
 
 
7. The Committee observes that the process of judicial appointment and pendency  
of cases are critical issues that require urgent attention. There must be synergy between 
the Judiciary and the Government to ensure timely processing of recommendations and 
appointments. The Committee feels that a coordination mechanism should be developed 
between the Judiciary and the Ministry of Law and Justice to track the status of 
appointments delays. 
 (Para 3.8) 
8. The Committee feels that an institutional mechanism may be developed wherein 
the process of the retirement of a judge and the appointment of his/her successor is 
aligned which would  ensure that the vacancy is filled immediately after the retirement.. 
The High Courts with the most significant backlog (Allahabad, Bombay, and 
Rajasthan) should be prioritized for judicial appointments.  The Committee feels that 
judicial workforce may be augmented by hiring more administrative staff, junior 
judicial officers, and court assistants to ensure smooth and efficient operations.  
(Para 3.9) 
9. During its recent study visit to the Kerala High Court, the Committee observed 
the successful deployment of Mobile Legal Aid Units (Mobile E-sewa Kendras) which 
get stationed periodically in the districts in remote areas. These units have been actively 
providing legal services to people in far-flung locations, particularly in large tribal 
population, where they have played a crucial role in delivering justice. Based on this 
effective model, the Committee recommends the expansion of this services to other 
remote areas to conduct awareness sessions and assist people in accessing legal services, 
in the Country. 
(Para 3.10) 
 
ASSESSMENT OF BUDGETARY SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT of JUSTICE 
 
Gram Nyayalayas 
10. The Committee notes that out of 488 entities notified across various states, only 
319 are functional. It is observed that states like Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and UTs 
like Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh have notified entities but none are functional. The 
Committee feels that these states/UTs should prioritize operationalization of the notified 
entities through development of their infrastructural facilities and deployment of 
required workforce. The Committee also opines that that states with partially functional 
entities (e.g., Odisha, Maharashtra, Jharkhand, Punjab, Haryana) should address their 
challenges such as funding allocation, administrative bottlenecks, and workforce 
shortages.   
(Para 3.20) 
 

 50 
11. The Committee feels that Gram Nyayalayas should operate every working day so 
that the backlog of cases can be handled more effectively instead of just two days a 
week. The current limited sitting schedule  of just two days a week significantly reduces 
the capacity of these courts to deal with the volume of cases. The Committee opines that 
prioritizing the recruitment of Nyayadhikaris (Judicial Officers) and ensuring the 
timely filling of vacancies may help in providing uninterrupted functioning of Gram 
Nyayalayas. 
(Para 3.21) 
12. The Committee suggests that an extensive public awareness campaign may be 
launched about Gram Nyayalayas which will  include information on the schedule of 
mobile courts, the process for filing cases, and the availability of legal support. The 
Committee further recommends the jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas may be clearly 
defined to avoid overlap with regular courts.  
(Para 3.22) 
 
 Designing Innovative Solutions and Holistic Access to Justice (DISHA) 
 
13. The Committee appreciates the concept of DISHA scheme that endeavours to 
address the legal needs of the people.  Given the success of the 56 TV programs 
broadcast under the "Vidhi Jagriti Abhiyaan" initiative, the Committee  recommends 
that the department may collaborate with the Doordarshan to expand the content and 
increase its reach. 
(Para 3.24) 
 
14. The Committee further suggests that to increase the program's impact, 
interactive formats should be explored, such as call-in programs, where viewers can ask 
legal questions directly to experts. The Committee feels that social media campaigns 
and online discussions can engage younger audiences. 
(Para 3.25) 
e-Court Mission Mode Project 
 
15. The Committee is not aware of the reasons for the low fund utilization rate of 
18.23% under the e-Courts Project Phase-III as of December 31, 2024 which ultimately 
highlights the need for a more efficient fund disbursement mechanism. Since funds are 
released based on requisitions from the eCommittee, Supreme Court of India, a 
streamlined process should be established to ensure timely allocation.  
(Para 3.29) 
Fast Track Courts  
 
16. The Committee recommends that the budget allocation of the FTSCs may be 
increased to meet their actual financial requirements. As of 31st December 2024, 747 
FTSCs are functional, falling short of the target of 790 for the year 2024. The 

 51 
Committee urges the Ministry to take immediate steps to expedite the establishment of 
the remaining FTSCs by providing additional resources and infrastructural setup, 
especially in states with high case pendency. 
(Para 3.33) 
SCHEMES/PROGRAMMES OF NALSA 
 
17. The Committee appreciates the efforts of NALSA, especially in recent years, for 
its exceptional work in providing legal services and raising awareness about legal 
entitlements among the poor and vulnerable sections of the country. The Committee 
recommends expanding the Legal Aid Defence Counsel System (LADCS) to more 
districts across the country. This expansion will ensure that those from marginalized 
backgrounds have access to experienced lawyers, which will help them in getting justice 
quickly.  
(Para 3.47) 
 18. The Committee recommends strengthening the E-Lok Adalat platform to 
improve its accessibility, particularly for rural population and those with limited 
technological access.The Committee opines that collaborating with local organizations 
will help in setting up digital access points in rural areas (e.g., community centers, 
libraries, or local panchayat offices). Further, Para-Legal Volunteers (PLVs) may be 
trained to assist people in navigating the digital platform.  
(Para 3.48) 
19. The Committee also feels that specialized legal aid units should be established 
within NALSA, focusing on women's and children's rights, and staffed with advocates 
trained to handle sensitive issues. Further, the Committee recommends that more 
number of NGOs and child welfare organizations may be collaborated with, to ensure 
that legal assistance reaches every woman and child. 
(Para 3.49) 
 
20. The Committee also recommends that regular assessments may be carried out to 
evaluate the effectiveness of  legal aid programs. The Committee feels that this can be 
achieved through conducting audits and surveys among beneficiaries to gather feedback 
on the quality and accessibility of the services provided.  
(Para 3.50) 
 
21. The Committee recommends that the Department should prioritize the approval 
of NALSA's proposals for creation of 46 additional posts and revival of 12 posts. The 
Committee feels that this will help bridge the significant gap between the current and 
required staff strength, enabling NALSA to efficiently execute and monitor its programs 
and schemes. 
(Para 3.53) 
 
 

 52 
National Judicial Academy, Bhopal 
 
22. The Committee recommends that the NJA should continue to enhance its 
curriculum by integrating emerging legal issues and international judicial trends. 
Regular assessments should be done to evaluate the effectiveness of existing programs, 
focusing on adapting to contemporary legal challenges. 
(Para 3.60) 
 
23. The Committee opines that the NJA should expand its collaborations with 
international judicial bodies and institutions. This will not only enhance the Academy's 
global outreach but also facilitate cross-border learning and the exchange of best 
practices. Partnering with countries that have diverse legal traditions will help enrich 
the curriculum and provide Indian judges with a broader perspective. 
(Para 3.61) 
24. While the current infrastructure and staff strength are sufficient for present 
activities, as reported by the NJA, the Committee feels that the NJA should prepare for 
future growth by expanding its infrastructural facilities, particularly in light of its 
increasing international engagements. Further, the Committee feels that the NJA should 
expedite the recruitment process for the 32 vacant positions. 
(Para 3.62)

R E P O R T 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
 
Ministry of Law & Justice 
1.0 The Ministry of Law & Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by the 
British Parliament. The Ministry comprises the following three Departments under the overall 
charge of the Law and Justice Minister assisted by a Minister of State. Each of the three 
departments is administratively headed by an independent Secretary. 
. 
 
1.1  The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in administration 
of justice; furnishing legal advice to the Government of India and defending Government of 
India in various Courts and Tribunals; drafting Supreme and Subordinate legislations for 
Government of India; appointment, resignation and removal of Judges of the Supreme Court 
of India and High Courts in States; Legal aid to poor; access to Justice; Justice Delivery and 
Legal Reforms etc. 
1.2 In this report the demands allocated to Department of Legal Affairs (Demand No. 65) 
have been analysed and recommendations of the committee have been made at the end of 
each headings/sub-headings.  
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
Functions of the Department 

 
11 
1.3 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department 
of Legal Affairs has been allocated the following matters:  
(i) Advice to Ministries on legal matters including interpr etation of the Constitution 
and the Laws, conveyancing and engagement of counsel to appear on behalf of the 
Union of India in the High Courts and subordinate Courts, where the Union of 
India is a party. 
(ii) Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India , and other Central 
Government Law Officers of the States, whose services are shared by the 
Ministries of the Government of India. 
(iii) Conduct of cases in the Supreme Court of India and the High Courts on behalf of 
the Central Government and on behalf of the G overnments of States participating 
in the Central Agency Scheme. 
(iv) Reciprocal arrangements with foreign countries for the service of summons in civil 
suits for the execution of decrees of Civil Courts, for the enforcement of 
maintenance orders, and for the a dministration of the estates of foreigners dying in 
India intestate. 
(v) Authorization of officers to execute contracts and assurances and of property on 
behalf of the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution, and authorization 
of officers to sign a nd verify plaints or written statements in suits by or against the 
Central Government. 
(vi) Indian Legal Service. 
(vii) Treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of civil law. 
(viii) Law Commission of India. 
(ix) Legal Profession including the Advocates Act, 1961  (25 of 1961) and persons 
entitled to practice before High Courts. 
(x) Enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India and the conferring 
thereon of further powers; persons entitled to practise before the Supreme Court, 
references to the Supreme Court under Article 143 of the Constitution of India. 
(xi) Administration of the Notaries Act, 1952 (53 of 1952). 
(xii) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. 
1.4 Besides the above, the Department also administers the following acts: 
(a) The Advocates Act, 1961 
(b) The Notaries Act, 1952 
(c) The Advocates’ Welfare Fund Act, 2001 
(d) The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 
(e) The India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019 
1.5 The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) and the Law Commission of India also 
fall under the administrative purview of the Department. The Department is the cadre 
controlling authority for Indian Legal Service (ILS). It also handles the appointment of 
Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India, and Additional Solicitor General of 
India. Further, in order to promote studies and research in law and for improvement in ADR 
Ecosystem in the country the department sanctions grant –in- aid to institutions engaged in 
these fields such as Indian Law Institute and Indian Arbitration Centre. 

 
12 
Structure of the Department 
1.6 Department of Legal Affairs has two tier set up namely, the Main Secretariat of the 
Department which is located in New Delhi, and Branch Secretariats located at Bengaluru, 
Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai. The nature of duties discharged by the Department is broadl y 
classified into two areas - Advice work and Litigation work. The Main Secretariat is headed 
by the Law Secretary, assisted by Addit ional Secretaries, Joint Secretaries  and Legal 
Advisers.  
1.7 There is a Central Agency Section in the Department, which is currently led by the 
Law Secretary and supported by Officers from the Government Advocates cadre of the  ILS 
and other supporting staff for handling  litigations at the Supreme Court on behalf of all 
Ministries/Department of the Government of India as well a s administration of the Union 
Territories. The Judicial section of the Department defends Government of India in all courts 
and Tribunals where Government of India is a party. The litigation work in High Courts and 
CAT (Principal Bench) is handled by the L itigation (High Court) Section and in Lower 
Courts by the Litigation (Lower Court) Section.  
1.8 The Department has a separate cell called the 'Implementation Cell' to handle the 
implementation of the recommendations of the Law commission of India and the 
administration of the Advocates Act, 1961 and the Advocates Welfare Fund Act, 2001. This 
Cell also administers the subject of 'Legal Education' as provided under Entry 26 of List III to 
the 7th Schedule of the Constitution of India.  
1.9 The Department tenders legal advice to all Ministries and Departments of the 
Government of India. The legal advice team of the Department is generally headed by an 
Additional Secretary or a Joint Secretary & Legal Adviser, who, in turn, is assisted by other 
officers at different levels. 
1.10 Under the Digital India initiative, the Department has created a web based application 
namely, Legal Information Management & Briefing System (LIMBS) for monitoring all 
court cases where Union of India is a party. It is an innovative and easy to access online tool 
which is available 24x7 to all the stakeholders, viz., senior Government Officials, Nodal 
Officers and users of Ministries/Department.  
1.11 Further, the following Institutions/organizations are under the overall supervision of 
the Department of Legal Affairs: 
(i) Law Commission of India (LCI): - The Law Commission of India is a non-
statutory body, constituted by the Government once in three years. The present 23rd  
Law Commission was constituted on 01.09.2024 and will run up to 31.08.2027. The 
Commission is assisted by Law Officers of Indian Legal Service and a few 
consultants having experiences in legal research. A small group of secretarial staff 
looks after the administration. The Law Commission works on projects based on (a) 
Reference received from the Central Government and/or from Supreme Court of India 
and High Courts; and (b) Suo motu Cognizance - keeping in view the importance of 
the subject matter, the Commission may initiate study on specific subjects.  

 
13 
(ii) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT): - ITAT is one of the oldest Tribunals, 
set up under Section 252 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to hear second appeals in all 
matters of direct taxes and appeals against the revision orders of Administrative 
Commissioners as well as o rders denying registration under Section 12A or under 
Section 80G of the Income -tax Act 1961.  It functions as the final fact finding 
authority in the matters concerning Income -tax, wealth -tax, gift -tax etc. The orders 
passed by the ITAT are final; an appea l lies to the High Court only if a substantial 
question of law arises for determination. The Tribunal consists of 63 Benches, which 
is spread over 30 stations (including 02 Circuit Benches) throughout the country.  
(iii) Bar Council of India (BCI): - The Bar Council of India is a statutory body 
constituted under Section 4 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and it has been empowered, 
among other things, to lay down standards for professional conduct and etiquette for 
lawyers, and to maintain and improve standards of legal education in the country.  
(iv) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute is a premier legal research 
institute founded on 27th December, 1956. The prime objective of the Institute is to 
promote advanced studies and research in law and to contribute substantially in 
reforming the administration of justice, so as to meet the socio-economic aspirations 
of the people through law and its instrumentalities. The Institute has been granted 
Deemed University status in the year 2004. 
(v) The India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC):- The IIAC was established 
in December, 2022 with a view to provide cost effective and timely services for the 
conduct of arbitration and conciliation at national and international level, facilitate 
conduct of international and domestic arbitration and conciliation and impart training 
in alternative dispute resolution and related matters in field of arbitration, conciliation 
and mediation. Its purpose is to bring reforms in the field of arbitration and 
conciliation and to develop it as a flagship institution for domestic and international 
arbitration. It will facilitate and provide administrative assistance for conduct of 
arbitration and conciliation proceedings in a professional and time-bound manner and 
in the most cost-effective way. It will also set up an arbitration chamber to empanel 
professional arbitrators at national and international level and set up an Arbitration 
Academy to train arbitrators in India, so as to empower them to compete on par with 
reputed arbitral institutions in the world. IIAC has empanelled 161 Arbitrators and 51 
Arbitrators have been empanelled separately for conduct of International Commercial 
Arbitration since the year 2023 and is planning to conduct Arbitration proceedings 
online in near future. So far it has registered a total of 15 Arbitration till date, out of 
which 13 are domestic arbitrations  and 2 are International arbitration. Justice Hemant 
Gupta, retired Judge, Supreme Court of India was appointed as Chairperson.  Shri 
Ganesh Chandru and Shri Anant Vijay Palli have been appointed as Part-time 
Members in the Centre vide notification dated 23.12.2022. The Central Government 
has nominated Dr. Ajay Sahai, Director General, Federation of Indian Export 
Organizations as Part-time Member of the Centre and the Secretary, Department of 
Legal Affairs along with  Financial Adviser, Ministry of Law & Justice is the ex-
officio Member of the IIAC.

written submission stated that the Law Commission of India was allocated Rs 11.835 crore in 
RE 2024-25 and its expenditure as on 31.01.2025 was Rs. 6.689 crore only which is about 56 
% of the allocated budget. The department in their presentation informed that the term of 22nd 
LCI ended on 31.08.2024 and Government has  constituted the  23rd LCI on  01.09.2024. 
However, the Chairperson and Members have not been appointed till date. Due to this,  the 
budget utilization has been lower than expected in this financial year as the salaries and

activities and expenditures. However, once the chairperson and members are appointed and

amount of Rs. 1.5 Cr. could not be debited to NDMC towards payment of license fee for LCI 
office premises, and the said amount has not be considered in the utilized budget.

Commission in September, 2024, the appointment of Chairman has not been made till

role in legal reforms and policy  recommendation. The Committee, therefore, urge the 
department may take necessary steps to appoint the Chairman and Members of the  
Law Commission at the earliest. In future, a clear timeline may be desired for

ENGAGEMENT OF LAW OFFICERS AND ADVOCATES 
 
3.16 Law Officers for Supreme Court are appointed by the Department i.e. one Attorney 
General of India, on e Solicitor General of India and eleven Additio nal Solicitors General of 
India. In addition, the department also appoints Law Officers for High Courts i.e. 25 
Additional Solicitor General and 31 Deputy Solicitors General.  
Besides Law Officers, the Governm ent also engages Panel Counsels to conduct litigation 
before various courts and Tribunals in the Country. The panel counsel for various High 
Courts are engaged by this Department to represent Union of India for a particular term and 
their engagement is not  made against any civil post. At present, there are more than 7000 
Advocates empanelled under various categories of Panel counsel for various judicial fora.  
 
3.17 Presently, there is no criteria / methodology to project the required number of panel 
counsel for a court / tribunal. Advocate are engaged by this Department on need basis and 
keeping in view the size of High Court, number of Central Govt. litigations etc. appropriate 
number of counsel are engaged as and when required. 
  
3.18 However, keeping in view the size of High Court, number of Central Government 
litigations and so forth, appropriate number of counsel are engaged with the approval of 
Hon’ble Minister for Law & Justice on the basis of their interest, qualification, experience, 
reputation, exp ertise, professional competence and standing at Bar, and interviews are not 
conducted for this purpose. Further, empanelment/engagement of Advocates as panel counsel 
is an ongoing process and projecting actual total number of panel counsel for a High Court on 
an earlier date is not feasible due to expiry of terms, deaths and resignation etc.  
 
3.19 Though the Government has been making efforts to appoint best Panel Counsels, 
many are not forth coming for reasons best known to them, thus i t has resulted in  not 
getting favourable outcomes in the litigation process. The committee, therefore, 
recommends a systematic, transparent, and performance -oriented approach  may be 
adopted for selecting legal counsel s. Further, having clear qualification criteria and 
utilizing technology for performance tracking, the appointment process can be made 
more efficient and effective. This in turn will help in reducing  delays and improve 
litigation outcomes thereby ensuring that only the most competent and thoroughly 
vetted legal p rofessionals are selected. In addition, the Department may consider 
implementing a feedback mechanism to evaluate the quality of legal services provided 
by the counsels, in the respective departments.  Based on it, contract renewal criteria 
linked to performance may be introduced.

INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT)  
3.28 The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal is a quasi -judicial body headed by a President 
and assisted by Zonal Vic e-Presidents, and at present there are 57 Judicial Members and 53 
Accountant Members. It has 63 Benches whic h are spread across 30  cities. The powers and 
functions of ITAT are exercised and discharged by the Benches constituted by the President 
of the Tribunal from amongst the Members thereof, which generally consists of one Judicial 
Member and one accountant Member. The orders passed by the ITAT are final; an appeal lies 
to the High Court only if a substantial question of law arises for determination.

Additionally, there is a shortage of Registry Officers and other officials. Another aspect

point out that all these have  contributed to a growing backlog of cases, impacting the

recruitment process is streamlined all vacancies can be filled up the bac klog in 
disposing of cases  can be considerably reduced . Additionally, the Committee suggests 
the extensive use of virtual courts for ITAT may be explored , which will also help in 
disposing of cases quickly. 
INDIA INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION CENTRE (IIAC) 
 
3.36 The India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC) has been established by the India 
International Arbitration Centre Act, a statute promulgated by the Parliament of India. The 
purpose of this enactment is to create an independent and autonomous regime for institutional 
arbitration. IIAC has been declared as an institution of national importance. The dispute 
resolution processes that are in place have a huge impact on the Indian economy and the 
global perception on doing business in India. To this end, the IIAC aims to inspire confidence 
amongst parties (both domestic and international) by providing a neutral dispute resolution 
platform for resolution of commercial disputes through a seamless arbitral process.  
 
3.37 The Chamber of Arbitration, established  by the IIAC, will scrutinise the applications 
for admission to the panel of arbitrators and thereafter empanel arbitrators. The Chamber of 
Arbitration shall consist of experienced arbitration practitioners of repute (at national and 
international level) a nd persons having wide experience in the area of alternative dispute 
resolution. The IIAC has been set up with an overall objective of promoting and developing 
India as a major arbitration hub by facilitating a quick and efficient dispute resolution 
mechanism.  
 
3.38 The current composition of  the IIAC is Justice Hemant Gupta  (Retd.), Former 
Judge, Supreme Court of India as  the Chairperson. Dr. Ajay Sahai, Part-time Member,  Sh. 
Anant Vijay Palli, Part-time Member, Mr. Ganesh Chandru, Part-time Member, Dr. Rajiv 
Mani, Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry  of Law and Justice, Member -ex 
officio, Ms. Ranjana Chopra,  Additional Secretary &  Financial Advisor, Department of 
Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice, Member -ex officio. The recruitment process of 
the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), who is also Member-ex officio has been completed and 
appointment letter has been issued. 
3.39      As on date, the Secretariat of IIAC comprises of the following staff appointed  o n 
contractual basis. One Regist rar, One Deputy Registrar, Two Counsels , One Assistant 
Registrar, One Executive Assistant, One Assistant Registrar (Accounts), One Executive 
Assistant (Accounts), One Private Secretary attached to the office of Chairperson, One 
Private Secretary attached to the office of Registrar, One Private Secretary attached to the 
office of Deputy Registrar. 
3.40      The Committee was informed that IIAC is continuously taking steps for augmenting 
its infrastructure, both physical and ICT related. The arbitration room s, meeting rooms, 
library, cafeteria, lounge and arrangements for the officers and staff of the IIAC are being 
provided so as to make it at par with other International Arbitration Centres of repute 
worldwide and for overall development of IIAC as a major arbitration hub. IIAC 
administers arbitration as per the India International Arbitration Centre (Conduct of 
Arbitration) Regulations, 2023. IIAC has developed a Software for conduct of Arbitration 

 
31 
Proceedings as per above said Regulations which went live o n 25 November, 2024 for the 
smooth and efficient working of the conduct of Arbitration Proceedings through online 
mode. In order to make its services cost effective IIAC with the previous approval of the 
Central Government has made the India International Arbitration Centre (Conduct of 
Arbitration) Regulations, 2023 which provides for efficient and time bound process of 
arbitration including day to day hearings. 
3.41 IIAC offers competitive structure of  Administrative Fees and  Arbitrators Fees in  
comparison with other  reputed national  and international institutions. The Schedule 
appended to the aforesaid Regulations provides for the fees and other charges for conducting 
arbitration under the aegis of IIAC.  
3.42 IIAC has also made IIAC (Conduct of Micro and  Small Enterprises Arbitration) 
Regulations 2024 to  contribute to the  sustainable and holistic growth and development  of 
the Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE) ecosystem by promoting faster and more effective 
resolution of disputes affecting Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE).  
3.43 The Committee was informed that the major challenges faced by the IIAC are the 
requirement of funds and enablement of parties to agree to refer their disputes to the IIAC 
for arbitration. For promoting IIAC administered arbitration as per its regulations, IIAC has 
been taking steps to  promote institutional arbitration. IIAC  has since its establishment, 
conducted various workshops, conferences and seminars for various stakeholders in  the 
arbitration ecosystem and encouraged parties to consider adopting IIAC institutional 
arbitration to enable time bound, efficacious and cost -effective dispute resolution.  With 
larger dissemination of  IIAC's efficient operations and  functioning and the support that  
IIAC provides to  the parties over a period of time can contribute in parties agreeing to 
conduct arbitrations under the aegis of IIAC. 
 
3.44 The Committee notes that  even after establishment of IIAC  many arbitration 
cases are still being conducted outside the country, and not many international cases are 
dealt with. One of the factors that is affecting the IIAC is lack of sufficient funds.   To 
transform the IIAC into a globally recognized premier arbitration center known for its 
efficiency, expertise, and neutrality, the Government may prov ide sufficient budget 
allocation to it . Focus should also be placed on enhancing infrastructure, capacity 
building, and international outreach. Though, the Department has taken various steps 
to appoint 161 Arbitrators of Domestic Arbitration and 51 Arbitrators for International 
Arbitration. Considering the number of cases pending in various courts, the strength of 
Domestic Arbitrators should be increased. The Department may also take steps to 
appoint the most qualified arbitrators to the IIAC panel, so that IIAC can be positioned 
as a trusted and influential hub in global arbitration. 
 
MEDIATION COUNCIL OF INDIA 
 
3.45 The Mediation Council of India as envisioned in the 2023 Mediation Act, is a 
proposed body meant to regulate and improve mediation in India pa rticularly for commercial 
disputes. The Council will focus on commercial disputes, aiming to promote alternative 
dispute resolution methods and reduce reliance on traditional court procedure. 

 
32 
 
3.46  The Department during the presentation before the Committ ee has informed that the 
Mediation Council of India is yet to be established. Proposal for creation of 60 posts for 
Mediation Council of India was sent to Department of Expenditure. DoE has approved the 
creation of 21 posts. The following rules under the Mediation Act, 2023 have been notified in 
the Gazette of India:- 
(i) The Mediation Council of India (Salary, Allowances and other Terms and Conditions of 
Service  of Chairperson and Members) Rules, 2024; 
(ii) The Mediation Council of India (Travelling and o ther Allowances for Part -time 
Chairperson and Part-time Members) Rules, 2024; and 
(iii) The Mediation Council of India (Forms and Manner of Annual Statement of Accounts) 
Rules, 2024.  
Section 31 to 38 of the Act which deals with various aspects of the Coun cil have been 
brought into force vide notification dated 09.10.2023. 
 
3.47 The Department further informed that Section 45 of the Mediation Act, 2023 provides 
for a fund called the Mediation Fund for the purposes of promotion, facilitation and 
encouragement of mediation under the Act, to be administered by the Mediation Council of 
India. The Central Government is enabled under the Section 45 to provide grants to the 
Mediation Council of India which will be credited to the Mediation Fund. Upon 
establishment of the Mediation Council of India, the funds would be provided to the Council 
in terms of the statutory and policy provisions.  
 
3.48 The Mediation Council of India is also enabled to frame and notify various 
regulations to facilitate the creation and impl ementation of a framework for institutional 
mediation in the country. These include regulations for manner of conducting mediation 
proceeding under sub-section (1) of section 15; standards for professional and ethical conduct 
of mediators under sub-section (3) of section 15; conditions for registration of mediators and 
renewal, withdrawal, suspension or cancellations of such registrations under clause (d) of 
section 38 and manner of process of conducting online mediation under sub -section (2) of 
section 30.  Section 38 further enable the Mediation Council of India to lay down the 
guidelines for the continuous education, certification and assessment of mediators by the 
recognised mediation institutes.  
 
3.49 In this regard, it may also be noted that for recomm ending draft subordinate 
legislation under the Act a working group/committee chaired by Shri P. K. Malhotra, former 
Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice, was constituted. The 
said working Group/Committee had submitted its report to the Department on 31.08.2023 and 
had recommended draft of the rules and regulations for operationalization of the Mediation 
Act 2023. Once the Mediation Council of India is established, the Council shall thereafter 
take steps for the formulation of regulations, recognition of mediation institutes for training 
and other steps in this regard. 
 
3.50 Further, at present training to Mediators is provided by the Mediation and 
Conciliation Project Committee, Supreme Court of India. NALSA allocates grants to  the 
Mediation and Conciliation Project Committee, Supreme Court of India, to support mediation 
activities including training.  

 
33 
 
3.51  One of the main aim for enacting the Mediation Act and establishment of 
Mediation Council is to promote both pre - and pos t-litigation mediation,  which will 
effectively reduce the backlog of cases in courts. However, the Committee notes that the 
Department is yet to establish  Mediation Council of India. The Committee desires it 
may be expedited, so that the purpose of enacting the Act can be achieved.  
3.52 The Committee  desires that a comprehensive awareness campaign across the 
country, at both the state and district levels, through all possible channels  may be 
launched as many are not aware about its establishment . This cam paign will help in 
knowing the existence of the Mediation Council of India and enable the shift of public 
mindset from a litigation-oriented approach to a pre-litigation mediation mindset.

CHAPTER – II - OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
 
BUDGET 
1. The committee recognizes that legal representation is essential for the effective 
defense of government interests, but the rising costs call for a thorough review of 
expenditure patterns and potential measures for optimization. Therefore, the committee 
recommends that the department strengthen the pre-litigation process by promoting the 
use of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) and taking steps to reduce frivolous and 
repetitive litigation. To support this, all government departments and PSUs may review 
all the ongoing cases by setting a team of officers and withdraw those that are weak in 
nature. Additionally, a periodic review of the empanelment and performance of legal 
counsel may also be conducted. (Para 2.8) 
LAW COMMISSION OF INDIA 
2.  The Committee notes that despite the approval of the Constitution of Law 
Commission in September, 2024, the appointment of Chairman has not been made till 
date. This act hinders the effective functioning of the Commission, which plays a crucial 
role in legal reforms and policy recommendation. The Committee, therefore, urge the 
department may take necessary steps to appoint the Chairman and Members of the  
Law Commission at the earliest. In future, a clear timeline may b e desired for 
appointment of Chairman and Members of Law Commission of India. (Para 2.12) 
ITAT 
3. The Committee is pleased to note that ITAT Office at Delhi location has been 
shifted to its own building in July, 2024. While, on other 26 locations they are operating 
from the premises given by the Central Government and other Government bodies and 
on 7 locations from buildings of private owners. The Committee urges the Department 
to take steps to move the ITAT Office from the rented premises either to Governm ent 
premises at the earliest. The ITAT may approach the Department to help in this matter. 
The Department may also consider allocating suitable land and adequate funds to ITAT 
for constructing its own premises at these locations at the earliest. (Para 2.14)
