CHAPTER - I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
1.0 The Ministry of Law and Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by 
the British Parliament and it is one of the oldest limbs of the Government of India. In 
accordance with the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Ministry 
comprises three Departments under the overall charge of the Law and Justice Minister 
assisted by a Minister of State. Each department is administratively headed by an independent 
Secretary. 
 
1.1.  The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in administration 
of justice; giving legal advice to Government of India and defend Government of India in 
various Courts and Tribunals and draft Supreme and Subordinate form of legislations for 
Government of India, etc. 
1.2. In this report, the demands allocated to Legislative Department (Demand No. 65) and 
Election Commission of India (Demand No. 66) have been analyzed and recommendations of 
the Committee have been made at the end of each heading/sub-headings. 
 
1.3. Legislative Department  acts as a service  provider to the Ministries/Departments in 
drafting of principal legislation and vetting of subordinate legislation. The Department is also 
involved in Drafting of Ordinances promulgated by the President, Presidential Acts for the 
States and the President' s Rule, Presidential Regulations to be made by the President under 
Article 240 for Union Territories, Constitution Orders etc.  
 
1.4. This Department also deals with the matters related to Elections to Parliament, the 
Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Offices of the President and Vice -President.. 
This Department also drafts the Finance Bill to give effect to the financial proposals of the 
Central Government every year, which is undertaken in the Legislative Department on the 
budget proposals being brought before it by the Ministry of Finance.  The Department is also 

 
9 
involved in the Publication of Hindi translation of selected judgments of the Supreme Court 
and High Courts on cases pertaining to constitutional, civil and criminal laws in the for m of 
law Journals (Patrikas).  
 
1.5. Further, Ordinance promulgated by the President of India, Regulation made by 
President of India for Union Territories, Electoral Laws and Electoral reforms, maintenance 
of the updated Central Legislation under Bharat Sanhita (India Code) and authoritative 
translation of Central Legislations and Constitution of India in languages specified in the 
Eight Schedule to the Constitution under the Authoritative Text (Central Laws) Act 1973, 
publication and preparation of standard legal terminology, delimitation of Parliamentary and 
Legislative Assembly Constituencies, etc. are also assigned to the Department under 
Allocation of Business Rules, 1961. The Department also imparts training in legislative 
drafting to Officers of the Union/State Government and UT administration through the 
Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research (ILDR). 
 
1.6. It inter-alia administers Personal laws, Electoral laws, the Indian Contract Act, 1872, 
the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the Evidence Act, 1872, the Indian Trust Act, 1882, the Code 
of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Limitation Act, 1963, the Election Commission (Conditions of 
Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991, the 
Representation of People Act, 1950 and the Representation of People Act, 1951. It also 
facilitates procurement of Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) for the Election Commission of 
India, Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) Machines and reimbursement of election 
expenditure to State Governments and UT administrations. 
1.7. Legislative Department does not have any statutory or autonomous body under its 
control. It has two oth er wings under it, namely, the Official Languages Wing and Vidhi 
Sahitya Prakashan, which are responsible  for propagation of Hindi and other Official 
Languages in the field of law. 
(i) Official Languages Wing (OLW): The Official Languages Wing is a 
successor organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission 
under the Legislative Department and is responsible for preparing and 
publishing standard legal terminology and also for translation of Hindi, all the 
Bills to be introduced in Parliament, all Central Acts, Ordinances, Subordinate 
legislations, etc. as required under the Official Languages Act, 1963. The 
Official Languages Wing is also responsible for arranging translation of the 
Central Acts, Ordinances, etc., into the Official Languages as specified in the 
Eighth Schedule to the Constitution as required under the Authoritative Texts 

 
10 
(Central Laws) Act, 1973. The Official Languages Wing also grants-in-aid to 
various registered voluntary organisations engaged in promotion and 
propagation of Hindi and other regional languages and those organisations, 
which are directly engaged in the publication of legal literature and 
propagation of Hindi and other Languages in the field of law.  
       
 (ii) Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP): VSP is a wing under the Legislative 
Department, Ministry of Law and Justice. This wing was set up under the 
recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on Official Languages in 
the year 1968 for promotion and propagation of Hindi in the legal field and for 
this purpose a monthly Hindi law journal for publication of reportable 
judgements of Supreme Court was started under the name and style of 
Uchchttam Nyayalay Nirnay Patrika. Thereafter, in the year 1969, another 
Hindi law journal was started under the name and style of Uchch Nyayalay 
Nirnay Patrika for publication of Hindi version of the judgements passed by 
various High Courts. In the year, 1987, Uchch Nyayalay Nirnay Patrika was 
divided into two Hindi law journals i.e. civil nirnay partika and dandik nirnay 
patrika. In this way VSP is publishing three journals for promotion and 
propagation of Hindi in the legal field. Apart from these three law journals, 
VSP is also publishing standard law text books in Hindi written by eminent 
jurists. This Prakashan is also responsible for sale of official diglot edition of 
Central Acts, Constitution of India, Election Manual, Legal Glossary etc. This 
Prakashan also organizes exhibition and sale of official diglot edition of 
Central Acts, Constitution of India, Election Manual, Legal Glossary, law 
journals etc. and also conducts seminars and workshops for promotion and 
propagation of Hindi all over India. 
 
1.8. The organisational set -up of the Legislative Department includes the Secretary, 
Additional Secretary, Joint Secretary & Legislat ive Counsel, Additional Legislative 
Counsel, Deputy Legislative Counsel, Assistant Legislative Counsel and other 
supporting staff. The work relating to legislative drafting, scrutiny and vetting of 
subordinate legislation have been distributed among variou s Legislative Groups, and 
each group is headed by a Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel or Additional 
Secretary. The Secretary of the Legislative Department also acts as the Chief 

 
11 
Parliamentary Counsel and the Additional Secretary is in -charge of all sub ordinate 
legislation. 
ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
1.9. The Legislative Department is the administrative Department for the Election 
Commission of India, an autonomous constitutional authority created under Article 324 of 
Constitution for superintendence, direction, control of elections to Parliament, State 
legislatures, and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President of India.  The 
functions, responsibilities, structure and power of ECI are enlisted in the Articles 324 to 329 
of Part XV of the Constitution of India. Article 324 of the Constitution of India bestows 
electoral powers, duties and functions on the ECI, while Section 14 of the Representation of 
the Peoples Act, 1951 provides for conduct of the elections to constitute a new Lok Sabha 
before the expiry of its current term. 
1.10. The Election Commission of India is a multimember body (since 1993) headed by the 
Chief Election Commissioner, who acts as Chairman of the Commission. The Chief Election 
Commissioner and Election Commissioners a re appointed by the President of India and have 
tenure of six years, or up to the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The Commission is 
assisted by Deputy Election Commissioners, Chief Electoral Officers (CEO), District 
Election Officers (DEO) and Electoral Registration Officers (ERO), appointed by the 
Election Commission under Representation of People Act, 1951.  
1.11. It registers political parties and allots symbols to them and ensures inner party 
democracy in their functioning by insisting organizational elections at periodic intervals. 
Political parties registered with the Commission are granted recognition at the State and 
National levels on the basis of their poll performance at general elections according to criteria 
specified by it. It implements Model Code of Conduct (MCC) for smooth conduct of free and 
fair elections. It also observes 25th January as National Voters' Day to encourage young 
electors to take part in election process.  
1.12. The electoral expenses on account of conduct of elections  to the House of the People 
and the State Legislative Assembly are borne by the Central Government and the concerned 
State Government, and case of simultaneous elections, the expenditure is to be shared on 
50:50 basis between Central and the concerned Stat e Government. The initial expenditure is 
borne by the respective State Governments, and on submission of the audited report, the 
Central Government’s share is reimbursed through the Legislative Department.  

 
12 
1.13. The Election Commission has its independent  Secretariat for the work relating to the 
smooth conduct of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, and t here is an exclusive 
demand (Demand No. 66) i.e. voted expenditure under which budgetary allocation is sought 
for running the activities of Election Commission of India.

Repeal of Obsolete Laws  
 
2.37  The Department in its written submiss ion has stated that the Government, as a part 
of its resolve to bring reforms in the legal system had constituted a two Member Committee 
in 2014 to undertake comprehensive review of laws with a view to remove obsolete and 
redundant laws. On the basis of th e recommendations of the said Two Member Committee 
and the Law Commission, the Legislative Department had identified 1824 redundant and 
obsolete Acts. After due examination and consultations with concerned Ministries and 
Departments, a total of 1562 Central Acts have since been repealed. Presently, a total number 
of 76 obsolete and redundant laws have been repealed in 2023 through the Repeal and 
Amending Bill, 2023 (Act No. 37 of 2023) by the Government of India. Total 1486 obsolete 
laws were repealed since  2014 till the last Demands for Grants . Further, the Twenty -third 
Law Commission of India has been constituted with a mandate inter alia to examine 
review/repeal of obsolete laws. 
 
2.38  As far as repealing of Obsolete laws is concerned, the Committee appreciates 
the work done in this regard  and that 1824 reduntant and obsolete laws have been 
identified to be repealed. The Committee also feels that the laws prevalent in a coun try 
should be representative of the political and social structure  existing at that time. The 
Committee hopes that the department will undertake such exercise of identifying and 
repealing the obsolete laws on regular and continuous basis in future also.

3.11      The Committee is given to understand that whenever the elections are 
announced in states, the Model Code of Conduct comes into place immediately on 
announcement and trade gets hit. Though, Digital transactions have made a huge 
impact, still a large portion of the country’s economy is cash economy. In the pretext of 
implementation of the Model Code of Conduct, even the genuine transactions of the 
traders are seized which impacts the trader and the economy. The Committee desires 
that ECI should have a mechanism to verify the purpose for which the money is being 
transacted. On verification, if it is found to be for legal purpose, then the entire money 
should be released immediately.

DELIMITATION COMMISSION 
6.1 On a specific query raised about the progress of delimitation work, the Ministry submitted the 
following written reply:- 
 “The Delimitation Commission was constituted in July, 2002. It became functional in 
November/December, 2002. The Commission - in terms of the Constitutional provision - 
was to delimit the constituencies on the basis of 1991 census figures. By June, 2003 the 
Commission had completed almost 60 per cent of its work. The totality of the Commission’s 
work (all the Parliamentary constituencies and th e Assembly constituencies in all the states 
in the country) would have been completed by November/December, 2003. But it could not 
be done because the Parliament amended the Constitution by the Constitution (Eighty-
Seventh Amendment) Act, 2003, which provides that the delimitation work shall be done by 
the Commission on the basis of the 2001 census and not the 1991 census figures. As a 
consequence, the work done by the Commission on the basis of the 1991 census became 
non-est by the operation of law. The Commission, however, started preliminary work on the 
basis of the provisional 2001 census figures, which were available. But the preliminary work 
could not be taken to the logical extent becau se; even the provisiona l 2001 census figures 
regarding the schedule castes and schedule tribes were not available. 
 The 2001 Census figures for most of the States were published on December 31, 2003. 
Thereafter the Commission took-up the work of collecting data and tabulating the same. 
While the process was going on, the Lok Sabha was dissolved and fresh elections were 
declared. The Commission has five Lok Sabha  Members from each State as its associate 
members. Where the number of MPs in a Stat e is less than five, all of them become 
Commission’s members. With the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the associate members 
ceased to be members by operation of law. Even otherwise during the elections, the 
fieldwork by the Commission was almost stopped. After the constitution of the Fourteenth 
Lok Sabha, the Commission requested Hon’ble Speaker to nominate associate members to 
the Delimitation Commission from each State.  After receipt of the nominations, the 
Commission restarted the delimitation work which is progressing on a tight schedule. 
  The delimitation of the Lok Sabha and assembly constituencies in all the States is a 
time consuming work. Under the scheme of the Act associate members are to be associated 
with the delimitation work from the very beginning. As a consequence there have to be more 
than one meeting with the associate memb ers from each State. Thereafter, the draft 
delimitation proposals are published in newspapers and suggestions and views are invited 
from the public. Finally, the public meetings are held by the Commission in all the States 
and the draft finalized, after that. 

 Delimitation work in all the States in the country is at different stages. Four States viz; 
Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal and the Union Territory of Pondicherry are 
scheduled to go to polls in May, 2006. Out of these, Final Delimitation Order has been 
issued in respect of the State of Kerala, West Bengal and Union Territory of Pondicherry and 
published in the State and Central Gazette on 31.3.2005, 31st May, 2005, 31st March, 2005 
and 15th February, 2006 respectively. For Assam and Tamil Nadu the Commission has 
decided that further discussion relating to the above mentioned two States would be held 
after the Legislative Assembly election to th e States is over and new set of Associate 
Members (five MLAs) are appointed by the Speaker of the new Legislative Assembly. 
 It may be added that under Article 82 of the Constitution, the readjustment of 
constituencies for the House of the People ‘shall take effect from such date as the President 
may, by order, specify’. Similarly under Article 170 (3) of the Constitution, the readjustment 
of constituencies for the State Legislative Assemblies ‘shall take effect from such date as the 
President may, by order, specify’. The question of elections to be held on the basis of the 
new delimitation exercise will be dependent on the date determined by the President of 
India.”

NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY (NALSA) 
7.6 Budgetary allocation (2006-07) for NALSA has been  made as Rs. 10 crore which is the same as 
in the previous year was made. 
7.7 National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) has been constituted under section 3 of the Legal 
Services Authorities Act, 1987 in the year 1995 to  provide free and competent legal services to the 
weaker sections of the society with the objective to  ensure that opportunities for securing justice are 
not denied to any citizen for the reason of economic or other disabilities. To be eligible for seeking 
legal aid under the NALSA, the annual income limit fixed by the Central Government for the cases 
before the Supreme Court is Rs. 50,000 at present. Out of twenty eight States Legal Services 
Authorities, and 7 Union Territories, 18 State Legal Services Authorities and 3 Union Territories have 
raised the income ceiling limit to Rs. 50,000 per annum to provide free legal aid under Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987. This has resulted in an increase of number of beneficiaries. During the period 
from the 1st April 2005 to the 31st December 2005, more than 5.70 lakh persons have been benefited 
through legal aid services. Out of them, 54811 persons belong to the Scheduled Castes, 15716 to the 
Scheduled Tribes, 51577 persons were women and 6582 were children. 

7.8 The Committee is satisfied that its reco mmendation (6th Repo rt on the Demand for 
Grants 2005-06), that more and more States and UT s should raise the income-ceiling limit, has 
resulted in 18 States and 3 UTs raising the limit to the prescribed level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should  speed up the entire process so that income-
ceiling limit throughout the eountry remains uniform and la rger number of persons can get 
benefit under the scheme. The Committee also fe els that the counsels engaged for the poor 
under the legal aid programme are paid meager ly; and as a result thereof good and reputed 
lawyers do not come forward to take up the case s. Even Senior Advocates do not take up such 
cases. As a result the poor liti gants feel that legal aid being pr ovided to them is mere eyewash. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the fee structure for the legal aid counsel should be 
reasonably enhanced so that the experienced  and competent lawyers are attracted and 
motivated to take up / accept the cases of the legal aid beneficiaries with full enthusiasm 
Moreover, the fee structure should be made uniform throughout the country.

Assistance Fund. 
7.11 The Committee notes that NALSA has la unched a laudable mission for legal 
empowerment of all the sections of the society, ye t, certain grey areas need to be addressed by 
the Ministry. 0ne such problem rel ates to lack of proper planning. Moreover, non-utilisation of 
grants by the States Legal Serv ices Authorities is another area  of concern. The Committee feels 
that NALSA has not prepared a consolidated sc heme, covering all its schemes and programmes 
for formulating a Centrally Sponsored Scheme due to which the target set was not achieved. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that NALSA  should submit as early as possible a 
perspective plan covering all it s schemes to the Ministry at th e earliest, for consideration. The 
Ministry should effectively moni tor not only utilisation of the f unds but also implementation of 
the schemes and programmes of NALSA. Th e Committee, therefore, recommends that 
constraints of funds should not come in the way of successful implementation of the scheme. The 
Ministry should, therefore, allo cate additional funds to he lp operationalis e the various 
programmes to be undertaken by NALSA at RE st age. The Committee also feels that the actual 
benefit of this scheme is not gaining access to po or litigants. The programme is confined to high 
profile areas or capital cities only. In this direction, the Committee acknowledges the historic 
Maha Lok Adalat organi sed by Hon’ble Justice A.P.Shah, Chief Justice,  High Court, Madras 
and Patron-in chief, Tamil Nadu State Legal Serv ices Authority on 15/04/2006 who along with 
Justice P.D.Dinakaran and others at High Cour t Legal Services Committee, Madurai Bench of 
Madras High Court, Madurai made  quick disposal of all the case s at the Madurai Bench of the 
High Court, by bringing all the Judges of High Court and Subordinate Courts as well as 

litigants at one place. The Committee feels such proactive steps would go a long way in disposing 
off the pending cases with in a prescribed time frame. 
7.12 Lok Adalat is an important constituent of NALSA. Permanent Lok Adalats under section 19 of 
the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 have been established in almost all the States However, 
Permanent Lok Adalats for Public Utility Services under section 22B of the Legal Services 
Authorities Amendment Act, 2002 have been established only in Eight States viz. Assam, Bihar, 
Haryana, Jharkhand, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim and U.T. of Chandigarh. The State Governments of 
Kerala and Delhi have also approved the proposal of their Legal Services Authorities for 
establishment of Permanent Lok Adalat  u/s 22B of the Act and establishment of Permanent Lok 
Adalats in these States is under process. So far as Jammu and Kashmir is concerned, amendment to 
the Act is required. During the period from 1st April, 2005 to 31st December, 2005, 38,261 Lok 
Adalats were organized. These Lok Adalats sett led 9,60,202 cases. The remaining State Legal 
Services Authorities have informed that their pr oposals for establishment of Permanent Lok Adalats 
are pending with the State Governments. The State Authorities have been impressed upon to get their 
proposal cleared from their respective State Government. The NALSA has also taken up the matter 
with the State Governments to expedite the matter but the progress in this matter is slow due to 
paucity of funds. 
7.13 The Committee notes that only eight States have established so far the Permanent Lok 
Adalats for public utility services and such prop osals have been cleared so far by Kerala and 
National Capital Territory of Delhi. The remai ning States/Union Territories are still in the 
process of consideration of the proposal. The Committee expresses its concern over the slow 
pace of establishment of Permanent Lok Adalats fo r public utility services. It also notes that 
after amendment of the Legal Services Authorit ies Act in 2002 establishment only a few such 
Permanent Lok Adalats manifests a lackadai sical approach. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry should make all out efforts in th e direction of establishing Permanent Lok Adalats 
in the remaining States and UTs. It would be appropriate if the Ministry chalks out a time-
bound programme in consultation with the State Legal Services Authorities for establishing 
these Lok Adalats and monitor the pace of implementations thereof. 
LAW COMMISSION OF INDIA 
7.14 Implementation of reports of the Law Commission has been engaging the attention of the 
Government as well as the Committee. The Committee in the 2nd Report (Para 41) recommended:— 
“The Committee was informed that the Law Co mmission has so far presented 188 Reports to 
the Government, out of which 47 Reports are pending implementation at various stages/levels 
and for variety of reasons. The Committee recommends that the Department of Legal Affairs, 
being the nodal agency for monitoring the implementation of the Law Commission’s Reports, 
may ask all the administrative Ministries/Departm ents to keep record of various stages of 
implementation of recommendations contained in the Reports of Law Commission. The 
Committee has observed that there has been inordinate delay in implementing some of the 
Reports of the Law Commission. It may not be ou t of place to mention that the Sixth Report of 
the Law Commission presented to Government in 1957 is yet to be implemented. In this 
context, the Committee feels that it would be be tter to apprise Parliame nt once in a year the 
status of implementation of various Reports of Law Commission. Thus, Government may lay 
before each House of Parliament, an annual  statement to that effect which could inter alia 
contain reasons for delay in implementing certain recommendations of the Law Commission.” 
7.15 The Committee has now been appraised that the Law Commission has since submitted 195 
reports out of which 51 are still pending. The pr esent Seventeenth Law Commission has presented ten 
Reports (186th to 195th reports) so far out of which four reports (192nd, 193rd, 194th and 195th) are 
under examination. The Committee notes that the Mi nistry has started laying of the statement of 

pending Law Commission’s Reports once in a year before the parliament. The Committee further 
hopes that the Ministry would be pursuing the Administrative Departments/Ministry for 
implementation of pending Reports of Law Commission. 
7.16 The Committee feels that the Law Commission’s  reports form the basis for review of the 
judicial system and framing, am ending and repealing the legislat ions as per the needs of the 
changing circumstances. Thus, the role of the Commission assumes special significance in the 
Indian judicial and legislativ e system. The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the reports 
of the Commission should be implemented in le tter and spirit and the Ministry should make 
concerted efforts to ensure timely implementa tion of the recommendations contained therein. 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry  should consider providing statutory backing 
to the Law Commission on the pattern of other co untries like U.K. and Cana da, etc., so that it 
could function more effectively with the desired empowerment.

SOME CONNECTED ISSUES  
REVISION OF ELECTORAL ROLLS
 
7.30 The electoral rolls are revised by the Election Commission every year. All persons who attain  
18 years of age or above are eligible for inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls and can apply 
for the same. Budget Estimates for 2006-07 for meeting expenses on revision of electoral rolls are 
covered under sub head 00.103. 
7.31 The Committee has been apprised by the Ministry through their action taken reply that keeping 
in view the elections to the Legislative Assemblie s of Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and 
Pondicherry 
due in 2006, the electoral rolls for these States/UT have been revised w.r.t. 01.01.2006 as the 
qualifying date. In Assam final publication was made on 10.02.2006. As on that date about 1.74 crore 
electors were 
enrolled in the State. The electoral rolls in Kera la (except for Assembly constituencies falling in 
Kasargod and Palghat districts) were finally published on 27.02.2006 and that of Assembly 

constituencies falling in Kasargod and Palghat districts were published on 04.03.2006. About 2.12 
crore electors stood enrolled in the State. The electo ral rolls of West Bengal were finally published on 
22.02.2006 and as on that date about 4.89 crore electors stood included in the rolls. The electoral rolls 
of Tamil Nadu were finally published on 7.03.2006 and as on that date about 4.64 crore electors stood 
included in the rolls. In Pondicherry the electoral rolls were finally published on 24.02.2006 and 
25.02.2006 and approximately 6.5 lakh electors were enrolled. 
 In all the four States of Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and UT of Pondicherry, the 
electoral rolls have been computerized and are avai lable on the website of respective Chief Electoral 
Officer and also on the website of the Commission. In the State of Kerala and UT of Pondicherry, the 
electoral rolls are with photographs. For the first time the General Elections to the Legislative 
Assemblies of Kerala and UT of Pondicherry have the facilities of having electoral rolls with 
photographs of electors for poll purpose. In the state of West Bengal, electoral rolls in respect of 46 
assembly constituencies have been prepared/printed with photos of electors. The electoral rolls with 
photographs while on one hand helps establish identity of voters; on the other it eliminated the 
chances of impersonation. 
7.32 During the meetings of the Committee some Members expressed concern about the revision of 
electoral rolls in different Parliamentary as well as the Assemblies Constituencies. It was observed 
that there had been numerous complaints of the voters all over the country about irregularities 
committed in preparation of these rolls. The Committee feels that such irregularity impedes the 
successful implementation of the schemes and should be avoided. The Committee is happy to note 
that the process of revision of the electoral rolls in Assam, West Bengal, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, UT of 
Pondicherry are completed and computerized. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier 
recommendation (para 7.32 of 6th Report) that to overcome such shortcomings, the Election 
Commission should consider establishing its offices  for this purpose at the district levels and 
district level officer would be made accountable for revision of the rolls. The Committee further 
recommends that the process of revision of the electoral rolls must be completed within a 
specific time frame. 
ELECTRONIC VOTING MACHINES (EVMs) 
7.33 The Election commission of India had purchased the Electronic Voting Machines for the first 
time in the year 1989-90 and started their use on experimental basis in November, 1998 onwards only. 
While 
referring to the successful experimental use of Electronic voting Machines in the then held 
Parliamentary and Assembly Elections in many constituencies/States on selective basis, the election 
commission sought to use these machines on regular basis in elections and requested the government 
for making available adequate number of these mach ines so as to over all polling stations in the 
country. 
 Non-plan Budget Estimates for the year 2006 -07 for Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) has 
been increased to Rs. 300 crores as compared to  the allocation of Rs. 100 crore during 2005-06. The 
Government has explained the reason for this variation by stating that this increase has been for 
purchase of new EVMs. The Ministry has also apprised the Committee through their action taken 
reply that upgradation of the Electronic Voting Machines has been completed by the two 
manufacturing firms (i.e. M/s ECIL, Hyderabad and M/s BEL, Bangalore) in consultation with and as 
per the suggestions of the commission. Finally, before approving the upgraded EVMs for use in the 
elections, the upgraded EVMs are being got technically evaluated by an Expert Committee, headed by 
Professor Indiresan, retired Professor, IIT, Delhi. 
7.34 The Committee was informed that some State El ection Commissioners have been requesting to 
provide them with EVMs for conduct of elections  to the local bodies. The Election Commission has 
convened a meeting of all State Election Commissioners at Hyderabad on 18th April, 2005 in which 

the issue of utilization of EVMs in local bodies was also discussed. The Ministry of Law and Justice 
through their Action Taken Reply has said that the decision regarding giving EVMs on loan to the 
State Election Commissions for the local bodies elections on certain terms and conditions has been 
taken and the State Election Commissions of Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tripura, Union Territory of 
Andaman & Nicobar islands and Union Territory of Daman & Diu, were allowed to use EVMs, on 
case to case basis. 
7.35 The Committee feels that being one of the largest democracies of the world, the Ministry 
constant endeavor should be directed to ensure th at elections are held in free and fair manner. 
Necessary infrastructure of which, EVMs constitute  a part should, therefore,  be in place at the 
time of holding elections. The Committee is satisfied that its recommendation for upgradation of 
old EVMs has been implemented by the Mini stry. The Committee hopes that the process 
of procurement of new upgraded EVMs would also be completed as early as possible. 
ELECTORS PHOTO IDENTITY CARDS (EPIC) 
7.36 Issue of Photo Identity Cards to voters is one of the constituents of the budget of the Legislative 
Department. Budget Estimates (Non-plan) for the year 2005-06 under this heading was rupees 72.72 
crores as compared to rupees 42.24 crores during the current financial year (2006-07). After 
comparing the BE of 2005-2006 with the RE 2005-2006 it can be said that due to slow pace of work 
the target fixed was not achieved. The Commission feels that this will continue in the current financial 
year that is why there has been a further decline in the Budget Estimate of 2006-07. 
7.37 The Committee notes that as on the 1st Janua ry, 2005, total electors in the country were 
680,508,403 and the number of the electors, who have been issued with Identity Cards, is 
478,251,225, which constitute 69.87 per cent of  the total voters. Thus, there remains a shortfall 
of nearly 30 per cent of those who are yet to be covered under the EPIC scheme. The Committee 
also notes that the Election Commi ssion has started a campaign fo r this purpose by identifying 
some States for a pilot project. The Committee fe els that the Commission has not achieved the 
desired goals despite the fact that considerable ti me has elapsed since the inception of the EPIC 
scheme. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation (Para No. 7.5 of the 
2nd Report and Para No. 7.37 of  the 6th Report of the Committ ee) that the Commission should 
devise a time-bound programme for achieving 100 per cent EPIC coverage. The Committee also 
feels that a unique multi-purpose identity card is the need of th e day, which can be used by the 
citizens as an all-purpose card for identification , proof of residence, citizenship, date of Birth 
etc. In view of this expenditure incurred on Election photo identity cards, and the time taken for 
achieving the targets, the Committee impressed upon the Ministry for ma king efforts on war 
footing basis for making available the cards to all its citizens.

not be utilized. Accordingly, the Committee in its 2nd Report (Para 66) and 6th Report (Para 7.40)

No.A.45011/13/2001-Adm.I(L.D) dated 29th September, 2004, 21st October, 2004, 20th May, 2005 

and again on 20th March, 2006. The response from the Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty

7.40 The Committee notes with concern that allotm ent of land for building of the Institute of 
Legislative Drafting and Research, for which an  amount of Rs. 1.55 crore was kept in the 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2002-03, has not been materialized so far. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recomm endation that the Mini stry should take up 
this issue on priority basis and make concerted efforts to acquire land for construction of 
building for the Institute. The Ministry should also ensure th at financial constraints to 
materialize the proposal should not come in the way of ma terialization of the proposal. The 
Committee also feels that the Institute should not confine itself to imparting training in India 
only, rather it should think on expanding its area outside India. To begin with, the Institute can 
chalk out a raining programme in legislative dr afting for the neighbori ng Asian Countries so 
that the participants coming to attend such courses can be trained in legislative drafting. Similar 
courses can be run for th e participants coming from the diff erent States. For that purpose, the 
Institute should devise a proper fee structure for running these courses. Similarly, Institute 
should try to explore means by which drafting can be done in oth er regional languages so that it 
can be of a reat help to the State Governments. 
SIMPLIFICATION OF LEGISLATIVE LANGUAGE 
7.41 The Committee notes that the process of simplific ation of laws is the need of the day. The 
Committee observes that legisl ative language is often quite  technical, intricate and 
incomprehensible for the common man for whom la ws are made. It feels that, laws should be 
drafted in national or regional languages to convey th e purpose and intent of framing laws and 
all central laws should be translated into Hindi  in order to make the provisions known to the 
masses. Even a common law country like En gland has started simp lifying its laws. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that  the Ministry should explore 
ways and means to simplify laws so as to be understood even by the people having no specialized 
knowledge of legal formulations. In other words, Legislative Department should act as a catalyst 
for launching a movement for plai n language drafting of laws and instruments of subordinate 
legislation.

8.3 The Committee has been informed that till 1992-93, the budget of the Department of Justice was 
salary oriented. From 1993-94 onwards, the Demands of the Department of Justice also included 

provision for the Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to infrastructure facilities for the judiciary and 
the National Judicial Academy. From 1996-97, provision was also being made for the First National 
Judicial Pay Commission. The Commission has been wound up w.e.f. 1.12.2003. From 2001-02 
onwards the project for computerisation of City Civi l Courts in four metropolitan cities of Chennai, 
Delhi, Mumbai and Kolkata has been included. From  2002-03 onwards specific allocations are being 
made for setting up of Family Courts and for recons truction or extension of High Courts buildings. 
Provision for 50 per cent recurring expenditure on Family Courts under Non-Plan side has been made 
during the year to support the cause of women in view of strong recommendation of the Parliamentary 
Committee on Empowerment of Women. This is being continued in the year 2006-07 also. 
8.4 The Department of Justice is a small Department having staff strength of 37 persons only. The 
Budget Estimates and Revised Estimates of the De partment for the year 2005-06 are Rs.80 lakh and 
Rs.85 lakh respectively. In the Budget Estimates 2006-07, a provision of Rs.90 lakh has been made. 
DELINKING OF DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE FROM THE MINISTRY OF HOME AND 
CREATION OF A SEPARATE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE WITH A FULL TIME 
SECRETARY OF JUSTICE 
8.5 The Committee has been recommending persistently that the Department of Justice should be 
separated from the Home Ministry and provided with a full fledged Secretary of its own. This long 
standing recommendation of the Committee can be traced in its 2nd Report on the Demand for Grants 
of the Ministry of Law and Justice (2004-05) under the heading “Delinking of Budget of Department 
of Justice.” wherein the Committee had observed  “the Committee on Home Affairs has been 
reiterating its view since 1995, either to make the Department of Justice an independent Department 
or to merge its budget with the Ministry of Home Affairs.” 
8.6 The Committee was informed that the Government of India had taken a conscious decision in 
1971 to continue administrative association of the Department of Justice with the Home Ministry. The 
position 
emerging as of now seems to be that the Department of Justice is a full- fledged separate Department 
headed by a Secretary who has to be the Home Secr etary. The position held by the Ministry has been 
that the mere fact that the Home Secretary holds ad ditional charge of the Department of Justice, does 
not affect the status of the Department as an independent full-fledged Department. 
8.7. The Committee on Home Affairs also in its 86th Report had made detailed observations that, 
“the Committee has been persistently recommending to set right the anomaly relating to the budget 
presentation 
and administrative control over Department of Justice since 1995 through its 17th Report (1995), 31st 
and 34th Reports (1996), 39th Report (1997), 45th  Report (1998), 56th Report (1999), 61st Report 
(2000), 69th and 72nd Report (2001) to either make it an independent Department or merge the budget 
with the Ministry of Home Affair.” While making final recommendations the Committee on Home 
Affairs had observed that it finds it difficult to understand the advantages for the Government in 
keeping the anomaly intact. The need and justification for making the Department of Justice a full-
fledged Department with a Secretary of its own was thus explained by the Committee on the 5th April, 
2006 as under:- 
“What is the rationale behind attaching the Justice Department to the Home Ministry? 
Today, the Home Ministry is the busiest Ministry in the entire set up of the Government. 
Problems have grown beyond our expectations. New issues have cropped up. Today, the 
very security of the country is at stake. Naxalism has developed beyond our imagination and 
scale. Today, our hands are full with problems and it is no exaggeration if it is said that 
howsoever devotional we may be, we will not be able to give full attention to the Department 
of Justice, which also deserves much more gr eater attention today than at any time in the 

past. It is beyond doubt when we say that the time has come that we should think of 
separation of Justice Department from Home and create a separate full-fledged Department 
of Justice, with a full-fledged Secretary devoted fully to this Department. It is unfair to the 
Home Secretary to burden the Justice Department when their contribution can only be in 
improving governance in various States and making sure that court dealings are done. It is 
earnestly suggested that the Government should take a policy decision on this issue as there 
is a valid reason for this.” 
8.8 From the above observations, the Committ ee finds it reasonable to deduce that the 
rationale behind keeping the Department of Ju stice under the Administrative control of the 
Home Secretary might has been logical at that ti me but the situation has gone sea change since 
then. Keeping in view the fact th at the department of Justice has been assigned a distinct task 
under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Committee 
understands and notes that the Department of Ju stice has been performing sensitive functions 
pertaining to judiciary and the administration of justice. Seen in this context and also of the fact 
that there are about 3 crore cases pending in different courts thus shaking the faith of the people 
in the judicial system, it would be more appropri ate if the Department is  accorded a distinct 
identity including strong administ rative structure of its own. It  is in this context that the 
Committee is of the considered opinion that for the sake of administrative efficiency and 
exigency, the Department is separated from the Home Ministry and provided with a full-fledged 
Secretary. It this context the Committee again reit erates and recommends that it is a high time 
that this long standing recomm endation is implemented in le tter and spirit with immediate 
effect. 
PLAN SCHEMES 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to infrastructural 
Facilities for the judiciary 
8.9 The Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the development of infrastructure facilities for the 
judiciary is being implemented by this Department since 1993-94. The scheme includes construction 
of court- 
buildings and residential accommodation for judicial officers/judges covering High Courts and 
Subordinate Courts. The expenditure on the scheme is shared by the Central and the State 
Governments on 50:50 asis. The Central share is however restricted to the allocations made as per 
criterion laid down by the Planning Commission. However, the States are free to spend more amounts. 
Expenditure in respect of the Union Territories is fully met by the Centre. 
8.10 From 1993-94 upto 2003-04, an amount of Rs. 631.39 crore has been released to various 
States/UTs. With the matching States’ share, (Union  Territories are not required to provide matching 
share) the 
States/UTs were required to spend an amount of Rs. 1071.12 crore on the basis of release upto  
2002-03. The State Governments/Union Territories are expected to submit the Utilization Certificates 
within 18 months from the date of release of an amount. Against this, the State Governments and 
Union Territories have spent an amount of Rs. 1162.34 crore upto 31.12.2004. 
8.11 So far, 91 extension buildings in various High Courts have been completed and work on 17 
extension buildings is in progress. About 125 judges’ residences of various High Courts have been 
completed and work in respect of 175 residences is going on. As regards Subordinate Judiciary, 1037 
District/Subordinate Court complexes have been completed and construction work on 986 
District/Subordinate Courts is in progress. As many  as 2061 residential quarters for judicial officers 
have been completed whereas work on 1410 residential quarters is in progress. 

8.12 The Committee feels that the Centrally Spons ored Scheme relating to infrastructural 
facilities, though started in 1993-94, has not b een executed effectively due to the absence of a 
proper planning. Similarly, availability of Stat e Governments’ matching share for the scheme 
has been a problem area. Consequently, the succe ss of implementation of the scheme has not 
been assessed properly. As informed by the Depa rtment of Justice, there was no focussed or 
final target for completion of physical infrastructure,  and States have defaulted in providing 
matching share in time. It ha s been decided on the advice of the Planning Commission to 
prepare a 10 year perspective plan for the required physical infrastructure state-wise. The 
Committee welcomes the move of the Ministry but  a t  t h e  s a m e  t i m e  i t  c a u t i o n s  t h a t  t h e  
perspective plan should not be a mere pretext to lengthen implem entation of the scheme. There 
should be proper monitoring of the scheme in te rms of achievement of ta rgets, allocation of 
funds etc. This is more so because the Committ ee has been given to understand that even the 
basic infrastructural facilities li ke transport and Housing are not available to the Magistrates 
and Judges at lower judiciary level and they have to encounter many difficulties. These 
infrastructural lacunae may hamp er to a great extent, their functioning. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation (P ara 8.8 6th Report) that the Ministry should 
consider all these components seriously and include them in the perspective plan. 
COMPUTERISATION OF JUDICIARY 
8.13 The Committee has been apprised that an improved case management technique and extensive 
computerisation have reduced Supreme Court’s arr ears from 1.05 lakh cases in 1991 to 29,315 cases 
in 
July, 2004. As regards pace of computerisation in  High Courts and subordinate Courts it requires 
upgradation and new-generation hardware. The computerization of subordinate courts, civil and 
criminal, has been implemented so far in two stages. About 700 city courts in four metros such as 
Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai have been comp uterized at a cost of Rs. 17.26 crore. Another 
900 courts located in state capitals, or in cities where the High Court is stationed, have been covered 
under computerization programme launched during 2003 -04 of the Department of Justice at a cost of 
Rs. 24.24 crore. 
8.14 There are in total 14,948 subordinate courts, including 1734 Fast Track Courts, which function 
at the district-level and below. Excluding the aforesaid 1600 courts, which are being computerized by 
the 
Department of Justice, there is a balance of 13, 348 courts which require Rs. 384.53 crore for their 
computerization. 
8.15 When these courts are com puterized with appropriate local area network and wider area 
network, and the accessory systems are in place, then all the judicial courts in the country, from the 
apex to the lowest, will be computerized on one electronic grid. 
8.16 NIC has prepared a detailed project report for the computerization of the remaining 13,348 
courts. It will require a sum of Rs. 384.53 crore at  the estimated cost of around Rs. 3 lakh per court. 
The Department of Justice has circulated the EFC memo for approval of this project. 
8.17 In the 2004-05 budget of the Department of Just ice, there is an outlay of Rs. 110 crore in R.E. 
out of which it is proposed to re- appropriate Rs. 103.05 crore for the computerization of 3475 
subordinate courts. The Planning Commission has provided ‘in principle’ approval for this project. 
 Meanwhile, the government constituted an E-Committee to advise on technological 
communication and management related changes in the judiciary. The E-Committee submitted its 
report on National Policy and Action Plan for implementation of Information and Communicatien 
Technology in the Indian judiciary at  a cost of Rs. 854 crores in three phases spread over a period of 
five years. In view of E-Committee’s proposal, the project of computerization of District and 
Subordinate courts was kept in abeyance and the NI C was directed to implement the proposal of the 

E-Committee. The Government has prepared a revise d proposal for computerisation of the Indian 
Judiciary on the Action Plan of the E-Committee. 
8.18 For the year 2005-2006, in BE, Out of Rs. 22 0.00 crore, an amount Rs. 214.00 crore (Rs. 192.00 
crore computerisation + & 22.00 crore for NE) was ear marked for computerisation of district courts. 
In the RE stage, this has been reduced and out of  Rs. 100.00 crore, an amount of Rs. 86.16 crore has 
been earmarked for Computerisation of district & subordinate courts. For the BE 2006-2007, Out of 
total plan allocation of this Department, amount of  Rs. 137.95 crore is kept for computerisation of 
district & subordinate courts. 
8.19 The Committee expresses satisfaction over the pace of computerisation of the City Courts 
in four metropolitan cities of Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai and in  the courts located in 
the State capitals or in cities where the High Co urts are located. The Committee, however, feels 
that the rate of computerisation in the subordinate courts including the Fast Track Courts need 
to be augmented. The Committee is of the view that computerisation of judiciary would be an 
effective tool to bring down pe ndency of cases as has been ex perienced in the Supreme Court. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that th e Ministry should ensure that necessary 
budgetary allocations for this pur pose should be made and the targets set to computerise the 
entire judicial system are met. 
FAMILY COURTS 
8.20 The Family Courts Act, 1984 mandates setting up of Family Courts in areas with a population of 
one million or more or in such places where it is deemed necessary. The Parliamentary Committee on 
Empowerment of Women in their Twelfth report has recommended setting up of a least one Family 
Court in each District throughout the country. As on date, 159 Family Courts have been set up all over 
the country. During the year 2004, these family cour ts disposed of 93502 cases out of which 27939 
ended in reconciliation of family disputes. The Central Government bears 50 percent of the cost of 
construction of Family Court building and also the annual recurring cost of running such Family 
Courts. The State Governments have been requested to set up as many Family Courts as possible. 
During the year  005-06 an amount of Rs. 95 lakh was provided in BE which was reduced to Rs. 85 
lakh in RE. Out of Rs. 85.00 lakh, Rs. 30.00 lakh was being released to the States. About setting up of 
a family court in Goa the Committee was informed that as per the Family Court Act, 1984 family 
courts are set up by the States in the cities having population exceeding one million. 
8.21 The Committee feels that the present position  of setting up of the Family Courts is not 
satisfactory. The Committee, therefore, reiterat es its earlier recommendation (Para 8.18 6th 
Report) that Ministry should fix a target for es tablishing at least one Family Court in each 
district so as to resolve family disputes and rel ated matters expeditiously and in order to do so 
the Committee recommends to amend the relevant provision of the Family Court Act, 1984 
pertaing to eligibility criteria of population ex ceeding one million for setting up of a family 
court, so that at least one family court is set in each district particularly, in the states like Goa.
