PENDENCY OF CASES 
8.24 As per the latest information available as  on November/December, 20 05, 33,635 cases were 
pending in the Supreme Court; 34,24,518 in different High Courts and 2.44 crore cases were pending 
in the ubordinate Judiciary. 
8.25 The Government has taken the following steps to clear the pendency:- 
 (a) The Government has been constantly reviewing the accumulation of arrears in Courts. 
Besides increasing th e Judges’ strength from time to time, various steps have been 
taken by the Courts, viz; grouping of cases involving common questions of law, 
constitution of specialized benches and organizing Lok Adalats at regular intervals, 
etc. 
 (b) The Government has also encouraged alternative modes of disposal including 
mediation, negotiation and arbitration. Special tribunals like Central Administrative 
Tribunal, State 
Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family Courts, Labour 
Courts, Consumer Courts etc. have been set up to expedite disposal of cases. 
Information technology is being used in generation of cause lists, providing 
information to the litigants/Advocates etc. for speedy disposal of cases. 
 (c) Fast Track Courts (FTC) for the disposal  of long pending cases, particularly sessions 
cases and cases involving under trials in jails are being set up. 
 (d) Central Government has sanctioned a grant of Rs. 502.90 crore, based on the 
recommendations of the Eleventh Finance Commission, for the creation of 1734 Fast 
Track Courts in the country. 
8.26 The Committee on Home Affairs in their 101st Report and the Committee on Personnel, Public 
Grievances, Law and Justice in their 2nd & 6th Reports, respectively, on Demands for Grants for  
2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06 of the Department of Ju stice had urged upon the Government to consider 
fresh initiatives to arrest pendency of cases in various courts. Government had initiated some 
measures to arrest and clear such pendency. It ha d also requested the State Governments/High Courts 
to earmarks portion of the Fast Track Courts to dispose of senior citizen’s cases, on priority basis. 
8.27 The Committee notes that notwithstanding its persistent recommendations to reduce 
pendency of the cases before the Supreme Court,  High Courts and the various subordinate 
courts all 
over the country, there has not been any major b reakthrough in the matter. Year after year, 
particularly from 1999 onwards the pendency of  cases has been conti nuously increasing except 
the Supreme Court where pendency has been arres ted to some extent due to extensive 
computerisation and a host of other initiatives.  The above trend is continuing inspite of a 
number of alternative me asures taken like setting up of fast  track courts, family courts and 
permanent Lok Adalats and disposal of a cons iderable number of cases by these courts. The 
Committee has been apprised that the Govern ment has been constantly reviewing the 
accumulation of arrears in Courts and the proble m is sought to be tack led by constitution of 

specialized benches and organizing Lok Adalats at  regular intervals; encouraging alternative 
modes of disposal, establishing Fast Track Courts and the proposed Gram Nyayalayas Bill 2006 
etc. The Committee finds that specialised benche s, Lok Adalats and Fast Track courts though 
created as an alternative mode of disposal of arrears of cases have been suffering due to 
infrastructural lacunae or financial constraints and thus are not able to meet the desired targets. 
The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation to call upon the Ministry to 
address the problem of pendency of cases by ca refully analysing the factors responsible and 
searching viable solutions in addition to the existing arrangements. 
VACANCIES OF JUDGES 
8.28 As against the sanctioned strength of 26 J udges, the Supreme Court of India has 23 Judges in 
position, leaving three vacancies to be filled up, as on 22.3.2006. 
8.29 In the High Courts, against the sanctioned strength of 675 Judges, 567 Judges are in position, 
leaving 108 vacancies to be filled up, as on 22.3.2006. 
8.30 Pursuant to the Supreme Court Judgement of October 6, 1993, read with their Advisory Opinion 
of October 28, 1998, the process of initiation of pr oposal for appointment of Judges of Supreme Court 
lies with the Chief Justice of India and for appointm ent of Judges in a High Court, it lies with the 
Chief Justices of respective High Courts. The Government has been requesting the Chief Justices of 
the High Courts, Chief Ministers and Governors of the States, from time to time, to initiate proposals 
for 
filling up of the present as well as the anticipated vacancies, during the next six months. 
8.31 The Committee held detailed deliberations on the procedure for filling up of vacant posts of 
judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts, as per the pre and post 1993 dispensations. 
The Committee noted that this issue has been engaging the attention of the Committee on Home 
Affairs since long, as also of the present Committee. The Committee on Home Affairs examined the 
subject in detail in its Eighty-fifth Report on Laws Delay: Arrears in Courts. That Committee was, 
inter alia, of the view that the delays in judicial appointment was a matter of serious public concern 
and pointed out that the failure to fill up judicial vacancies promptly could not be shielded or defended 
in the name of judicial independence (Para 32.2 ibid) 
8.32 The Committee observes that there has not been any perceptible improvement in the 
position of vacancies of Judges in Supreme Court and High Courts under the post 1993 
arrangement. The Committee feels that time  has come when the issue has not only 
to be deliberated at the highest level, but also to be debated in  the public domain so that there 
could emerge an alternative system which co uld bring about an overall improvement in the 
situation. The Committee, therefore, calls upon th e Ministry to come forward with a concrete 
alternative, addressing the issue of appointment of Judges of th e higher judiciary by evolving a 
suitable mechanism through the Executive d ecision with judicial scrutiny, instead of  allowing 
the judiciary alone to choose the judges. This can avoid a vicious circle created in the judiciary 
so that the vacancies could be filled up on the date of their occurrence. 
BENCHES OF SUPREME COURT 
8.33 The Committee has been recommending time and again for setting up of benches of the 
Supreme Court in far-flung areas, with a view to  providing justice to th e poor, for whom it is 
impossible to visit the national capital. The Committee’s recommendations for setting up of benches 
of Supreme Court in Southern, Western and North-Ea stern parts of the country have been considered 
by the Supreme Court and they found no justification in setting up benches of the Supreme Court. 
8.34 The Committee, in its Second and Sixth Report, dealt with the issue and felt that establishment 
of benches of Supreme Court in Southern, Wester n and North-Eastern parts of the country would 
facilitate 
the litigants to avail justice from the apex court, without traveling to Delhi from far away places. The 

Committee, accordingly, recommended that Government should decide its course of action to resolve 
the matter expeditiously. 
8.35 In its Action Taken reply to the above recommendation, Department of Justice has informed the 
Committee that the subject matter of establishing benches of the Supreme Court in other parts of the 
country was discussed at a full meeting of the Hon’ble Judges and that the full court is of the 
considered opinion that the demand for establishment of the benches of the Supreme Court can not be 
accepted. 
8.36 The Committee is not satisfied with the persis tent opposition for es tablishing benches of 
the Supreme Court in other parts of the country  without giving any convincing reasons or 
justification 
thereof. The Committee, therefore, endorses its earlier view that establishment of benches of the 
Supreme Court in other parts of the country woul d be of immense help to the poor who cannot 
afford to travel from their na tive places to Delhi. The Committee, therefore, feels that the 
Ministry should come forward with a necessary Constitutional  amendment to address this 
deadlock. 
FAST TRACK COURTS 
8.37 The Eleventh Finance Commission had sanctioned setting up of 1711 Fast Track Courts, for 
expeditious trial of long pending sessions cases and also cases involving under trials, who remain in 
jails for a period of more than two years. By the close of the financial year 2005-06, 1562 courts had 
become functional. They have disposed 8 lakh cases, out of 15.28 lakh cases, transferred to them. The 
Fast Track Courts were started on the basis of the recommendation by the Eleventh Finance 
Commission for the period 2000-05.  
8.38 The Committee has been apprised by the Department of Justice through their detailed 
explanatory note that the term of the Fast Track Courts, recommended by Eleventh Finance 
Commission, expired on 31.3.2005. As the Twelfth Finance Commission had not made any 
recommendation for the continuation of the Fast Trac k Courts, Department of Justice proposed to 
continue the 1562 Fast Track Courts, which were functional as on 31.3.2005, for a further period of 5 
years i.e. upto 31.3.2010 with a provision of Rs. 509 crores and the same was approved by the 
Government. 
8.39 The Committee in its 6th Report on the Demand for Grants (2005-06) had also recommended 
(Para 8.40) in favour of continuance to the Fast  Track Courts. The scheme was jeopardized in the 
lurch after the expiry of the term of the Eleventh  Finance Commission as there was no mention of any 
recommendation for continuity of the scheme in the Report of the Twelfth Finance Commission 
beyond 31st March, 2005. It appears that the Department of Justice acted upon the assumption that 
Twelfth Finance Commission would adopt a positive approach in this case. However, the report of the 
Twelfth Finance Commission could not be made available before finalization of the budget process of 
the Department as a result of which the Department could not get time to pursue it further. The 
Committee then gave the recommendation that the Department of Justice should vigorously pursue 
this issue with the Ministry of Finance or the Planning Commission and till the scheme is finalized, 
take up the matter with the State Governments for providing funds to be reimbursed subsequently by 
the Central Government. The Committee feels satisfied that the Government has given extension to 
Fast Track Courts for another five year i.e. beyond 2010 otherwise the good job done by the FTC and 
purpose for its creation would have been defeated. The Supreme Court also had at that time enquired 
from the Government about the state of further extension of the scheme. 
8.40 The Committee is satisfied that extension has been given to the 1562 Fast Track Courts by 
the Twelfth Finance Commission for a further p eriod of 5 years. The Committee hopes that the 
Department of Justice would be monitoring functioning of the Fast Track Courts. 

 The Committee further notes that there ar e some anomalies in absorbing Fast Track 
Court Judges on regular basis in the mainstre am of the Judiciary. Thus the Committee feels 
that it should be looked into  by the Ministry and anomalies,  i f  a n y ,  s h o u l d  b e  a d d r e s s e d  
properly. 
THE JUDICIARY IN INDIA : AN OVERVIEW 
Judiciary - From Supreme Court to Subordinate Courts 
8.41 The Preamble to the Constitution of India adopted in the Constituent Assembly on 26 
November, 1949, provides to resolve to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic 
Republic and to secure to all its citizens justice-social, economic and political. 
8.42 The concept relating to “separation of power s between the Legislature, the Executive and the 
Judiciary’ as well as the fundamental concept of an independent judiciary are elevated to the level of 
basic tructure of the Constitution. To achieve the purpose of imparting justice to the common man, the 
Supreme Court of India as an Apex Court, and the 21 High Courts as well as Subordinate Courts have 
been established. 
8.43 The Constitution initially provided for a Chief Justice of India and not more than 7 Judges in the 
Supreme Court. However, with the passage of time, and keeping in view the quantum of work in the 
Supreme Court, the number of judges in the Supreme Court has been raised to 26. 
8.44 Appointment of judges in the Supreme Court of India is made by the President under article 124 
of the Constitution, after consultation with Supreme Court/ High Court Judges, except the 
appointment of Chief Justice of India himself. 
8.45 Article 214 of the Constitution provides that there shall be a High Court for each State. 
However, article 231 also provides that Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for 
two or more States, or for two or more States and a Union Territory. In keeping with these provisions, 
there were only 18 High Courts all over the countr y till November, 2000, number of which rose to 21 
on the creation of 3 new States. 
8.46 Appointment of Permanent Judges and Additional Judges of High Courts are made by the 
President under article 217 and article 224 of the Constitution, respectively, after consultation with 
State constitutional uthorities/Chief Justice of the High Court and after consultation with the Chief 
Justice of India. 
8.47. Under article 235 of the Constitution of Indi a, the administrative control over the members of 
Subordinate Judicial Service vests with the concerned High Court. Further, in exercise of powers 
conferred under proviso to article 309 read with articles 233 of the Constitution, the State Government 
frames rules and regulations in consultation with the High Court. The members of the State Judicial 
Service are governed by these rules and regula tions. Therefore, the service conditions, including 
appointment, promotion etc., of judicial officers of  the District/Subordinate Courts are governed by 
the respective State Governments. It has been observed that at any given point of time, 25-30 percent 
of the vacancies in the Subordinate Courts remain unfilled. 
8.48 The Department of Justice, Union Ministry of Law and Justice which deals with appointment of 
judges and their conditions of services as well as various courts in the country, has taken some major 
initiatives to address the problem of delay in cour ts and huge pendency of cases. The initiatives are 
both for seeking long-term solutions as well as for dealing with the immediate problem of pendency. 
8.49 The Indian judiciary comprises of nearly 15,0 00 courts situated in approximately 2,500 court 
complexes throughout the country. The total pend ency of cases in these Courts as on the 31st 
December, 2005 was 2,91,21,117; the individual break up being - Supreme Court- 33,635; High 
Courts- 35,31,774 and the District and Subordinate Courts- 2,55,55,704. 

8.50 Judiciary is always held responsible for mounting arrears of Court cases. But, it doesn’t control 
the resources of funds and has no power to create additional Courts, appoint adequate Court staff and 
augment the infrastructure required for the Courts. Ideally, judiciary should have autonomy with 
regard to the creation of posts, allocation of budget and incurring of expenditure. However, Financial 
Autonomy at to the High Courts always remains a distant dream. 
8.51 Stagnation in courts, particularly lower judiciary, where more than 22 million cases are pending, 
and high transaction cost due to such delay, ultimately lead to denial the justice to the poor and 
disadvantaged. This is the core concern, which warrants judicial reform. Presently the reform projects 
are being monitored by two national-level Steering Committees headed by sitting-Judges of the 
Supreme Court of India. In every state, where the project is being implemented, there is a Project 
Monitoring Committee (PMC) headed by a sitting judge of the High Court of that state. 
8.52 The objective of judicial reform is to enhance judicial productivity both qualitatively and 
quantitatively by eliminating arrears and making the justice delivery system affordable, accessible, 
cost effective, transparent and accountable. Due to la ck of scientific data about judicial process in the 
form of real time judicial statistics performance au dit of the Judiciary as an institution and individual 
judges is difficult. This onstitutes a significant stumbling block for addressing the problem of judicial 
arrears. Currently real time data about cases can be made available through information technology 
tools and this is being currently addressed by the Government. 
8.53 There is a need for measures to rationalize an d standardize the infrastructure of the courts. The 
need of proper facilities, particularly at mufassils or  at taluka level in backward areas is imminent as 
there, most of the courts function from dingy, dilapidated and outdated structures with poor hygienic 
conditions even for judicial officers, not to mention Members of the Bar or litigants and witnesses. 
The Indian State in the 21st century, flush with economic boom, must meet the modern standards in 
courts’ infrastructure the world over and provid e ‘Plan’ funds in ratio commensurate to the 
requirements. 
8.54 The e-Committee, set up by the Union Government to advice on technological communication 
and management related changes, has submitted its National Policy and Action Plan for 
implementation of nformation and Communication Tech nology (ICT) in the Indian Judiciary at a cost 
of 854 crores in three phases spreading over a period of 5 years. 
8.55 Based on the National Policy and Action Plan, a revised proposal for computerisation of the 
Indian Judiciary has been prepared for the cons ideration of the Expenditure Finance Committee and 
submitted for the approval in December, 2005. 
8.56 There was an overwhelming realization in the judicial sector in favour of devising a National 
Policy and Action Plan with appropriate spread and phasing to implement Information and 
Communication Technology (ICT) in courts across the country and their web-based interlinking.  
8.57 Based on the inputs received from persons having expertise in diverse domains relevant for 
change management in India Judiciary, the E-Committee framed the national Policy and Action Plan 
for mplementation of Information and Communication Technology in the Indian Judiciary. 
8.58 The Department of Justice, Union Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India has taken 
up the computerization of the 29 Capital City Courts in technical cooperation with the National 
Informatics 
Centre. The computerization project of Capital City Co urts in States and Union Territories is a central 
scheme with 100 per cent funding from the Central Government. The scope of the Capital City Courts 
Computerisation is to develop, deliver, install and implement automated Decision-making and 
Decision support Systems in all the 900 courts located  at capitals States and Union Territories. It will 
help the judicial administration in streamlining its routine activities, reduce the pendency of case by 
implementing appropriate automated process, and pr ovide easy and transparen t information access to 
litigant public. 

 The objectives of the Scheme are :— 
 (i) To help the judicial administration of the District and Subordinate Courts of States 
and Union Territories in streamlining their day to day activities,  
 (ii) To assist the judicial administra tion in reducing the pendency of cases. 
 (iii) To provide transparency of information to the litigants,  
 (iv) To enhance access of judges to legal and judicial databases. 
8.59 The plan scheme of the Government - Ce ntrally Sponsored Scheme for Development of 
Infrastructure in Judiciary includes construction of  court buildings and residential accommodation for 
Judges/Judicial Officers, covering High Courts and subordinate Courts. The Central Government’s 
share is restricted to the funds made available by  the Planning Commission and the expenditure under 
the Scheme is hared by the Central and State Governments on 50:50 basis. 
8.60 The Union Ministry of Law and Justice also proposes to provide for the establishment of Gram 
Nyayalayas at the Panchayats at intermediate level. The Gram Nyayalayas will have both criminal and 
civil jurisdiction. The Gram Nyayalayas will also have jurisdiction to try all original suits of civil 
nature as the lowest courts. This will address th e problem of access to justice to the women and rural 
masses who have no means of seeking redressal through the existing judicial process. 
8.61 The Supreme Court in the Salem Bar Association Vs Union of India has given certain directions 
to the Central and State Governments with respect to providing funds for the creation of more courts 
and anpower for the Judiciary and also to assess the impact of legislation upon the courts. The 
directions have been circulated to the States and Departments and the Ministry of Law and Justice is 
in the process of finalizing its views. 
Role of Registry of Supreme Court 
8.62 The Committee, in its meeting held on 4th April, 2006 observed as under:- 
"........ The Supreme Court Regist ry can call for the data keep ing in view th e subordinate 
courts also. We need not depend upon the pre ss reports, where there is a comment that the 
lower courts are not having even a manual typewriter. There is no need for agitation. These 
types of reports need not come. This is the work of the Ministry of Law. But we can have 
firsthand information from the Supreme Court Registry regarding the subordinate judiciary 
in this matter. It can make a mega plan and present it to the Committee. We will study it and 
submit in our eport so that the Parliament and the Government can be asked to deal with that 
subject. That is why we want everything to be sorted out here within the four walls of this 
Parliamentary system instead of having everything being commented upon by the press and 
media. That is the roblem we are facing. That is  why we want to thrash out the points within 
the four walls so that we can think about it an d we can have some arrangement for it. In the 
same way, the Chief Justices, the Law Ministers and others say about the pending litigations, 
accumulation of cases and huge a rrears of cases. All these things can be made up in a better 
way as a report and if it comes from the Supreme Court Registry, the Committee and the 
Parliament can consider it. That will have the authenticity and that can be taken into 
consideration by the Parliament. That can be looked into and discussed.........". 
8.63 In view of the facts mentioned in the fo regoing paragraphs, the Committee is of the 
opinion that there should be so me body/agency which would appr ise the concerned authorities 
of the needs of the subordinate j udiciary, which are being neglected on some pretext or other at 
the macro level. The Committee expresses the desire that Government should evolve a 
mechanism for having an overall view of the needs/hindrances of the judicieary by inviting an in 
house deliberation. 

8.64 The Committee is seized of the fact that Chie f Justices Conferences ar e convened periodically 
by the Chief Justice of India. Heads of Judiciar y in the States meet and deliberate under the 
Chairmanship of the Chief Justice of India, in th e presence of two senior most Judges of the Apex 
Court and take policy decisions on the matters which are vital to and which materially affect the 
functioning of Judicial dministration. 
8.65 In that backdrop the Committee recommends th at a Conference of all Registries of the 
High Courts and Administrative  Heads of Subordinate/Lower co urts should be convened at 
least once in a year under the overa ll supervision of the Registry of the S.C. The authorities can 
ventilate the problems faced by them and narrate  the bottlenecks, while participating in such 
fora. This would ensure that the benefits would percolate down to the lower Courts also. In 
order to achieve this object ive, the Committee recommends that the Supreme Court Registry 
can call for the data, keeping in view the needs of the subordinate Courts also. 
Role of Ministry of Law and Justice 
8.66 The Committee further recommends that the De partment of Justice, Ministry of Law and 
Justice can provide necessary infrastructure and funds for convening such conferences annually 
on the line of seminars of Collectors/District Magistrates being organize d by the Ministry of 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. Wh en such efforts are made, the Ministry can 
consider the needs of the lower judiciary in a better and effective manner and place them before 
the Committee for consideration. The Committee is confident that these discussions would 
certainly prove to be a milestone for the Departme nt of Justice for formulating policy decisions 
in the matter of Judicial Reforms. 
JUDICIAL REFORMS 
8.67 After introduction of economic reforms and globalisation and revolutionary technological 
innovations, new challenges and complexities have cropped up before Indian Judicial System 
imposing enormous urden upon the courts. As the so ciety has become more aware, the law, the image 
of the court system and administration of justice suffer a loss of  public confidence. In this context, it 
has become all the more important that the grey areas confronting Indian Judiciary need prompt 
attention. 
8.68 The Committee feels that it is time to consid er application of the principles and techniques 
of modern management in solving some prom inent problems like law’s inordinate delays, 
arrears of cases and increased workflow in the court system. This requires scientific study of the 
problems. For this, the judiciary is required to develop skills to manage its resources, setting 
targets and evolving concepts like case management and time  management. Simultaneously 
there is need to increase output. 
8.69 The Committee has been informed that the Judges in the United Kingdom and the United States 
of America has applied some innovative methods. These methods have been successful in certain 
areas. For xample, Annual Judicial Statistics Report, published by the Chief Justices in the United 
Kingdom and the United States every year, help to enable the public to understand the performance of 
the judiciary. imilarly, in the United States, every Bill is accompanied by Judicial Impact Statement 
describing the likely effect of the legislation upon the workload of the courts. The Committee also 
notes that the Electronic udicial Resource Management is gaining importance and it has been found 
the most effective tool for judicial  reforms. In Indian context, no new legislation is required as the 
Information Technology Act 2000 has already incorporated the requisite provisions. 
8.70 The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlie r (Para 8.48, 6th Report) view that the above 
measures would have significant impact on ref orming the Indian Judi cial System and the 
Ministry should, explore the possibility of introducing these methods. 

ALL INDIA JUDICIAL SERVICE 
8.71 During the discussion a point was raised regarding setting up of All India Judicial Service. In a 
written reply, the Committee was informed that the 1st, 8th and 11th Law Commissions had inter-alia 
recommended the formation of All India Judicial  Service. The Supreme Court of India also 
recommended vide its judgments delivered on 13th November, 1991 in W.P. No. 1022 of 1989 and 
24th August, 1993 in Review Petition No. 249/92 in the matter of All India Judges Association for 
setting up of an All India Judicial Service. 
 The Ministry has also stated that as the creati on of an All India Service requires cooperation of 
the State Governments and the High Courts, their views were sought earlier. Most of the States did not 
support creation of All India Judicial Service. The National Commission to Review the Working of 
the Constitution submitted its report on this matter stating that after examining the responses received 
from the public and after detailed deliberations, the Commission decided that the formation of All 
India Judicial Service would not be a better alternat ive to the present system. In the light of these 
observations of the National Commission, the matter of formation of All India Judicial Service could 
not be proceeded with. The Government has further stated that as the matter of creation of an All India 
Service is gaining momentum, the proposal for setting up of an All India Judicial Service is proposed 
to be re-examined on merits after ascertaining views of the all concerned including consultations with 
Hon’ble Chief Justice of India and the State Governments. 
8.72 In view of the position explained by the Ministry the Committee recommends that all out 
efforts, including the amendment in Constitution, if necessary, may be taken up expeditiously to 
set up All India Judicial Service. The Committ ee presumes that the consultations with the 
Ministry of Finance, Mi nistry of personnel, Public Grievan ces and Pensions and also the UPSC 
would be necessary in the matter. 
CHANGING THE NAMES OF SOME HIGH COURTS 
8.73 Some Members of the Committee raised the issu e of changing the nomenclatures of the Madras, 
Calcutta and Bombay High Courts in view of the fact that after renaming of the Metropolitan Cities of 
Madras, Calcutta and Bombay as Chennai, Kolkata an d Mumbai respectively, there is a need to bring 
in corresponding changes in the names of the High Courts situated in these cities. It was argued that if 
names of these High Courts remain the same it may create confusion and mislead the public and 
appear to be anachronistic. 
8.74 The Committee, therefore impresses, upon the Ministry to consider initiating necessary 
action for changing the names of the Madras, Calcutta and Bombay High Courts in line with the 
official names of these metropolitan cities. The Committee feels that this is an administrative 
matter and must be changed as early as poss ible as recommended by the Committee in its 
previous report. 
DEMAND NO. 62 : SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
8.75 Demand No. 62 in the detailed Demands of Grants of the Ministry pertains to the Supreme 
Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the Supreme Court of India is ‘Charged’. The total 
Budget Estimates of the Supreme Court of India fo r the year 2006-07 under the Revenue Section are 
Rs. 43.27 crore as against Rs. 42.21 crore in Revised Estimates for the year 2005-06. 
8.76 The Committee held discussion with the Represen tatives of the Registry of Supreme Court on 
their Demand for Grants. The Regist ry Stated that since the number  of employee working in Session 
Court was limited, the expenditure was limited and more over, any additional amount required, the 
same is granted at Revised Estimate Stage.  
8.77 The Committee was also apprised that Computeris ation of all the courts up to Magistrate level 
was in full swing and was being implemented through NIC with estimated cost of Rs. 105 crore. They 
had lso been working on Video Conferencing facility to expedite the judicial process. The Committee 

was also apprised about the constitution of an e-Committee by the Government to advice on 
technological, 
communication and management related changes in the Judiciary. The Committee had already 
submitted its report on the National Policy and Action Plan for implementation of Information and 
Communication 
Technology in the Judiciary and the same was under consideration. The Registry also briefed the 
Committee about their separate website on which latest judgments had been made available for the 
public. 
8.78 The Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice while discussing the Demand 
for Grants (2006-2007) of the Ministry of Law and Justice held its meeting on 4th April 2006, heard 
the views/ suggestions of the representative of the Registry of the Supreme Court who gave its 
presentation on the subject. After their presentation was over some Members of the Committee asked 
some questions, the Registry of the Supreme Court had promised that the information would be sent in 
due course. In the meantime, the Committee vide its letter No. RS. 3/2/2006/P&L dated 13th April 
2006 has asked the Registry, Supreme Court to send information regarding some queries by the 
Members latest y 21st April, 2006. Later on the Registry of the Supreme Court through their letter 
dated 18th April 2006 communicated the Committee Secretariat as follows: 
“As regards your request to supply the information asked for during the meeting, it is stated 
that most of the information is to be collected from various High Courts which is likely to 
consume some time and therefore, it cannot be sent before 21st April, 2006. It would be sent 
as soon as the requisite information is made available to this office.” 
8.79 The Committee endorses with the view of th e Supreme Court that the collection of data 
from various High Courts of the country is certainly a time consuming one, but the Committee 
also feels that the requisite information must be gathered as early as possible and submitted 
before the Committee. The Committe e also feels that the Supreme Court Journals, containing 
all important judgements and cases should be  publicized and commercialized to get wider 
publicity and even unreported cases should also get references in th e journals. In the same way, 
different High Courts of the country can also  publicize and commercialized their judgements 
and cases through their journals and can make reference of unreported cases in that.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee undertook study visit to all the North -Eastern States (except Mizoram) 
to assess the infrastructural facilities available in those states. The Committee found that 
among the North -Eastern States, Meghalaya has performed best in terms of utilizati on of 
funds under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for creation of infrastructural facilities for su b-
ordinate judiciary. The process followed by Meghalaya in terms of compliance of the cond i-
tions laid down by the Department of Justice and Ministry of Finance  for release of funds, 
needs to be emulated by others to derive maximum benefit from the Scheme.   (Recommenda-
tion No. vi) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 The recommendation of the committee has been noted. 
 
 

pg. 9 
 
CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE GOVERN-
MENT  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 It is the duty of the State to provide access to justice to all its citizens and create jud i-
cial infrastructure to provide efficient, economic and timely delivery of justice. The status of 
judicial infrastructure in the North Eastern States can at best be termed as work in progress 
and a lot of work still needs to be done to meet the requirement at the lower end of the spe c-
trum. It does not augur well for a vibrant and aspirational democracy to have Courts which 
are functioning from dilapidated rented premises with insufficient space and which lack basic 
amenities like toilets, water connection, proper electricity supply, etc. Although, the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for Judicia ry, is a ray 
of hope in otherwise gloomy scenario, it is imperative to enhance the share of North eastern 
States  under the Scheme.  (Recommendation No. i) 
Action Taken 
2.1 The budgetary allocation done for the Scheme every year is required to be distributed 
to all the 28 States and 8 Union Territories.  To take care of the interest of the NER, there is 
mandatory allocation of at least 10% of budgetary allocation for the NE Region. Against total 
allocation of Rs.1051 crore for the scheme in the FY 2023-24, a provision of Rs.111 crore 
was kept for the NE Region.   
2.2 As per the laid down process, in the beginning of the financial year, based on the 
weightage formula as provided in the scheme, the tentative allocation for all the states is done 
and made known to them for preparing their action plan. They are required to seek funds im-
mediately and latest by June, after fulfilment of all the conditions, primary among which is 
the utilization of funds released earlier. However, after June, the release can be made to the 
States w.r.t. their requirements and need. The scheme guidelines provide for allocation of en-
hanced budgetary support to the needy States, having good pace of expenditure, if some other 
States are not in a position to seek their allocated funds and thus some savings are available.  
 2.3 Thus, subject to  the utilization of the funds released earlier and having the need and a 
good pipeline of projects, the NER States can also seek enhanced funds, if available, as indi-
cated in para above. In the FY 2023-24, against allocation of Rs.111crore, on account of 
these provisions, funds to the tune of Rs.130.14 crore were released to the states in NE Re-
gion.  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.4 The revised procedural guidelines fo r release of CSS funds under the new Public F i-
nancial Management System (PFMS) has apparently, slowed down the pace of release of 
funds. Due to stringent conditions attached for release of funds, most of the States are finding 

pg. 10 
 
it difficult to get their quo ta of funds despite having huge requirements for funds for their 
projects both ongoing and new. From the data provided by the Department, 3 out of 8 NE 
States did not get any funds during 2022 -23 due to such norms. The Committee is happy to 
note that the D epartment of Justice has made commendable efforts to ensure that funds are 
released to the states on time and that all of them become PFMS compliant. The Committee, 
however, recommends the Department to approach the MoF to get the guidelines on release 
of funds under the CSS relaxed, wherever the States are facing genuine difficulties in the i m-
plementation of such guidelines.  (Recommendation No. ii) 
Action Taken  
2.5 As per the guidelines of Ministry of Finance regarding the release of funds under the Ce n-
trally Sponsored Schemes in vogue in 2023 -24 not more than 25% of the funds earmarked to a State 
can be released at one go. Release of further instalment can only be done after the utilization of the 
previous funds released to it along with the State matching share. The purpose of these guidelines is to 
ensure efficient utilization of funds and to avoid parking of funds. As mentioned above, the scheme 
guidelines also provide for allocation of enhanced budgetary support to the needy states, having good 
pace of expenditure, if some other states are not in a position to seek their allocated funds and thus 
some savings are available.   
2.6 Fund is released to the States as soon as they reduce their unspent balance (Central share + 
state share lying with them) to  the permissible level. The funds using these procedures are released, 
on need basis and only those States get benefited which have exhausted the funds released to them 
earlier and have the capacity to utilize more funds and have ongoing/new projects to ut ilise the 
funds.   
2.7 The States which are not able to utilize the previous funds, are not provided more funds, so as 
to avoid unnecessary parking of funds at the level of the State Government. In the FY 2022 -23, funds 
could not be released to the States of Nagaland, Tripura and Mizoram, as all these States had unspent 
balance of funds available in their respective Single Nodal Agency (SNA) accounts.   The State-wise 
position is as under: 
 Nagaland: Funds to the tune of Rs.13.27 cr ore were released to the State in the F.Y. 2021-22. 
However, as the State did not utilize these funds, it did not become eligible for release of 
funds in 2022 -23. It was only after utilization of unspent balance of funds, that funds to the 
tune of Rs.4.3925 crore were released to the State in FY 23-24. 
 Mizoram: Funds to the tune of Rs.9.5 cr ore were released to the State in the F.Y. 2021 -22. 
However, as the State did not utilize these funds, it did not become eligible for release of 
funds in 2022 -23. It was only after utilization of unspent balance of funds that funds to the 
tune of Rs.8.855 crore were released to the State in FY 23-24. 
 Tripura: Funds to the tune of Rs.7.74 cr ore were released to the State in the F.Y. 2020 -21. 
However, as the State did not utilize these funds, it did not become eligible for release of 
funds in 2021 -22 as well as in 2022 -23. It was only after utilization of unspent balance of 
funds that funds to th e tune of Rs.40.4869 cr ore were released to the State in FY 23 -24. It is 
relevant to mention that  in F.Y.2023-24, Ministry of Finance was also  approached to relax 
the condition to enable this Department to release more than 25% of funds at one go to the 
States. However, this was not agreed to by the Ministry of Finance.

CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE GOVERNMENT AND REI-
TERATES ITS RECOMMENDATIONS    
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 Apart from general PFMS related issues, the North -Eastern States face other cha l-
lenges in creation of infrastructure due to their remote location, hilly terrain, availability of 
unencumbered land. Also the NE States and other hilly States have a short working season 
which makes movement of men and material difficult over the treacherous terrain and ther e-
by making contract implementation difficult with increased time and cost overruns. Because 
of limited railways connectivity in the region, the cost of transportation becomes much higher, 
leading to substantial increase in cost of material. Other reasons include late receipt of project 
proposals and non-receipt of utilization of certificates from the respective state governments. 
The department should take these factors into account while prescribing the modalities of 
fund release. (Recommendation No. iv) 
Action Taken 
3.1 The Department is aware of the challenges in creation of infrastructure due to  remote 
location, hilly terrain, availability of unencumbered land etc. in North Eastern Region (NER). 
These peculiarities, in addition to problem of short working season, limited railways connec-
tivity, are hindering the creation of necessary infrastructure in the North Eastern Region. The 
Department is committed to releasing funds to all the States, particularly to States in NER as 
and when a particular State has utilized the funds previously released to it. As far as the prob-
lem like high transportation cost leading in NER States, the State contribution has been kept 
at only 10% as compared to 40% in other States in respect of funds sharing pattern under the 
scheme.  
3.2 It is relevant to illustrate an example of State of Arunachal Pradesh. In January 2023, 
against the request of the State seeking around Rs.122 crore for ongoing and new projects of 
Court Halls and Residential Units, after due approvals, a  sum of Rs. 32.38  crore wa s r e-
leased to the State in January 2023.  Thus funds to the tune of Rs. Rs.35.97 cr ore (Rs.32.38 
crore central share plus Rs.3.59 crore matching State share) were available to the State. How-
ever, the State has incurred only an expenditure of only of Rs.13. 26 crore (2023-24) out of 
these funds. Thus, the State could not get any funds in the financial year 2023-24, as it is hav-
ing a huge unspent balance of the previous year and is accordingly not eligible for receipt of 
more central funds. One of the importan t conditions for claiming funds under the scheme is 
utilization of funds released to the State earlier. Thus, speedy utilization of funds by the 
States is a pre-requisite for release of further central funds.   
Further observation 
3.3 The Committee takes n ote of th e reply of the D epartment. The C ommittee also 
understands that there is a n issue of non-utilization of the funds released earlier  in the 
north-eastern states which hinders the release of further installments in the scheme for 

pg. 12 
 
the creation of i nfrastructure.  The Committee further emphasizes that a system of p e-
nalties or incentives may be introduced in the scheme so that States may get motivated 
to improve their financial management practices and ensure that funds are used  fully 
and effectively. This could also create a sense of urgency among the States for  timely 
utilization of funds. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.4 The funding pattern under the CSS for the 8 North Eastern States and two Himalayan 
states is 90:10 (Center: State). However, in some cases the States are finding it difficult to 
even contribute 10% of the funds leading to delay in completion of projects. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends the Department to explore the possibility of providing a better deal 
in terms of enhanced allocation of funds and relaxation of spending norms under the Scheme, 
considering the peculiarities of the NE States. It is further recommended that the 10% of the 
state quota may also be relaxed for the NE States subject to subsequent recovery from the 
concerned state, so that the ongoing projects are not stalled for want of such meager amount  
of money. (Recommendation No. v) 
Action Taken 
 
3.5 As already mentioned the basic issue, which hampers release of funds to the States, 
including NER States is non-utilization of the funds released earlier. Also, the funds sharing 
patterns are prescribed by Ministry of Finance for all Centrally Sponsored Schemes across 
various Ministries of Union of India. Further, the primary responsibility of development of 
infrastructure facilities for judiciary rests with the State Government, the contribution of Cen-
tral Government through the scheme is supplementary in nature. For the contribution under 
the scheme being supplementary in nature, 10% of the State share is alrea dy a relaxation in 
comparison to States where the State share is 40%. 
 
Further observation 
3.6 The Committee takes note of the reply of the Department. However, the commi t-
tee reiterates its recommendation and suggests the Department to approach the Mini s-
try of Finance with the recommendation of the Committee and seek relaxation for the 
States of the North-eastern region of the country.  
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
3.7 During the interactions with the Committee, the Kohima Bar Association made a r e-
quest for a separate High Court for the State of Nagaland. The President of Bar informed that 
the States like Tripura, Meghalaya and Manipur which came under the jurisdiction of Gauhati 
High Court in 1971 have now established their own High Courts. However, the State of Na-
galand which has been under the jurisdiction of Gauhati High Court since 1963 does not have 
its own High Court. The Committee feels that there is merit in the demand for a separate 
High Court by State of Nagaland and the Ministry of Law and Just ice must coordinate with 
Ministry of Home Affairs to address the demand. (Recommendation No. iii) 

pg. 13 
 
Action Taken 
3.8 The Chief Minister, Nagaland vide his letter dated 25.06.2021 conveyed the decision 
of the State Cabinet taken on the 07.04.2021 for setting up a separate High Court for the State 
of Nagaland.  The proposal to set up a High Court for the State of Nagaland essentially i n-
volves amendment to the North -Eastern Area (Reorganization) Act, 1971, which mandates 
that the Gauhati High Court shall be the common High Court for the States of Assam, Aru n-
achal Pradesh, Mizoram and Nagaland.   
3.9 The matter is currently under examination, in consultation with the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
Further observation 
3.10  The matter of establishment of High Court for Nagaland has been in motion 
since 2021. The North-Eastern States like Tripura, Meghalaya and Manipur which were 
under the jurisdiction of Guwahati High Court along with Nagaland have got their     
respective High Courts established whereas the matter of e stablishment of High Court 
of Nagaland is still under examination. T he Committee recommends that the Depar t-
ment of Justice should expedite the necessary process such as consultation with the Min-
istry of Home Affairs etc. for early set up of High Court of Nagaland.

CHALLENGES IN LOK ADALATS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 Lok Adalats are being organized by NALSA and State LSAs for amicable settlement of 
disputes. Though Lok Adalats  are designed to expedite case resolution, they encounter 
challenges due to their limited powers compared to regular courts. They also don't have to adhere 
to any proper procedures. Further, they cannot compel the parties to appear for the proceedings. 
Many times one of the parties does not appear for the hearing and then there is a delay in the 
disposal. Therefore, there is a need to have a relook into the powers and procedures of 
conducting Lok Adalats for making them more effective and efficient. The Lok  Adalats should 
have powers to ensure the presence of parties for finding the scope of an amicable settlement. 
(Para 23) 
Action Taken: 
I. The Lok Adalats are governed under Chapter VI (Section 19 to 22) of the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987. As per Section 19 (5) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 
the Lok Adalats  "have jurisdiction to determine and to arrive at a compromise or 
settlement bet ween the parties to a dispute". The Lok Adalats are statutory bodies 
established for the purpose of amicable settlement between the parties in dispute. Section 
22 of the LSA Act 1987 states that the "Lok Adalats have the same powers as are vested 
in Civil Court under the CPC, 1908, while trying a suit ... ". Overall, the Lok Adalats are 
based on a participatory approach of dispute resolution and the proceeding in Lok 
Adalats are usually not adjudicatory. 
II. With respect to the issue of delay in disposal becaus e of absence of the parties, it is 
submitted that NALSA regularly engages with the SLSAs to conduct pre -Lok Adalat 
meetings for ensuring the attendance of the parties and consequently increasing the 
disposal rate. The data below shows the consequent increase in disposal rate. 
III. In the year 2023, National Lok Adalats disposed the highest ever number of cases with 
more than 110% increase in total cases disposed in comparison to the previous year. The 
disposal of cases at the State Lok Adalats also increased in the F.Y. 2023 -24 from 
8,51,309 to 9,97,494. 
IV. It is proposed that NALSA will strengthen Lok Adalats through extensive awareness 
campaigns on Lok Adalats as an Alternative Dispute Resolution platform to enhance the 
participation of parties in the Lok Adalats which will in turn increase the disposal rate. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.2 Thus Strengthening and streamlining Lok Adalats becomes imperative to make them 
more effective in resolving disputes efficiently. Lok Adalats often suffer from inadequate 
infrastructure, facilities, staff and training. This affects their efficiency and quality of service. 
Accordingly, the Committee feels that Lok Adalats need to be provided with adequate 

 
9 
infrastructure, equipment, staff and training. They also need to adopt mode rn technology and 
methods to streamline their processes and reduce delays. (Para 24) 
Action Taken: 
I. The Lok Adalats are organized on a non -working day of the Courts so that the Court s' 
existing infrastructure can be used for periodic Lok Adalats. 
II. NALSA grants cannot be used for infrastructure development and are only to be used for 
carrying out the various legal services activities and programmes including organizing of 
Lok Adalats. 
III. The referral judges and the judges deputed at Lok Adalats are regularly trai ned at the 
judicial academies as per the State's judicial training schedules. 
IV. It is proposed that SLSAs to take up the issue of infrastructure, facilities and staff for 
strengthening Lok Adalats at the State level with the respective State/UT Governments 
and High Courts. 
 
INCREASED ACCESS TO LEGAL-AID TO THE PRISONERS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 The Committee is, therefore, of the view that access to justice, especially to the

I. It is submitted that NALSA has  developed a centralized application processing system

II. Further, access points for Legal Aid to undertrials are established at all points of their

at the police station. For strengthening a ccess to legal aid services at the police 
station, a roster of legal aid lawyers is put up at 4,126 Police Stations and the process 
is ongoing for the remaining police stations. 
B. At Courts: Under the above-mentioned framework, 9,372 remand lawyers are deputed 
at all concerned courts in the country for enabling prompt access to legal 
representation to arrested persons produced before remand courts. In the year 2023,

set up at a common area in prison which is accessible to prisoners. There are 1,171

Recommendation/Observation  
2.1  Further, the Committee expresses its concern on the plight of vulnerable sections, 
where NALSA should have been involved effectively. As per the data available in the 
public domain, out of total number of prisoners  in the country, approximately 70 percent

under trial prisoners have spent more time in jail than the actual sentence prescribed 
under the relevant Sections/ Acts in cas e if they have been convicted. A large number of 
prisoners are unable to arrange bail due to non-furnishing of personal bail bonds/surety.

I. As per the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) data, the proportion of under  trial

A. In 2022, there were 1.42 crore arrests for offences in IPC, offences under State &

B. 18.04 Lakh persons were admitted to prisons during the year 2022, however, the 
prison population only increased by 19,186 from 2021 to 2022 which shows that 
majority of the prisoners admitted during the year were r eleased either on bail or 
acquitted. 
II. The above-mentioned point is further substantiated by the fact that 69% of the under  trial 
prisoners as on 31 st December, 2022 had spent less than a year in the prison. Further 
break-up of this data point shows that 32% of the under trial prisoners had spent only upto 
3 months in the prison. This reflects that the majority of the under  trial population in 
prisons is a floating population. 
III. To keep a check on avoidable arrests and imprisonment of accused persons due to 
absence of legal representation, NALSA is augmenting legal services at pre -trial stages 
through the 'Early Access to Justice at Pre-arrest, Arrest and Remand Stage' framework.

focusing on legal aid at pre-trial stages to keep a check on avoidable imprisonment: 
A Suspects provided legal aid at police station 27,521 
B Suspects not arrested by police 9,948 (36% of A)

D Persons provided legal aid at remand stage 1,70,912

E Bail applications filed at remand stage 66,294 (39% of D)

IV. Under trial Review Committees (UTRCs) are district level bodies chaired by the DLSA

CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE DEPARTMENT 
AND REITERATES ITS RECOMMENDATIONS 
LACK OF AWARENESS AND LEGAL EDUCATION 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.1  Therefore, empowering individuals through education and creating awareness about their 
rights and the role of legal aid is essential to bridge this informational gap. Accordingly, the 
Committee is of the view that Government may take an extensive mass media campaign to 
educate the eligible population about the legal aid avenues available for them to get justice. (Para 
10)  
Action Taken:  
 
I. It is submitted that National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) is bridging the 
information gap among the eligible population with its ongoing awareness programmes. 
During the year 2023, 3,44,580 physical legal awareness programmes were organized 
which benefitted 3,21,50,1 78 persons. The increase in number of persons availing legal 
services reflects the impact of existing awareness programmes: 
A. The number of persons availing free legal services including legal representation, 
assistance, and advice increased by 36% in the year 2023 (14.9 lakh) in comparison to 
the year 2022 (10.9 lakh). 
B. The number of persons availing legal services at pre-arrest stage, arrest and remand 
stage increased by 30% from 1. 7 lakh in the year 2022 to 2.2 lakh in the year 2023. 
II. NALSA regularly conduc ts legal aid camp -based awareness campaigns across the 
country and has developed a NALSA 'theme song' for media -based awareness on the role 
of NALSA. However, NALSA has not yet ventured into mass -media campaigns at the 
national level. For mass -media campai gns, there will be need of specially qualified 
human resource having experience in media and communications for designing, 
coordinating, and analyzing mass -media campaigns. In order to bridge the information 
gap, it is proposed that NALSA will adopt following two pronged approach: 
A. Strengthening the existing awareness programmes/ campaigns: 
Conducting Pan-India beneficiary category wise targeted legal awareness campaigns, 
as per a fixed calendar/schedule of campaigns. The campaigns would include: 
i. Legal Literacy and Awareness camps: Tailored programs will be developed with 
focused attention on specific subject matters and rights & obligations, and 
processes under related laws. 
ii. Community outreach: Public events/meetings, street plays, etc. by students and 
PLVs. 
iii. On-spot legal services: Legal counselling & assistance camps by engaging 
lawyers (Panel Lawyers and Legal Aid Defence Counsels {LADCs}) with 

 
17 
subject-matter expertise; 
iv. Information Dissemination: Outreach -kits containing flyers, posters, etc. in local 
languages regarding the role of Legal Services Institutions (LSIs) and legal 
services schemes, programmes, etc. will be distributed. 
v. Mobile clinics for remote areas: Utilize vehicle based legal aid clinics for remote 
areas and small communities, including nomadic and semi nomadic communities. 
vi. Student PLV involvement: Encourage University based legal aid clinics for 
conducting follow-up legal awareness and outreach camps in areas in the vicinity 
of their institutions. 
vii. Reporting and Feedback: District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) will 
prepare categorized data of the campaigns which will be analyzed at the state 
level by the State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs) and at the national level by 
NALSA for identifying improvement areas and sharing of good p ractices among 
SLSAs. 
B. Building capacity for "extensive mass media campaign to educate the eligible 
population about the legal aid avenue ": 
i. NALSA will take assistance of a special government agency in designing, 
executing, and analyzing mass media campaign s, from the earmarked funds for 
this purpose. 
ii. Local campaigns will focus on digital and physical dissemination of NALSA's 
Information, Education & Communication (IEC) material such as posters and 
flyers on legal services schemes, eligibility under Section 12 of the LSA Act 
1987, platforms/means for accessing legal services, etc. 
iii. These mass -media and physical campaigns will be synchronized with the 
scheduled targeted campaigns as proposed in part 'A' of the proposed action. 
iv. To enhance the dissemination of th e 'theme song', NALSA will coordinate & 
collaborate with mass -media platforms such as All India Radio, Doordarshan, 
Rajya Sabha TV, Lok Sabha TV, etc. for playing NALSA's theme song. 
v. SLSAs and DLSAs will ensure the widespread distribution of NALSA's theme 
song at public events, market areas, community fairs/carnivals, etc., in the local 
language.

3.2 Despite NALSA's commendable efforts, legal awareness remains limited, 
particularly in rural and marginalized communities. Awareness is crucial for the success of 
legal aid mechanisms. Therefore, the Committee recommends that NALSA collaborate 
with educational institutions and NGOs to integrate legal literacy into curricula, leverage

effectiveness. 
 
BUDGETARY CONSTRAINTS AND ALLOCATIONS 
Recommendation/Observation 

 
18 
3.3 It is an admitted fact that the prevalent social and economic disparity in the country is 
eroding the democratic objective of 'justice for all'. As majority of our population lacks legal 
awareness and necessary means to approach the courts, they are compelled to suffer in silence.

Services Day 2023 to enhance the reach of Legal Services Institutions and bridge the gap

III. It is proposed that NALSA will increase the number of PLVs on the basis of a need-based

challenge in achieving the intended outcomes of legal services programmes. Section 16

Recommendation/Observation 
3.4   In this regard, the Committee observes that the majority of the Indian population are eligible 
for legal aid. However, as per 'India Justice Report, 2019' published by the Tata Trust, per capita 
free legal aid s pend in India is just 0.75 paisa  per annum (in 2017 -18), which is perhaps among 
the lowest in the wor ld. Though funding legal services authorities is also one of the 
responsibilities of States, there is a dire need to significantly enhance the expenditure on this

I. The majority of the population is 'eligible' for legal aid as per the wide eligibility criteria

framework ensures that no one in need of free legal services is rendered ineligible to

II. During the F.Y. 2022 -23, Rs. 190 crore were provided to NALSA as Grant -in-Aid for

Budget Estimate stage. Further, the Government of India  has approved a new Central 
Sector Scheme namely Legal Aid Defense Counsel System (LADCS) Scheme for three 
years (F.Y. 2023-24 to F.Y. 2025 -26) with outlay of Rs. 998.43 crore (including Rs. 200 

 
19 
crore for F.Y. 2023 -24 for implementation and operationalizat ion of LADCS Scheme) 
with 100% Central share. Hence, total Rs. 400 crore were provided to NALSA during the 
F.Y. 2023-24.  
III. In absence of adequate funds from the State governments, SLSAs are dependent on 
NALSA grants only. To address this issue, it is propos ed that NALSA will take steps for 
deliberating this issue at appropriate platform for finding sustainable and decentralized 
funding solutions. 
IV. It is further proposed that NALSA will request a specialized government agency such as 
NITI Aayog to conduct a pa n-India survey for demand and supply of free legal services 
as well as to map the anticipated increase in demand. Such a study will be crucial in an 
objective determination on the required funds and human resources to meet the demand. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.5 Budget limitations impede the scalability and effectiveness of legal aid programs, 
affecting infrastructure, staffing, and outreach activities. The Department of Justice's 
DISHA program, which reached 1.53 million individuals through legal awareness 
initiatives as of June 30, 2024, demonstrates the potential impact of well -funded programs. 
Therefore, the Committee advocates for a fixed percentage of state GDP to be allocated to 
legal aid, encouraging state contribut ions through matching central grants, and exploring 
partnerships with the private sector and CSR initiatives to supplement funding and ensure 
sustainable resource allocation.

Recommendation/Observation 
3.8 To overcome these challenges and enhance the utilization of PLVs Committee feels that 
some immediate measures should be taken like providing regular and comprehensive training 
and capacity building of PLVs. They should also be provided with adequate resour ces and 
support to perform their duties effectively. PLVs should be paid or compensated adequately for 

 
21 
their work, so that they remain interested in their work. They should also receive recognition and 
appreciation from the legal system and the society. Th is would enhance their motivation and 
commitment to serve the people. Further, the legal services authorities and the Lok Adalats 
should conduct awareness campaigns and outreach programs to inform and educate the people 
about the role and functions of PLVs . In turn, the PLVs should also build trust and rapport with 
the people and address their concerns and grievances. (Para 26) 
Action Taken 
I. There are 42,782 PLVs, out of which 17,765 (41.5%) are female, 235 are transgender 
persons and 24,782 are male, who ha ve been given induction training. In addition to the 
induction training, 7,407 PLVs have been provided special training through various  
capacity building programmes during the last five F.Y. i.e. 2019-20 to 2023-24. 
II. As per the Scheme for Para -Legal Volunte ers (Revised), the PLVs' tenure may be 
extended for more than a year if the Chairperson, DLSA finds the PLV's performance 
satisfactory based on regular review. 
III. NALSA periodically organizes national level programmes for PLVs for recognizing and 
commending t heir performance. The State authorities also regularly organize similar 
programmes at the State level. 
IV. In reference to the issue of providing adequate resources to the PLVs, it may be noted 
that the expenses incurred by the PLVs in performance of their dut ies, including travel 
costs, are reimbursed as per the 'Scheme for Para Legal Volunteers (Revised).' 
V. In reference to the issue of payment and adequate compensation to the PLVs for their 
services, it may be noted that the SLSAs and DLSAs decide the honorar ium for the PLVs 
as per the revised Scheme (referred above). As per the Scheme, revised in the year 2013, 
the honorarium of the PLVs shall not be less than Rs. 250 per day. As of January, 2024, 
the honorarium for PLV in different SLSAs ranges between Rs. 250 to Rs. 1800 per day. 
VI. It is proposed that NALSA will ensure that intensive subject-specific trainings for PLVs 
are conducted at the district level based on their area of work and experience, in 
collaboration with the local organizations and government bodies. Further, SLSAs will be 
asked to ensure that the PLVs are empanelled under all categories as mentioned in the 
revised scheme. 
VII. It is further proposed that the agenda of revising the minimum fee structure for PLVs will 
be taken up in the next Central Au thority meeting of NALSA. In addition, all campaigns 
of NALSA will include awareness about the specific roles of PLVs. Pamphlets and 
posters displaying the details of the PLVs in the district/taluk a along with their subject -
specific roles will also be publicized at relevant public places. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.9 Para-Legal Volunteers (PLVs) remain an underutilized resource despite their 
potential to connect marginalized communities with essential legal services. Their 
effectiveness can be significantly enhanced through expanded roles, targeted training, and 
meaningful recognition. To bridge existing gaps, the Committee recommends training 

 
22 
programs should incorporate digital literacy, mediation techniques, and specialized legal 
skills relevant to local needs. Performance-based incentives must be introduced to motiva te 
consistent excellence, while peer -review mechanisms can foster collaboration and identify 
best practices for replication. Recognizing top -performing PLVs through awards and 
public acknowledgment will further enhance their commitment and inspire broader 
participation, ultimately strengthening the grassroots reach of legal aid services. 
 
MANNING THE NALSA  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.10 The Committee notes that NALSA's activities have increased manifold since its inception 
and it is actively engaged in taking the legal aid movement in India to every nook and corner. 
However, its existing sanctioned staff strength of 34 only is too low considering its mandate and 
reach. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Government to sanction additional 40 posts 
as requested by them. (Para 33) 
Action Taken 
I. It is submitted that NALSA is working on the proposals for creation of additional posts 
for NALSA and Department of Justice will act on it as per due process. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
3.11 The Committ ee has repeatedly emphasized the urgency of this issue, but the 
Department's responses have been consistently vague and non -committal. NALSA has 
frequently highlighted this concern during its depositions, underscoring the critical 
need for adequate staffin g to fulfil its expanding mandate. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department of Justice provide a clear and actionable timeline 
for the creation and recruitment of the requisite officers and staff in NALSA. Such a 
commitment is essential to ens ure the effective functioning of NALSA and the 
fulfilment of its objective to provide accessible and efficient legal aid services across 
the country.
