Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 The Committee notes that it is quite evident from the table, the maximum 
number of officers recruited are from Technical and medical background. Above 70 
per cent of the recruits in the civil service by UPSC nowadays are from technical 
streams. Every year, hundreds of technocrats are thus being lost, who are likely to 
work in other specific areas which is also a requirement for the nation.   So, doctors 
and top technocrats are being lost who can perform as very good doctors and 
engineers.  The allurement to become civil servant is perhaps also adversely aff ecting 
other fields of working.   Hence, the Committee opines that it is high time to have a 
rethink about the whole process of recruitment for the Civil Service. (Para 2.7)          
Action Taken 
3.1 Union Public Service Commission has constituted Expert Committees in 
consultation with the Government from time to time in the past to assess the efficacy 
in selecting the most suitable candidates through the Civil Services Examination. 
Based on the recomm endations of such Committees, necessary changes have been 
carried out in scheme of Civil Services Examination accordingly. The last such 
Committee i.e. Baswan Committee, was constituted on 12 -08-2015 which submitted 
its report on 09 -08-2016. The Commission  conveyed its views on the 
recommendations of the Baswan Committee in March, 2017 to Department of 
Personnel and Training, for consideration. The Report of the Baswan Committee is 
under consideration in the DoPT. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2 The Committee notes that the each recruitment test conducted by UPSC as of 
now, takes anywhere between six months to one year to complete. This long drawn 
process involves a lot of expenses for the competing candidates and also 
contributes to the erosion of human cap ital. In view of this, the Committee desires 

55 
 
to know whether UPSC is contemplating to make any change in the pattern of civil 
services examination to curtail the length of the examination cycle.      (Para 2.9)  
Action Taken 
3.3 It has been the constant endeavour of Union Public Service Commission  to 
compress the time -cycles of all its Examinations including the Civil Services 
Examination. The examination process involves several steps including 
Notification of Examination Rules a s well as reporting of vacancies by the 
Government. The Commission publishes the Calendar of Examinations well in 
advance, as per which these Examinations are conducted. 
3.4 As regards the Civil Services Examination, following are submitted: 
(a)       This Examination has following stages (i) Preliminary Examination 
(Objective type) for screening of candidates for the Civil Services (Main) 
Examination (ii) Civil Services (Main) Examination (Descriptive type) and (iii) 
Personality Test/Interview. A statement showing the time taken at different stages of 
the Examination during the period from 2017 –2021, i.e. from the stage of 
advertisement (Notification of the Examination) to declaration of final result is 
attached as Annexure I. 
 
(b)       As per the current  trend, number of applications for the Civil Services 
(Preliminary) Examination comes to over a million every year. The 2023 
Examination was held at 79 Centres (cities) across the country at 2,538 Venues to 
accommodate 10.27 lakh candidates. For ensuring s mooth conduct of this 
Examination, numerous activities are required to be completed by the Commission 
viz. (i) selection of Venues in each Centre; (ii) processing/ scrutiny of applications 
received in order to allow only eligible candidates; (iii) distribu tion of candidates 
(after availability of exact count on completion of application process) to these 
Venues; (iv) preparation and release of e -Admit Cards of the candidates; (v) 
preparation of Scannable Attendance Lists of candidates, printing and dispatch  of the 
same to the Venue Supervisors; (vi) packing/dispatch of OMR sheets/stationeries to 
the Venues; (vii) preparation/ despatch of sensitive material to the Centres; (viii) 
deployment of large number of examination functionaries at different levels to t hese 
centres and venues; (ix) release of funds to the Centres and Venues; (x) conduct of 
meetings with various stake holders like police, postal authorities, railway authorities, 
Centre Supervisors, Inspecting Officers etc.; (xi) issue of number of   letters from 
different levels to number of authorities etc. 

56 
 
(c)        All these processes are to be executed with extreme care following 
various checks &  counter-checks at different levels in coordination with the 
examination functionaries to rule out any possibility of any error/mistake at any 
stage. It would be seen from the attached statement that the time duration for such 
activities has been within the range of around 2.5 to 3 months. Hence, this much lead 
time is a bare minimum for successful conduct of Examination of this scale. It may, 
thus, be appreciated that there is hardly any scope for further compressing the time 
between the date of advertisem ent (notification) and date of holding the Civil 
Services (Preliminary) Examination owing to the reasons cited above. 
  
(d)       After taking due care and completing all the processes, presently result 
of the Preliminary Examination is declared within 12 days from the date of conduct 
of the Examination. Earlier, time taken to declare the result was somewhere between 
40-50 days. Again, for smooth conduct of the Main Examination, which is a 5 days 
affair having 9 descriptive type papers, the drills of arrang ement are almost the same 
as those of the Preliminary Examination except the level of scale involved. The 
average time gap between declaration of the result of the Preliminary Examination 
and conduct of the Main Examination is about 2 -3 months. At this sta ge, the 
Preliminary Examination Qualified Candidates are needed adequate time to prepare 
for the Main Examination because of the number of papers and their toughness level. 
Any attempt to reduce this gap may invite grievances from the candidates. Therefore , 
there is hardly any possibility to bring down this time gap of three months. 
 
(e)       The Civil Services (Main) Examination, being a 9 Papers -Examination 
of descriptive type, it takes more time for evaluation of answer scripts i.e. about more 
than two months as nearly 1.20 lakh scripts of different subjects are evaluated by 
different teams of experts. Therefore, at this stage also, there is little scope of 
reducing the time-line between the date of completion of the Main Examination and 
the declaration of its result. 
 
(f)        After declaration of result of the Main Examination, as per existing 
scheme, the successful candidates are required to fill up Detailed Application Form 
(DAF-II) for which, time is given to them. Once these  DAFs-II are received from 
them, the same are processed for generation of E -Summon Letter and scheduling of 
their Personality Tests. The Personality Tests are held at the UPSC, so the candidates 
are required to come to the UPSC for attending the same from their places of stay 
across the country. Therefore, a lead time is to be given to them for arranging their 
transport, necessary documents and stay in Delhi. As such, the Personality Tests 

57 
 
cannot be scheduled immediately after the declaration of result of t he Main 
Examination. Further, maximum 12 candidates are interviewed in a day by one 
Personality Test Board, which is the optimal number which cannot be increased in 
order to maintain the quality of the Personality Test process and awarding of marks to 
the candidates as per their skills and capabilities. Besides, these Personality Test 
Boards are chaired by the Hon’ble Members of the Commission. Hence, the number 
of such Boards depends on the availability of Hon’ble Members. Furthermore, the 
entire duration of the Personality Test process is dependent on this aspect as also on 
the number of candidates, which in turn depends on the number of vacancies to be 
filled up on the basis of the Examination. On completion of the Personality Tests, 
final result of the Civil Service Examination is declared within 4 days. As such, there 
is also hardly any scope of reducing the time -line for completion of Personality Test 
process. 
 
(g)       It may be seen that the time cycle for the Civil Services Examination 
has been opti mized to the extent possible despite increase in the number of 
candidates, Centres and Venues over the years after analysing the time taken in the 
pre-examination and post examination activities in detail. One of the most vital 
factors that go into the det ermination of the time schedule of an Examination is the 
need to maintain the utmost confidentiality and the integrity of the examination 
process. Various checks and balances have been integrated in the examination 
system, which have been gained through ye ars of experience to eliminate the risk to 
the confidentiality and integrity, so that the Examination is conducted in an utmost 
fair and transparent manner. 
3.5 Further, it may also be appreciated that the UPSC presently holds another 12 
Structured Examinations and, therefore, it takes due care to also keep the time cycle 
of these Examinations at the optimum level besides optimizing the time cycle of the 
Civil Services Examination. Further, the UPSC ensures that a judicious balance is 
maintained at all stag es of all its Examinations including the Civil Services 
Examination. 
3.6 Furthermore, this issue was also referred to the Baswan Committee. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.7      The Committee earnestly recommends a comprehensive re -examination 
of civil services recruitment framework. The objective is to strike a careful 
balance between drawing exceptional talent into public administration and 
retaining the country’s finest doctors, engineers, and technocrats in the fields 

58 
 
where their skills are irreplaceable. At present, the examination cycle stretches 
across almost an entire year. This not only delays the entry of competent officers 
into service but also compels highly skilled professionals to step away from their 
core vocations for prolonged periods. The nation quietly loses valuable expertise 
in medicine, engineering, and other vital sectors. Therefore, the Committee 
believes the recruitment process must be rationalised and streamlined. Its 
duration should be curtailed. Stages of as sessment must be harmonised to 
improve efficiency, without compromising the integrity or quality of selection. 
Moreover, new and flexible pathways should be explored. Such mechanisms 
would allow technical and medical experts to contribute meaningfully to 
governance, while still advancing in their professions. This approach would 
ensure that the nation’s human capital is not only preserved but fully optimised.  
The Committee reiterates  DoPT to establish a clear timeline for implementation 
of the Baswan Commi ttee’s reforms by  forming a dedicated team to monitor 
progress in the direction of  exam restructuring. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.8 The Committee appreciates the UPSC and SSC for conducting the diligence 
exercises before publishing the answer keys. Howe ver, the Committee is of the 
view that this will become further more credible if the feedback of the candidates 
are taken through a dedicated portal and then keys are published. The Committee 
hopes that this process will be followed in future. Further, UPSC should explore the 
feasibility of declaring the answer key of Civil Services Preliminary exams after the 
Preliminary Exam stage is over and not after the declaration of final results of the 
Civil Services examination. Candidates should be allowed to raise objections at this 
stage only and on that basis any discrepancies related to the answer key of the 
Preliminary examination should be resolved.   This should be taken into account 
before publishing the result of candidates qualifying for the next stage, i. e. Civil 
Services Mains examination. (Para 2.39) 
Action Taken  
3.9 Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)  is already having an online 
Question Paper Representation Portal (QPRep ) in its website where candidates can 
submit their views on any aspect of a question. This portal remains active for an 
exam for a period of 7 days from the next date immediately after the conclusion of 
that exam. In respect of the release of the answer ke y, it is stated that the 
Commission releases the answer key of the Civil Services (Preliminary) 

59 
 
Examination (objective type) after completion of the entire process of the Civil 
Services Examination. This policy of the Commission is being followed in all 
Examinations of the Commission and it has been working smoothly. Further, 
candidates can make representations on the questions through the dedicated portal, 
as explained above.  As the above system of disclosing keys after the final result of 
the Examination  is working fine since inception and serving the larger public 
interest very well, no requirement is felt to change the same. Further, the issue of 
releasing answer keys is presently sub -judice in W.P. No. 8626/2023 filed by Shri 
Himanshu and others vs  UPSC & Others before the Hon’ble Delhi High Court. 
This case was last heard on 01.12.2023 and listed for next hearing on 21.05.2024. 
3.10 Staff Selection Commission (SSC)  has informed that   in order to ensure 
greater transparency in the examination - system, and in the interest of the 
candidates, the SSC already as the following process in the place: - (i) The tentative 
answer keys of all computer based examinations are uploaded on the Commission’s 
website soon after the conduct of the examination, affordin g the candidates with an 
opportunity to make representations/ challenges against discrepancies, if any, in 
Question Paper/ Tentative Answer Keys.; (ii) On receipt of the challenges, the 
Commission, through a panel of experts, exercises due diligence before  preparing 
the Final Answer keys. Thereafter, the result is declared on the basis of the Final 
Answer keys. The Final answer keys are also uploaded on the website of the 
Commission whereby the candidates are able to judge their performance in the 
examinations.; (iii) Marks secured by the candidates in various examinations 
conducted by the commission are also hosted on website for the information of 
individual candidates. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.11 The Committee recommends that UPSC consider establishing a 
dedicated portal for collecting candidate feedback and objections on the 
provisional answer keys of the Preliminary Examination. It should aim to 
release these keys soon after the exam, following S SC’s transparent model, 
and provide a clear window of 7 to 10 days for raising objections. An expert 
panel should review all submissions before Mains results are announced, and 
final corrected answer keys should be published to help candidates understand 
the evaluation process. Additionally, UPSC and SSC must ensure that all 
related communication is timely and widely disseminated through official 
channels to keep all candidates informed. A uniform, standardised policy for 
handling answer keys across all UPS C examinations may be adopted for 

60 
 
clarity and consistency. The Committee also suggests that UPSC consider the 
outcome of the ongoing court case on this issue and review its approach 
accordingly. Benchmarking these practices against those of global public 
service commissions could further strengthen fairness and credibility. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.12 With respect to Railway Recruitment Board, the Committee emphasized that 
number of centers have to be increased for the candidates appearing for the 
examination. The examination centre should be within the zone where the 
candidate is residing, precisely within the State. (Para 2.52) 
Action Taken  
3.13 Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) conduct examination covering 
different Geographical locations/ States all over the country even as far as all seven 
North-East States, Islands of Andaman & Nicobar as well as Lakshadweep &  
Kashmir valley in north. Due to large number of candidates i.e. more than one 
crore, it is not always possible to allot centres near the pla ce of residence of the 
candidates. However, in allotting of centre it is ensured that Persons with 
Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) & female candidates are allotted centres near their 
residence. In the recent examinations to avoid long distance travel, it was  decided 
that as far as possible no candidates should travel more than 500 kilometers.  A 
massive recruitment exercise has been completed recently for empaneling 1,39,050 
candidates by conducting Computer Based Test (CBT) of approximately 2.37 crore 
candidates. CBT for Centralized Employment Notification (CEN) 01/2019 for Non-
Technical Popular Categories (NTPC) was conducted for 1.26 crore candidates in 
133 shifts in 68 days across 211 cities and 726 centres in 15 languages. Similarly, 
CBT for CEN-RRC 01/2019 (Level-1) was conducted for 1.11 crore candidates in 
99 shifts in 33 days across 191 cities and 551 centres in 15 languages. These 
processes were carried out with absolute fairness and transparency. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.14 The Committee acknowledges the immense scale and effort involved in 
conducting examinations for large numbers of candidates across diverse 
regions; however, it stresses the need to further expand the number of 
examination centres, with a focus on allotting  centres within a candidate’s State 
or zone of residence wherever possible. While it appreciates the special 
provisions for PwBD and female candidates, the Committee recommends 

61 
 
extending similar consideration to all candidates, particularly those from rura l 
or remote areas, to reduce travel burdens. It also suggests that RRBs consider 
adopting a zonal preference -based allocation system during the application 
process. The Commission further recommends improved coordination with local 
authorities and private infrastructure providers to identify additional venues. 
These measures would not only ease logistical challenges but also  lower travel 
expenses, and promote equitable access to the recruitment process across all 
regions.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.15 The Committee advocates to examine the following in details by IBPS. 
(i)    An assessment of the cost for an applicant to reach to the 
examination centre from his house and pay the fee.   
(ii)      The strike rate for a candidate to get a job.   
(iii)      An assessment of the cost of an unemployed person to only apply 
and not get the job.   
(iv) The Committee notes that on an average approximately 95 per 
cent of the candidates who apply are not able to get selected and left 
without job. However, every one is being charged and mostly they are 
unemployed.  Hence, the Committee recommends that it would be fair 
and can be explored that the State or the Central Government bear part of 
that cost so that it does not burden the unemployed youth.  (Para 2.76)  
Action Taken  
3.16 With respect to Point (i) to (iv), Department of Financial Services has 
furnished following information/inputs 
i. Noted for information 
ii. It is at about 0.75%, as number of vacancies are less as compared 
to number of applicants competing. 
iii. Noted for examination 
iv. At present, no such proposal exists. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.17 The Committee notes the limited response from the Department and urges 
that a more detailed and structured study be undertaken by IBPS, in 
coordination with the Department of Financial Services, to assess the financial 

62 
 
burden borne by unemployed youth who apply for competitive examinations but 
do not secure employment. In light of the extremely low strike rate of around 
0.75% and the fact that nearly all ap plicants, many of whom are unemployed, 
are charged examination fees and incur significant travel and other related 
expenses, the Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Government  
may explore mechanisms to subsidise a portion of these costs. This could be done 
through direct financial assistance, fee waivers for certain categories, or 
establishing a common subsidy framework for unemployed candidates 
appearing in public recruitment processes. Such measures would reflect a more 
empathetic and inclusive approach to support  youth in their efforts to secure 
gainful employment and reduce the financial strain on economically vulnerable 
applicants. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.18 The Committee notes the travelling undertaken by the candidates to appear in 
the examination and advises RRBs and IBPS to analyze and assess from which 
areas they get a large number of applications. If from a particular State or area they 
are getting a large number of applications, then contemplate increasing the number 
of centers in that area so that the agencies which are being hired for conducting 
exams set up more centers. It should be planned in such a way that it would be 
convenient for candidates. They should not travel more than 100 kms. or 200 kms. 
Also, for candidates who are travelling from far away distances to sit in the 
examinations, it should be ensured that measures are taken to make the travel more 
humane and comfortable. Some special trains  may be run for the purpose. The 
Committee feels these measures would ease the burden of the candidates. (Para 
2.77) 
Action Taken  
3.19 Department of Financial Services  has informed that IBPS deci des upon the 
number of centers/ venues in any particular State according to the number of 
candidates expected in the examination, and endeavors to provide candidates their 
choice of center as close to their opted city as possible. If number from a particular 
area is larger than expected,  new centers are added. Even in relatively very 
inaccessible areas (e.g., Lakshadweep), test center is provided regardless of very 
low number of candidates. The number of grievances of candidates in this regard is 
minimal. 

63 
 
3.20 Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) conduct examination covering different 
Geographical locations/ States all over the country even as far as all seven North -
East States, Islands of Andaman & Nicobar as well as Lakshadweep & Kashmir 
valley in north. Due to large number of candidates i.e. more than one crore, it is not 
always possible to allot centres near the place of residence of the candidates. 
However, in allotting of centre it is ensured that Persons with Benchmark 
Disabilities (PwBD) & female candidates are allotted centres near th eir residence. 
In the recent examinations to avoid long distance travel, it was decided that as far 
as possible no candidates should travel more than 500 kilometers. Moreover, 
Special Trains are operated as per requirements for ease of candidates. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.21 The Committee appreciates the efforts of IBPS and RRBs in expanding 
access of examination centres, including to remote and low -applicant areas. 
However, a more data -driven and proactive approach is needed. Recruitment 
agencies should identify high -application-density regions in advance and plan 
additional centres accordingly. This will help  in ensuring that candidates travel 
less than 100 kilometres for exams.  The Committee stresses the importance of 
making the process more candidate -friendly, especially for those from rural, 
remote, and economically weaker sections. It also recommends special transport 
arrangements—such as reserved coaches or special trains—in coordination with 
Indian Railways and State Transport Authorities. These should be planned well 
ahead of major exam dates. Information about such services must be widely 
publicised to help candidates plan their travel, reduce stress, and lower costs. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.22 The Committee suggests that a standard feedback module be prepared by the 
organizations which are responsible for conduct of the examinations. Once the 
students have completed the examination cycle, they may be given an option to fill 
in this standardized module. This module may contain various heads like syllabus, 
time taken to complete the exam, constraints faced, infrastructure issues like 
internet connectivity etc, logistical issu es and so on. This will help the 
organizations make the recruitm ent cycle even more streamlined and fast . (Para 
2.104) 
  

64 
 
Action Taken  
3.23 `Feedback' module is available on the webpage of the UPSC 
(i.e. https://www.upsc.gov.in), where  any person can record his/her views/ 
comments/ suggestions in respect of any examination of the Commission including 
the CAPF(AC) Examination, which is conducted by the Commission for 
recruitment to the posts of Assistant Commandants in CAPFs. This feedba ck 
window remains available on 24 X 7 basis. Further, the people can also make 
representation through emails and other modes as they deem appropriate.  
3.24 Staff Selection Commission follows a transparent system of examination and 
continuous feedback of t he examinees is an integral part of the system. As part of 
the process of the examination system, the answer keys of the questions are 
finalized after getting due feedback from the candidates. Continuous feedback is 
also received in the form of representations/ grievances/ other references etc. These 
inputs are considered and appropriate measures taken. Based on such feedback, the 
Commission has started the practice of providing a window for correction of online 
application forms. This has enabled the candi dates to rectify the mistakes, if any, 
committed by them during the filling up of online applications. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.25 The Committee appreciates the existing feedback mechanisms of both 
UPSC and SSC . However, it  recommends a uniform, structured feedback 
module for all recruitment agencies, including UPSC, SSC, IBPS, and RRBs. 
This module should be mandatory at the end of each examination cycle and 
cover aspects such as syllabus relevance, question design, time ma nagement, 
infrastructure issues, language options, accessibility, logistics, and other 
constraints. Feedback should be collected in a consistent, analyzable format to 
enable regular assessment and improvement and the data should be periodically 
reviewed to enhance transparency and demonstrate responsiveness. A uniform 
framework would help identify systemic issues, improve the candidate 
experience, and streamline the recruitment process . The Committee also 
recommends that, in the event of an abrupt cancellat ion of an examination due 
to technical or procedural issues, appropriate steps should be taken to conduct a 
re-examination within three months, in the interest of the aspirants.

65

R E P O R T 
  
 This Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Legislative 
Department (Ministry of Law and Justice) on the Recommendations/ Observations of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and 
Justice in its One Hundred and Forty Nine (149th) Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants 
(2025-26) of the Legislative Department (Ministry of Law and Justice), which was presented to the 
Rajya Sabha on 27th March, 2025 and laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha on the 27th March, 2025. 
2. The Committee had made 11 recommendations/observations in its 149th    Report. Replies of 
the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters on the basis of 
satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I: Recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry: 
Para:- 2.20 (Total- 01). 
Chapter – II:   Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the replies given by the Ministry: Paras:- 2.35 and 2.38 (Total-02).  
Chapter – III:   Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry: Paras:- 2.21, 2.22, 2.27 and 2.36 (Total-04). 
Chapter – IV:   Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry 
have not been received by the Committee: Paras:- 3.5, 3.6, 3.10 and 3.11  
(Total-04).  
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed Action 
Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the Committee in 
Chapter – III of this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in the succeeding 
pages. For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report (i.e. of 149th Report) have been 
mentioned at the end of each Recommendation/Observation.   
  

2 
 
CHAPTER I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee observes that the Department has been able to spend about 80% of the RE 
(2024-25) upto 31st January, 2025. The Committee appreciates the Department for incurring the 
expenditure uniformly as a whole till 31st January, 2025 keeping in view the instructions issued by 
the Ministry of Finance (MoF), wherein the expenditure in the last quarter has to be restricted to 
33% ceiling and in last month (March) expenditure has to be restricted to 15% of ceiling. The 
Committee hopes that the Department shall strive to utilize the budget uniformly in the remaining 
part of FY 2024-25 and in forthcoming financial year 2025-26.             (Para 2.20)  
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 Recommendations/ observations made by the Committee have been noted for future 
compliance. The Legislative Department will put in its best efforts to comply with the prescribed 
ceilings of expenditure per quarter/month of the financial year, as provided by the Department of 
Expenditure, Ministry of Finance.

3 
 
 
CHAPTER II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1  The Committee in its previous reports, 101st, 107th, 114th and 130th reports on Demands for 
Grants suggested the Department to take the work related to translation of the Constitution in 
scheduled languages on priority. The Committee also observes that translation work have been 
done upto 106th Amendment in Hindi, Maithili, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Sanskrit and Urdu 
this year, as the updation work upto 105th amendment was done till the last Demands for Grants. 
However, so far 106 Amendments have taken place.               (Para 2.35) 
Action Taken 
 
2.2 As regards the Committee’s observation, it is submitted that besides Hindi, Maithili, 
Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Sanskrit and Urdu, the Constitution of India is updated up to 106th 
Amendment in Kashmiri language also. The publication of updated version of the Constitution of 
India in Telugu is ready to be published soon. The Central Institute of Indian Languages has been 
assigned the work of translation and updation of the Constitution of India in Assamese, Bodo, 
Gujarati, Konkani, Nepali, Odia, Santhali and Sindhi, and the work is under process. This 
Department is making all efforts to speed up the updation and translation of the Constitution of 
India in Bengali, Dogri, Kannada, Manipuri and Tamil languages, with the cooperation of 
respective State Governments. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
2.3 As far as repealing of Obsolete laws is concerned, the Committee appreciates the work done 
in this regard and that 1824 redundant and obsolete laws have been identified to be repealed. The 
Committee also feels that the laws prevalent in a country should be representative of the political 
and social structure existing at that time. The Committee hopes that the department will undertake 
such exercise of identifying and repealing the obsolete laws on regular and continuous basis in 
future also.                    (Para 2.38) 
 

4 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.4 As regards the Committee’s observation, it is stated that the present Government, as part of 
its resolve to bring reforms in the legal system had constituted a two Member Committee in 2014 to 
undertake comprehensive review of laws with a view to remove obsolete and redundant laws. On 
the basis of the recommendations of the said Two Member Committee and the Law Commission, 
the Legislative Department had identified 1824 redundant and obsolete Acts. After due examination 
and consultations with concerned Ministries and Department, a total of 1562 Central Acts have 
since been repealed through various Repealing and Amending Acts, Finance and Income Tax Acts. 
Apart from this 14 more pre-constitution Acts have been repealed through various Acts. Further, as 
different Ministries and Department are allocated different subject Matters, this Department has, 
vide its various D.O. letters, time and again requested all Ministries/Departments to take immediate 
necessary action to ensure the obsolete laws administered by them are repealed or re-enacted if so 
required as expeditiously as possible. Further, the Twenty-third Law Commission of India has been 
constituted with a mandate inter alia to examine review/repeal of obsolete laws.

projections made to the Ministry of Finance for the year 2025-26 under various heads have been

and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (about 27%) on the revenue Side and EVMs for Election Commission

CHAPTER - IV 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.1 It is also observed that out of the total allocation of Rs 361.76 crore in RE(2024-25), Rs 
268.34 crore has been spent upto 31st January, 2025, which is approximately 74 percent of RE 
(2024-25). The Committee appreciates the Commission for incurring the expenditure uniformly as a 
whole till 31st January, 2025 keeping in view the instructions issued by the Ministry of Finance 
(MoF), wherein the expenditure in the last quarter has to be restricted to 33% ceiling and in last 
month (March) expenditure has to be restricted to 15% of ceiling. The Committee hopes that the 
Commission will be able to utilize the remaining budget for the remaining part of Financial year 
2024-25 uniformily.                            (Para 3.5)  
4.2 However, the Committee, also observes that out of the total allocation of Rs. 27.91 crore in 
RE (2024-25) under the Capital head, the commission has been able to spent only Rs. 3.93 crore 
upto 31st January, 2025 which is about 14 percent of the RE (2024-25). The Committee fails to 
understand the reason behind such under-utilization of funds. Low capital expenditure utilization 
(14% of RE 2024-25 spent as of 31st January, 2025) indicates either inefficiencies in fund 
deployment or delays in procurement. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the ECI to improve 
its spending capacity on its capital side and ensure timely utilization of allocated capital funds, as 
non- expenditure tantamount to under-utilisation of resources.                   (Para 3.6) 
4.3 The Committee observes that out of the total 850 post, 275 posts are vacant which is about 
32% of the total sanctioned strength. The Committee shows its concern as a large number of 
vacancies still exist, especially at the level of Assistant Section Officer, Senior Secretariat Assistant, 
Steno Grade 'D', Junior Secretariat Assistant, MTS which is hampering its working. The vacancies 
in the Commission have accumulated over a period of time and accordingly, recommends the 
Commission to expedite the process of recruitment.                    (Para 3.10) 
4.4 The Committee is given to understand that whenever the elections are announced in states, 
the Model Code of Conduct comes into place immediately on announcement and trade gets hit. 
Though, Digital transactions have made a huge impact, still a large portion of the country’s 
economy is cash economy. In the pretext of implementation of the Model Code of Conduct, even the 

13 
 
genuine transactions of the traders are seized which impacts the trader and the economy. The 
Committee desires that ECI should have a mechanism to verify the purpose for which the money is 
being transacted. On verification, if it is found to be for legal purpose, then the entire money should 
be released immediately.                       (Para 3.11)  
Further Recommendation/Observation:  
4.5  The Committee has not received replies to recommendations of the Committee of the 
above paras i.e., 3.5, 3.6, 3.10 and 3.11 from the Legislative Department/Election Commission.  
The Committee would like to remind the Department that Action taken Replies should be 
furnished before the Committee within three months from the day when Report on Demands 
for Grants is presented in Parliament.

R E P O R T 
 This Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by 
the Department of Justice(Ministry of Law & Justice) on the recommendations/observations 
of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public 
Grievances, Law and Justice in its One Hundred Forty Seventh (147th) Report of the 
Committee on “Demands for Grants (2025-26)” pertaining to the Department of Justice 
(Ministry of Law & Justice), which was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 27th March, 2025 
and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 27th March, 2025. 
2. The Committee had made 24 recommendations/observations in its 147th Report. 
Replies of the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters 
on the basis of satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the 
Department, i.e. in respect of paras:- 2.5, 2.6, 2.10, 3.24, 3.25, 3.48, 3.49,  
3.50, 3.53 and 3.60(Total -10).  
Chapter – II:  Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the replies given by the Department, i.e. in respect of 
paras:- 3.21, 3.22, 3.29, 3.33, 3.47, 3.61 and 3.62 (Total -07).  
Chapter – III:   Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not 
accepted the replies of the Department, i.e. with regard to paras:- 2.12. 
2.15, 3.2, 3.8 3.9, 3.10, and 3.20 (Total -07). 
Chapter – IV:   Recommendations/observations (Nil) in respect of which final replies of 
the Government have not been received.  
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the 
Committee in Chapter – III of this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in the 
succeeding pages. For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report (i.e. of the 
147thReport) have been mentioned at the end of each recommendation/observation.   
  

2 
 
CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE DEPARTMENT 
 
ASSESSMENT OF BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.1  It is observed that the allocation to the Department has increased since 2023-24.  
However, as of January 31, 2025, the expenditure stands at Rs.2520.683 Crore, which is 89% 
of the Revised Estimates (RE) of Rs.2817.47 Crore for 2024-25.  The Committee appreciates 
the Department for its proper utilization of funds under different heads during the financial 
year 2024-25 and hopes that the department will continue to utilize the funds on the same 
pattern in future.                      (Para 2.5) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 The observations of the Committee are duly acknowledged. The Department remains 
committed to ensuring optimal and effective utilization of the allocated funds, as reflected in 
the financial year 2024-25. Efforts will be made to maintain the same level of fiscal discipline 
and efficiency in future financial years as well. 
 Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.3         The Committee observes that there is a significant increase in BE for 2025-26 when 
compared to the RE 2024-25.  A detailed review of expenditure trends may be conducted to 
ensure that budget estimates may accurately measures the actual usage of funds with respect 
to expenditure.                                                      (Para 2.6)   
 
Action Taken 
 
1.4 The observations of the Committee are duly acknowledged. The Department has been 
conducting regular review meetings with the involvement of States/UTs and other 
stakeholders to closely monitor expenditure patterns and ensure effective implementation of 
schemes. These reviews facilitate improved alignment of Budget Estimates (BE) with actual 
fund utilization. A detailed comparison of BE 2024-25, RE 2024-25, actual expenditure for 
2024-25 and BE 2025-26 is provided below, reflecting prudent financial management and the 
rationale behind the projections for 2025-26:

1.5 The Department will continue its data-driven approach to budgeting and monitoring 
to ensure that future estimates remain closely aligned with actual fund requirements and

4 
 
 
Assessment of Budget Allocated to National Legal Servies Authority (NALSA) 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.6       The Department has provided Rs.400 Crore as grant-in-aid to NALSA, considering its 
activities against its projection of Rs. 730.73 Crore for F.Y. 2025-26 which may still be 
insufficient.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendations made in its 116th and 
128th Reports to increase the Grant-aid-aid for NALSA, to enable them to conduct all 
activities on time.  The committee feels that without adequate budgetary provisions, both 
ongoing and newly implemented schemes and activities of NALSA will not take off.  The 
Department of Justice and NALSA should once again reach out to the Ministry of Finance 
and press the matter with greater emphasis.                (Para 2.10) 
 
Action Taken 
1.7 As per the Budgetary Estimates 2025-26, an amount of Rs. 200 crore has been 
provisioned as Grants-in-Aid to NALSA under Head 2014.00.119.01.00.31 – Grants-in-Aid 
General, under Demand No. 65 of the Ministry of Law & Justice, against the proposed 
Budgetary Estimates of Rs. 300.00 crore for the Financial Year 2025-26. Under this head, the 
implementation of various legal aid schemes / programmes framed under the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987 are undertaken, which may be adversely affected due to low budgetary 
allocation. Highlighting the implication, the matter for additional grants will be suitably taken 
up with the Ministry of Finance at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage, as per requirement. 
 
1.8 In addition, an amount of ₹200 crore has been provisioned as Grants-in-Aid for the 
Legal Aid Defense Counsel System (LADCS) Scheme in the Budgetary Estimates 2025-26 
against the proposed Budgetary Estimates of Rs. 430.73 crore for the Financial Year 2025-26. 
Presently, the LADCS Scheme has been implemented in 654 District Legal Services 
Authorities (DLSAs) and expansion to all DLSAs across the country in F.Y. 2025-26 is 
underway. Accordingly, demand for additional funds will be taken up with the Ministry of 
Finance at the RE stage, as per requirement. 
 
 
Designing innovative solutions and Holistic Access to Justice (DISHA) 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.9      The Committee appreciates the concept of DISHA scheme that endeavours to address 
the legal needs of the people.  Given the success of the 56 TV programs broadcast under the 
“Vidhi Jagriti Abhiyaan” initiative, the Committee recommends that the department may 
collaborate with the Doordarshan to expand the content and increase its reach.                                                                                   
                                                                                                                               (Para 3.24) 
 
 
 
 
 

5 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.10 Under the DISHA Scheme, the Department of Justice, in collaboration with 
Doordarshan, developed and aired 56 television programmes focused on legal awareness. 
These programmes addressed key issued related to the empowerment of senior citizens, 
persons with disabilities, women, children and transgenders.  
 
1.11 The episodes were developed in eight languages, i.e., Hindi, English, Bangla, 
Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil and Telugu and were broadcasted across 11 national 
and regional channels of Doordarshan, namely,  DD National, DD News, DD Punjabi, DD 
India, DD Assam, DD Bangla, DD Chandana, DD Malayalam, DD Sahyadri, DD Podhigai 
and DD Yadagiri. The series was telecasted between February and September 2024, reaching 
over 70 lakh viewers.  All 56 episodes are currently available on the YouTube channels of the 
respective DD platforms. 
 
1.12 As part of the initiative, information about the Tele-Law mobile app and the Tele-Law 
toll-free number (14454) was disseminated through on-screen Scrolls and L/Aston Bands 
during the telecasts. Furthermore, the Tele-Law movie was also broadcast on Doordarshan to 
expand awareness. 
 
1.13 In collaboration with Prasar Bharati, a 30-second radio jingle promoting the Tele-Law 
campaign was aired over 61 days, from 18 December, 2023, to 16 February, 2024. The jingle 
was broadcast across: 25 FM Rainbow channels, 4 FM Gold channels, 42 Vividh Bharti 
stations and 201 primary/local radio stations. 
 
 1.14 Additionally, the campaign included special spot broadcasts under the "Nayi Soch 
Nayi Kahani" programme on FM Gold Delhi, which was aired from 01 August, 2023, to 31 
August, 2023. 
 
1.15 The Committee’s recommendation has been noted for compliance. Department would 
further expand its outreach from support from Doordarshan to increase the legal literacy and 
awareness among the masses. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.16       The Committee further suggests that to increase the program’s impact, interactive 
formats should be explored, such as call – programs, where viewers can ask legal questions 
directly to experts.  The Committee feels that social media campaigns and online discussion 
can engage younger audiences.                  (Para 3.25) 
  
 
Action Taken 
 
1.17 The suggestion of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
 
 
 

6 
 
SCHEMES/PROGRAMMES OF NALSA 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.18       The Committee recommends strengthening the E-Lok Adalat platform to improve its

Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.11         The Committee observes that the process of judicial appointment and pendency of 
cases are critical issues that require urgent attention.  There must be synergy between the 
judiciary and the Government to ensure timely processing of recommendations and 
appointments.  The Committee feels that a coordination mechanism should be developed 
between the Judiciary and the Ministry of Law and Justice to track the status of appointments

(Para 3.8) 
3.12         The Committee feels that an institutional mechanism may be developed wherein the

which would ensure that the vacancy is filled immediately after the retirement.  The High

Action Taken (Para 3.8 & Para 3.9)  
 
3.13 The Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are appointed under Articles 124, 
217 and 224 of the Constitution of India in accordance with the procedure laid down in the 
Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) prepared in 1998 pursuant to the Supreme Court’s 
judgment of October 6, 1993 (Second Judges Case), read with its Advisory Opinion of 
October 28, 1998 (Third Judges Case). 
 
3.14 As per the MoP, the responsibility for initiating proposals for appointment of Judges 
to the Supreme Court lies with the Chief Justice of India, while for High Courts, it lies with 
the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court. The MoP stipulates that High Courts should 
send their recommendations at least six months before the anticipated vacancy; however, this 
timeline is rarely adhered to by the High Courts. For appointments to the High Courts, the 
views of the concerned State Government are obtained in accordance with the MoP. The 
recommendations are also examined in light of reports available to the Government regarding 
the proposed names. Recommendations from the High Court Collegium, the State 
Government and the Government of India are then forwarded to the Supreme Court 
Collegium (SCC) for its advice. Only those candidates whose names are recommended by the 
SCC are appointed as Judges of the High Courts. 
 
3.15 The appointment of Judges to Constitutional Courts is a continuous, integrated and 
collaborative process involving both the Executive and the Judiciary. It requires consultation 
and concurrence from various constitutional authorities at both the State and Central levels. 
While every effort is made to fill up existing vacancies expeditiously, vacancies in High 
Courts continue to arise due to retirement, resignation, elevation of Judges to the Supreme 
Court and also due to periodic increases in the sanctioned strength of Judges. 
 

18 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.16 The Committee takes note of the Ministry’s response detailing the constitutional 
and procedural framework governing appointments to the Supreme Court and High 
Courts as prescribed under the Memorandum of Procedure (MoP). However, it is 
constrained to observe that, despite clearly defined timelines, several High Courts 
continue to delay the submission of recommendations so at least six months prior to 
anticipated vacancies.  The Committee finds this situation deeply unsatisfactory, as 
these delays adversely affect judicial capacity and impede the timely dispensation of 
justice.   The Committee reiterates that effective coordination between the Judiciary 
and the Executive is crucial to ensure timely appointments. 
3.17  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a structured coordination 
mechanism be instituted between the Ministry of Law and Justice and the Judiciary to 
regularly monitor the status of pending recommendations, compliance with the 
timelines under the Memorandum of Procedure (MoP), and projected vacancies. The 
Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that High Courts with the heaviest 
pendency particularly those of Allahabad, Bombay, and Rajasthan be accorded priority 
in the appointment process.

3.22 Section 3(1) of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 provides that the State Governments,

Nyayalayas mandatory for State Governments.

2. The Committee had made 21 recommendations/observations in its One Hundred Forty 
Sixth Report. Replies of the Departments of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances 
and Pensions and Pensioners‘ which have been categor ized and scrutinized under four  
chapters on the basis of satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as 
follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations which have been  accepted by the 
Ministry: Paras:- 2.2, 2.7, 2.9, 2.13, 3.5 and 3.34. (Total- 06). 
Chapter – II:   Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the replies given by the Ministr y: Paras:- 3.9, 3.11, 3.17, 
3.32, 3.36 and 3.56. (Total- 06).  
Chapter – III:  Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not 
accepted the replies of the Ministr y: Paras:- 2.5, 2.15, 3.18, 3.23, 3.30 and 
3.42. (Total- 06). 
Chapter-IV: Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
ministry have not been received: Paras:- 3.53, 3.54, and 3.55. (Total- 03). 
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the 
Committee in Chapter – III of this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in the 
succeeding pages.  For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report (i.e. of 14 6th 
Report) have been mentioned at the end of each Recommendation/Observation.   
  

 
2 
 
CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Overall Assessment of the Demands for Grants 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 It is observed that the budgetary allocation for the Department has been steadily 
increasing during the past few years. BE for the financial year 2025 -26 of DARPG is Rs. 
174.37 crore , which is an increase of Rs. 42.412 Crore  (32.14% approximately) over RE 
2024-25. The Committee notes that except for the year  2022-23, where the Department was 
able to spend almost the entire budget allocation, in subsequent years, the Department has 
not been able to fully utilise the allocation, while the allocations kept on increasing. The 
Committee hopes the Department would be able to spend the allocation as it has already 
done in 2022-23.                                                                                                      (Para 2.2) 
Action Taken 
1.2 The Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances  has one Scheme , 
i.e., ‗Scheme for Administrative Reforms‘ which was recast into a new Scheme with two 
components (i) Administrative Reforms Component , and (ii) Comprehensive S ystem for 
Redressal of Public Grievances Component, with the following budget outlay:

1.3 An amount of Rs. 100.00 core has been allocated under the ‗Scheme for 
Administrative Reforms‘ for both components in B.E 2025 -26 against amount of Rs. 80.00 
crore which was allocated in BE 2024 -25. Further an amount of Rs. 50.57 crore under Non -
Scheme and 2.30 crore under Capital outlay and Rs. 21.50 crore under Grant -in-Aid for 
NCGG. Accordingly, an amount of Rs. 174.37 crore has been allocated to this Department 
during 2025-26 against the total allocation of Rs. 124.41 crore in B.E 2024-25. 
1.4 During the financial year 2024-25, the funds could not be fully utilized due to: 
● Prime Ministers Awards 2023 could not be conferred on 21.04.2024 due to General 
Election 2024 to Lok Sabha. 
● ‗Next Gen CPGRAMS Project‘ under the component of Comprehensive Redressal of 
Public Grievances, could not be materialized due to non- completion of tender process. 
1.5 An additional allocation in BE 2025 -26 was projected by this Department for 
organizing Prime Ministers Awards 2023 & 2024. Also, this increased budget requirement in  
B.E 2025-26 was due to proposed revamping of CPGRAMS ―NextGen CPGRAMS‖ Project. 
1.6 The existing CPGRAMS, developed in 2006, required a major overhaul to keep pace 
with the rapid advancements in technology. An upgraded system was essential not only for 
ensuring faster and higher -quality resolution of public grievances, but also for transforming 
CPGRAMS into an intelligent platform capable of predicting risks related to policies, 
processes, and personnel —thereby enhancing accountability across the governanc e 
ecosystem. It was decided to engage a System Integrator to design and implement an end -to-
end solution for the Next Gen CPGRAMS. The Department of Expenditure approved a 
comprehensive proposal for the development of this enhanced system, with a total out lay of 
₹128.10 crore. Of this, ₹ 87 crore was earmarked specifically for the creation of a new IT 
infrastructure and an advanced analytical dashboard. 
1.7 The Department had floated a Request for Proposal  (RFP) through Central Public 
Procurement Portal for selecting the System Integrator for this project. Since, this was highly 
technical project, the Department had scheduled multiple stakeholders consultations and 
industry consultations. The validity of RFP was extended multiple times on demand of  the 
prospective bidders. Further, the date of submission of POC/presentation was also extended 
on request of bidders who qualified in the pre -qualification criteria. Due the process, the 
finalisation of bids was delayed. This delay resulted short expenditure in the respective heads 
allotted for PG. The Department would be able to spend the allocation made in the Budget 
Estimate 2025-26. 

 
4 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.8 The Committee notes that there is an increase of 81.91% in Non -Scheme 
allocation. The Committee desires that the key areas driving the rise may be identified to 
ensure that administrative and operational expenses remain constant and do not lead to 
excessive overheads. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to utilize the 
funds more uniformly throughout the year.                                                           (Para 2.7)                                                                          
Action Taken 
1.9 The reasons for increasing of about 81.91% under the Non-Scheme heads of this 
Department are mainly as under: 
a. An amount of Rs. 10 crore was allocated to this Department under head ‗Rents, 
Rates and Taxes‘ during B.E. 2024 -25 which was enhanced to Rs. 25 crore in R.E. 2024 - 
25 for payment of monthly rent of Office space.  
b. For B.E. 2025 -26, an amount of Rs. 30.00 crore has been allocated due to 
escalation in rental charges. In object heads of Salaries and Allowances, 8.54 % and    
41.70 % funds increased respectively due to periodical revision of salary & allowances . 
In addition to the above, the increment in some other object heads has been made to meet 
the regular expenses.  
1.10 The expenditure is being monitored regularly in Senior Officers Meeting and all 
efforts are being made to utilize the funds uniformly throughout the year. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.11 The Committee notes that there is a significant variation of 52.81% between BE  
2024-25 and BE 2025 -26. The Committee feels that improved forecasting and budget 
management processes may be used to reduce the variation. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that regular monitoring of expenditures by the Department should be done to 
optimize fund utilization.                                                                                             (Para 2.9)                                                                                                   
Action Taken 
1.12 The observations made by the Committee is noted. The NCGG furnishes the 
utilization certificate with every request for release of funds to Department Administrative 
Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) which is a useful tool for monitoring of the 
expenditures and Budget by DARPG. The final allocation to NCGG for FY 2024 -25 was Rs. 
19.00 crore and the BE 2025-26 has been projected for Rs.21.50 crore. 

 
5 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.13 The Committee observes that the Revised Estimate (RE) for 2024 -25 is 104.10%  
higher than the Budget Estimate (BE) for the same year, indicating a substantial increase. 
Additionally, there is a 70.91% increase from BE 2024 -25 to BE 2025 -26. Furthermore, the 
BE for 2025 -26 is 10.05% lower than the projections submitted to the Minist ry of Finance 
(MoF). The Committee feels that the Department should take adequate steps to utilize the 
funds timely, completely and efficiently in future.                                                    (Para 2.13) 
Action Taken  
1.14 The increase in budget in RE 2024 -25 over BE 2024 -25 was due to  direct tenancy 
with NDMC as per office area available/allotted to the Department.  The annual estimation 
for the rent is Rs. 7.00 crore. However, only Rs. 2.50 crore were allocated in BE 2024 -25. 
Further, funds were sought in RE 2024 -25 for procurement of MSQL software for 
Bhavishyawhich is procured at Rs. 4.41 C rore. As per the expenditure statement for FY 
2024-25, the percentage of expenditure over RE 2024-25 is 93.39%. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.15 The Committee appreciates the 10-step CPGRAMS reforms process that was adopted 
by DARPG for improving the quality of grievance disposal and reducing the time lines. The 
Committee commends the Department for faster rate of di sposal of grievances by reducing 
the average disposal time from 32 days in 2021 to 16 days in May 2023.  To further improve 
the disposal rate, the Committee recommends the Department to integrate State portals with 
CPGRAMS, standardize naming conventions, and establish a feedback mechanism to 
monitor and enhance the quality of grievance redressal.                                           (Para 3.5)                                      
Action Taken  
1.16 In order to enhance the quality and pace of grievance redressal, the Department 
launched the 10-Step CPGRAMS Reforms in April 2022. These reforms aim at streamlining 
operations through end -to-end digitization, intelligent routing of grievances, real -time 
performance monitoring, and inclusive service delivery. A significant aspect of these reforms 
has been the integration of State grievance portals into CPGRAMS to create a unified 
national platform. To date, all States and Union T erritories, except West Beng al have been 
integrated. In addition to platform integration, DARPG has undertaken the standardization of 
grievance categorization, enabling precise routing and monitoring of grievances. Over 
1,03,840 Grievance Redressal Officers have been mapped as per th e categorization structure. 
This has led to a reduction in average disposal time from 45 days to 30 days in 2022, and 

 
6 
 
further to 21 days in 2024. 
1.17 The feedback mechanism has also been significantly strengthened. Upon resolution of 
a grievance, citizens  receive SMS and email notifications inviting feedback. In July 2022, 
DARPG operationalized a multilingual Feedback Call Centre to capture direct responses 
from citizens. As of 28th February 2025, over 20.48 lakh feedback calls have been completed. 
A dedic ated feedback portal, developed by DARPG, now enables Ministries and 
Departments to analyze monthly trends and take corrective action in areas with low 
satisfaction ratings. This continuous feedback loop is instrumental in shaping departmental 
responsiveness. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.18 To alleviate the burden on pensioners regarding the submission of annual life 
certificates, the Committee recommends the Department to promote the use of the Aadhaar -
based Digital Life Certificate (DLC) system, which will enable online submissions without 
their physical presence. Furthermore, life certificates attested by authorized officials of 
Indian Embassies, High Commissions, or Consulates may be allowed for submission for 
pensioners, residing abroad eliminating t heir need for travelling to India solely for this 
purpose.                                                                                                                     (Para 3.34) 
Action Taken  
1.19 The Department has taken a number of steps to spread awareness and provide access 
to digital technology for Life certificate generation. For this DoPPW has collaborated with 
India Post Payments Bank (IPPB), Pension Disbursing Banks, M/o Railways, M/o Defen ce, 
D/o Posts, D/o Telecom, Pensioners‘ Welfare Ass ociations, MeitY& UIDAI.  This 
Department has issued a comprehensive guidelines dated 9th August, 2024 on Nationwide 
DLC Campaign 3.0. 
1.20 Face Authentication technique has digitally empowered the pension ers and they no 
longer need to visit bank branches/ service centers for submission of Life Certificates. 
Through this App a pensioner can submit a Digital Life Certificate from the comfort of home 
using any Android smart phone or on the iOS platform of iPhone. 
1.21 For submission of Annual Life certificates in respect of pensioners/ family 
pensioners‘ residing abroad, DoPPW has issued OM No. 11(15)/2022 -P&PW ( H) dated 
15.10.2024 (Annexure- I). Hence, the recommendation has already been complied. 
***** 

 
7 
 
CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE MINISTRY 
Overall Assessment of the Demands for Grants 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1 The Committee feels that the Department should enhance capacity-building initiatives 
for Grievance Officers (GROs) by strengthening partnerships with ISTM, ATIs, and ASCI. 
Regular training programs, b oth online (iGOT  Karmayogi) and offline, may be conducted 
with updated content and practical case studi es. Further, the Sevottam scheme may be 
reviewed and expanded for better grievance redressal.                                              (Para 3.9)                                                   
Action Taken 
2.2 Taking cognizance of the Committee‘s views on enhancing the capacity of Grievance 
Officers, the Department has stepped up efforts to provide structured training through 
collaborations with reputed institutions. A sustained partnership with the Institute of  
Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM) has enabled the creation of a cadre of master 
trainers for CPGRAMS. Additionally, ISTM has been instrumental in developing online 
courses hosted on the iGOT Karmayogi platform, making learning more accessible. 
2.3 The Department has also deepened its engagement with State Administrative Training 
Institutes (ATIs) under the Sevottam programme. This initiative focuses on three pillars —
Citizen‘s Charter, Grievance Redress Mechanism, and Capability Building. Over the last 
three years, financial assistance has been extended to ATIs for establishing dedicated training 
cells. A total of 756 training sessions have bee n conducted, benefiting 24,942 Officers across 
States. 
2.4 DARPG has partnered with the Administrative Staf f College of India (ASCI) to 
conduct a Training Needs Assessment (TNA) of Grievance Officers. This will culminate in 
the development of a standardized training curriculum and andragogical framework, enabling 
uniformity in training delivery across States. F urther, the Department organized two national 
workshops—in Pune (May, 2023) and Bhopal (February , 2025)—with participation from 22 
States/UTs to showcase best practices in grievance redress and capacity building. 
 
 

 
8 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.5 The Committee observes that the feedback of grievance redressal measured through 
Grievance Redressal Index, indicates positive progress with a significant rise in satisfaction 
rates and reduction in appeals, wherein the overall satisfaction rate of 52% in 2024 still 
points to considerable room for improvement. The 61% satisfaction rate for the top 10 
Ministries/Departments is a moderate outcome, suggesting that more efforts are needed to 
achieve higher citizen satisfaction.                                                                            (Para3.11) 
Action Taken 
2.6 The endeavour of the government is that the individual citizen‗s voice must be heard, 
and the citizen must be empowered adequately to repose trust in the system. In this regard, 
DARPG ha s introduced several measures for strengthening CPGRAMS and improve the 
quality of the public grievances and citizen satisfaction as under:- 
(i) Introduction of Appeal Mechanism to increase the accountability and quality of 
grievances. 
(ii) Operationalization of feedback call centre to ensure that the every voice must be 
heard. 
(iii) Conducting monthly meeting with all Nodal PG officers of Ministries/Department of 
Central Governments and States with the focus to ensure the redressal timely and as per 
citizen expectaction. 
(iv) Capacity building through Sevotttam to ensure effective redressal. 
2.7 Besides, in pursuance to the direction of Hon‘ble  Prime Minister during the 
PRAGATI meeting held on 26th February, 2025, Department of Administrative Reforms and 
Public Grievances (DARPG) has operationalized a dedicated module for review of public 
grievances by Secretaries to the GOI in CPGRAMS. The Modu le enables 
Ministries/Departments to structure meeting agenda, monitor the progress in a systematic 
manner. In the module, the Ministries/Department can also review the close case to monitor 
the quality of the disposal by the GROs. A D.O. letter from Cabinet Secretary and O.M. from 
Secretary (DARPG) were also issued to all Ministries/Departments for compliance 
(Annexure-II). As on 8.4.2025 26 Review meetings were conducted by 
Ministries/Department through this module, wherein, more than 50 individual CPGRAM S 
cases were reviewed. 
2.8 Further, to make CPGRAMS more sensitive, accessible and meaningful to the citizen, 
the Department had issued Comprehensive Guidelines for Effective Redressal of Public 

 
9 
 
Grievances on 23rd August 2024. These guidelines envisage int egration of various public 
grievance platforms, creation of dedicated grievance cells in Ministries/ Departments, 
appointment of experienced and competent nodal officers, emphasis on root cause analysis of 
grievances and action on feedback, strengthening e scalation processes by appointing 
appellate authorities, and grievance closure guidelines with further reduction in upper limit of 
resolution time from 30 days to 21 days. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.9 The Committee observes that, adopting e -Office mechanism requires establishing 
24/7 support, conducting regular user training, and promoting awareness of new features. 
Integration with other government platforms and a stronger feedback mechanism are 
essential for continuous improvement. Further, the Committee feels that Cyber -Security 
through audits and multi - factor authentication for data protection may be ensured to 
improve efficiency.                                                                                                    (Para 3.17) 
Action Taken 
2.10 There is a multi -level support mechanism in place for the e -Office project to handle 
issues on daily basis and escalate to the next level if needed. A 24*7 help desk 
[https://servicedesk.nic.in/] is already available. Users can register issues online or call the 
24*7 available NIC Service desk support number at 1800111555. 
2.11 User training and promoting awareness of new features is provided by the eOffice 
Project Division through regular structured training and support to help users transition to the 
eOffice platform. Training includes a 4-day structured program covering theory and practical 
application, with additional customized training at the user organization‘s premises and 1-day 
sessions for senior officials. 
2.12 Integration with other government platforms – External entities, like Parichay SSO or 
equivalent (e.g. SAML, Active directory), Web VPN, eSign, Applications, Bhashini and 
Kanthasth for languages are already integrated with eOffice. Further, eOffice serves as a 
feeder to other eGovernance systems by offering read/write APIs for seamless integration 
with external applications. To meet the generic requirements for interaction with other 
eGovernance systems, the 'eOffice Web Services' are available to provide read/write APIs for 
seamless integration and provide information to other dashboard services as well. 
2.13 The eOffice Project Division has a feedback mechanism for receiving feedback from 
all its user organizations for continuous im provement, and are maintained and recorded 

 
10 
 
centrally, on a structured platform. These feedbacks are assessed, prioritized and then 
released into the application in an iterative and incremental continuous delivery process. 
From January 2024 until March 2025 , 39 features were released in six different versions of 
the eFiles application. Application security audits are done regularly along with continuous 
vulnerability assessment. Annual comprehensive audit are also conducted. E -Office access is 
restricted to NICNET/NKN or through VPN only and 2-Factor authentication is enabled. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.14 A fluctuating trend can be observed in the number of cases received and disposed 
over the years. In 2021 -22, 66,736 cases were received with a 95.26% disposal rate, which 
declined to 91.8% in 2022-23 despite a lower number of cases received (58,964). In 2023-24, 
cases received surged to 94,108, but the disposal rate slightly dropped to 90.88%. The trend 
continued in 2024-25 (till 27.01.25) with a sharp rise in cases (1,05,058) and a further dip in 
disposal rate (87.1%), indicating a growing backlog and potential challenges in handling the 
increased workload efficiently. Therefore, the Committee recommends the Department to 
improve its efficiency, by enha ncing its staff strength and adopting automation, and 
streamline workflows. The Committee also feels that coordination and leveraging digital 
tools will ensure timely resolution and prevent backlog amidst rising volumes of cases.           
(Para 3.32) 
Action Taken 
2.15 DoPPW constantly coordinates with other Ministries/ Departments through meetings, 
e-mails and reminders for ensuring expeditious redressal. Also, monthly Inter Ministerial 
Review Meetings (IMRMs), through VC, and Pension Adalats have prov ed their utility in 
redressal of long pending grievances. The recommendations of Parliamentary Standing 
Committee have been noted and it is submitted that the frequency of interaction with 
Ministries/Departments having majority of long pending cases, would  be increased through 
issue of DOs and physical meetings with the concerned Nodal Officers. For this, adequate 
manpower would be deployed.  
2.16 The DoPPW is also in the process of introducing technological advancements, 
thereby reducing redressal time. Fo r this, meetings with the stakeholders, especially 
Ministries/Departments having majority of the pension grievances, are being convened on the 
issue of auto forwarding of the grievances directly from the complainants to the concerned 
GROs and auto lateral movement of the grievances among Ministries/ Departments as the 
redressal of pension grievances require action from different stakeholders. 

 
11 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.17 The Committee observes that rate of grievances have increased drastically, 
particularly in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) [72%], which remains a major concern for 
pensioners of PCDA, Pension Allahabad and Department of Ex -Servicemen Welfare, 
indicating persistent issues in pension processing. Further the trends in other ministries like 
Railways, Financial Services, and Posts show s a decline, which means that Mo D requires 
targeted intervention rather than general reforms. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
the Department to establish a specialized grievance c ell with representatives from M oD, 
PCDA, and Ex-Servicemen Welfare to identify key bottlenecks and expedite timely resolution 
of grievances.                                                                                                            (Para 3.36) 
 Action Taken 
2.18 In the backdrop of increased receipts of the Defence pension grievances, the level of 
interaction with Ministry of Defence was elevated and meetings with Secretary (Defence), 
Secretary (ESW) and Controller General of Defence Accounts (CGDA) were conducted on 
regular intervals, apart from monthly Inter-Ministerial Review Meetings (IMRMs). However, 
the recommendations of Parliamentary Standing Committee  have been noted and 
nominations, not below the rank of Director, are being sought from the major stakeholde rs, 
viz., CGDA, PCDA(P), Prayagraj, DESW and Department of Military Affairs. On receipt of 
the same, the specialized grievance cell would be constituted. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.19 The Committee appreciates the Department of Pension and Pensioners Welfare for its 
overall performance and hopes that it will continue good work to bring about 'ease of living' 
for pensioners, especially for super senior citizens and family pensioners.             (Para 3.56) 
Action Taken 
2.20 The Ministry has noted the recommendation/observation of the Committee.  
2.21 DoPPW is committed for the welfare of Pensioners‘ especially super senior citizens 
and family pensioners. The Face Authentication Technique is a game changer and very 
beneficial for pensioners as no external device is required and DLC generation is very fast, in 
less than a minute. It can be submitted through any smart phone and is being widely used 
which ensures ease of living for Pensioners. 

 
12 
 
2.22 Pensioners‘ Awareness Programmes , Bankers‘ Awareness Programmes and Pre - 
Retirement counseling workshops are held on regular basis, both physically and online to 
familiarize and popularize DLCs and the Face Authentication Technique.  Pensioners were 
apprised of new initiatives by Government of India through social media also.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN FOR NOT
