Overall Assesement of the Demands for Grants 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1 The Committee observes that the Department should ensure timely implementation 
and efficient utilization  of allocated funds of Rs. 97.00 Crore by establishing well -defined 
performance indicators. The en hancement of CPGRAMS through AI -driven analytics and 
regional language support is imperative to improve the accessibility and inclusivity. The 
Committee hopes that the proposed Data Strategy Unit will leverage advanced technologies 
to enhance governance efficiency. Strengthening collaborations with premier institutions like 
IIT Kanpur will further drive innovation and technological advancements, in upgrading 
CPGRAMS.                                                                                                                 (Para 2.5) 
Action Taken 
3.2 In alignment with the vision for Next Generation CPGRAMS, the Department has 
adopted a comprehensive approach to introduce measurable performance indicators and 
operational benchmarks for technology deployment and public grievance redress. The 
enhancement of CPGRAMS with AI -based analytics is currently underway through 
collaboration with premier institutions such as IIT Kanpur, where efforts are focused on 
predictive grievance routing, automatic prioritization, and detection of habitual complaints. 
Furthermore, a regional language interface is being developed in partnership with Bhashini 
under MeitY, to make the platform inclusive and accessible to every citizen in their native 
language. Simultaneously, the proposed Data Strategy Unit, now operational, is ta sked with 
generating actionable insights and thematic analytics to improve overall governance 
efficiency. These measures are fully aligned with the Committee's expectation of leveraging 
advanced technology and institutional collaborations to ensure citizen -centric grievance 
redressal. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.3 The Committee notes the Ministry’s comprehensive response regarding the 
enhancement of Next Generation CPGRAMS, including the adoption of performance 

 
14 
 
indicators, AI -driven analytics, regi onal language support, and institutional 
collaborations. However, the Committee observes that the Ministry has not provided a 
definitive timeline for the full operationalization of the Next Generation CPGRA MS. 
Additionally, the status and expected completi on timeframe for the development of the 
regional language interface may be specified.  
3.4 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should  furnish a 
detailed and time -bound action plan outlining the milestones for the complete 
deployment of the Next Generation CPGRAMS. This should include  the phased rollout 
of the regional language interface. The Committee feels that s uch clarity will enable the 
Department to timely implement and efficiently utilize allocated funds.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.5 It may be observed that there are significant variations of Non -Scheme (Revenue) 
budget estimates, revised estimates, and actual expenditures over the last three financial 
years. In 2023-24, the revised estimate (₹14 crore) w as substantially higher than the budget 
estimate (₹9.03 crore), with actual expenditure (₹13.74 crore)close to full utilization. In 
2024-25, the revised estimate (₹21.67 crore) shows a sharp increase, but actual expenditure 
as of 20.01.2025 remains lower ( ₹7.62 crore). Even if the figure of ₹8 crores is included, 
then also the actual expenditure is significantly lower when compared with the allocated 
budget. The Committee hopes that in the rest of the period, the Department would be able to 
fully utilize th e allocated sum. Further, the Committee desires a detailed reason for under -
utilization of funds during the year 2024-25.                                                            (Para 2.15) 
Action Taken

and a brief of the budget is as under.

Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.7 The Committee observes that as on 20.01.2025, the actual expenditure reported 
was only ₹7.62 crore . Moreover, even after accounting for the payment towards rent of 
the premises . i.e. ₹8 Crore, which was to be made in F Y 2024-25, the estimated 
expenditure amounts to  ₹15.62 Cr ore. Y et, by the end of the financial period, the 
expenditure rose sharply to ₹ 21.04 crore. The Ministry has not explained how such a 
substantial expenditure was incurred within  a short span of time. Further, the 
Committee finds that no explanation has been given for the significant variations 
observed in the Non -Scheme (Revenue) budget estimat es, revised estimates, and actual 
expenditures over the last three years. The Department may  furnish a comprehensive 
statement detailing the reasons for the sharp expenditure increase in the closing period.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.8 EPFO- It has come  to the notice of the Committee, that in the form of public 
grievances a large number of employees who work in private sector where funds are under 
the watch of EPFO, the employer do not pay their share of contribution and even sometimes 
do not even pay th e employees contribution as well. Secondly, some of the private sector 
organizations have made trusts and employee and employer’s contribution is kept in the 
trusts. The money is also not paid to the employees. The hard earned money of employees 
which have  been mandatorily deducted and employer’s share is not credited to the 
employee’s EPFO account. In such instance when any grievance of such type is received by 
the Department, the Committee feels that it should take up with EPFO.                 (Para 3.18)                               
Action Taken 
3.9 With reference to the Committee‘s concern about grievances related to EPFO, 
especially regarding defaulting private employers, the Department plans to intiate targeted 
action. Pursuant to the Hon‘ble  Prime Minister‘s directive during the PRAGATI meeting of 
26th February 2025, DARPG activated the grievance review module for EPFO -related 
complaints. In the April 2024 review meeting with Nodal Officers, the Secretary of DARPG 
specifically raised the matt er of increasing grievances involving non -payment of 
employee/employer contributions and the misuse of employee trusts. 
3.10 DARPG has started compiling a list of such grievances and will coordinate with the 
Ministry of Labour and EPFO for redressal. The D epartment will ask EPFO to review 
previously disposed cases using the Secretary -level grievance review module to assess their 
quality. Additionally, in collaboration with Common Services Centre (CSC), DARPG plans 

 
16 
 
to organize a Facebook Live session with EP FO in May 2025 to directly engage citizens on 
these matters and guide them on grievance resolution procedures. This outreach initiative is 
expected to bridge information gaps and address the concerns highlighted by the Committee. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.11 The Committee acknowledges the Department’s prompt action in addressing 
grievances related to EPFO contributions and misuse of employee trusts, including the 
activation of the grievance review module and planned citizen engagement initiati ves. 
However, the Committee is concerned about the continuing incidence of defaulting 
employers and the impact on employees’ hard -earned funds. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department and EPFO expedite the resolution of pending cases 
and s trengthen monitoring mechanisms to prevent future defaults. The Committee 
further desires that the Ministry may devise a result-oriented effective action plan.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.12 The Committee observes that the training sessions had covered only 224 Indian 
officials across s elect States, which is insufficient for nationwide impact. However, it is also 
observed that States with high grievance redressal needs (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, 
Maharashtra) were not adequately covered. The Committee r ecommends that, to enhance the 
effectiveness of CPGRAMS, the Department should focus on expanding domestic outreach by 
integrating digital learning platforms and strengthening post training assessments.        
 (Para 3.23) 
Action Taken 
3.13 The observation s made by the Committee is noted. As far as NCGG is concerned, 
CPGRAMS, which has revolutionized the grievance redressal and monitoring system of the 
Government of India, is introduced as a topic in Capacity Building Programmes for the 
international Civil Servants. Earlier in the reply, it was emphasized that NCGG has trained 
224 domestic Civil Servants of the State of Arunachal Pradesh and the UT of Jammu & 
Kashmir. As such with regard to the recommendation, NCGG does not conduct any capacity 
building programme specifically for CPGRAMS. 
 
 
 

 
17 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.14 The Committee is of the view that capacity building for CPGRAMS should be 
extended to all Civil Servants across the country in a phased manner. In the initial 
phase, priority may be given to officials from States with high grievance redressal 
requirements, followed by others in subsequent phases. The Committee also emphasizes 
that NCGG should design and conduct dedicated capacity -building programmes on 
CPGRAMS. This would significantly  contribute towards enhancing the efficiency and 
responsiveness of the public grievance redressal system. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.15 The Committee feels that as the mortality rates among the employees within the first 
two to three years post -retirement remain elevated, the Department should implement 
comprehensive pre -retirement counselling programs for all the retiring employees. These  
programs should be universally accessible, utilizing both online and offline platforms, to 
prepare employees for significant lifestyle changes and associated challenges.       (Para 3.30) 
Action Taken 
3.16 Department of Pension & Pensioners‘ Welfare has been organizing Pre -Retirement 
Counseling (PRC) Workshops regularly for the benefit of retiring Central Government 
officials. So far, 55 PRC Workshops have been conducted in different parts of the country 
which have benefited more than 10000 retiring centr al government officials. In order to 
facilitate the smooth transition for the retiring employees, various sessions on Retirement 
Benefits, CGHS, Investment modes, BHAVISHYA portal, Integrated Pensioners Portal, 
Family Pension, CPENGRAMS, ANUBHAV and Digita l Life Certificate etc. are conducted 
in the workshops. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.17 The Committee appreciates the Ministry’s initiatives in organizing pre -
retirement counselling workshops and informing retiring officials about welfare schemes 
and retirement benefits. However, the Committee observes that these programmes 
mainly focus on government benefits . It  should also cover broader opportunities 
available to retirees  like agricultural and digital entrepreneurship  and avenues for 
pursuing hobb ies and talents. Enhanced guidance on productive engagement beyond 
voluntary work, such as leveraging retirees’ experience and skills in various domains, 
will support their well-being and make post-retirement life more rewarding. 

 
18 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.18 The Committee appreciates the Department for holding Pension Adalats every year 
since 2017. The Committee is of the view that, while the Nationwide Pension Adalats have 
played a crucial role in grievance redressal , the resolution rate of 71.38% indicates that 
nearly 29% of cases remain unresolved, which raises concerns about efficiency. The 
Committee therefore, desires that efforts may be made to address the unresolved cases by 
constantly pursuing them with the concerned Departments.                                     (Para 3.42) 
Action Taken 
3.19 The objective of the Pension Adalat is to provide on -the-spot resolution of unresolved 
and chronic grievances in CPENGRAMS. After giving advance notice to all the stakeholders, 
involving the Head of Office (HOO), Pay and Account Office (PAO), Central Pension 
Accounting Office (CPAO), Pension Disbursing Bank , etc., and representative of the 
Pensioner are called on a common platform for resolution of the grievances across th e table. 
Most of the cases taken up in Pension Adalats are resolved on the spot. However, due follow -
up with the respective Ministry/Department is carried out and Action Taken Reports are 
sought for the cases that are resolved. The unresolved cases are rev isited and their status is 
considered before holding the next Pension Adalat. There is a slight overall improvement in 
the redressal of pension grievances, increasing from 71.38% to 71.44%. This Department has 
decided to organize 3 Pension Adalats each yea r to resolve more long -pending grievances 
with increased success rate. This will enable the consideration of additional grievances and 
more effective redressal, thereby reducing the duration of pendency and enhancing 
efficiency. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.20 The Committee appreciates the decision of the Department to organize three 
Pension Adalats every year to ensure early redressal  of pension grievances. However, 
the Committee is of the considered view that, in order to further expedite the resolution 
of long -pending and chronic grievances, the Pension Adalats may be conducted on a 
quarterly basis. This will facilitate more frequent  review and resolution of cases, 
thereby improving the overall efficiency and effectiveness of the grievance redressal 
mechanism. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may take 
necessary steps to institutionalize quarterly Pension Adalat s for enhanced grievance 
redressal.

exercise should be stopped immediately.                                                                  (Para 3.55)

R E P O R T 
 
 This Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Committee deals with the action taken by the 
Department of Legal Affairs (Ministry of Law & Justice) on the 
recommendations/observations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its One Hundred Forty Eight (148th) 
Report of the Committee on “Demands for Grants (2025-26)” pertaining to the Department of 
Legal Affairs (Ministry of Law & Justice), which was presented to Rajya Sabha on the 27th 
March, 2025 and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 27th March, 2025. 
2. The Committee had made 16 recommendations/observations in its 148th Report. 
Replies of the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters 
on the basis of satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the 
Ministry: Paras:- 2.12, 2.14, 3.9, 3.15 and 3.33 (Total-05) 
Chapter – II:     Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the replies given by the Ministry: Paras:- 2.8, 3.7, 3.8, 
3.19, 3.22, 3.27, 3.51 and 3.52 (Total-08) 
Chapter – III:      Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not 
accepted the replies of the Ministry: Paras:- 3.23, 3.35 and 3.44 (Total-03) 
Chapter – IV:     Recommendations/observations (Nil) in respect of which final replies of 
the Government have not been received.  
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed 
Action Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the 
Committee in Chapter – III of this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in the 
succeeding pages. For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report (i.e., of the 148th 
Report) have been mentioned at the end of each recommendation/observation.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT

Recommendation/Observation 2.1 The committee recognizes that legal representation is essential for the effective 
defense of government interests, but the rising costs call for a thorough review of expenditure 
patterns and potential measures for optimization. Therefore, the committee recommends that 
the department strengthen the pre-litigation process by promoting the use of Alternative 
Dispute Resolution (ADR) and taking steps to reduce frivolous and repetitive litigation. To 
support this, all government departments and PSUs may review all the ongoing cases by 
setting a team of officers and withdraw those that are weak in nature. Additionally, a 
periodic review of the empanelment and performance of legal counsel may also be 
conducted.                             (Para 2.8)  Action Taken 
2.2 During the past decade, the Government of India has taken various initiatives in the 
realm of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms. The major policy and 
legislative initiatives taken by the Central Government over the years in this regard include:  
i. the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 has been progressively amended in the 
years 2015, 2019 and 2021. These amendments aims at ensuring timely conclusion of 
arbitration proceedings, neutrality of arbitrators, minimizing judicial intervention in 
the arbitral process, promotion of institutional arbitration and quick enforcement of 
arbitral awards. 
ii. The India International Arbitration Centre Act, 2019, was enacted to provide for the 
establishment and incorporation of the India International Arbitration Centre for the 
purpose of creating an independent, autonomous and world class body for facilitating 
institutional arbitration and to declare the Centre to be an institution of national 
importance. 
iii. The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 was amended in the year 2018 to provide for Pre-
Institution Mediation and Settlement (PIMS) mechanism. This is aimed at providing 
an opportunity to the parties to resolve the commercial disputes through mediation 
before approaching the court. 
iv. The Mediation Act, 2023, was enacted recently, to lay down the legal framework for 
mediation to be adopted by parties to a dispute, especially institutional mediation. 
Section 5 of the Mediation Act, 2023, provides for voluntary pre-litigation mediation 
as well. 
v. The Department and the India International Arbitration Centre continue to take steps 
including organizing of conferences and seminars to disseminate the advantages of 
arbitration and mediation. 
 2.3 As regards periodic review of the empanelment and performance of legal counsel is 
concerned Advocates are empanelled as panel counsel generally for a term of three years 
after that either new panels are formed or terms of earlier panel are extended by this 
Department keeping in view the requirement of litigation, performance, etc. reviewed at the 
level of Hon'ble Minister of Law & Justice. Besides, there is already a system of litigation in-
charge as defined in this Department's OM dated 21.10.2019 (Annexure-I) who are to submit 
monthly reports on allocation of cases, performance of counsel, etc. Further, Ministries /

Departments also report their issues with the performance of panel counsel which are 
examined and decided on merits.

CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE 
DEPARTMENT AND REITERATES ITS RECOMMENDATIONS 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.1 The Committee feels that addressing the backlog in various courts requires a 
multifaceted approach, including judicial reforms, adoption of latest technology, promotion 
of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), and streamlining of procedures. The Committee is 
of the opinion that if mandatory pre-litigation mediation is introduced for commercial, 
family, and civil disputes before allowing litigation in a large extent it will reduce pendency. 
Additionally, the expansion of Lok Adalats and the establishment of fast-track courts may be 
prioritized for small claims, consumer disputes, and contract enforcement. The use of AI-
based Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) may be explored to streamline the resolution 
process.                                                                                                   (Para 3.23) 
 
Action Taken 
3.2 The Commercial Courts Act, 2015 as amended in 2018 provides for Pre-Institution 
Mediation and Settlement (PIMS) mechanism for commercial disputes. Under this 
mechanism, where a commercial dispute of specified value does not contemplate any urgent 
interim relief, the parties have to first exhaust the mandatory remedy of PIMS before 
approaching the Court. 
3.3 Further, the Government had introduced the Mediation Bill, 2021 in December, 2021 
which inter-alia provided for the mandatory pre litigation. However, the DRPSC in its 117th 
report on the Mediation Bill, 2021 vide para no. 3.96 had suggested for introducing voluntary 
prelitigation mediation. The relevant observations of the committee is as under: 
 “3.96 The Committee further notes that making pre-litigation mediation mandatory may 
actually result in delaying of cases and may prove to be an additional tool in hands of 
litigants to delay the disposal of cases. The Committee also notes the views of few 
experts that not only pre-litigation mediation should be made optional but also be 
introduced in a phased manner instead of introducing it with immediate effect for all 
civil and commercial disputes and the challenges faced in implementing Pre-Litigation 
Mediation under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 should be studied before mandating 
it across other categories of cases.” 
3.4 Pursuant thereto, official amendments to the Mediation Bill, 2021 were moved and 
Section 5 of the enacted Mediation Act, 2023, now provides for voluntary pre-institution 
mediation as against mandatory pre-institution mediation as provided in the Bill. As regards 
ODR, the Mediation Act, 2023 inter-alia provides a separate chapter, i.e., chapter VII on 
online mediation. The process of online mediation is to be conducted in the manner to be 
specified by the Mediation Council of India. The Mediation Council of India would consider 
the role and requirement of AI, in the process as well.  
 
 

10 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.5 The Committee suggests expanding and modernising of Lok Adalats and 
establishing fast track courts for small claims, consumer and contract disputes will 
ensure timely resolution. Integration of AI based Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) 
mechanism supported by Mediation Council of India will enhance accessibility, 
efficiency and transparency in the justice delivery system. 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
3.6 The Committee notes that Government has appointed  17 Judicial Members and 20 
Accountant Members in 2024, however, many positions for Members are still vacant. 
Additionally, there is a shortage of Registry Officers and other officials. Another aspect that

timeliness of case resolution. The Committee, therefore, desires that if recruitment process is 
streamlined,  all vacancies can be filled up the backlog in disposing of cases can be 
considerably reduced. Additionally, the Committee suggests the extensive use of virtual 
courts for ITAT may be explored, which will also help in disposing of cases quickly.  
                                                                                                            (Para 3.35)

R E P O R T 
 This Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Department 
of Personnel and Training (Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions) on the 
recommendations / observations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its One Hundred and Forty Fifth (145th) Report on 
"Demands for Grants (2025-26)", which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 27th March, 2025 and 
laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha on the 27th March, 2025. 
2. The Committee had made 31 recommendations/observations in its 145th Report. Replies of 
the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters on the basis of 
satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I:  Recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry: 
Paras:- 2.14, 2.59, 2.63 and 6.15 (Total- 04) 
Chapter – II:  Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the replies given by the Ministry: Paras:- 2.8, 2.17, 2.22,  2.44, 2.49, 
3.3, 3.4, 3.7, 3.16, 4.19, 4.23, 5.7, 6.3, 6.9, 6.12, 6.25, 6.27 and 6.36 (Total- 18) 
Chapter – III:   Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry: Paras:-  3.15, 4.10, 4.14, 5.8, 6.6, 6.20, 6.30, and 6.33 
(Total- 8) 
Chapter-IV: Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the ministry 
have not been received: Paras:- 4.6 (Total- 1) 
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed Action 
Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the Committee in 
Chapter – III of this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in the succeeding 
pages. For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report (i.e., of 145th Report) have been 
mentioned at the end of each Recommendation/Observation.   
 
  

2 
 
CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Ministry received an increased Revised Estimate (RE) for 2024-25 (₹2,576.15 crore) 
compared to Budget Estimates (BE) (₹2,328.56 crore), a 10.63% rise. However, as of January 31, 
2025, only ₹2,020.45 crore has been utilized, indicating underutilization of funds. DoPT has utilized 
only 80.22% of its RE. The Committee urge the Ministry to make realistic projection based on past 
expenditure trends.                      (Para 2.14) 
Action Taken 
1.2 Pace of expenditure during the initial part of the FY 2024-25 was on the slower side. 
However, against the RE 2024-25 allocations of Rs. 2576.15 crore, the actual expenditure incurred 
in FY 2024-25 was Rs. 2509.65 crore (97.42%).  
1.3 The suggestions by the Committee have been duly noted and measures to achieve higher 
pace and quality of expenditure are being implemented by various organizations of the Department 
to ensure an even pace of expenditure. The pace and quality of expenditure of all Departmental 
organizations is being closely monitored at senior levels in the Organizations as well as in the 
Department, regularly. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.4 The budget allocation for the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) has increased 
marginally from ₹51.31 crore in BE 2024-25 and RE 2024-25 to ₹52.07 crore in BE 2025-26. While 
this marginal increase of ₹ 0.76 crore may acknowledge the Commission’s financial needs, it 
remains modest given inflation, operational expansion, and the increasing complexity of vigilance 
activities. The Committee observes that CVC’s expenditure trend indicate effective financial 
management and is in line with planned allocations. The Committee expects CVC to maintain 
efficiency in resource utilization while ensuring adequate funding for its critical vigilance functions.  
(Para 2.59) 
Action Taken 
1.5 Recommendation has been noted for compliance. 
 

3 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.6 The Committee notes that audit observations from previous years have been progressively 
addressed, reducing pending issues to 10 in 2023-24. While progress has been consistent, the 
complete settlement of outstanding paras requires timely action. The Committee emphasizes the 
need for timely resolution of pending audit paras to maintain financial transparency and 
compliance. It recommends that UPSC expedite its responses and ensure quicker settlement of audit 
observations in the future.                   (Para 2.63) 
Action Taken 
1.7 The recommendation of the Committee for quick settlement of Audit Observations is noted 
for compliance. 
1.8 With regard to 10 pending Audit paras in 2023-24, it is submitted that out of 10 paras, 9 
Audit paras pertain to Audit conducted w.e.f 14.10.2024 to 25.10.2024 for which Audit Report 
2023-24 was received on 6.12.2024. Replies are being sent to Director General of Audit, Central 
Expenditure for settlement of the Observations. For the remaining 1 Para, reply has been sent to 
Audit. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.9 The Committee recommends that a Centralized Digital Case Repository (CDCR) should be 
established by the Central Vigilance Commission to store attested copies of all documents submitted 
to Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs). Competent Authorities must be given secure access to 
retrieve case records instantly. A mandatory timeline may be in place/implemented for 
administrative authorities to submit their views on prosecution sanctions, with accountability 
measures for delays. Regular audits should be conducted to ensure compliance with record-keeping 
protocols. Further, an interdepartmental coordination mechanism should be introduced to expedite 
document sharing. Training programs must be conducted to ensure vigilance officers and 
administrators adhere to streamlined sanction procedures.               (Para 6.15) 
Action Taken 
1.10 Ministry of Electronics & IT (MeitY) has Centralised Digital Case Repository as 
DigiLocker, for accessing and managing documents by organisations.  Further its Digital Archiving 
and Management Division develops the record keeping applications for organisations. The 
recommendation of the Committee will be taken up with MeitY.

CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THECOMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE GOVERNMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances, and Pensions informed the Committee that 
it had projected an outlay of ₹3,859.97 crore to the Ministry of Finance during the Pre-Budget 
Meeting under Demand No. 74 for BE 2024-25. However, the Finance Ministry approved only 
₹2,328.56 crore, which is 60.32% of the projected amount. A detailed review of the Ministry's 
expenditure pattern for the same fiscal year reveals that, as of 31.01.2025, it had utilized only 
₹2,020.45 crore against the sanctioned BE of ₹2,328.56 crore. Despite this, the allocations were 
increased to ₹2,576.15 crore in the Revised Estimates (RE). This discrepancy highlights 
shortcomings in budget projection and expenditure planning. The Committee, therefore, urges the 
Ministry to adopt more accurate budget forecasting and expenditure planning to ensure optimal 
utilization of funds.            (Para 2.8) 
Action Taken 
2.2 Against the RE 2024-25 allocations of Rs. 2576.15 crore, the actual expenditure incurred in 
FY 2024-25 was Rs. 2509.65 crore which is 97.42% of RE allocation.   
2.3 A conscious effort is being made to fully utilize the allocated budget in FY 2025-26 and for 
this purpose, expenditure trends are being closely monitored regularly by Heads of various 
Organizations as well as by the Senior Officers of the Department. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.4 The Committee notes that during the financial year 2024-25, out of 14 organisations, 
07 organisations, i.e., UPSC, SSC, LBSNAA, CAT, CBI, CVC and SPV Karmayogi Bharat have 
utilized above 77% of the funds allocated to them while PESB, IIPA, CIC and CBC have not 
been able to utilize the allocated funds optimally up to 31st January, 2025. The Committee 
observes that ISTM and Lokpal have poor utilization of funds spending below 50% of the 
allocations and moreover, data shows that NRA has not spent any money out of the BE and RE 
allocation of ₹10 crore. The Committee recommends that the Department may take corrective 
action in this regard.                     (Para 2.17) 
 

5

primary jurisdiction is in Delhi and other Union Territories. As per the statute, DSPE (CBI) needs

not a Union Territory or Railway area. Section 5 of DSPE Act entitles the ’Central Government’ to

constituting the Inquiry Wing and in approving the organisational structure of both the 
Inquiry and Prosecution Wings. The Committee also notes the interim efforts made to utilise 
deputation-based arrangements until regular appointments are made. However, 
operationalisation of these statutory wings remains incomplete. The Committee desires to be 
apprised of the latest status of the communications sent to DoPT along with the action taken 
by them regarding posting of officers requested by the Lokpal. 
3.56 With regard to the Prosecution Wing, the Committee notes that although the Full 
Bench has resolved to constitute it, progress has been limited in view of the small number of 
cases presently before courts. The Committee, however, reiterates that statutory compliance 
cannot remain contingent on the volume of cases and urges that the constitution of the 
Prosecution Wing be taken forward expeditiously. The Committee further seeks an update on 
the status of the Lokpal’s request to DoPT for notifying a Special Court under Section 35 of 
the Act of 2013 to exclusively hear cases arising from the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 
pursuant to sanctions granted under Section 20(7). 
3.57 In view of its earlier recommendation that both Wings be fully constituted within six 
months, the Committee reiterates that urgent steps be taken to operationalise the Inquiry and 
Prosecution Wings through regular appointments or deputation, so that the Lokpal may 
effectively discharge its statutory mandate without further delay. 
***** 
  

40 
 
CHAPTER IV 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.1 UPSC informed the Committee that it publishes the preliminary examination answer key 
only after completing the entire selection process. This delays candidates' ability to challenge 
potential errors before advancing to the next stage, undermining transparency and fairness. Such a 
practice can demoralize candidates and raise concerns about the validity of the examination. 
Despite rigorous scrutiny, the possibility of errors in the answer key cannot be entirely ruled out. 
To enhance credibility, fairness, and candidate confidence, the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation contained in para 4.5 of its 126th  report that UPSC may explore and take steps to 
release the answer key immediately after the preliminary examination and provide candidates with 
an opportunity to raise objections before proceeding further.     (Para 4.6) 
 
Action Taken 
4.2 The Commission opens a Representation Window on its web-portal for a week for the 
candidates of the said examination to represent against any of the Questions of the Examination. 
The observations made by the candidates in their representations are carefully considered in the 
Commission through the subject experts and remedial action is taken, if required. So far as releasing 
of Answer Keys is concerned, it is stated that answer keys of objective type examinations 
conducted by the Commission are disclosed only after the entire process of the examination.  
4.3 Further, the matter of releasing answer key after completion of Preliminary Examinations, 
i.e., before the final result of the respective Examinations is presently sub-judice in 
W.P.(C)No.118/2024 filed by Shri Himanshu Kumar & Ors Vs UPSC &Ors, pertaining to Civil 
Services Examination, before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India. The court has appointed Shri 
Jaideep Gupta, Sr. Advocate as Amicus Curiae in this regard.

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairman of the Committee on Personnel, Public Grieva nces, Law and Justice, having been authorised 
by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Sixteenth Report of the Committee on the 
Representation of the People (Amendment) Bill, 2006.* 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee, the Hon’ble 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha re ferred** the Bill on 27 th March, 2006, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 17 th February, 
2006 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report. 
3. The Committee considered the Bill in 5 sittings held on 5 th June, 11th, 12th and 26th July and 2nd August, 2006. 
3.1 In its sitting held on 5 th June, 2006, the Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative 
Department, Ministry of Law and Justice on the Bill. 
3.2 The Committee heard the views of the representatives of  the Ministries of Home Affairs; External Affairs; 
Overseas Indian Affairs; Law and Justice; and the El ection Commission of India at its meeting held on 11 th July, 
2006. 
3.3 The Committee took up clause-by-clause consid eration of the Bill in its sitting held on 12th July, 2006. 
3.4 The Committee further heard the views of the repr esentatives of the Legislative Department and the 
Department of Legal Affairs of Ministry of Law and Justice and the Election Commission of India on the clauses of 
the Bill in its meeting held on 26th July, 2006. 
3.5 The Committee considered and adopted the draf t Report on the Bill in its sitting held on 2nd August, 2006. 
4. In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the following papers/documents:- 
 (i) Background note on the Bill received from the Le gislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice; 
 (ii) The Representation of the People Act, 1950;

and 
 (viii) The comments/replies rece ived from the Ministry of Ex ternal Affairs, Ministry of 
Overseas Indian Affairs, Election  Commission of India and Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative 
Department, Department of Legal Affairs), on the points raised by the Chairman and 
Members in the sittings of the Committee.

  E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN

** Published in the Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part-II (No. 42997) dated the 28th March, 2006. 

 
 
REPORT 
 The Representation of the People (Amendment) Bill, 2006 (Annexure A) seeks to amend section 20 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) to make provision for enabling the Indian citizens, absenting 
from their place of ordinary residence in India owing to their employment, education or otherwise outside India, to 
get their names registered in the electoral rolls of the con cerned constituency of their place of ordinary residence in 
India, had they been in India, so that they would be in a position to cast their votes in the elections to the Lok Sabha 
and to the State Legislatures in case they happen to be in their constituency at the time of the polls. The Bill seeks to 
make an enabling provision for these c itizens to be able to contest the elections. The Bill has a legislative purpose so 
as to extend the right to vote to the Indian citizens residing abroad (colloquially known as “Non-Resident Indians” 
i.e. NRI). The Government feels that conferring such a right will enable them to participate in the democratic process 
of elections in their motherland and will also boost their involvement in the nation-building. Accordingly, following 
the persistent demand of Indian citizens residing outside I ndia and having considered all the aspects of their demand, 
the Government has proposed to make provision thro ugh this legislation by amending section 20 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1950, as the Government considers that it is a legitimate right of the Indian citizens 
residing outside the country. In the opinion of the Government, it cannot be ignored that the contribution by way of 
foreign exchange by the citizens of India employed outside India is considerable and it is the duty of the Government 
to safeguard their interests and the sense of belonging and to protect their legitimate democratic rights. 
2. In the Background Note on the Bill, the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice has informed the 
Committee that:- 
“.... the Legislative Department exam ined all aspects of the demand afresh in consultation with the other 
concerned administrative Ministries/Departments, name ly, the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of 
External Affairs, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs and the Election 
Commission of India and decided to take steps to confer voting rights to the citizens of India absenting from 
their place of ordinary residence owing to their employment, education or otherwise outside India, by 
suitably amending the relevant law. It is, therefore, proposed to amend section 20 of the Representation of 
the People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) so as to amplify the definition of ‘ordinarily resident’ contained therein 
for enabling non-resident Indian who have absented themselves from their place of ordinary residence 
owing to employment, education or otherwise to get th eir names registered in th e electoral rolls of the 
concerned constituency of their place of ordinary residence in India had they been in India so that they 
would be in a position to cast their votes in elections to the Lok Sabha and to the State Legislatures in case 
they happen to be in their constituency at the time of polls. 
***  *** ***  
 The amendment proposed in the Bill will entitle the eligible citizens of India who are absenting from 
their place of ordinary residence in India owing to their employment, education or otherwise outside India 
to get themselves enrolled in the electoral rolls and cast  their votes when they are in their constituency and 
thus fully participate in the democr atic process of nation building and uphold their pride and prestige as 
citizens of India. This will give the NRIs a sense of belonging to their motherland. 
 The detailed modalities of enrolment of the ne w category of electors would be worked out in 
consultation with the Election Commission at the time of amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 
after the proposed law is passed by Parliament.” 
3. To achieve these objectives, the proposed amendment seeks to insert a new clause under Section 20 ibid. - 
“(1AA) A person absenting himself from his place of ordinary residence owing to his employment, 
education, or otherwise, outside India, whether temporar ily or not, shall not, by reason thereof, cease to be 
ordinarily resident in India.” 
4. In the Statement of Objects and Reasons ap pended to the Bill it is stated as under:- 

“Section 19 of the Representation of the People Ac t, 1950 provides that every person who is not less 
than eighteen years of age on the qualifying date and is ordinarily resident in a constituency shall be entitled 
to be registered in the electoral ro lls for that constituency. The meaning of ‘ordinary resident’ is laid down 
in section 20 of the said Act. At present, a person who is absenting from his place of ordinary residence by 
reason of his employment, education or otherwise outside India is not qualified to get his name registered in 
the electoral rolls and thus cast his vote in elections to the Parliament and to the State Legislatures. 
There are a large number of citizens of India residing outside India due to their employment, education, 
etc. They have been persistently demanding for conferring them with voting rights. Though the issue of 
conferring voting rights to the citizens if they are absenting from their place of ordinary residence in India 
owing to their employment, education or otherwise out side India has been recei ving the attention of the 
Government for quite some time, yet the same could no t be acceded to owing to th e practical difficulties in 
enrolling them in the electoral rolls of the concerned constituency and allowing them to cast their votes 
outside India within the short span of time available in the election process. 
*** *** ***  
The Government has considered all aspects of th e demand and it has been decided to enable the 
Indian citizens absenting from thei r place of ordinary residence in India owing to their employment, 
education or otherwise outside India to get thei r names registered in the electoral rolls of the 
concerned constituency of their place of ordinary residence in India ........."  
5.  In the light of the above, the Re presentation of the People (Amendment) Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 17 th February, 2006. It was referred to the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice on the 27 th March, 2006 for examination with instruction to report 
within three months. 
6. However, while considering the B ill, the Committee felt that it would not be possible for it to complete the 
consideration of the Bill and Report thereon to Parliament within the stipulated time, keeping in view the importance 
of the Bill requiring the vast range of discussions, issues involved and the consideration of memoranda received from 
a cross-section of the society. Accordingly, the Committee sought an extension of time upto the last week of the 208th 
Session of Rajya Sabha or the Monsoon Session of the year  2006 from the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, which 
was acceded to. 
7. Keeping in view the public impo rtance of the Bill, the Committee decide d to invite views/suggestions from 
various individuals/organisations thereon. It, accordingly, authorised the Secretariat to issue a press advertisement for 
inviting views/suggestions. 
7.1 In response to the press advertisement issued on the 20th April, 2006 which was published in the major English 
and Hindi dailies and vernacular news papers all over the country on the 25 th April, 2006, a number of 
representations/memoranda were received. 
7.2 The major points raised in the memoranda are as follows:- 
 (i) The proposed amendment clause is of very wide  amplitude having far reaching effects and may create 
non-resident representation if the NRIs are allowed to contest elections as well. 
 (ii) People who abandon their motherland and go to  other countries for education and employment may not 
be able to cast their votes in favour of the most suitable candidate, thus, conferring of such right may 
prove to be counter productive and will only add to the election complexities. 
 (iii) The proposed amendment is unjustified as the NR Is do not pay any tax and they will get the right to 
elect the Government. 
 (iv) It is a wrong notion that the right to vote to the NRIs will boost their involvement in the nation 
building, rather this futile action may jeopardize th e purpose of nation building as the NRIs will not be 
aware of the political climate of Indian States. 
 (v) Such a right if granted, may jeopardize the security and sovereig nty of the country and may result in 
catastrophy. 
 (vi) The proposed amendment does not sound logical and is against the principle of equality. Presently, at 
the time of revision of electoral rolls, the names of the persons who are not residing at the place of their 

ordinary residence continuously for 6 months irrespective of the fact whether they live outside India or 
within India, is deleted from the respective electoral rolls. This w ill create a legal priviledge in favour 
of the non-resident Indians. 
 (vii) Foreign funds will start playing a negative role in Government formation especially in case of split 
verdict. 
 (viii) On the face of it, it appears to be a noble idea to give voting right to the Indians living abroad but to 
give them the right to contest elections too appears to be uncalled for. They will enjoy all the privileges 
without any accountability. 
 (ix) Voting rights should be restricted to those NRIs who pay Income Tax in India and have valid PAN 
numbers in India to obviate the instances of fraud and electoral malpractice. 
 (x) The Bill will not create any ne w category of voters as once they ar e back in India they can get their 
names registered in India. Further, they have to be  physically present at the time of election to be able 
to cast their vote. 
 (xi) A person who is residing outside whether tempor arily or permanently cannot understand the needs of 
the people of his constituency. Hence NRIs should not be allowed to contest elections. 
 (xii) If the right to vote is allowed to the NRIs, th en the cost of canvassing and electioneering for the 
contestants will go up. Some mechanism needs to be devised for regulation of the right. 
 (xiii) Before according the right to vote to an NRI, hi s past record should be cons idered to find out whether 
he has clean antecedents as there is criminalization of politics and politicisation of criminals. Further, 
clear provisions for the procedure of casting votes by  the NRIs should be envisaged well in advance. It 
would be appropriate if such voters are provided with I-cards. Related rights, if accruing to them in any 
form must clearly be specified. 
 (xiv) Average NRI has a poor knowledge and understanding of the representatives and the economic, 
political and social problems of different regions of their native country, therefore focusing on their 
right would be futile, instead the target should be the optimization of local voter turn out rather than 
NRI turnout. 
7.3 The Committee forwarded the memoranda so received to the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and 
Justice for their comments. The comments of the Department were received on the 11th July, 2006. (Annexure-B) 
7.4 The Legislative Department was also forwarded a Ques tionnaire on the Bill, the replies to which were also 
received on the 11th July, 2006. (Annexure-C) 
7.5. The Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice in their written reply/comments on the 
Questionnaire/memoranda mainly focussed on the following points:- 
 1. Summary of comments on the Questionnaire:- 
 (i) In a democratic set up, the citizens particip ate in the governance and this is achieved mainly 
through their legitimate political right to cast their votes. Under Arti cle 326 every person who 
is a citizen of India and who is not less than eight een years of age on such date as may be fixed 
in that behalf by or under any law made by the appropriate legislature and is not otherwise 
disqualified under the Constitution shall be entitled to be registered as a voter. 
 (ii) The privilege, to be registered as a voter, to  the citizens is conferred by virtue of being a citizen 
of our country and can be availed of by a pe rson moving from one place of his ordinary 
residence in India to another place of ordinary residence in India. 
 (iii) The Representation of the People Act, 19 50, at present do not allow persons who are not 
ordinary resident in a constituency in India to  register themselves as voters. To remove the 
discrimination meted out to the citizens of India solely on the ground of non-residence, it is 
proposed to confer the right to register their na mes in the electoral rolls of their constituency in 
India had they been in the respective constitue ncies but for their proceeding abroad owing to 
their employment, education or otherwise. 

 (iv) The voters list are prepared on the basis of territorial constituencies in India, it has become 
necessary that the citizens of India residing ab road owing to their employment, education or 
otherwise are allowed to enroll themselves in the electoral rolls in their respective constituency. 
This could be done only at the place of their ordi nary residence in India on the legal fiction that 
they would have continued to reside at the place of their ordinary residence in India but for 
their proceeding abroad. 
 (v) The proposed amendment seeks to allow all citizens of India living abroad to enroll themselves 
in the electoral rolls of their respective constitu ency in India irrespective of their period of 
residence abroad so long as they continue to be the citizens of India. 
 (vi) The expression “otherwise” as used in the proposed amendment covers the case of dependents 
of persons employed or otherwise staying outside India. The reasons for residence are only 
illustrative and not exhaustive. 
 (vii) It is proposed to insist for the passport and the permanent address in India shown in the 
passport as the condition to identify the cons tituency where the person concerned could get 
himself enrolled in the voters’ list. 
 (viii) The amending clause is intended to allow enro llment of their names in the electoral rolls of the 
concerned constituency of their place of ordinary residence in India, had they been in India. 
 (ix) They would thus be in a position to cast thei r votes in the election to the Lok Sabha and to the 
State Legislatures in case they happen to be in their constituency at the time of polls. 
 (x) They may also be able to contest the Pa rliamentary and Assembly elections if they are 
otherwise eligible as per law. 
 (xi) Conferring such voting right will enable them to participate in the democratic process of 
elections in their motherland and will also boost their involvement in nation building. 
 (xii) The citizens living abroad will come to Indi a along with their travel documents and passport 
and in case such person is found involved in anti -national or subversive activities, the security 
agencies of the country will keep a watch on them. 
 (xiii) The proposal is limited to allowing them to cast their votes in the concerned polling booth 
earmarked. 
 (xiv) There is no proposal to lay down any additiona l condition for contesting election in respect of 
the citizens of India living abroad owing to their employment, education or otherwise. 
 (xv) Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs have  stated that USA, UK, China and Italy are some 
countries giving voting rights to their non-resident nationals. 
 2. Summary of comments on the Memoranda:- 
 (i) The proposal is to provide an enabling provision in the law so that a citizen of India living 
abroad in case he happens to be in India will have the opportunity to cast his vote. 
 (ii) Whatever provisions of law are applicable to the resident In dians would be equally applicable 
to the citizens of India living abroad also. 
 (iii) A Member of Parliament or of a State Legislature who remains absent without leave for more 
than a particular period may lose his membership. 
 (iv) After addition of name in the voting roll, the Indian citizen residing outside can cast his/her 
vote and also contest the election if he/she is otherwise eligible. 
 (v) The right of a citizen of India to vote is a po litical democratic right and the elector has a right to 
choose amongst the contesting candidate as per his conscience and judgment. 
 (vi) The name of the spouse of the citizens of Indi a living abroad will be allowed to be added in the 
electoral rolls only if such spouse is a citizen of India. 

 (vii) Income-tax is assessed for an assesssee as pe r the Income Tax Act, 1961. The citizens of India 
living abroad will exercise their voting right as per the provisions of the Constitution of India 
and the election laws. 
 (viii) The proposal is to involve the citizens of In dia living abroad to contribute in the process of 
nation building. 
 (ix) Indian citizens who are living abroad only will be given voting right under the proposed 
legislation. Constitution of India does not recognise dual citizenship of Indian citizens for the 
purpose of voting right. 
 (x) The resident Indians have the right to get themselves enrolled at the place of their ordinary 
residence which can be only at one place. The law does not allow to have the names enrolled in 
two different places at a time. The resident Indians can get their names changed from one 
constituency to another at their place of ordinary residence. 
 (xi) The proposal is to remove the discrimination  meted out to the citizens of India solely on the 
ground of place of residence. 
 (xii) It is not correct to say that  if an Indian citizen living abroad is conferred voting right, it would 
affect our sovereignty. 
 (xiii) The name of the citizens of India living outside India will be included in the voters list in India 
only if he continues to be a citizen of India and fulfils other requirements as per law. 
 (xiv) Once elected they will be governed by the rules made by the legislature for its Members. 
 (xv) The existing law is strong enough to check use of money power in elections. There are ceiling 
on election expenses. 
 (xvi) The right to cast vote could be considered as one of the primary privilege of a citizen of a 
sovereign democratic republic. The elected repr esentatives enjoy privileges and are bound by 
duties as are provided under the law and prescribed by the Houses of which a person is a 
Member. 
 (xvii) Only those persons will be allowed to vote who continue to hold Indian citizenship. There will 
be no change in the other legal requirements in respect of a resident Indian and a citizen of 
India living out of India. 
 (xviii) After getting the right to vote during elections the citizens of India living abroad will be treated 
equally with the citizens of India living in their constituency. 
 (xix) The voting right has to be exercised by the citizens of India living abroad in person by coming 
to his constituency. This way of casting of vote is  no doubt difficult but it is very simple and 
clear. It is not practically possible to allow them to cast their votes by proxy or postal ballot. 
There is no proposal to allow the citizens of India living abroad to cast their votes outside 
India. 
 (xx) Having regard to the number of days a person has to work as a legislator, there is no need of 
laying down any condition of residence in India. 
 (xxi) The average NRI may keep knowledge of representatives after getting the right to vote. 
 (xxii) The errors in voting list may not become hurdl e in conferring on the voting right to citizens of 
India living abroad. They will have clear identity by way of their passports. 
 (xxiii) There cannot be any time limit regarding the stay of NRIs abroad. It depends on what type of 
visa/permit such NRI is holding while staying abroad. 
 (xxiv) There is no need of any separate list State- wise. Only the name has to be added in the electoral 
rolls. 
 (xxv) No defence or security point is touched by extending the voting right to citizens of India living 
abroad. 

 (xxvi) The citizens of India are livi ng in various parts of the world. It is only because of the practical 
difficulties in arranging polling booth outside India safely and within the time limit, that the 
voting right would be exercised only in India. 
 (xxvii) The facility is not for dual citizens. It is only for the citizens of India living abroad owing to 
their employment, education or otherwise. 
8. The Committee took up the consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on the 5 th June, 2006. It heard the 
presentation of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministiy of Law and Justice in the same meeting. 
8.1 The Committee further heard the views of the Ministries  of External Affairs, Over seas Indian Affairs and the 
Home Affairs in its meeting held on the 11th July, 2006. 
8.2 The Committee also heard the views of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice and the 
Election Commission of India in its meeting held on the 12 th July, 2006. The Committee also took up clause-by-
clause consideration on the Bill in the same meeting. 
8.3 Having regard to the wide implications of the propos ed amendment sought to be effected through the present 
legislation, the Committee further held discussions with th e Secretaries of the Departme nt of Legal Affairs and the 
Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law and Jus tice and the representatives of the Election Commission of 
India in its sitting held on the 26th July, 2006. 
8.4 The Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice in his presentation briefly traced the 
background of the present Bill, the main provisions of the Act of 1950 as they exist, the reasons for the proposed
